This is my second attempt at a review. The first one was after I rage quit. I left an unfavourable review and was summarily attacked by Germans who, as it turns out, are not all "smiles und sunshine!"
YMMV - I feel this needs to be said.
Battle Brothers is not a bad game. In fact, this will be more of a mixed review with the intent to help others who have not already purchased the game. I purchased the game during Early Access based on many of the reviews at the time.
First of all, congratulations to Overhype Studios for creating a polished, detailed and, from what I can tell, bug-free game.   I am excited to see what else they will do!
Battle Brothers - A Turn Based Tactical RPG:
Yes, the combat is turn-based. I prefer this style of turn-based combat when compared to games like The Banner Saga, for example. Here each combat participant, ally and enemy, is given a turn with the order based on their initiative. Resolve and fatigue also play a role? You can defer all or part of your action points until later in the combat round, if you choose. This is extremely well done and opens up a lot of nice strategy options. In The Banner Saga, the turn order always staggered the allies and enemies. This meant if you were down to one enemy, it would get a turn between each of your allies, until it was dead. Battle Brothers combat is much more elegant.
RPG? The RPG elements are the weakest part of this game. There is some background flavour text you can read when you hire your mercs. Events may occur based on backgrounds and traits so it matters who is in your party. Your choices in these events may have consequences, some good, some very bad. There are also random events that occur throughout your travels. It is open world, so areas of interest will also appear on the map. You can select perks when you level. You can also increase your stats. As far as RPG, these perks are for combat pursposes only. There are no classes in the traditional RPG sense. Your mercs are either ranged, melee, or both. It would be a nice touch to hire a blacksmith or healer (non-combatants) for your group. I tried hiring mercs with traits like greedy, tiny, superstitious, etc., in hopes it might add more to the game... Quests are contracts. You can have only one a time. By completing or failing contracts, you develop reputation with the towns and noble houses. The game grinds. Even a lot of positive reviews will tell you that. The map can feel mostly empty for a sandbox. Since Early Access, the game has added ambitions and end-game scenarios. I was hoping those might improve story and gameplay more. The game is called Battle Brothers for a reason...
Combat. Here the game should shine. It can and does, most of the time. As there are so many positive reviews, this one will try to cover some of the negative combat aspects. This is not a dungeon crawl game. Combat happens outside, always. This is surprising considering a lot of locations are forts and towers. Your party usually starts on the left, unless you intervene in combat already started. The variety is the terrain. You can have swamp, tundra, forest, hills, etc. The terrain can add definite strategy. It can also be very clunky. There are obstacles like logs, and shrubbery ("Ni!"). All you can do is move around them, and that can take a lot of turns and fatigue build up. They will easily create bottlenecks based on AI zones of control, which really only succeed in prolonging combat. This is not a stealth game. Backstabbing perk adds bonuses based on how many other allies surround the enemy. I tried to create a traditional rogue type but did not succeed. Despite being directly behind an occupied (and stunned) opponent, I consistently hit the shield! The AI is very good (Veteran). If you are squishy, you will be targeted. So, you adapt. Ultimately, combat started to feel the same and grind as well. Sure traits, perks and equipment will improve your chances, but they had a minimal effect on the overall tactics. I wish there were an option to allow the enemy to surrender. In my last fight, I outnumbered my two near-death opponents 6:1. The next round I could not deliver the killing blow so I watched as a raider crit-hit dead two of my well-equipped yet fatigued mercs. RNG. Many do love the game for this reason. I just saw it as a waste of my time. Time I would rather spend doing something else.

Double Fine generally produces some fine games and Stacking is certainly one of them. Stacking is a puzzle game which teeters on the casual line. It’s gameplay and core concepts are based on the Russian matryoska stacking dolls, hence the name: Stacking. You play the smallest doll of them all, named Charlie, as you set out on a quest to rescue your chimney-sweeping family from the evil industrialist Baron. If you haven’t already guessed, Stacking is set in a miniature Victorian world inhabited by matrioyska dolls. Even the cut scenes are presented like silent movies on a stage. It is not quite to the same scope as Brutal Legend as it is less than 10 hours long, and it’s not quite to the same calibre as Psychonauts, but Stacking upholds the fine name of Double Fine.
Stacking does have the charm factor turned all the way up with a saloon soundtrack, a miniature world and an unlikely hero. When all the dolls get excited, they jump up and down, like they’re being moved with an invisible hand. Stacking doesn’t take itself too seriously. It was produced as a small side project while Double Fine were working on Brutal Legend and feels like one too. While I was happy with the $10 purchase, I would not pay more than that as there’s just not enough substance overall.

Overall if given the choice I would give this game a positive rating, but the game punishes you for playing risky, and by that I mean anything that isn't 100% safe is potentially game ruining. Any mission with 3 skulls is so risky that it isn't even worth doing, so you spend hours and hours doing 1 and 2 skull missions. I've started over 50 games and had 4 long campaigns (30 days or more game time), and if things don't go perfectly for you in the first 3 day game time, and I mean PERFECTLY, you better just quit and restart because it will catch up to you. If you lose 1 guy in your first mission, restart the game, because you've lost too much and you will be playing catch up the rest of the game.
My last campaign that will probably make me quit I spent 40 days game time doing 1 and 2 skull missions. During that 40 days I lost 1 Battle brother. So I thought "well, I've been playing this campaign for a week all my characters are level 5-9, I guess I should try a 3 skull mission". I do the mission, win but lose 4 characters in the process, basically ending my game. Sure, I could go hire level 1 new recruits but they will be targeted and killed by the more difficult enemies I'm already encountering, and I lost some high level gear during that battle too.
In the end, it is a good game, but you feel pretty empty when 1 mistake or rng completely ruins a game you put hours or days into.

Double Fine never ceases to amaze me with the sheer amount of charm and originality they can squeeze into a game, and Stacking is perhaps the best example of this yet. An adventure puzzle game starring Russian nesting dolls, it's designed around the principle of, ahem, stacking your character inside other dolls in order to gain control over them. Each doll has a unique ability based on the character they play (for example a bear can scream at the crowd, or a seasick child can literally toss his cookies), and it's in using these abilities that you are able to open up new paths and solve problems in any number of different ways.
And that's what I found so enjoyable about Stacking. It's not so much the actual task of solving a puzzle that's fun, but finding the myriad of alternative, often hilarious ways in which you can solve a dilemma that proves so satisfying. Sure I can simply take control of the chef and toss the caviar in the gutter to stop buffet, or I could use the Pide Pipper to draw a band of rats into the kitchen and have then overrun the place. Even when the solutions become too nonsensical to guess, a surprisingly handy hint system points you in the right direction without completely spelling out the answer.
And of course all of this is wrapped with as much charm and personality as you'd expect from a Double Fine game, with terrific characterizations for the dozens of unique dolls, a brilliant vintage art direction, and excellent cutscenes that pay homage to silent movies. It's absolutely brimming with character and manages to tie it all back in to its clever puzzle mechanics, making a cohesive whole that might possibly be my favorite of Double Fine's recent games. It's a hard call, but regardless of my personal ranking, Stacking is a joy to play and you'd be missing out if you let something so fun and uplifting pass you by.

A charmingly goofy puzzle game, Stacking has you stacking into fellow Matryoshka dolls in order to solve challenges. Each doll has their own performable action which adds a bit of personality to the solutions themselves. The level prologues are told with 1920s film cards and a theatre stage which lends originally to the exposition and sets the mood well for the antics ahead. Hobos are cast as helpers and industrialists as effigy which, along with the child labor issue that sat quietly at the center of the story, suggested a greater commentary that wasn't elaborated on past that basic point. The same can be said about the act of stacking itself. It's sort of implied that the protagonist's ability to stack into other dolls is fairly unique, but neither that nor the fact that these other dolls have lost control of themselves and done things, often against their own interests, is ever commented on. Seriousness certainly isn't the focus of the game, but it ends up feeling rather like the dolls that populate it, hollow and with a fixed expression. It proves to be an enjoyable, if short,  romp all the same. Just don't go in expecting a whole lot more.

My Let's Play of Dog Sled Saga:
My Review:
Mechanically speaking, there are only a handful of actions that are required of you whilst you are Dog-Sleding.  You click and hold the mouse button to initiate a variable trajectory with which you try and hurl dog biscuits into your awesome dog's mouth.  You'll know your dogs are hungry by their panting breath against the cold pixel-y wind.
It is actually quite easy to blunder this up.  First if you try and feed your dogs before they are hungry, it will comically bounce off their noggin and you'll have lost a doggy biscuit.  Second if you just clearly miss (some dogs seem to be better catchers than others) well then you're probably going to lose the race.  But sometimes you can miss because you aren't paying attention to the huge TREE INCOMING sign.
So what happens if your dogs are hungry?  Well, aside from going slow they trip up the works.  You'll have to, in real-time, adjust the length of rope dividing the dogs to make sure it has proper length to avoid getting tangled.  Outside of that, I'm not really sure.  I never went that far without feed my dogs.
Dog Sled Saga is surprisingly deep despite being pretty shallow.  All of the game can be controlled via the mouse and one mouse button.  You don't really need to tend to your dogs outside of the races, like a tamagotchi.  The only thing you need to concern yourself with is if they are tired and if they get along with other dogs on your team and what type of position they like to be in.
Despite all of this, I did find myself becoming attached to my Dog Sled Saga team.  The pixel art is wonderful to watch and the music, my goodness the music.  It is great!  I mean, the music is 8-bit style, but it's SO WELL DONE.  Truly gets stuck in my head.
I am a fan of Dog Sled Saga even though right now it seems kind of bare-bones.

Don't fret if you did not play the first one, as this review is for you if you're skeptical.
In a nutsnell, this is a game of, erm, fate. You, the player, are playing a game about your life- a card game in which every card is an event from your memories. Death, however, makes your memories a little hazy. Did you stop to help that overturned cart? Was it actually an ambush? And didn't you meet that priest before encountering the cart? Why is there a desert card in this city?!
Worry not, as you can decide (to an extent) what cards you wish to use for every level. Have a level with tons of undead? Better shuffle that holy warhammer into your deck. And speaking of levels, every level has several seperate mechanics. It could be "just reach the end boss", or perhaps "rescue soliders along the way, who can then assist you for the final boss". You might have to search a burning undead-filled city for survivors and lead them out. Every level is interesting.
And then their's The Dealer... oh boy did I miss him. Although he will (probably) never steer you wrong, he won't make it easy for you. Wise-crackin' and ever-doubtful of your abilities, he's GLaDoS cranked to 11. He will often remark on every event or action you take. Keeping a specific beneficial card in your deck to get a free item? He'll call you out on it. Fail a dice roll? Hoo boy, he'll try to contain his laughter.
Outside of the cards and roulettes, there is the combat system. If you've played any batman game you probably know how it goes. You can roll outta the danger, you can block certain attacks, combo attacks to strike with a powerful ability, yada yada. If you haven't had such combat experience, you should be able to get into it just fine. Worry not if you get frustrated- I was a hardcore Hand of Fate player and even I had some challenging scrapes at times.

Started playing this game with a buddy of mine as we were looking for something with co-op capability the whole way through. We've played korean based MMORPGS before so we are familiar with the common practices such as the flashy cash shop, the limited character customization on start and the need to physically buy or obtain armor (costumes) that will change your visual. None of this bothers us. You know why? Once you actually get into the game, you realize that these shortcuts the cash shop offers are just that - shortcuts. Everything can be obtained in-game through working the auction house, and even at 65 you have tons of opprotunities to find chests with random costume pieces and end-game gear from. The combat only gets better no matter which advanced class you play. I have a 65 warp mage, a 59 catspaw and am currently working on leveling a 35 Doomblade to 65 to be my main end-game character. This game is far from perfect, however. More often than not, me and my friend pick out odd things in the voice acting, or NPC character design and laugh at them. However, it's these random quirks that also make the game stand out. I came from playing Grand Chase, a 2.5D side scroller somewhat similar to this. You make characters, go into instanced dungeons with up to four people and kick the crap out of everything you can, with the end-goal being big shiny numbers from leveled, specced gear and a costume set you're happy with in a class you decided to play.
We've played almost every hour together, and so far have not had any problems doing so. This games charm is something you will either hate or love, but definitely give it more than 0.4 hours like I see most people doing on here. You don't get to see any of what the game actually has to offer.
As well, this game was not MADE by the same company that made TERA. It was published by En Masse, the same as TERA. En Masse handles the translations and what not that involve this game being ported over from Korea. Korea still has much more content, as it all hasn't been translated etc. Therefore Kritika online and TERA have completely seperate developers. (Kritika developer is ALLM and TERA is developed by Bluehole.)
Out of all the classes I've played so far, the gameplay is entirely different. I go from a warp mage, who excels in AOE crowd control and focuses heavily on dishing out massive amounts of damage with lasers/beams and the sort, to my Catspaw who.. ironically enough, grows cat ears and makes a bunch of weird cat noises for fan service.. i guess.. who spends 90% of her time in the air doing positional combos and fast paced, multi-hit abilities that decimate large groups of enemies at ease.
I've also found that this games in-game community is really good! We've found a guild that we keep all of our characters on that has at least 10 people online at most times, will offer help for end-game runs, dailies, pvp missions, as well as help in form of knowledge to lower level people.
Seriously, try this game if you like Beam Em' Ups! I'm nearing 60 hours played and I've spent $40 during the premium currency sale and was able to buy everything I wanted in terms of convenience and looks available to me, still with some left over for the future shop updates. Compare that amount of money spent and my playtime to a majority of the 500+ games I own on steam alone and you'll see, I was able to get my moneys worth and will continue to do so for some time.
Hope this review allows some people who may have looked the other way a chance at trying, and possibily liking this game!

This game surprised me a little.
I went in expecting a clicker, but it's more of a very minimalist visual novel with intervals of clicker-like gameplay.  Despite having very little dialogue spread throughout the game and taking place in pretty much a single location, it somehow manages to introduce a variety of interesting characters and a twist that I don't think you'll expect.  You get little pieces of their stories when completing objectives, and the writing is simple yet amusing.
I'd like to make it clear that this game is not very exciting, it's strength is that it is simple enough to pretty much mindlessly play.  So, similar to a clicker, it is more of a game to pass the time when you don't have anything else to do.  It does this task admirably, providing just enough interaction to keep the player engaged; especially in the late game.  The gameplay is oddly addictive and I found myself coming back to the game frequently.
The visual novel portion of the game does have an ending, and a true ending after that (though you can continue playing afterwards).  My only gripe is that the very end is a bit drawn out, especially if you want the true end.  All in all, you'll probably have close to 20h of gameplay when you unlock the final achievement, with the option to keep playing if you find it especially enjoyable.
The art style of the game is visually pleasing and easy to look at, with interesting character designs being especially eye catching.  While the art is nice, the sound design is a bit much near the end of the game.  I personnally turned the sound effects down alot because the game gets very busy near the end.
I recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a game to fill in the boring parts of their day, or anyone who is interested in a light-hearted bite-sized gaming experience.

If you have ever played Van Helsing series from the same dev, and loved them. You will also love this one.
--- below is the generic detailed review, but not in-depth. I tried to be spoiler free as much as I can, short version is available in overall topic ----
edit1: fix some typing errors
::: Visual :::
The graphic is nice in its own genre, nothing special. There are some nice details here and there, but you won't notice them anyway when the waves come. The FX is visually served its purpose for the genre, though, it would be better to see some visual variation of the same enemy. (different headgears, weapons, horns, sizes, etc.)
::: Sound :::
The repeated audio can be annoying at times (which is expected from this genre). however, there are several things that is missing, which I think should be included in the patches, one of them is pinging notice (Attention, Help, Back). You can see it in the minimap, but when things get messy, you won't be seeing it anymore, so the sound is need. (maybe the sound is there, but i tried them, but heard none, just ping in minimap)
::: Gameplay :::
There are 13 official maps, each map has 4 variation (depending on number of players), 4 tiers for each map. Map designs are very good imo, you cannot just use the same setup on every map, and each can be done in several different styles. There are also some challenges maps available after complete normal maps too. Finish all maps, and all tiers ? you can continue with custom maps from others or make one (or more) yourselfs.
Apart from the normal difficulty, you can customized one yourself when you reach certain level, there is also an endless mode for your hardcoreness. I haven't try the custom diff and endless, still in the middle of tier 2 with these hours in.
Each map can be different depending on number of players, more lanes, more cores, chaotic ai paths, different enemies in waves, more enemies. They are really nice, but just one thing ..., the wave is patterned wave, not a dynamic wave in normal mode (random enemies orders). It is not really disappointed, but it would be a blast if it is a dynamic wave.
There are 3 classes (currently), which are melee, range, and magic class. each classes has several active and passive skill, which encourage different playstyle. Skill trees design to progress nicely with your playthrough (from tier 1-4). It doesn't really encourage the abused xp farming at all, but a lot of players still doing it. There are some balancing issue, but nothing major.
Items and Equipments can be purchased from store (random), or crafted in lobby. They can also be earned as rewards from completing maps and some optional objectives. They are what you can expect from general action-rpg game, so nothing special. Bonuses from equipment is what you expected, but with the right setup, it is more than enough.
In order to build traps, you need bases for them, each base is trap-type specific. (you cannot just build anything on any bases) there are some special traps (map specific traps) in some maps which can be used for your advantage (or not). You need essences to build them, which can be earned from killing hordes, and completing waves. in co-op games, the essence will be divided according to number of players, so you share your earning, but your spending is yourself.
Each trap has 2 passive skills and 3 upgradable skills (3 level each). They can be ranked up with Research Points, which can be earned from complete maps, optional quests. They are not infinite, but I can say that there are enough for you to progress to each tier maps.
Skills and upgrades can be reset at anytime during your journey through tiers 1-4 in lobby with some costs. This allow you to change your playstyle back and forth freely, however, this can be minimized with co-op plays.
::: Overall :::
If you are looking for a good TD game, this is your game. Apart from traps, heroes also play the huge part in the game. You can customized your loadout (traps' upgrades, and heroes' skills and equipments). You can be a dedicated trapper, a meat wall, or balanced between the two, depending on your loadouts. CO-OP play is fairly balanced, as the difficulty scales with the players in-game.
It requires some balancing here and there, but nothing major to prevent you from enjoying a good TD.
Final word, please DO NOT CHEAT (or whatever you called) in CO-OP games, do it alone if you want to.

Kinda disappointed with this game because it turned out to basically be a clicker game and I expected more of a puzzle game after having 100% completed and loved This Starry Midnight We Make which was also made by Cavyhouse. That's my own misconception, though, so I won't hold it against the game. I just wanted to warn you right off the bat, though, if you don't like clicker games, you probably won't like this game.
On it's own, it's certainly a well-made clicker game and it has plenty of the Cavyhouse style that TSMWM has. My one complaint is how slow the game is to get started. You start with basically nothing: one tree and a watering can. However, you eventually have a screen full of stuff that requires constant clicking. Basic clicker game mechanics, in other words. That one tree and watering can you start with, though, stick around a bit too long. You first have to grow 1 kidney. Then 5. Then 10. Then 15. Then 30. During this part you're not doing much aside from waiting on the watering can to fill and then watering your one tree and finally harvesting when the fruits are ready. I think this initial 20 or so minutes of gameplay should have been condensed down to like 5 minutes.
After that, though, the ball gets rolling as you get more plants and machines, your upgraded plants begin to bear more fruit and you start ordering animals that also need tending. At this point you constantly have things to do.
There is one main difference between this game's mechanics and most other clicker games that bears mentioning: the lack of automation. In most clickers the game plays itself, only requiring input from the user to speed up the current gameplay or to upgrade the automation. This game lacks any real automation. If you stop watering plants, they stop growing; if you don't harvest your fruit, you won't get any more; if you don't fill your mincemeat grinder, you won't get mincemeat; etc. You can walk away from the game at any point and you don't have to worry about plants dying or anything but your production will halt, regardless. This is kind of a controversial difference so I won't say it's a good or bad choice. It's really up to what the player wants and expects.
Like in TSMWM, the story is delivered by short dialog cutscenes that occur every few quests you complete. Various people from town come to the shop for their own reasons and you learn of their situations that way. It's a nice bit of world-building but doesn't have any real bearing on the gameplay.
Since the gameplay here is very simplistic there's not much else to say about it. If you like clicker games, you should check this out since it's well-made and has some great themeing but if you don't like clicker games, I'd avoid it simply because it doesn't do anything interesting enough to win you over.

I have not played a game that so perfectly recaptures the hopeless, decaying world of Glen Cook's Black Company series or the old Myth games by Bungie. But far from being a simple nostalgic romp, Battle Brothers is an amazing tactics game with numerous potential ways to build your mercenary company.
It is a challenging game, but rarely patently unfair. I find myself holding my breath on archer shots and heavy two-handed swings knowing that someone's life could very well end if they missed - but unlike previous games, a fatality or two in a mission does not feel completely game ending like it did the XCOM series. It was just a grim reminder of how sudden violence is in a world where mercenaries are needed to keep the roads safe from bandits and goblins.
Every part of this game was made with clear polish and loving attention to detail; the writing is spot on and ranges from grim to black humour, the mechanics feel tight and properly balanced, the different enemy factions provide completely different sets of tactical challenges from one another (keep each fight fresh! A strategy that works on brigands will not serve you against goblins!), the art is amazing, and the soundtrack is superb.
I have not had this much fun in a singleplayer game for a long time.

The monetary toll of treating the injuries or just the price to you reputation will suck, but not nearly as much as starting over. 2. Close fights are often not a challange of tactics and praying for at least decent RNG, often they are another opportunity to run away. Notice you are faced with a fairly comperable force, you have enough money and food for a couple more days without this contract AND you aren't getting paid enough to replace at least of few of the inevitable friendly corpses? Then your job is to realize that and peace out, not try and beat these random enemies through a feat of tactical prowess. Sorry employer, you obviously needed to hire a stronger company or pay me waaaay more.
With a great overworld features and tactical battles, Battle Brothers is a no brainer for fans of the genere looking for a challenge. No go buy it and enjoy running away =D

Sentai Filmworks is proving to be quite interesting by bringing anime to Steam; although I'll never buy another Blu-Ray from them again since they won't get rid of their cheap, screen-covering yellow subtitles, it sure doesn't hurt to rent a movie on a stormy Tuesday night, and being able to customize the subtitles in Steam's video player is a neat touch.
To be straightforward, Loups=Garous is a solid B- movie; low-budget and derivative with no liberties taken, but still worthy of your time if you don't have much else to do. There's no outstanding faults in either the dub or sub, but not much in the way of original content either. Despite that, there still exists a fair degree of care in the presentation of the movie's themes, with the top two being totalitarianism & man's "suppressed monster".
Background art and music is what we've come to expect from Production I.G.- sublime, world-building, and decadent. Would probably be even more remarkable if given enough time.
Animation quality is a mixed bag; the design is representative of the source material's intentionally lifeless atmosphere, but translates poorly to anime, since everybody is, well.... lifeless. The lack of detail in even the most basic shots undermines what the narrative has to offer, which makes it difficult to root for anybody currently in a scene. Sometimes I feel as if this would be better as live-action, especially when it gets edgy in a few parts.
In spite of Loups=Garous great themes, it's definitely not character driven. Most, if not all characters in the film seem like flat, pre-established archetypes too often seen in modern I.P.-
-Ayumi's a stoic, anti-societal kuu-dere
-Haduki's the clumsy, overly anxious type that has trouble expressing her emotions
-Mio's a half-baked Mary Sue that appears out of nowhere in the beginning to assist the characters with superb hacking skills, having no in-depth explanation as to how she acquired those skills, for which Loups=Garous relies on the audience to make assumptions about her character
It also doesn't help that Sentai Filmworks labels Ayumi as a guy, going so far as giving "him" a male voice actor in the dub and even retaining that gender-swap in the subtitles, when said character is a definite female in original Japanese, regardless of character design. It might of been an okay marketing decision for their Blu-Ray, but it's still glaringly misleading.
Although the characters felt unoriginal, I certainly didn't hate them. They carried the movie fairly well when they had to, and managed to pull off the sentiment charm when it was required. Not everyone will feel the same way though.
There's nothing wrong in expecting Production I.G. to go all out when they make anime movies (since they definitely nailed Break Blade & Eden of the East), but even if corners are cut, movie's like this can still be worth looking at, if you're willing to give 'em a chance.

The core gameplay focuses on learning how to properly manage a team of dogs, and how to maximize race efficiency. Races use simple click and timing mechanics to manage factors such as sled position, hunger, jumping, and untangling. Proper racing is rewarded with speed and happy dogs. Awesome moments are rewarded with fame that can lead to sponsorship upgrades.
Learning about each individual dog is important to team management. Each dog has a unique personality that will affect their natural sled position, likes, dislikes, happiness, and rapport with teammates. Dogs will have their own favorite things, skills, and faults. They will also have different levels of athleticism that will affect their fatigue and hunger.
All of the information about races and dogs will serve one purpose: managing the team. The overall goal is to earn money from victories and move on to more advanced leagues. The time outside of races is used to rest dogs to lower fatigue, fill the journal, change leagues, and hire new dogs. Raleigh will offer a piece of advice (chosen by you) at the end of each race. This information will be used to fill the journal and provide gameplay tips. The first couple of leagues seem easy once the core gameplay is understood, but that seems subject to change based on in-game progress and future updates.

Battle Brothers is an excellent game that combines a simple management and levelling mechanic with an enjoyable turn based battle system. The premise is to hire a band of mercenaries and wander the world doing various contracts, until your company either perishes, or you deal with one of the end game crises (though you can continue beyond this point and do all three if you like).
As such the meat of the game is the combat mechanics, and these hold up very well. Your mercenaries and your opponents each have a number of action pooints, with actions dependant on the weapons and other items they are carrying. Unusually for a game of this ilk, armour realistically trumps, yet at the same time, heavy armoured mercenaries will become bogged down in fatigue, making tactical planning necessary not only at the set up of an engagement, but also as it plays out.
The idea of endless battles, even against a varied set of enemies, only works if there is a reason for it, and this is where the campaign comes into play. You hire and fire, starve and march your mercenaries around the world, growing your reputation and deciding the kind of company you want to run. Some of your men will become familiar and treasured, others just a pile of rotting bones and a name in the roster of the dead: "Disembowelled by Shagra the Slayer", "Beheaded by a raider".
By the end of it, one way or the other, you will have gathered up a mighty collection of these, for the game is hard, especially before you get the hang of when to run and when to fight - though you can to some extent choose when to lower your goals in order to stay alive. Yet at the same time that does make it more rewarding when you finally get your company up to a decent strength and manage to sustain it, building your named men to higher levels.
And a word also needs to go to the developers who stay constantly in contact with their players, adding and tweaking and listening to the ideas. What is clear is that they have produced a game they love themselves, and this has resulted in one that should be enjoyed by many of the turn-based genre ... and for the first time in a while I can give a 'what's it worth' recommendation of full price.
What's it worth: Full price

I must say that all Heroes have quite good stats and are easy to use in the battles against the creatures withing the dungeons. You can level up easily and also collect different items for your hero from three chests: Wooden, Silver and Golden. Items can be bought as well from the Shop found in every dungeon and you don't have to worry about currency. You will get enough gold once you start killing creatures.
Even if you don't get the chance to see a story in this game, that's not really a matter as the game is already dynamic and you will always be busy to keep destroying monsters than do anything. But in order to pass the dungeon you have to activate Marks which bring along different packs of monsters. You have to clean and activate all those Marks in order to meet The Redemeer, a selfish guy who will try to steal your soul. (No, not in a romantic way )
The soundtrack is quite playful, but you will not really pay attention to it, since the game's action is that catchy. However, the sound effects are quite powerful, especially the projectile's sound effect. You will not miss for sure if something is attacking you from the distance.
Graphics are quite typical for a 2D game and I like the fact that the characters are still somehow detailed, I mean you are not seeing some undefined pixeled spots, but some cute tiny characters.
Even though there are not that much features implemented in the current version, Dungeon Souls is very fun to play and entertaining and I strongly recommned this game to anyone. Still, we are expecting new features and goodies in this game in the future.

Dungeon Souls is one of those instantly-accessible, immediately fun-to-play games. Choose a character and fight hordes of enemies to survive as long as you can while looting tons of equipment along the way.
Controls are very responsive and each character offers a unique gameplay experience. I found my favourite in the Thief. Coupling his high-rate of attack and critical damage chance with items that fan the area of impact with flames is fantastic fun. Certain requirements are needed to unlock other characters. Unlocking and rambling around with the slow, but powerful
Necromancer, buffed with a demon eye that attacks enemies automatically and minions to swarm my enemies was also a joy.
Being a rogue-like game, there ought to be enough variety in gameplay and equipment to keep you coming back. This is certainly the case: enemies are fairly diverse and loot adds very interesting, powerful effects that make you want to come back to discover more. Unlocking characters is definitely something you'll want to do too, because they add a significantly new dimension to your dungeoneering.
In short, Dungeon Souls is just as fast-paced, frantic and enjoyable as the videos portray.

The concept of "Action Movie X: The Video Game", formerly known as "Just Cause 2", being enhanced with a multiplayer mode had me turned on when I first downloaded the game on my Xbox 360. The very concept alone of a game where you're encouraged and rewarded to blow crap up seemed absolutely brilliant to do with a friend, especially since many of the vehicles operate as two-seaters, and thus when you use them in the singleplayer, you only get to use one thing at a time.
Well, this game, I suppose, wasn't what I had fantasized about. It wasn't awful, but it was in a galaxy far, far away from good. That has mostly to do with how repetitive it got, similar to its host game. I know I hyped it up as a game where the one goal is to destroy everything, but in terms of creative-ish ways to solve problems and kill enemies, the Just Cause series kind of fell short of games like Far Cry 3 and Aliens vs. Predator. The issue here is that Just Cause 2 HAD problems that you could solve creatively; these of course came in the form of missions and military installations. This game doesn't have either in any of the servers I've tried to get into - that would be shy of a dozen, and NO, I'm not going to waste the time combing through ALL of them just to verify. I've wasted enough of my time on those dozen alone.
So basically all Just Cause 2: Multiplayer Mod has to offer is in its title, in that it lets you drive, fly, swim and shoot around with your friends in an open world setting, and the trail abruptly ends there.

A fun mash-up of metroidvania-style exploration, run'n'gun gameplay and bullet hell elements.
Despite the description above, Greedy Guns is as simple as it gets: you run, shoot enemies on the way and collect money to buy weapons. Besides that, there are a few secrets to be found and some abilities that you'll get that will then allow you to explore sections of the game that were earlier blocked off.
And as far as simplicity goes, it works very well in this game - it's fun the way it is, while also presenting at least some challenge due to the bullet hell elements. And, of course, it's double as fun when played coop.
The biggest problem with the game is that it's awfully short for a metroidvania game. There isn't much exploration to be done, even after you've gotten new abilities. Mostly, re-exploring earlier sections will grant health pieces (4 pieces increases the character's max HP) or money and there is an extra weapon to be found as well, but that's about it.
It also doesn't help that, for a game called "Greedy Guns", collecting money is actually quite irrelevant. It's easy enough to collect money to buy new weapons and there is nothing else to be done with money then.
Greedy Guns sadly suffers from wasted potential - if the game was longer, exploration was more meaningful and there were more uses for collected money, the game would have been MUCH better.
However, issues aside, one important thing to mention is that the game has local coop (as mentioned above). So while the single player experience is short and somewhat lackluster, the game is potentially a lot more fun if played with a friend since, as mentioned, the game's premise is simple enough, which makes it perfect for having two characters going around shooting the hell out of enemies while dodging bullets.
I'm hoping the game will have updates in the future that will include more content and then make good use of the game's potential.

Ahnayro: The Dream World is a cryptic puzzle which requires you to not only have good general knowledge, but also be willing to search the internet for information that will help you to guess some very specific words from a jumble of letters on a dial. If that sounds truely boring, then you are probably right. If, however, you enjoy cryptic puzzles, then you may enjoy it more than you think.
The game has a terrific atmosphere. The way the clues are presented to you is quite spooky in a supernatural way, like a shoebox of somebody else's trinkets and memorabilia. Each puzzle has a spoken recording to accompany the objects and pictures.
Every day you are allowed five hints, without which most people would struggle to get anywhere. It's enough to make the answers guessable and the fact you have to wait a day for some more hints keeps you returning for more.

On the plus side, you'll get to search and learn about all sorts of really obscure history.  The downside is that this isn't really a self-contained puzzle game. It's more like an online scavenger hunt where the game gives you the next hints, and less like any of the other puzzle games you'll find here.
It's made well, with a lot of thought and hard work.  I wasn't sure what 'the waking world' was meaning in the context of the game, and it means 'searching online'.  If you like hunting down online history and scavenging for common links in history, then this game is for you.  If you were looking for a puzzle game where the answers are actually in the game itself, I might recommend trying something else.

The first thing that should catch your eye upon viewing the game’s store page is its extraordinary graphics/art style. Or its absurd premise: pick one. But is the game truly absurd, or is it just a beautiful, tender story wrapped in total weirdness? I’m not sure either to be honest, not yet, but maybe we can find out together? I’m almost sure we will know the answer by the end of this review, so... shall we begin?

I thought I knew what the game would be about, roughly, but I was surprised to see that I was actually completely wrong this time. I expected a casual time management game, but what I got was actually a clicker game. You know, clicker games… like Clicker Heroes and Sakura Clicker. Where you just use the mouse to complete objectives. Except My Organic Garden has a story to tell, and unlike most of the other clicker games (I haven’t played them all) you can actually complete it given enough time.
In fact, there are several stories to follow. You have a main story, which involves you (Organa, an apprentice) learning the profession of organ harvesting, which I will get to in a minute. And then there are several side quests that contain shorter stories.
All of the stories are told in a style similar to visual novels, but the conversations are always kept to a minimum. The stories are also broken up, so every now and then you get to see a new part of it. A wise choice, because it keeps the game more interesting and makes you want to continue playing. Usually you play these sorts of games for 30 minutes or so – sure, there are exceptions – and then close them and open them a day or two later to see if ‘you’ have made some progress. Not in this case. Because of the story you might want to return to it faster than normal. In reality it still remains a clicker game, though, so this means that if you have little or no interest in these sorts of games this most likely doesn’t apply to you. Another reason to return to it sooner is the fact that the game doesn’t continue harvesting whenever you close the game. All harvesting has to be done by the player him- or herself (and with the help of your animals).
The gameplay consists of first having to manage one tree. Give it enough water and kidneys will grow on it. Give the tree even more water and the kidneys will grow until they’re finally ripe for harvesting. Harvesting levels up the tree and giving it water levels up the water can. Each time you level up you can do more. The water can, for example, allows you to have more water in it, while the tree allows you to plant even more kidneys. Later on you will also be able to grow even higher quality kidneys, as well as hearts and meat, for example. Since there’s a lot of micromanaging involved you ultimately have to purchase some animals from the (a different?) shop. There are frogs and birds, among a few other animals. Frogs will fill up the water can faster and birds allow you to produce more meat. These animals can all also be leveled up. In fact, I haven’t yet seen one thing that I wasn’t able to level up. Everything levels up, it’s crazy. Crazy, but necessary if you want to make good progress, though. There is no time limit, or any limit whatsoever, so you can take your sweet time growing organs and clicking things. The story does progress once you have completed enough or the right quest(s), though.
The quests themselves are simplistic and easy. They can just take a lot of time to complete. Invest enough of your time into the game and you’ll be able to finish all of the available quests. The goal is to always level up more, buy more and harvest more. There’s no real depth to them and the stories aren’t interesting enough (thus far) to make me care about any of the involved characters. I really want to see the complete story, including the side quests, but I don’t want to spend hours of my time just mindlessly (a keyword in case you want to argue!) and frantically clicking things.
Ultimately I guess it can be either a soothing experience if you really take your time, or it can be a really stressful experience if you’re the OCD kind of person or if you just fail to see the logic behind it. I fall into that last category I think. I don’t see the logic behind clicker games, although this game does have more to offer, but I also don’t find these games soothing or relaxing. And unlike the other clicker games Forget Me Not My Organic Garden isn’t free. Would the game be that much more enjoyable if it was free? Probably not, but I would rate it differently I think.
The music is kind of cheerful. To be honest I expected a sad, dramatic game, but it’s actually the opposite. It’s a strange feeling, hearing happy music during more serious moments. But it’s a feeling I seemed to enjoy nevertheless. There’s no voice acting at all: the animals do make some noises, however, and there are some sound effects to indicate you’re making progress (completing quests, and leveling up items and animals). Other than that, the music seems to be the main focus here.
Forget Me Not My Organic Garden uses a lot of fade-in and fade-out techniques. These techniques are accompanied by beautifully shaded and colored – sometimes (very) blurry - graphics, but except for a few animations most of the art is static. The few animations are shown in a way that it looks like stop-motion, but I thought it was a bit messy, because animals were moving to all sorts of places. It’s certainly unique, I’ll give it that, but it doesn’t help you when you have to keep track of so many things at the same time. I wish this was done a bit differently.
I’m not sure what the total length of the game is - I might get there eventually – but apparently the game is about 15-30 hours long from what I’ve read and seen. That’s impressive, but also understandable, given the mechanics. I personally consider it lengthy, but if we compare it to other clicker games it clearly isn’t, of course. Despite that, you can still get more than enough gameplay out of it. Just don’t expect as much.

Forget Me Not My Organic Garden is a well-made game all things considered. However, it isn’t what I expected it to be. I personally expected something a little… deeper, purely based on the screenshots. But if you enjoy frantically clicking your mouse then there’s plenty of fun to be had here, no doubt about it. I wouldn’t say it’s a case of style over substance (the stories might just give the game more substance in the end) but in the first few hours it will definitely feel like that.
Pros:
+ Excellent art style
+ Cheerful music
+ Multiple stories
+ Easy to learn and play
Mixed:
+/- Can be soothing if you take your time, or just plain stressful
Cons:
- Repetitive gameplay
- Too much micromanaging
- ‘Stop motion’-like animations make you lose track of things
(Ratings aren’t calculated based on a formula, but on my personal feelings)

Ahnayro: The Dream World was a beautiful puzzle game. What started out to be a mesh of trivia fun, turned into a timeline of History. Most of it comes from American History, from figures, places and other artifacts.
Players begin on what appears to be an empty astral clock. Completing each puzzle will advance us to the next, to where the entire clock is complete. The puzzles, themselves, are linked in to the respective point on the board, and consists of word searching games; find and connect a letter, or letters (up to 3) to form a word, or a phrase. While the controls and tutorial were easy, it was a major challenge for me. Unless you are a historian, more than not you will have to do research in order to find the answers. Luckily, the clues are in the photographs and quotes provided.
Aside from this inspiring objective, the visuals and effects were also amazing. The heirlooms and antiques provided in the backgrounds gave an ancient feel to the atmosphere, as well as the color scheme. The colors used were very monotone. The old-styled photographs, supported this theme too, having the aged crippling and creases on them. Another design added to this, was the astral clock, and the glowing animation that is triggered when finished with a puzzle. The sound and music also added, to the latter effect. Both were well-done, and suited the atmosphere of the game.
My only complaints are in the lack of an undo button. For clues that require a lengthy answer, one mis-click and you have to just … spam click the remaining letters until the slots reset. This can be annoying. The ending, was also, kind of underwhelming. Once the boards been complete, that's it. Checking the screenshots of this game also establishes that. Apart from the external links you have access to from each artifact point, nothing else really happens.

But, despite this, it was a fun game. I've definitely learned more than a thing or two, after playing Ahnayro: The Dream World, and I recommend playing!

After playing this game for more than 350 hours so far (of which 200 hours were invested since the beta update last month) and without any indication of being bored by it anytime soon, i just had to write a review for it, even though i never wrote one before and english is not my native language (as you probably can tell by now).
So instead of repeating all the things other reviews already told you, like that you manage a mercenary company and doing contracts in a random generated open world, i will entirely focus on the (for me) biggest strenght of this game. Even so the game is put in the genre of tactic-rpgs or strategy, i find it's more accurate described as a turn-based medieval combat simulation. All the things, that were of great importants for skirmishes with very few combatants 500 years ago, considering weapons, armour, skill of the fighters and terrain, are all taken into account, as well as morale and fatigue and the historical accurate role of every medieval weapon. To clarify my arguments i will provide some examples, but will hide them under spoilers, because for me, figuring these things out by myself was part of the fun (and challenge) of this game. So if you don't want to spoil yourself, you have to believe me without getting examples (maybe this review will be marked as helpful a lot to be a little more trustworthy ;)), but if you, on the other hand, are a fan of realistic, turn-based medieval combat and the high amount of positive reviews still not convinced you, you might as well give it a shot and look into the spoilers.
Your company in Battle Brothers will start with unexperienced fighters and low funds so which equipment would provide the most benefit in such a scenario?
Most reviews are mentioning, how easy your brothers can die, so how complex can a combat system be, if keeping the own men alive is relying on pure luck of RNG? But while it's not easy by all means, and not losing men sometimes is impossible (at least on ironman), the game provides you with the necessary tools to avoid it most of the time.
All weapontypes have a role they fulfill and using the right one against the right enemy will make the game much easier.
Going from early to late game simulates to some extend the progress of warfare in the medieval times. Starting only with light armour in the beginning, having access to heavy one later on allows you to change your playstile to some extend.
While having all these tactical options at your disposal, i want to clearify that so have the human enemies you fight. They are having the same combat skills, they use the same weapons with the same stats, the same armour and taking their perks from the same pool you do, too (and they have the same level requirements for more advanced ones, so a level 1 thug will have no perks at all). They get no bonus to hit chance, or malus, in a situation were you wouldn't. The game is what i call fair in this regard and i really like this. The only disadvantage you have, which other reviews pointed out as well, is the limitation of 12 men you can bring to each battle while the enemys have no limitation at all.
With containing fantasy aspects, the game has the justification of providing you with different challenges like Orcs and Goblins, who, of course, have perks you can't possess, weapons you can loot but usually only use with penaltys and their unique tactics, so that you have to adapt to be sucessful. They are all very well implemented and the way to beat them always feels reasonable
All these aspects of the complex combat mechanic would still be shallow and unsatisfying, if the AI couldn't make use of it. Fortunately she does a really good job. To be honest, i can't remember the last time, the AI in a turn-based game was this challenging and smart (without cheating of course). That doesn't mean she is perfect, there are some flaws and misscalcualtions at times, especialy when she is using specific perks, but they are very minor in comparison (and maybe get fixed in the future). Furthermore, the AI behavior is custom for every type of enemy, so Orcs act other than goblins or humans.
While playing, you can clearly see, that programming a good AI was really important for the devs and it paid off.
So if you consider yourself a fan of challenging but fair turn-based tactical combat simulation in a grounded, low-fantasy setting with high replayability, i assure you, you will not be disappointed. Please consider buying this game for 30 bucks, you get more value than most AAA singleplayer games the past years provided and the developers of Battle Brothers would like to add more content to the game (modding, dlc, translations) if it's success justifies it, so you help us all :)

Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Your name is Organa, you work in a greenhouse at the back of a… let’s say, a slightly different shop and you have lot to learn from your Master Irene. Well, she is going to teach you how can grow and harvest something totally…..out there! Yes, you are going to learn how to grow and harvest “Organ Fruits” from their respective trees!  EXCUSE ME, WHAT DID YOU SAY…?
Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden is a Novel/clicker type of game (and to be totally honest with you, the first game of it genre that I have played). The story is laid out as a visual novel. Throughout the story, you will meet different characters and you will be given tasks to achieve to keep moving forward in the story.
In the greenhouse, you will start with 2 trees and a watering can. Apparently, it is the conversional equipment for the organ fruit grower. But be assured you will get up to 5 trees and you will be able to produce Hearts, Kidneys, Stomachs, Livers and Colon fruits. Each time you pick a fruit from its tree, you will get points. Accumulate enough points to level up your trees and produce even faster and better fruits but you will also get money to spend in a catalogue. Oh, before I forget, you will be able to use your Tranquilade to produce pickled fruits, and a meat grinder to produce mincemeat.
In the catalogue you will be able to purchase frogs (one of my cousins went for an audition), butterflies, lizards, moles, woodpeckers and Homunculis. They will assist you in the greenhouse.
The artwork is different but nice. I really like the soundtracks; different music each time you meet a new character which changes the ambiance.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Interesting concept & artwork
-	Easy and enjoyable to play
-	Achievements
-	Trading Cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Kind of repetitive

The story revolves around Charlie, who is basically a midget child that everyone makes fun of for being so small, and his family, whom, at the hands of an evil Baron, are sent off to slave away mining coal, forced to work on ships, and generally anything that is considered a violation of child labor laws. He then hatches the brilliant plan to master the art of body-snatching, and sets off on a wild adventure to rescue his family from the Baron by occupying the bodies of keymasters, flatulent old men, an ill-bladdered german boy, and a slew of insanely wild characters, all of which will have you laughing emmensely and enjoying yourself way more than the price tag would infer. The point I'm trying to make is, it's an awesome game if you're looking for something whimsically challenging, full of comical humor, with just a touch of serious slave trading.

Starbound is a 2D space/extraterrestrial sandbox game from Chucklefish that, after several years in Early Access, has been released as a full game. Earth and an organization made up of seven races, the Protectorate, have been destroyed by an ancient and powerful foe. As the last surviving member of the Protectorate, it is your responsibility to defeat this evil foe! Or you could completely ignore the main quest, go to a far away planet, build some houses and get rich from the rent payments. It's up to you really.

You see, when Chucklefish describe their game as a sandbox, they really mean it. Sure, there are limits to it, but there's a hell of a lot of stuff you can do. Starbound does have a story, and even if you want to focus on other stuff you're probably going through the story quests. The story is a tad bit ridiculous but then so are the Novakids, people made out of neon gas. These quests, the first few of them anyway, are also used to teach the player about core mechanics and they do a fairly good job of explaining the basics. You can focus on the story if you want to or you can do any number of things, perhaps you just want to build a house and a farm on a faraway planet, or maybe you want to create a colony of Avians, hell I've heard there's someone trying to recreate the Death Star so you could even do something crazy like that.

One of the most important parts of the game is your character's ship. You have the ship from the get go but its FTL drive is completely caput, you can travel within your starting system but that's it. Completing a few story quests will get your ship repaired and then the game gets interesting. Once you have your ship you can do whatever you want. Your ship is fueled with a resource called Erchius Crystals which can be found on natural satellites (you'll need special breathing equipment before you can survive on them). When fueled, the ship can be used to jump to different star systems and then can be moved to positions over whatever planet or satellite you wish to visit. The ship is quite small to begin with (still big enough to build all of the crafting stations) but you can increase the size of the ship by hiring new crew members and then using upgrade modules at certain numbers of crew. Your ship ends up being pretty big so if you want to go for the whole space nomad thing it's possible.

When it comes to the planets themselves, there's a reasonable amount of variety. There are quite a few different types of them, ranging from lush forest worlds to worlds so cold you'll freeze to death without the proper equipment. They all have risk factors, the safest worlds are classed as Low Risk but they also have the lowest tiers of ore (Copper, Silver and Gold). You'll be wanting to visit more challenging planets fairly quickly so you can upgrade all your different crafting stations to access new armour, weapons, tools etc.

From what I've seen so far, all planets have some wildlife, most of which will attack you but some animals don't pay much attention to you. Sometimes this is all you'll find on a planet apart from some random chests and the odd travelling vendor. However, some worlds will be home to some pretty cool stuff. Perhaps you'll get lucky on an ocean world and find an underwater Hylotl city or maybe you'll find a Floran settlement in the middle of a jungle (completing quests for NPCs in settlements is how you get new crew members in the vanilla game). Some worlds are home to Penal colonies full of prisoners armed to the teeth, others are home to long abandoned Apex Labs. There's no way to know what a planet will have before you get there (something I find a tad frustrating) so it can be tough to find what you're looking for but when you do find them whatever it is you want, it's very satisfying.

No matter what you decide to do in Starbound, you're going to spend a fair amount of time collecting resources with your Protectorate Matter Manipulator. The MM is basically a combination of the basic tools you usually find in this kind of game, it can be used for mining chopping down trees etc. It can also be upgraded with special upgrade modules that improve its effectiveness. Unfortunately, mining for ore is one of the weakest parts of the game. The mining itself isn't so bad (though the lack of a quick way back to the surface sucks), the problem is that you never find large deposits of ore, I've never seen more than seven or eight bits of ore together. Not a huge issue by itself but when you consider the fact that you've probably gone to that planet specifically to look for ore it can be aggravating to spend half an hour doing it and ending up with 30 or 40 ore, that’s not going to last long.

Another big issue with the game is its performance but it seems to be a case of luck of the draw as to whether or not you'll actually have any problems. Some people have had issues that make the game unplayable, other have had issues with the game simply not performing as well as it should. I've been pretty lucky and the only performance-related issue I've had is some trouble getting fullscreen to work but there's no guarantee that you won't have any performance trouble. The only way to know if you're going to run into trouble is to buy the game and see if it works, not particularly helpful I realize but worst case scenario you can just refund the game and wait for fixes.

A couple more things I'd like to mention. Firstly, Starbound has an awesome modding community. Starbound is definitely enjoyable if you're playing Vanilla but there are some fantastic quality of life mods as well as complete overhauls out there that make it even more fun to play. Secondly, the game's drop-in multiplayer works very well and while singleplayer is a lot of fun I find the game even more enjoyable when playing with a friend.


Starbound is far from perfect but that doesn't stop it being a super enjoyable space sandbox game with plenty to do. It's well worth the price of admission.

As a fan of the Original X-COM/UFO: Enemy Unknown, I whole heartedly recommend this game. Battle Brothers is a turn based strategy game with real time management elements. The premise is simple, you lead a company of mercenaries through a medievil fantasy realm (inspired by Germanic origin) with Greenskins, Undead and Brigands to fight against. The story is relatively barebones and that in my humble opinion is a good thing because it's a game about your dudes and what happens to them. They can die, they WILL die and some will survive with severe injuries. The game is easy to understand, as opposed to 1994's X-COM, the UI tells you everything you need to know, and the game in my opinion does a great job of easing the player into the role of Mercenary Commander.
Combat works based on initiative stats (highest goes first), with every action building up fatigue. The combat is nice and quick and very rarely will it exceed more than 10 turns, which addresses a big problem I have with turn based games, often the tactical combat can go on forever, thankfully Battle Brothers does a great job of keeping them short and sweet. The brilliance of this game is your dudes can level up and become stronger, but they can also die (much like in X-COM). In one battle I went up against a Nachzehrer (Ghoul), in brutal combat with one of my men who did amazingly in a previous battle I quickly found his head went flying clean off, his fellow men wavered but as a unit brought the beast down, this will often be the story at least in the early game! But being bested in combat isn't always the end, as these people can survive battles and see more... However you may find they are debuffed from battles, they may suffer brain damage, they may have lost an eye making it harder for them to hit their target, these make the game exciting and constantly add a level of tension I haven't experienced since X-COM.
The overworld sees you exploring the realm and looking for fights, quests and trading, whilst buying new gear for your dudes and keeping them fed and paid. I do have criticisms of this though in that I wish there was a seed generator for this part of the game, whilst I love the core gameplay, I believe that sharing these worlds and their challenges would have been a good idea, not only that but the ability to revisit those realms would have been nice, also if the game memorized your companies that could have made for some interesting clashes, as you face off against your old companies, but that's just a thought (maybe Battle Bros 2, eh?) *wink* *wink* *nudge*. I like to think of the overworld like an Open ended version of The Banner Saga. Whilst the world design is great and shows it's (Medievil European) inspiration, I would have liked some deserts to be included with their own set of challenges.
The art style is heavily reminiscent of a board game, characters are represented by "pieces" and it really works for the game. Characters die brutally, show armour damage and represent their armours. You can even customize your dudes if you find a Barber and that is really awesome!
Overall I love Battle Brothers, I've spent years looking for my next game to surpass the influence X-COM had on me, and I genuinely believe I have found it. The game is WELL POLISHED and doesn't ever fail to entertain, a world generation tool would have been nice as well more biomes but what we've got here is an excellent package and an incredible entry title from Overhype Studios, I hope this game is supported with post launch DLC and I personally cannot wait to see what Overhype Studios choose to work on next!

Loot, mob fights, and epic boss battles look no further for a fun 8 bit dungeon crawler that will keep you entertained for hours.You start off with having 8 characters to choose from which can satisfy your play style, 2 of the characters are locked and can be unlocked by defeating certain bosses. You’re character has upgradable stats and abilities to improve their performance, along with collectable items you find throughout the levels. If your character dies you lose all your items, but your character itself levels in rank which gives it bonuses. It would seem that there is a plan for stats being able to improve your abilities as well. There are 5 dungeons in total for every difficulty. Each dungeon has 3 levels, the first 2 is where you gather items, gold, and experience from slaying enemy mobs and the 3rd one is where you face the boss! You have to activate a certain number of spawn nodes in order to proceed to the next level. You must be careful though every level has traps and super mobs, they can get the best of you regardless of how strong your character may be!
What this game is doing right so far is the gameplay and items you collect, you can have a ton of fun destroying monsters left, right, and centre  with your abilities and the items that enhance your damage. The boss battles are fun yet frustrating, you will be scratching your head how to overcome certain patterns of a bosses play style. They need to improve on certain enemy designs, some of them starting from the winter dungeon level with the purple square eye mobs seem way to simple, same with the flies in the cathedral. I found that range characters seem to have a disadvantage against certain mobs, the range character typically has low health, high damage, and above average movement speed. There are certain enemies who will rush up to you and start knocking down your health points and before you know it you’re dead, this can be frustrating when there is a lot going on when fighting enemy mobs. The traps need to have a more eye catching notification that they’ve been activated as well following under when there is a lot going on when fighting enemy mobs. melee characters have a great advantage against bosses or enemies who shoot projectiles because their basic attack can stop it.
Overall this game is a lot of fun, it certainly has kept me entertained with the progression of your character, the selection of characters, and collecting items. I haven’t defeated the final boss yet…I will soon! I definitely recommend this game to any dungeon crawler fan because it’s just in early access now and there’s a lot more to come!

I like this game. Dungeon Souls is a top-down roguelike hack 'n' slash dungeon crawler where you are attempting to delve deeper into a dungeon by finding locations on each level called "marks." There are the usual threats that come with a dungeon crawling roguelike; like traps, hangry demons and waves of skeletons. The game comes off as a mix between the Gauntlet Reboot and Rogue Legacy... so it falls somewhere around Hammerwatch which is definitely a good thing. It's all very fast paced and the combat is undoubtedly addicting, I love using the Archer and calling down an arrow storm on the bloodthirsty dungeon denizens! It also seems like it doesn't take too long to get good at the game and unlock all of the various characters as after about 2 hours in, I've already got most of them.
My only major complaints are the rather short length of the game (I'm sure more content will be added as the game is in early access) and the lack of tooltips or a tutorial that tell you all the controls and how to effectively play the game. I actually didn't find out that TAB opens a skill screen until I went into the Discussion Hub on steam. All in all, not a bad foray into a Dungeon Crawling Rogue-like.

Dungeon Souls is a top-down roguelike rogue-lite hack 'n' slash dungeon crawler. It is similar to Hammerwatch to a degree, so if you like that you will probably like this. The biggest difference between the 2 is that this is strictly single player as of the writing of this review. The game is in early access, so that might change. Generally I avoid early access due to a large amount of them being absolute garbage that will never be finished. I heard good things about this one though so I gave it a shot.
Starting out you have access to 3 characters, the melee based barbarian, the accurate archer, and the fast thief. There are 5 others, which are unlocked by beating certain enemies or finding certain items. There also looks to be more in the works, which will just add to the variety of play options. All the characters are fairly well balanced, none feel noticiably weaker or stronger than others, although they do all play different due to their skills and starting stats. The various characters have different emphasis, but none of them feel like support characters like in Hammerwatch. Please note that I like Hammerwatch a lot, am just explaining the difference. All of them have a basic attack, which is different for each character, and 2 special skills. The skills are unique to the characters as well. The thief for example can throw an AoE bomb and disappear for a couple seconds, while the archer has multi-shot for a few seconds and a devastating arrow rain. There are 4 difficulties, the higher 2 are locked until you beat the game on the previous one.
The music is decent, not bad for a dungeon crawler. But odds are your attacks, explosions, and what not are going to cover it up a lot, not to mention the almost bullet hell like nature of some of the boss fights. Sound effects are very nice. No voice acting but the game doesn't really need it either.
This game lacks in story, but it excels in REALLY FUN gameplay! The items you find from chests or in shops are random and some of them can completely change how you play. Due to items I found in one run I ended up with a tank that was near unkillable as long as I didn't try to die due to all the health regen he got. He died on a boss but until then that was an absolutely amazingly fun run. There are a ton of items that boost stats, give regen, bonus damage, statuses attacks, and other things. The dungeons are randomly generated although the way to move to the next level is set. Find and activate 2-5 large glyphs on the floor and go back to where you started that floor at to move on. Enemies are easy to identify, with them being tinted a different color if they're one of the random ones that are stronger than normal. I've only found one sprite that is overtly reused. A mage type enemy that come in 3 different colors, all of which attack completely differently. The floors are nicely done, and very atmosphereic. Dark enough to make them feel dangerous, but not so dark you can't see the things you're supposed to squish.
The game has a leveling system. Upon level up you get a stat point to put into (physical) damage, defense, magic (damage), speed, resistance, and accuracy. Most characters start with an accuracy of over 70%, 1 starts are 40%, one at 50%. If you are playing a non-melee range character you are going to get that up to 90%+ asap otherwise your attacks have the spread of a shotgun without the damage. You start the game with 1 skill point to toss into your basic attack or to unlock one of the 2 special skills of the character. You get more skill points as you level, but not every level. Both skill and stat points need to be spent wisely or you'll find yourself overwhelmed. Any money you haven't spent at the end of your run is added to the bank at character selection which can be used to buy passive global permanent upgrades for the characters. These upgrades are rather expensive but are very nice, especially for when you unlock the harder modes.
Dungeon Souls is also very easy to run. I do not have a high end PC by any means, and the game runs at a nice and steady 60FPS.
I have a few complaints about the game. First, the character unlocks seem either too quick or too easy. I unlocked 2 of the 5 locked characters on my first run by taking out basic mobs. And had them all unlocked in under 3 hours without actually trying to unlock them. Second, the game could really use a tutorial. It isn't stated anywhere to click on your skills once in a run to apply skill points. It again isn't stated anywhere that you use your potions by hitting the 1-3 keys. Or that you can bounce between special skills (which are used with the right click) by using the mouse wheel instead of Q and E.
Very good game, very fun. If you like the genre I'd say it should definitely be on your list of games to play. And early access status aside, this is a game that I would definitely buy again. I am actually looking forward to seeing the future updates for this game.

So far Hand of Fate 2 is one of my favorite games of the year, which comes as no surprise seeing as how the first game was incredibly fun as well. The combat is improved from the original, the cards and senarios are even more interesting than the original, as well as they delve more than just "you're gonna fight a boss". Yes, you do fight bosses at the end but the flavor around it is even better than the original which is surprising considering how well the original was at it.
Pros:
- Improved combat, more to do in combat senarios, combat is also more difficult.
- Even greater atmosphere than the first, including improved graphics.
- New elements of the game, including dice rolls and twitch chat interaction if you're a streamer.
- Graphical settings are fairly vast, the game also lets you rebind keys on keyboard or controller.
- Companions to accompany you that all seem to have a viarety of character.
Cons:
- Some of the music isn't fitting with the game, for example the music when you beat a final boss isn't exactly fitting to the tone in my opinion.
- Some janky animations, although improved from the original. Can affect hitboxes at times but not a huge issue.
- RNG could be considered a negative if you really dislike RNG affecting your game. If you don't like RNG in games, ie Darkest Dungeon, I'd stear away from this game. Personally, I'm fine with it.
If you enjoyed the first game, you'll definitely enjoy Hand of Fate 2. A fitting sequel.

The shooting is heavy and satisfying, permforming admirably on both gamepad and keyboard (though this IS a little sketchy without configuring it properly in the options menu). The Metroidvania aspects, though thin at first, gradually become more apparent, with secret areas and map memorisation soon becoming prevalant.
