In the game Heroes & Legends: Conquerors of Kolhar, by Cuve Games, you will be thrust into a world that is fighting against an upcoming apocalypse. You have been tasked to find an artifact of ancient power that might be able to seal off the portal to a hellish plane of existence. You will have to fight your way through hordes of monsters, and even deal with a couple of twists in the road to get to the end of the game. Will you be able to stop the evil and end of civilization, or will you be too weak, or too late to do anything.
Graphically this is a really nice looking game. I really like the character design, and I LOVE the fact that as the armor and weapons change you see a change in your character's appearance. In any given battle you will be working with 3 heroes on the left hand side of the screen. Your enemies will be on the right. There is going to be progress bars for each character/enemy to show you when they will be attacking next. By selecting a character you can see that the special abilities tab at the top of the screen will reflect the actions that that specific character can take, not only that but you will also see how many more seconds are needed to perform that ability again. Now to make things a little more hectic there is also an item bar that is going down the edge of the left hand of the screen. This shows you the items that you are currently going to receive if you get through the level. Now I will warn you this is like a conveyor belt, items might be added a different times so make sure that you keep an eye on this.
There's also the over-world map. There's no real exploring in this game, you get to see the next story area, a random encounter (I did a ton of these and tried to max out my characters), and there's also random events. All have their own icon, and all are easily distinguishable.
Now for the music in the game, it was kind of your standard middle of the road mideval fantasy music that after playing for quite some time just blends into the background. I really was hoping that there was going to be voice work in this game, but sadly all the in game dialogue is just text on the screen.
The controls are really straight forward, you are just going to have to be speedy with a mouse. You will use it to select abilities, to rearrange the items that you are going to receive, you are also going to be using it to shuffle your party while in battle.
So this was definitely a faster paced game than I had anticipated. When I first started I saw the turn base mechanics based on the character's speed, and that the enemies also worked in this fashion, but I soon learned that there's a ton of strategy that goes into this. You have the ability to shuffle your characters to different positions throughout the battle. You do this so that you can save your characters from death, because another character can do more damage, or because you need to have an ability cooldown taken care of. That's one of the more difficult things, your abilities don't refresh themselves if you do not have an enemy in front of you, so you can't just have your magic user sitting on the sidelines with no one attacking them and think that you are going to be able to regain your more powerful spells.
When you get further in the game you are going to notice that your best attack, at least mine, is to max out at least two of the characters when it comes to speed. You do this during any of the leveling up periods during the actual battle. You will be given a choice of options that have been predetermined and by clicking on one of those choices your stat for that specific stat will increase by one. I will warn you about one thing, pay attention to what the special ability stat icons are, if you want to increase efficiency you are going to want to raise those stats. Also if you have a wizard that is using a magical weapon, pilling on the melee damage stat is not going to do anything for you.
This game is filled with twists and turns, and a little bit of frustration. There are times where I wish that the game had a little bit more to do when it came to random encounters, there's only ever one on the board at a time, but I have found the way to refresh the option is to enter your inventory, or party selection screen and then exit right back out. That will also help with trying to get random events to constantly populate. Most of them will help your party, be it more resources to create your weapons and armor, improve a stat, or sometimes decrease a couple of stats, thanks to a curse. There is definitely a time in the game where you will be breaking down everything that you are earning through battles into resources. You will probably need the resources more than a couple of weapons you can't really use. Oh that does remind me though, the only time you can equip stuff is in battle, so if you think that you can just pimp out all your characters at the beginning of a battle, you are going to probably run into some issues because everything is happening at the same time, and there's a chance that killing an enemy might cause an item to populate your list, which in turn will get rid of one of the items you just made.
So I think it is clear that I really played this game a lot, I had quite a few HEAVY battles that kept me honest. I don't really know how I feel about retaining all the items that I had gain in a battle even if I lost it, but the thing that really ticked me off was the fact that at some point in the game, I'm not really sure, I have 2 of the 3 characters in my party completely armored up, but could not get the option to armor any of the other characters. It would not allow me to do so, either it was stuck on one armor, not allowing me to choose, or it was a blank screen for the armor section of the inventory screen.
Alright so lets get right to it, this is definitely a game where there's going to have to be more, if not the ending is terrible, and there was definitely a few bumps through the game, but in the end I couldn't put it down, and that's something that's hard to get me to do. So with that I have to say that this game gets a 9.2 out of 10.

Heroes & Legends: Conquerors of Kolhar is an RPG that came out of nowhere and at first glance reminded me of similar games that I’ve really enjoyed before. That’s about as far as it went though because Heroes & Legends had a bit more meat on its bones than meets the eye. It’s a mix of strategy and tactics, timing, RPG related bits like leveling and crafting, with an easy to follow and enjoyable story.
So there you are sent off by the queen on a quest to get this artifact that will end the coming cataclysm. That’s all well and good since no one really wants a cataclysm to happen anyway. Your starting party consists of an overzealous paladin named Allen, a grumpy mage named Benedict and a fighter who likes to stab things with sharp-pointed objects named Yaha. It’s a fun combination of personalities that merge well knowing the gravity of their quest. Later you meet a rogue-ish bard named Tysha whose personality was interesting, but ultimately forgettable. Lastly there’s a ranged-rogue Grenk named Jomon who joins you with guns and I like guns. I won’t tell you what’s up with him due to spoilers.
I wanted to like most of the characters, but  I had to drop Yaha due to poor DPS and Allen (even with his healing) couldn’t pull his weight. (Jeez, I sound like an elitist WoW guild.) In combat, there are time bars below your character’s health and when it fills up you (or the bad guys) attack. You also have additional special moves you can use when they are off cooldown. Even with picking mostly offensive stats when my characters leveled up, Yaha was lackluster and would have benefited from dual wielding sword-chucks (who wouldn’t be, even if they are hard to hold), but there isn’t any of that in Heroes & Legends, just a weapon in one hand and a shield in the others. Allen and his heal bomb was replaced when Benedict, Tysha and Jomon who all had a decent heal ability.
The combat was pretty interesting as well. First off you choose three of the five teammates, but then you have to pick the moves that would not only help you deal damage, but they’d have to benefit the party as well. You get a mixture of buffs, debuffs, stuns and other sorts of damage moves or evasive maneuvers. The heals were always nice to have and Tysha’s heal and damage buff was a no brainer; she needed to come along and jump into the action. You also get to move your characters around by swapping spots if you don’t want a certain person taking another hit (or getting exp for that bad guy dying). Then problem arrives when you realize that every fight is an endurance test with quite a few rounds that you had to survive in order to progress. At first what was interesting became tedious and that wasn’t even halfway through the campaign.
Combat is waiting game in Heroes & Legends. You’re either waiting for the bar to fill up or for a move to come off of cooldown. It’s neat, but not super engaging. Since you moves didn’t come off of cooldown if your character wasn’t in front of an enemy, you would sometimes hesitate on using a move since you may have to wait for longer than the cooldown actually lists. It’s a catch-22. One could say that it’s just more tactical and you have to plan accordingly, but it just didn’t really feel like that.
Crafting is where this game almost shines the most. Items drop in fights and you can equip them in mid battle. At the end of the fight you’re left with the five remaining items on the “loot bar” (good enough name right?) to either equip or recycle for parts. You can then trade up if you have too much of one lesser crafting ingredient and not enough of another that’s a single tier up (ten for one, it’s a bum deal, but one for the impatient player like myself).  What needed to happen here was to add another ingredient that would add some random status buff to the weapon. Too many times have I created a weapon only to have the same tier item drop in the next fight but with an attack buff on it. If an item your recycling has a stat bonus on it, there should be a chance to receive that back as well. The armor was the only thing that felt completely worth it. It had some combination of defense, attack, evasion or what-have-you that would usually go along with whatever playstyle you favored for that character. As a bonus, it also changed the aesthetics of the character too.
The story was well told until the end. The characters had changed and developed a bit and they even fleshed out some NPC’s. The problem is that the story is more epic in scope than is allowed here within the time frame it takes to finish the game. Heroes & Legends is set up as that epic game, but is not long enough. As such, some questions I had on why things went one way or why a character chose thus were left unanswered. The ending, while fitting, felt squished while still being complete. I knew “how” the story ended, but not completely the “why”. One of the main characters goes off on some grand plan for the aftermath of it all and how things will change and that felt like it came out of left field. I just remember reading it and thinking to myself, “Where in the crap is this line of thought coming from all of a sudden?” At the same time, they developed the story well enough that if fit the character’s profile, just not the situation and timing without much of the setup.
Score: Meh.../Gewd.
While it may have seemed like a lot of complaining, I don’t feel my time was wasted here. There were some wasted opportunities here that would have made a fairly decent difference in the enjoyment factor, but that’s not to say that it wasn’t enjoyable. I just wish the game was larger in scope. Shorten the fights and give use more of them with more of the story spread out. The writing was enjoyable up until the ending where while you can see what was said coming from who said it, it didn’t seem to fit with how you got there. There’s not much to the main campaign, but it’ll make you want to finish it. You can then replay the levels you want to level up more and max out on gear and the like after completing the campaign if you so choose. There is even a list of challenges that give you specific characters with specified move-sets that can prove quite difficult and that’s fun too. I just wanted more and like I’ve said before,

If you like Tower Defense or RPGs, this game is a must have!
The only game that is remotely comparable to Deathtrap is Sanctum2, where you can also join the battle after the building phase.
But Deathtrap has much more depth and customizations, you get loot, you can buy and craft items, you get xp and pick skills, just like a "real" rpg. And so far I have only played one of the three character classes...
Each Trap (=towers) has 5 different attributes that can be leveld up, so you have to specialize on something. Theres probably a lot of replayability, especially with the co-op multiplayer part, I havent even tried yet.
The only initial disappointment for me was, that you cannot freely place any trap anywhere. There are fixed positions on which you can place a certain class of trap, and you cannot block paths of the monsters. However, it turned out to be a very good design choice, it makes the game more fluid than this endless boring maze building that you have in almost every tower defense game.
I rarely review a game so early, but even though I've seen only a fraction of the content yet, it was already worth every cent.

I remember the day my family bought this game for me on Christmas of 2008. I also recall just how excited I was when I first played it on my xbox 360 so many years ago.
Left 4 Dead is an unique game. It is highly simplistic in its objective between each level. You grab a gun of your choice and some supplies then make a rush for the next saferoom until you make it to the end and call a way out of whatever terrible situation you are in, only to hold out for a tense few minutes until help arrives.
I picked this game back up again in 2014 on Steam and only now in the past few months have I been giving it a true go again. The fun is still there, even after all these years that have gone by. I truly believe the simplicity in this game is what keeps many returning. You don't level up and get a ton of skins or loot boxes like so many games do now a days.
The fundementals of this game are what keep me returning. The friends you play with also are a big selling factor for this game. There is just something satisfying about playing with a group of friends trying to survive on such a fast paced and action packed game.
You either like this game or you don't. Strictly speaking on a singleplayer format it can get dull fast. But when you add in buddies that is where the game shines. And that is one of the many reasons why I still play it to this day.

I really enjoy the way good strategy can mitigate the RNG but not remove it, so you'll need to react to unexpected opportunities and recover from misfortunes. Also, your little guys grow on you quite a bit as you go.
The equipment based skill system is also excellent; specialization can make a soldier a bit better but every character gets the special skills of their weapon just by equipping it. And every single weapon type has a unique use or gimmick. Even the humble dagger is incredibly useful in the hands of a skilled knife-fighter, who can stab an armored knight through the eyeslits and other weak points in his armor to attack his HP directly (and let you capture his armor after the battle). Pikes, bows, crossbows, spears, flails, all of them have a place in your line and the powers being unlocked just by equipping the item let you experiment and swap gear depending on the upcoming battle.
The art, writing, and music are good, and the sound effects add a lot of weight to combat even if there isn't much animation. You wince when you hear someone land a greataxe blow on one of your precious recruits. There's a nice sort of suddenness to the combat that emphasizes the dramatic moments when the fight turns one way or the other.
Enemy variety is good, with terrifyingly strong orcs, annoyingly cunning goblins, humans who fight like your men, undead who never tire or break morale, and savage wild animals.

I was fortunate enough to get my copy for free as a part of a contest the developers were running.  I have not yet completed the game,  so my views are based on getting midway through the 2nd stage.  It was not a condition of the contest to write a review (positive or negative), but I feel full disclosure is best for an effective review.
Ahnayro is primarily a game of riddles and finding connections, using still images and recorded audio as it's primary means of engaging the player.  It's a style that does a good job of making you study and examine all presented elements, looking for clues in a way that made me reminisce about old Agatha Christie stories.  As you are expected to actually do research and investigate via internet or even hard copy encyclopedia, it’s a good thing that the game is kept relatively low intensity in computing power.  However, what it lacks in advanced graphics it makes up for in well polished art direction and riddles that take more than just a few keywords punched into Google for a solution.
I’m giving this a thumbs up because I genuinely enjoy titles that I can play casually while chatting with friends or just as a way to relax and let my mind probe some problems that are not on a timed deadline.  And while I like the visual style so far, I hope some variations start appearing in the game’s future (video clips, objects that can be manipulated, etc.).
I recommend it to fans of the puzzle metaplot minigames from Assassin’s Creed, mystery novels, and casual games that challenge the mind more than the reflexes.

From what I have picked up so far, the story revolves around a person who is constantly plagued by terrible dreams. After using a certain technique, which I will not go into, the character is able to finally control themselves in the dream. You go through fragments of their dreams, piecing things together, and finding the relevance between each fragment, and slowly assembling the dream bit by bit. Only two sections currently exist, so they
expand more on the story later on.
"Ahnayro is a historically focused, narrative driven puzzle game exploring the world of dreams. You play as a person gifted with the ability to look beyond the veil of reality, investigating a universe that opens up to you every night; haunting you, beckoning you to solve the mysteries within.
Yet you are not in control of this world; you are at the mercy of mysterious individuals, who flow in and out of your mind. Your only hope of gaining control over this world is to piece together your fragmented visions and confront your tormentors.
As any dream, however, this new reality is structured on the waking world, and understanding one necessitates understanding the other."
Like I said, I
this game is more of an experience than your standard game. I would say that for this price, you should definitely jump at the chance of playing this. I feel that
game is worth every penny, and will continue to be for the months/years to come. I am not sure if it will be a continuing narrative like The Black Watchmen, but I

Starbound changed like a billion times during development because the devs couldn't decide on what they wanted the game to be. They made a procedural building-exploration game only to realize too late that not tying the key concepts of building and exploring together with something concrete (think Don't Starve, where you build to survive, explore to build and survive to explore further) made the game absolutely barren.
There's a billion, a trillion planets. You'll visit 20 of them at best, and forget about 18 of them. One will be your homebase (which you'll never move from, there's no advantage for building multiple bases). 2 or 3 of the same type of planet will be enough for you to gather Resource Lvl 1, upgrade and go to the next type of planet to do the exact same with Resource Lvl 2. Dungeons are literally the same - same enemies, same structure, sometimes even the same
, dude. You've seen one of each type, you've seem them all. They threw in a story that requires you to explore to try and make you actually explore a planet, because as I've said, other than seeing dungeons/towns for the first time and perhaps nabbing their stuff, nothing presses you to explore.
Ores? Weapons? Cash? They will all pretty much just fall into your hands. Open Random Wooden Box #3 and you'll find some weapon with crazy DPS. Open Iron Chest #5, 3 manipulator modules, 200 pixels, etc. Sell your junk and you'll get rich (until the next fall damage-related death). Most quests are random, given by colonists who you make homes for, because for some reason they decided that fixed characters in the Outpost with fixed sidequests was a bad idea? And the rewards for quests are simply ridiculous, being either a manipulator module, some random weapon or whatever, and if you've done enough quests, the colonist becomes a worthless crew member who gets trapped on everything and dies within being 5 minutes on the planet. You don't even need to explore for materials for the best armor in the game - you can just stumble onto random merchants that SELL one of the best sets. They're expensive, but you'll be swimming in cash most of the time.
Combat is shoddy. For some reason the game lags as if you were playing on a server all the time - your character moves normally, but monsters and blocks take a second to appear/move/attack, making hits not count a lot of the time. You'll also get ganged on a lot, then try to run and die from fall damage. Fall damage which could have been mitigated with a tech (Bouncy Ball) that they decided to pull from the game and put nothing on it's place.
The EPP is a tragedy. Get a couple of bars, craft some mcguffins and you can make an upgrade that allows you to explore some new planets without any sense of accomplishment. It eats your augments - you can't take one back and swap it for another, if you put one in over another the first one is just lost forever, no matter how rare or expensive. Why?
Scenarios and a main story were a decent idea, but executed poorly simply by lack of content and by lack of effort. There are 8 (if you count the tutorial) maps where you aren't allowed to break or place anything (can't complain about that) and follow a linear path to a boss. They're pretty, but you won't do much other than kill the odd monster and press the odd button. Puzzles could have helped a lot, but mostly the story and aventure maps fall through on simply not having enough to do. You'll save the universe and kill the Ridiculously Powerful God-Killing Evil Entity in like, 5 hours.
Moons are just lifeless gas stations, supposedly 'dangerous' because of the spooky ghost, but you'll only get killed if you stay in place. I have no clue why barren planets are in the game, and asteroids now have no valuable resources. Why they kept the gateways coded in being that after the first 20 minutes you'll have a shortcut to the outpost/ark right on your ship (and the only thing the gateways do is take you back there) is beyond me.
Still, Starbound isn't a bad game. You'll have some fun, and if you like building just for the sake of building, there are many pretty blocks and objects to use and collect. Then you'll forget about it and play it again three months later when nothing else in your library looks interesting.
As a game developer, Chucklefish is a great publisher.
TL;DR: Procedural building and exploration game where building and exploration have no connection whatsoever. Devs realized that making procedural exploration just for the sake of being procedural is a bad idea way too late and put in a story, but it's weak as hell and the game shoves everything you need in your face without having you make any effort whatsoever. Buy on AT LEAST a 75% off sale.

One Sentence Review:  It's... like a choose your own puzzle game?
"Please, Don't Touch Anything" is a strange, strange little puzzle game where... part of the puzzle is finding the puzzle.  It's unusual in that there are no real solutions, but multiple paths to discover.  So in one sense, it's like a "Choose Your Own Adventure" Game because the goal is to figure out all the endings... but finding the puzzles is the hard part!
Despite being just a single screen, there's a lot to do in this little oddity.  You have lots of cryptic clues and a big red button... and where you go from there is up to you.  There's hidden compartments, secret messages, things to unscrew and break... but what haven't you tried already?  How will you light up those other buttons?
It's a great little game and while definitely not for everyone I think anyone who likes point-and-click adventure will get their puzzle fix from this gem.

Core Gameplay:
============
For the players who have no clue what kind of game this is.
Dungeon Souls is a game you choose a character and try to get far as possible.

So the big challenge is to survive and get good in the game and upgrade your character good as possible.
Don't forget to buy items in the stores because these can help you on the way.

=======
What I find very weird about this game is that you play with mouse and keyboard.
Keyboards is for walking and using items and mouse for aiming.
This kind of games works perfectly with a controller for fast gameplay.
And just relax in the couch and play some on the big screen if possible.
Beside the controller part the game plays good with keyboard and mouse.
And controller your character feels really great.
Sounds & Graphics:
===============
The games looks as sounds like an old game.
They did a really great job with this.
The bit style graphic game play gives you the feeling you are playing an old game.
Just like old times for me '90 era of the Super Nintendo console.
Soundtrack as the small sounds are done very well.
Overall:
======
I think this one of the best Dungeon 8bit style games I played in years.
Playing this games feels very smooth and a lot of fun !!
It's haves a few classes to play with and some tactics to play this game.
I've try's a few round on easy as normal mode.
Controls really needs to get used to because there is no controller support this would be very nice if they fix this.
So you need to play this game with keyboard and mouse.
It's still a early access game when I played and made this review.
So some things will be made much better on the way they release this game.
It's a great and unique game to play and I can really recommend this game.

Pros:

Cons:
Pretty much everything bar the abovementioned points.
The game is an online co-op Action RPG that is being labeled as an 'MMO'.
Labeling a game that has no MMO features as an MMO is wrong, by both the devs and publisher.
This game is not an MMO, but a game based on the Mobile game Kritika The White Knights. Two different games, but share same features for the most part.
You never play with anyone, unless you have friends that play it and you invite them to a party.
In the quest 'hubs' you barely if ever see anyone else.
There is absolutely nothing massive about this game. It doesn't have any of the minimum requirements to be called an MMO or MMORPG.
The maps are smaller than any other game in the same genre. Even Diablo 3 have bigger maps. I'm not even sure you can call the 'maps' in this game 'maps', or just 'Paths' since they're just roads that goes from point A to point B and you can get from point A to B in a matter of seconds.
No character customization options besides costumes.
Genderlocked classes, though for this game it should be expected.
I can go on and on about the cons, but i'll leave it at that.
I tried it on the PC and played the mobile game for a while before i grew tired of it.
I can't recommend this game to anyone.

Double Fine is one of those companies that receives heaps of accolades from a stalwart handful of dedicated fans, but that those on the outside look at without the rose-tinted glasses the see the truth of the matter: Double Fine is, at best, an alright game creating company, definitely not great, probably not fine, and certainly not double fine. Stacking is the third game from this company I've played, and probably the worst of the lot. It has its charms, don't get me wrong, but they wore away quickly for me, until all that was left was a mediocre puzzle game bereft of any reason to be attached to it.
Strangely enough, the puzzle elements of this game remind me of the Hitman series, where there is a single or multiple goals in a fairlly small venue that need to be achieved through one of various means, with plently of disguises to be worn and crowds to be lost in. However, without the thrill of evading discovery or the danger of imminent death, Stacking fails to make the formula work. Without any danger and the barest of motivations, I was ready put the game away by the second area of the game, and becoming actually angry with it by the third. It is a puzzle game in the sense that it is puzzling how it is even considered a game. A definite pass.

Dungeon souls is an outstanding rogue-like action game, it reminds me so much of nuclear throne from how the game plays, except its focused more on your character's stats and abilities use.
There are about
seven characters in the game, goes from warrior, wizard, till nightblade, all are unique in their attacks and abilities.
Its a dungeon crawler each one having 3 levels and at the end is there's a boss fight, there are a LOT of pickups that improves your character, increases attackspeed, damage, defense and secret levels and more, now with the new update they can stack and can be changed.
You have 4 difficulty levels to choose from, easy, normal and the other 2 requires to be unlocked.
To finish each level you have to activate all marks across it, which is a magic circle that once you touch spawns enemies around it, once all marks activated the portal to the next level opens which is located at the beginning of the level.

Reason why I mentioned this is because there are some players who really dislikes having timed levels,
Each character has 2 unique spells that you can upgrade as you level up, making them stronger, you can also choose to use the skill point to upgrade your base attack power and each level up you get an extra +Stat to increase your str, speed, def... etc.
You get 3 slots to carry potions in and enemies drops a lot of them. Also you can carry only one active spell item that you might find.
Characters have ranks, once you achieve the highest one the character becomes different in appearance, name and becomes stronger.
Also you get to keep some gold with you after you die, which you can use to increase your character's passive's for the next run, you can increase hp, attack, and now you can use it also to craft weapons.

Everything from their weapons, armor, background, stats, perks, and traits comes into play. You also have to keep them fed, provide meds for healing, tools for repair, etc.

You can work for them via contracts, and even join in on full scale wars later in the game. There's also neutral towns too, and you build up relations with all the leaders on the map. If steam had a "neutral" option for recommending, I'd go for that.
Starbound changed like a billion times during development because the devs couldn't decide on what they wanted the game to be. They made a procedural building-exploration game only to realize too late that not tying the key concepts of building and exploring together with something concrete (think Don't Starve, where you build to survive, explore to build and survive to explore further) made the game absolutely barren.
There's a billion, a trillion planets. You'll visit 20 of them at best, and forget about 18 of them. One will be your homebase (which you'll never move from, there's no advantage for building multiple bases). 2 or 3 of the same type of planet will be enough for you to gather Resource Lvl 1, upgrade and go to the next type of planet to do the exact same with Resource Lvl 2. Dungeons are literally the same - same enemies, same structure, sometimes even the same
, dude. You've seen one of each type, you've seem them all. They threw in a story that requires you to explore to try and make you actually explore a planet, because as I've said, other than seeing dungeons/towns for the first time and perhaps nabbing their stuff, nothing presses you to explore.
Ores? Weapons? Cash? They will all pretty much just fall into your hands. Open Random Wooden Box #3 and you'll find some weapon with crazy DPS. Open Iron Chest #5, 3 manipulator modules, 200 pixels, etc. Sell your junk and you'll get rich (until the next fall damage-related death). Most quests are random, given by colonists who you make homes for, because for some reason they decided that fixed characters in the Outpost with fixed sidequests was a bad idea? And the rewards for quests are simply ridiculous, being either a manipulator module, some random weapon or whatever, and if you've done enough quests, the colonist becomes a worthless crew member who gets trapped on everything and dies within being 5 minutes on the planet. You don't even need to explore for materials for the best armor in the game - you can just stumble onto random merchants that SELL one of the best sets. They're expensive, but you'll be swimming in cash most of the time.
Combat is shoddy. For some reason the game lags as if you were playing on a server all the time - your character moves normally, but monsters and blocks take a second to appear/move/attack, making hits not count a lot of the time. You'll also get ganged on a lot, then try to run and die from fall damage. Fall damage which could have been mitigated with a tech (Bouncy Ball) that they decided to pull from the game and put nothing on it's place.
The EPP is a tragedy. Get a couple of bars, craft some mcguffins and you can make an upgrade that allows you to explore some new planets without any sense of accomplishment. It eats your augments - you can't take one back and swap it for another, if you put one in over another the first one is just lost forever, no matter how rare or expensive. Why?
Scenarios and a main story were a decent idea, but executed poorly simply by lack of content and by lack of effort. There are 8 (if you count the tutorial) maps where you aren't allowed to break or place anything (can't complain about that) and follow a linear path to a boss. They're pretty, but you won't do much other than kill the odd monster and press the odd button. Puzzles could have helped a lot, but mostly the story and aventure maps fall through on simply not having enough to do. You'll save the universe and kill the Ridiculously Powerful God-Killing Evil Entity in like, 5 hours.
Moons are just lifeless gas stations, supposedly 'dangerous' because of the spooky ghost, but you'll only get killed if you stay in place. I have no clue why barren planets are in the game, and asteroids now have no valuable resources. Why they kept the gateways coded in being that after the first 20 minutes you'll have a shortcut to the outpost/ark right on your ship (and the only thing the gateways do is take you back there) is beyond me.
Still, Starbound isn't a bad game. You'll have some fun, and if you like building just for the sake of building, there are many pretty blocks and objects to use and collect. Then you'll forget about it and play it again three months later when nothing else in your library looks interesting.
As a game developer, Chucklefish is a great publisher.
TL;DR: Procedural building and exploration game where building and exploration have no connection whatsoever. Devs realized that making procedural exploration just for the sake of being procedural is a bad idea way too late and put in a story, but it's weak as hell and the game shoves everything you need in your face without having you make any effort whatsoever. Buy on AT LEAST a 75% off sale.

Battle Brothers is a non forgiving tactical rpg-ish game that places the player in the position of leading a group of mercenaries.
Your first act as leader will be to name your band.
The second will be to participate in a scripted battle, where your former band is decimated to the last 3 men.
The third will be to seek revenge on the man that set up a trap for you and the lost souls.
From there and with those 3 companions - if they're still alive at that point - you will seek to rebuild what was lost.
Which means: gather gold and fame through fulfilling contracts available in your local towns and settlements.
Contracts provided by Mayors, Councillors and the most noble of the Houses...
Everything I detailed (other than the name you gave your company) is procedurally generated.
The towns, the people, the contracts, the 3 companions that you start with.
The worldset feels a lot like GoT with greedy men fighting and killing to get booze, fame and the like. While the land is inhabited by other things...
Where procedural games feel usually lifeless, here the devs managed to do something that breaths life (it still procedural, it has its limitations).
All the contracts you get are tied to ingame events that really take place; every win, every loose will push forward or backward entities (bandit groups, settlements, other mercenary bands, bounty hunters etc.).
Although there is no city expansion nor conquest. Still camps of bandits and nests of goblins will appear on the map as they thrive.
Be wary though, as towns can get destroyed. Which usually come after spending numerous hours playing to the point where dark events take place.
You can ignore those events and enjoy your daily routines, or take part in them and have an influence in their unfolding.
That's one of the many beauties of the game: play the way you want where every interference is skippable and nothing can stop you and your band other than death and misfortune.
Although there are two storyline ''arcs'' that you can complete, you can still keep playing after they are concluded (or not).
There is no experience nor level limitation onto your men, they can increase their skills as mush as you want. Past a certain level, they will not be able to pick perks but they will still be able to increase their skill (ranged, melee, HP, resolve etc.).
There are a tons of different backgrounds and a number of different traits that will help characterize the men that will seek your employ.
They come from different professions: fishers, farmers, hedge knights, brawlers etc.
Those background professions do have an impact on your band and its activities, but also in special events that will occur.
Some of them, other than their starting skills, will be more or less proficient at improving specific skills.
Basically, each time a merc level up, he can increase 3 of his skills once.
If one man has two stars (**) in melee, it means that he will get a good dice to increase that skill.
Because every increase of a skill is RNG. It isn't for the player to decide how much he wants to invest in a skill. The game generate a number, usually between 1 and 5.
Note that this amount is fixed. It isn't possible to save and  to reload to get better income: each time one merc levels up, the game lets the player know how much it is possible to increase that skill.
Let say you want to increase one of your men prowess in melee skill. But at the time of his level up, he got a bad dice of only +1.
Then, maybe, you'll decide to revisit your priorities and instead increase his melee defense, which got a solid +4.
The game oddities will sometimes make you deflect from your plannifications for better outcomes.
Picking men that are naturally proficient in learning one or another skill is critical for the higher levels and will help you to stay on track with your priorities.
Last words: the game does great what it does, but it does not try to do anything else.
This isn't a sandbox game where you have diverse things to do.
You are running a mecernary company: Pick up contracts, hire new recruits, buy provisions and weapons, sell the spoil of battle, decide for some goals for your company and ''manage'' relations with settlements and noble families through completing contracts.
Other than that... There is no buildings, no expanding your little company into different activities and groups, no crafting.
Just lead and make the right decisions.

Dungeon Souls is a top-down rogue-like dungeon crawler that draws inspiration from titles like Nuclear Throne, but ramps up the difficulty to an intense degree. I think this is best exemplified by their Hero Select screen, where you get to choose from three fallen heroes. You’re already dead at character select. That’s how tough this is, and they’re not trying hide that fact with anything more than a cute pixelated throwback to games of yesteryear.
There are three heroes to choose from, initially, each with their own unique skills that lend towards different playstyles. You have the Barbarian, for those that enjoy rushing into things head first, cleaving your way through baddies in a blood frenzied rage. Then, you have the Archer, who takes a more cautious approach by raining down arrows on their enemies from afar. Lastly, you have the Thief, for those of you more prone to sneaking around to find best position before you put a knife or bomb in just the right place. There are also five other heroes to be unlocked on your journey, but those are up to you to find.
Regardless of which hero you pick, this game takes a bit of caution and strategy as you wade through procedurally generated dungeons filled with waves of respawning baddies. Your goal in each dungeon is to collect as much loot, equipment and experience to level up enough to ready yourself for the next dungeon. As you level, you can custom tailor your character by spending points in attributes, and between your three skills. This allows a lot of unique builds that you have to take into consideration as you come to face greater foes in each dungeon.
In order to advance from one dungeon to the next, you have to active several glyphs which summon monsters all around you. Once all the glyphs are activated, you open a gate to the next dungeon, repeating the process until you reach the boss. These fights are where the game starts to feel like as skilled as you may be, you need a little bit of luck on your side as well. As you progress through each dungeon, you’ll get random drops from defeated foes, which can be something as simple as a medicinal herb, to something as powerful as a spiked, magically enchanted suit of armor. It’s all luck of the draw, and I didn’t feel too lucky as I progressed.
This game isn’t just difficult, it’s brutal, and most of it seems intentional. As you clear sectors of a dungeon, enemies respawn in your wake, which can leave you wondering if you should move on, or stick around and grind for more experience. This choice is made for you if you activate all the glyphs, which summons an undefeatable guardian that will sap your life from you until you move through the gate. This mechanic left me wondering what the developers had intended for their players to do, since they left open the possibility to grind, while ushering you out quickly once you’ve completed the level.
While this game did hold me at bay with it’s difficulty, I rarely felt punished, as if it were unavoidable. I just kept hacking away, learning the timings of the different enemies and adjusting my builds to suit my needs and playstyle. The mechanics were solid, leaving me with no complaints about hitboxes, animations or bugs, but there was a certain gameplay element that was incredibly irritating. Hallways. Time and time again, I was forced to walk through a long corridor taking countless hits from off-screen enemies that could see me across the entirety of the map. I can see why this happens, with the levels being procedurally generated and all, but I did feel cheated out of a few good runs because of it.
The only other complaint I had was the music, which was a single, atmospheric song that repeated through each dungeon I encountered. It is still the beta, though, and this could change, along with many other aspects of the game. All and all, I think that Dungeon Souls is another solid game that’s helping breathe life into the rogue-like genre. It’s still a little rough around the edges, but with a little polishing, this could be quite the gem.

If players can overlook the engine's quirks and dated visuals (part of the charm, imo), the moody and at times very unsettling tones allow one to easily lose his/herself in the game world. Those looking for a challenge will be sorely disappointed as even the "expert" level AI is downright moronic--and laughably so. Understandly, newcomers might be skeptical about older entries in the series after having played 2014's
--a flop of extremely linear proportions and objectively the most stripped-down of the Thief titles (though make sure to play Thief 4's side quests).
Enter the unofficial
patch coupled with the
mod, both of which are essential installations which catapult this stealth gem to new heights. With a few simple tweaks, Garrett's once haphazard and risk-free pickpocketing sprees will further require careful timing (as is expected from a master thief), and the City Watch will surely spot his beady lil' eye in the dark before the player can shout "Azkaban".
Prefer the classic Thief HUD? Modders got you covered. Completionists with a taste for the masochistic will rejoice as there are options to hide loot indicators -- or "sparkles" which compell the player to carefully rummage through the environment for valuable cups and coinpurses. And if these other tweaks aren't challenging enough, enable
patch's most punishing AI detection tweaks, roll the game on expert and prepare to be caught and hanged.

offers a special something for horror fans as well. In a notable chapter toward the end of the game, Garrett will encounter a rather unexpected change in pace and atmosphere as he steps from the shadows into true darkness, the legendary
--a long-abandoned asylum who's walls are coated in a thick, slow-brooding tension inspired by Silent Hill 2. The
experience is a deeply unsettling and expertly-paced audio/visual masterpiece who's influence has carried into modern jump-scare heavyweights, notably
.
From the perspective of someone who's childhood was largely made up of peanut butter sandwiches with a side of Thief 1 and 2,
in its patched form is arguably the best and most well-rounded entry in the series and it is now more accessible than it was at the time of its initial release.

This review will be amended as I play through the game. If you strongly disagree with any material in the review, please leave a comment on my profile and we can discuss it further.
The first thing you notice about Thief: Deadly Shadows are the load screens. These are understandable, given the higher level of graphical detail in this installment and being a home console release, but they are a bit disorienting compared to the much quicker load times of the previous installments. What's more noticeable are the various gameplay and story text blurbs included on these screens. For a series which previously established a noticeable lack of handholding the player, being reminded that you can knock enemies out with the blackjack is insulting.
But once you arrive at the title screen the problems really begin to pile up. There's no option to view the intro this time around, instead forcing players to idle at the title screen for a short time before the intro starts (more on it later). The carefully designed pre-rendered mechanical background has also been abandoned for a 3D Thief logo rotating Deus Ex-style against a 2D background. The background depicting the City lit up at night during a thunderstorm is also questionable. If I had to guess I'd say that the setting or story of Thief: Deadly Shadows is more nature-oriented, maybe revisiting the Pagans or some impending conflict judging by the storm.
The intro is noticeably lazier this time around, recycling a large amount of story art from the previous two games, as well as failing to provide any art that's relevant to the story in Deadly Shadows. The motion capture used during the action scene looks noticeably worse than what was seen in previous games, and the cheesy loot-collection jingle used during a cinematic made me roll my eyes.
In the options screen the ways in which Thief: Deadly Shadows restricts freedom for the players rears its head. There's no rope arrow, and the default binds for the various arrow types are different than the defaults for the previous two games. Forward leaning, an important part of collecting loot, is removed entirely, and the option to move forward slowly is gone as well. A button to toggle between a first and third person view exists as well, just so you know how much this game panders to a console audience.
The briefing screen has undergone a number of changes from it's previous iteration. Players can now perfom tasks while listening to the brief at the same time. This isn't really much of an improvement, since in the previous games briefings could simply be skipped with a button press. The briefings run for longer than in previous games and without the snappy editing and accompanying art they can be quiet boring to listen to on their own. There's no equipment to buy, and players are already told the explicit limit of what they can carry rather than just a large black box to group things in. An extra difficulty option has been added, and players can manipulate various difficulty factors such as AI behaviors.
From the first moments of gameplay is when Thief: Deadly Shadows makes some of its strongest impressions on the player. Since it's a sequel running on a new engine the first moments of the game will have to work hard to offset whatever difficulties people have to adjusting to the new engine. Deadly Shadows manages to accomplish this poorly, by asking the player to walk, showing motion that feels extremely restrictive. You can even switch to 3rd person to see how ridiculous Garret's walking animation is.
The tutorial level is a joke, plain and simple. The amount of handholding and bottlenecking the game does to introduce things to the player is a complete departure from how the series has operated before. Placing the player into situations devoid of tension do little to actually teach them about real gameplay.

I'm currently partway through the game, but I've played long enough to get an idea of what the game is like.
So here's the deal. This game is not perfect, it's nowhere near polished, and it has a score of problems. The visual style for the characters and creatures is often jarringly inconsistent, combat and gameplay are super imbalanced in the early game and it takes about an hour to really hit its stride (until then, there's this really wild swing from dull to way too hard to so easy it hurts). Level design in the early game is also terrible, though it gets way better as it goes on. Some parts of the game feel a bit unfinished, and certain parts of the tileset are just weird (certain bushes being set as above the characters, for one.) Spelling and grammar is often terrible, and the writing leaves much to be desired.
But, see, the single most important thing in a game is that it is ENJOYABLE TO PLAY, and that is one thing this game has in spades. For all its problems, I've never once been bored, and I'm still playing and intend on finishing it, which is more than I can say for a LOT of RPG maker games. The story is cute, the characters are fun, and the aesthetic, though a bit inconsistent at times, is overall colorful, imaginative, and delightfully sparkly. Also, there is this one absolutely ridiculous minigame involving cows that had me laughing out loud, and it was so much more fun than it had a right to be.
So, technically speaking, is this a well-made game? Far from it. It's unpolished and mediocre at best. And sometimes, when you're playing it, you think to yourself, man what were they thinking when they put this bit together. And there are some real 'wtf seriously' moments. But am I going to recommend you play it? Yes, yes, a thousand times yes. I can't NOT recommend it, not when every single play session has left me happy and contented with a big, goofy grin on my face. This is not a well made game. In fact, this is a pretty poorly made game. This thing is not winning any awards for quality. But it IS a thoroughly enjoyable game, and one you will not regret playing.

This game is all about realistic turn based medieval combat, set in a low fantasy world. You're the commander of a mercenary company, and have to manage your troops down to the individual man. You can work for them via contracts, and even join in on full scale wars later in the game. There's also neutral towns too, and you build up relations with all the leaders on the map. Your company also builds its' own reputation. Not to mention you can now go full rogue and raid anything you please! There's also trading, escorting caravans, and invasions from orcs or undead to deal with.
Get this game. It's absolutely stellar, not to mention rather difficult.

Battle Brothers is a non forgiving tactical rpg-ish game that places the player in the position of leading a group of mercenaries.
Your first act as leader will be to name your band.
The second will be to participate in a scripted battle, where your former band is decimated to the last 3 men.
The third will be to seek revenge on the man that set up a trap for you and the lost souls.
From there and with those 3 companions - if they're still alive at that point - you will seek to rebuild what was lost.
Which means: gather gold and fame through fulfilling contracts available in your local towns and settlements.
Contracts provided by Mayors, Councillors and the most noble of the Houses...
Everything I detailed (other than the name you gave your company) is procedurally generated.
The towns, the people, the contracts, the 3 companions that you start with.
The worldset feels a lot like GoT with greedy men fighting and killing to get booze, fame and the like. While the land is inhabited by other things...
Where procedural games feel usually lifeless, here the devs managed to do something that breaths life (it still procedural, it has its limitations).
All the contracts you get are tied to ingame events that really take place; every win, every loose will push forward or backward entities (bandit groups, settlements, other mercenary bands, bounty hunters etc.).
Although there is no city expansion nor conquest. Still camps of bandits and nests of goblins will appear on the map as they thrive.
Be wary though, as towns can get destroyed. Which usually come after spending numerous hours playing to the point where dark events take place.
You can ignore those events and enjoy your daily routines, or take part in them and have an influence in their unfolding.
That's one of the many beauties of the game: play the way you want where every interference is skippable and nothing can stop you and your band other than death and misfortune.
Although there are two storyline ''arcs'' that you can complete, you can still keep playing after they are concluded (or not).
There is no experience nor level limitation onto your men, they can increase their skills as mush as you want. Past a certain level, they will not be able to pick perks but they will still be able to increase their skill (ranged, melee, HP, resolve etc.).
There are a tons of different backgrounds and a number of different traits that will help characterize the men that will seek your employ.
They come from different professions: fishers, farmers, hedge knights, brawlers etc.
Those background professions do have an impact on your band and its activities, but also in special events that will occur.
Some of them, other than their starting skills, will be more or less proficient at improving specific skills.
Basically, each time a merc level up, he can increase 3 of his skills once.
If one man has two stars (**) in melee, it means that he will get a good dice to increase that skill.
Because every increase of a skill is RNG. It isn't for the player to decide how much he wants to invest in a skill. The game generate a number, usually between 1 and 5.
Note that this amount is fixed. It isn't possible to save and  to reload to get better income: each time one merc levels up, the game lets the player know how much it is possible to increase that skill.
Let say you want to increase one of your men prowess in melee skill. But at the time of his level up, he got a bad dice of only +1.
Then, maybe, you'll decide to revisit your priorities and instead increase his melee defense, which got a solid +4.
The game oddities will sometimes make you deflect from your plannifications for better outcomes.
Picking men that are naturally proficient in learning one or another skill is critical for the higher levels and will help you to stay on track with your priorities.
Last words: the game does great what it does, but it does not try to do anything else.
This isn't a sandbox game where you have diverse things to do.
You are running a mecernary company: Pick up contracts, hire new recruits, buy provisions and weapons, sell the spoil of battle, decide for some goals for your company and ''manage'' relations with settlements and noble families through completing contracts.
Other than that... There is no buildings, no expanding your little company into different activities and groups, no crafting.
Just lead and make the right decisions.

Battle Brothers is a game about raising a fledgling mercenary troop from clubs and pitchforks to a world renown company of fighters shod in shining plate mail.  You will spend the game scrambling from mission to mission to keep ahead of your operating expenses and scrape enough together to perhaps upgrade your equipment or hire new men.
The design for the overworld map is lifted directly from Mount & Blade, down to the NPC armies, travelling caravans, bandits, and all the various sizes footprints that describe how long ago they passed by.  Actually most of the game concepts are lifted directly from Mount & Blade, including the premise of the game.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing since the "meat" of the game, that being the combat, is entirely different.  Rather than action, Battle Brothers is turn based tactical.  Success depends on knowing how to arrange your men, with shield bearers protecting archers or pikemen.  Surround the enemy, use axes to break through shield walls, and watch your flanks!
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the experience of building up your fighters gradually through success in combat.

An amazingly well thought out puzzle game from Double Fine.  You play as a child Russian Matryoshka doll that has the ability to jump into other dolls slightly larger in size and control them.  Each doll has a different ability which is then used to solve different puzzles in the level.  You can keep stacking into larger dolls as you move up in size.  This allows you to accumulate abilities and to move different dolls around the stage that they might not have been able to get to normally.  This game mechanic is just executed perfectly.  There are so many different ways to play and solve puzzles that its sort of like Scribblenauts.  The game contains around 5 levels which should leave you with many hours of playtime to solve everything.  It's a definite recommend from me.

Whenever I see a game these days with the name ‘Souls’ in it I get a little bit anxious. A lot of games try to emulate the vibe and/or difficulty of the Dark/Demon Souls games (hence the ‘Souls’ part in the title). As you can judge by the screenshots the vibe isn’t what Dungeon Souls is aiming for, but is it tough-as-nails then? Or is it something else entirely and have I completely misjudged it by looking at its name alone?
I can happily tell you that - while there are some similarities, like pretty much every game – Dungeon Souls is nothing like the Souls series from From Software. Oh, it *is* hard, mind you, so I guess I was right about that, though. No, if I had to compare it to a different game, then I would sooner compare it to The Binding Of Isaac or Risk Of Rain. That is correct; we have a roguelike game on our hands here.
Most likely you will just start off running around the moment you spawn (there are several classes to choose from, by the way), hoping and praying that you know what you’re doing, but it probably won’t take long before your first official death. The game can get a bit hectic too soon and if you don’t exactly know what to do yet, or what effects an item will have on you (you usually don’t have enough time to stand still and properly read the descriptions) then you have basically already lost your first game. And then you retry again – because it’s a roguelike – and try to do better this time. And you will probably succeed in doing this, because you start to learn more about the world, the enemies and the items each and every time you play.
But every now and then, when things seem to go so well, the game intentionally decides to ruin one of your games by unleashing a trap on you when you’re in a small room with tons of enemies around. Sigh…
Ultimately the goal is to activate all of the marks in a level to open up the portal that will transport you to the next level. Activating a mark will always spawn a group of enemies, so you better be prepared and clear the room before you activate it. Killing enemies will level up your character, which allows you to unlock (a) skill(s). Enemies will become tougher, too, of course, so it balances out nicely eventually. Most of the time. But your enemies can still hit hard unfortunately and your health bar can be drained in a matter of seconds if you’re not careful enough, or if the game just thinks it’s time for you to die. It’s definitely challenging and without a doubt can be considered hard. Maybe even *too* hard. Thankfully this is still in an Early Access state so the difficulty can still be fine-tuned before the final release, but if you’re looking for a casual experience you better continue your search for now.
There are apparently 4 different environments and every few levels (if I’m not mistaken: 3) you will face a boss. Each level can take up to 5-10  minutes to complete usually, but time is of the essence: once all marks have been activated a timer will countdown and if it hits zero a ‘redeemer’ will appear who will chase you down and drain your health until you’re either dead or have proceeded through the portal. This feature was also available in Risk Of Rain and I didn’t really like it there either. There’s no need for rushing people through the game. Let people take their time and find out what can still be found and done here and there before they decide to finally move on to the next area. You want people to appreciate the work you put into the graphics and lore, don’t you? Well…, maybe you don’t. In any case, there are other ways to increase the difficulty.
Items you find during your quest to victory are random each time you play and you might not know about the effects of a specific item until you have actually used it. The results can be either helpful or critical/deathly but one thing is certain: it adds to the tense atmosphere. Will you risk using an item early on and hope it will make your life easier for maybe just a few minutes or will you save it for a different occasion, but risk that you might die before you’ll be able to use it? The risk/reward mechanic is generally speaking a good and fun feature to have, as long as it’s been implemented well. In this case it has been, sort of, but there’s always room for improvement. Especially considering the current difficulty. Because of it there absolutely needs to be some tweaking.
Not much to say about the sounds effects (nothing bad, at least) but the game only seems to have one, constantly repeated, track right now. That’s very limited and bound to annoy some people after a while.
Onto the graphics: the graphics are vibrant and reasonably detailed. Everything is also nicely animated. There were a few occasions where I couldn’t make out certain objects, though, but fortunately these moments were very rare. Because of the pixelated graphics things can also get a little hectic whenever there’s happening too much on screen. Pixelated graphics aren’t the best choice in situations like this. However, I can understand the reason why it was chosen, since it can be cost-effective. Other than that it all looks just fine, really. No (further) complaints here.
Depending on your skills and luck you could possibly blast through this game in 5-10 hours time. But then you would have to know exactly what you were doing. Most of us won’t be that lucky or smart so let’s say it would take about 5--20 hours before you finished your first game. Since the current price is €10 I’d say that’s more than fair. You can even try it again after that since there are multiple characters to choose from. Plus, the final release will have even more content. Plenty of content to be found here if you’re a roguelike-aficionado.
It’s still a work in progress and it needs more content and tweaking as we speak, but so far it shows promise. It doesn’t really introduce anything new, but I guess that’s to be expected with games in this genre. So if you don’t mind any of that go give it a try or at least add it to your watch- or wishlist.

After playing Finding Hope I was glad to see there was another game made by the same developer, so I played them one after the other. Beyond Magic has a lot of similarities to Finding Hope. Similar items and a lot of enemies have been carried over (I have a liking for games where you beat the crap out of cute things). There are a few of the same characters but the main protagonists and story have major differences. Game play is also pretty much the same, with the "If you follow the path you'll never get lost" and battles having the same mechanics. None of this is a bad thing because it all worked well in Finding Hope and I think it has been even more refined in this game. A small, but one of my favorite, differences is that your party follows you around while you travel the over world.
The story is funnier than Finding Hope but has a lot of similarities. It even takes a strike at it's story making fun of it towards the end. Damien's hair curse on Ace is hilarious! My main complaint story wise is the use of unoriginal fairy tale characters for people your interact with throughout the game. Rapunzel, Sleeping Beauty, and Snow White. Yes, it works with the game fine but I'd like to see some original characters to make this nice world feel more fresh.
I enjoy the art style. It is definitely a step up from Finding Hope and looks more refined. It reminds me of classic anime mixed with old school animated kid's movies.
The music is awesome. Aboslutely love it.
I do have few complaints. Just like in Finding Hope, the white text is hard to read when placed over art work and the characters during battle. There are also a couple spelling and grammar errors but they do not get in the way of the story at all. As for game play issues, I've been blocked by small things that shouldn't be in my way and not being able to pass the tops of palm trees but being able to walk through the middle of them. I have also almost gotten stuck under the platforms on the way to Rumpelstiltskin. This isn't really a problem but Rain is always cycling her walking animation even while standing still.
I greatly enjoyed this game and cant wait for Beyond Magic 2. Keep it up!

Double Fine do another brilliant game. Original and with it's own unique style, Stacking is a puzzle style game that uses Russian dolls as it's conduit to adventure. You play as a smaller than average (actually the smallest Russian doll in the game) Charlie, who is hunting down his family members who have been kidnapped by a mysterious group under the control of a man called Baron. Utilising his unique size he is able to go inside (literally) other Russian dolls to controll them and use their unique abilities to progress through the game. Unlike a lot of puzzle games, you are heavily rewarded for finding all the alternative ways of completing a puzzle, giving Stacking more play time then you would from a standard puzzle style game. The thing that I like the most about this game is the combination of unique game play and visuals that really get you hooked and encourage you to try out all the possible scenarios to complete the same objective, rather than creating an air of monotony or repetition. I would reccomend this game to anyone who wants something that is short, sweet and a breath of fresh air.

Put on your thief cap and play as Garret the master thief as you slowly...very slowly traverse through a stygian world and come to realise that this game is more than it surfaces to be.

Regardless of how you look at it, it's a slow paced game. To combat this the devs needed to inject it with diversity. At times the lack of fleshed out design imposes restrictions on player choice. Some levels are too linear though some have multiple ways around and multiple ways to tackle chokepoints. At your disposal you have a blackjack for knocking out enemies and diverse range of arrows (fire, water, noise, broadhead, moss etc) and other paraphernalia from holy water to mines. (Additional melee combat exists but it's fittingly pointless). I can't say how the game changes on the hardest difficulty. Maybe it requires you to get all the loot or maybe it makes loot more scarce so more importance is placed on player choice and sacrifice regarding item purchases. I'd prefer the latter.
The game lets you leave trails of cadavers but ideally you would just sneak past everyone for obvious reasons. The types of cadavers... well the devs weren't exactly liberal with enemy variety. Most react the same when you hint at your presence but later in the game they get a bit more anomalous and ergo stealth becomes more tense. Stealth is implemented well. It doesn't solely focus on realism as that would detract from the fun factor.
The cutscenes are flawlessly done which help spur you on through the intriguing story. The old fashioned art style in these cutscenes along with the inflated, overlapping and echoing sound also really help accentuate the fact that this game will indeed be an unsettling experience.
Though you can't talk unsettling without mentioning the Shalebridge Cradle. Not even nepenthes could calm the soul from what this level has to offer. Hope leaves and grief sets in and grows as you progress through the level. Dark paranoia consumes you via a richly constructed soundscape and haunting scenery. To this day the only game that I've found that competes at inundating you with complete foreboding ambience is the Ocean House Hotel (V:TM-B). Morbid curiosity poked me through to the end of both these levels and left me exhausted, relieved but also fascinated on how both areas exceed 99% of dedicated horror games. Maybe that percentage can be lowered with the highly anticipated collaboration between Kojima and Guillermoh♥♥♥♥youkonami...

It was little over a month since the Sons of Valor cheated death at the hands of Hoggart the Weasel's measly band of scoundrels, our company was on its way to scour a nest of Goblins that had been harrying the nearby fort of Schwertfeste at the behest of House Thurah.  After a harrowing encounter with a pack of wolf riders we came upon a far more taciturn sight: A procession of children, declaring themselves on a holy quest to spread the word of the Old Gods.
Now I was a leader of a band of cutthroats out to shed blood for coin, but I would be damned if I allowed a bunch of filthy brats to march out to their ends with greenskins about, so I looked to my Sergeant, an ex-holy man I knew as Bernhard The Preacher to set them straight.  I'd expected a beating and a chiding from the old battleaxe but to my surprise he knelt down and calmly explained to the children that they were not chosen to crusade for the Gods, but to be their messangers.  After all, here were we, a band of warriors set to protect the land from the iniquities that beset it (for a modest fee of crowns, hem hem) standing before them with our blades still fresh in the blood of Goblins that would have gladly stolen the tykes away to try their vile poisons on.  The children, happy with their new role as messengers of the Gods, gladly returned to Schwertfeste while we continued on.
When the battle was joined, Bernhard fought like a madman, slashing and decapitating whatever foul monster stood in his way until all that was left was a single archer that had harried us like mad through the entire battle.  Knocked senseless by our axeman, the goblin could only look with terror into the eyes of this holy warrior of the Gods as one slash with a falx he'd claimed from a run-in with the ancient imperial dead cleaved its head from its shoulders.
On that day Bernhard was a preacher no longer, baptized in the blood of the greenskisns, he became a that I would gladly call my Brother:
Bernhard The Paladin.

But there

Currently, one can rebind keyboard keys for instance, but solely from the Unity menu outside of the game and tutorial prompts don't reflect the change in-game. Animation is awkward and can be buggy. The greatest problem is the flavour text found in dialogues and journal. It's badly translated. Yeah, one can determine "what the poet wanted to say", but pacing of the text, syntax, idioms, metaphores - they all seem off. The text in game is not "All your bases" bad, but it's not well translated text either and young aspiring indie devs should maybe set higher standards. Stacking is the best game about mind control, child labor and Russian Nesting Dolls you will ever be able to find.
In it you play as Charlie, the youngest and littlest child of a family of chimney sweeps. Your family is kidnapped, so you head out to find them, possessing other dolls and using their abilities to solve puzzles and proceed. The storyline is a classic naturally, but it's the premise of the game that really stands out, and Stacking has a lot of fun with its premise. You have a lot of abilities to choose from, accessed by literally jumping into another character's hollow body, and the solutions to the puzzles are clever and entertaining. While the humor of the game sometimes swings towards the puerile, there's a little something for everyone.
There's limited voice-acting in the game- cutscenes are done in a 'silent movie' type style, complete with rolling projector film. The art is bright and distinct, and like the gameplay, toys with its character model's limitations. The characters move like you'd expect a Russian nesting doll to move, if that's something you've given much thought or worry towards.
This is a great game for achievement hunters as well- the achievements are tied into completing each level to 100%, and are sensible and fun to finish.

The main problem of the game is simple and easy to explain: UI. All the big problems with it stem from that one single feature.
The UI manages to tell you absolutely nothing, basic mechanics are never explained, stats have vague "this is what it does" statements while at other points the UI actively hurts the game. For a game that is about RNG management not to properly give enough informations about what something does is a sin against the genre itself. However, while it doesn't give enough information, it somehow manages to give too much. While it's not telling you one thing, the important information, it's telling you a long, wordy, fluff story that doesn't say anything about anything.
On the world map, you move from town to town and, in order to go into town, you'd think to click on the town or the flag or the name of the town, and you'd be right, but not really. Sometimes in order to open the town menu, you click on the flag, other times, you click on the buildings, and other times, you click on the nameplate. There is no definitive "click here" button.
However, the more problematic issue with the UI has to do with the art style and terrain height. Depending on the angle and differences in terrain height, you might not be able to see your units on the battle map. The hex and where to click to move there, can sometimes be UNDER another hex, making it tedius to find the right place to click.
Additionally, on the battle map, the unit roster for humans enemies and your troops is too similar. There is very little difference in the model for bandits and your actual troops. The "base" of the sprite is slightly different, but you'll be fighting enemies that look almost completely identical to you (and I've made some errors because of it). This also works incredibly poorly in combination with the aforementioned "height" problem, where your enitre unit model can disappear and almost becomes an invisible unit, but even the wrong angle can hide the "base" of the sprite, which is the main way to tell which is which. Luckilly, this problem goes away when you face the undead or orcs, as their sprites are suffeciently different enough to easily differentiate between your units and the enemy's.
The core game is basically Mount and Blade meets Darkest Dungeon. That sounds great, but as I play more, I find myself simply wanting to go play either Mount and Blade or Darkest Dungeon, and not Battle Brothers. It does both suffeciently well (minus the UI) but not great. It's a lite version of both, that is outshown by both. It lacks the depth and complexity of M&B and the charm and RNG management of Darkest Dungeon. Originally, I felt like the game did enough, but the more I play it, the more I see that I'd just rather play the other games I already had. Expansions/DLC would certainly help with its' "Jack of all Trades, master of none" problem, but I'm not sure if I'm invested enough into the game to care about DLC in the future.
Originally, I had made a positve "recommend" review (after, iirc, 4 hours game time), but quickly the love afair with the game died out. I mentioned the UI previously as annoying, but not a dealbreaker, but now, after having played it a few hours more, it has become a chore to use the UI and, as such, a dealbreaker imo. I've run into several bugs and issues that, while minor, are rather gamebreaking when it is a game about RNG management and you have a crossbowman who can't do anything because of a bug.
In my experience with this game, if you only plan to play about 4 hours of it, you'll love it. However, anything above 4 hours and the problems and annoyances will start to creep in there and ruin the game. Once the "new car smell" wears off, you'll realise that this is one half Mount and Blade, one half Darkest Dungeon with a terrible UI and stress the "half", a game that stives to be two games at once, but manages to be less than the sum of their parts.
