-Amazing graphics and soundtrack. These really do make the game great. The art is unique and appropriate, with a nice, gritty feeling that suits the tale of mercenaries. The music is very atmospheric, and really helps the long treks go by.
-A believable setting. The game does not delve deeply into the lore, but it does drop interesting hints. The noble houses vary between each other, with some honorable and others cruel, but they strike a good balance between themselves. The townspeople vary as well, but it ultimately sets realistic dynamics between the noble and the dastardly.
-Challenging gameplay. The enemies, and there are a lot of them, are all difficult in their own way. Some eventually lose their threatening status (Lookin' at you, Brigands), but the Greenskins, Nobles, and the Ancient Dead more than pick up the slack.
-Equipment variance. You can get a stunning amount of different armors and weapons in Battle Brothers. Arming swords, scramasax, pikes, warbrands, lutes, throwing javelins, butcher's cleavers, and military picks are just a small selection of the stuff you can fight with. What about armor, you say? Well, try a blotched gambeson, or a set of full plate, or scale mail, or just send them out in a potato sack with a bag over their head if you so choose!
Neutral:
-Permadeath. The threat of death is constantly looming over your men, and no one is safe. Some players love this, others not so much. The developers do help a bit with the Autosave feature in normal mode, but Ironman mode has no mercy.
-Fast Travel. There is a fast travel system in the game, by hiring a boat to sail you between port towns. It is by no means always comprehensive, as the procedurally-generated world may make only two ports and put them next to each other, but when it's not it makes several jobs much easier.
Cons:
-Lag. It's not often, but when it occurs it's bad. Normally, you'll never see it, but it's all too common in the end-game crises. The game simply isn't good at handling over 40-50 characters operating on their own, and when both sides can easily be 30-40 each...
-The !#$*&#% Necrosavants. I hate them. They are entirely OP. You can deal with two or three even in the midgame, but 7-15? Nope. You're donezo. They can teleport twice in one turn, have the Nine Lives perk keeping them alive when to rights they should be dead, have cleavers that devestate armor, and every point of damage they deal heals them. Usually they can easily be avoided, but when they can't you can have serious problems.
In conclusion, this game is awesome. It has its flaws, but none game-breaking. The game is fun and entirely too addicting. The fights are brutal, and it even reminds you that "Death is fun". The world is fleshed out, but not so much as to deny future expansions. Battle Brothers is a nice, unique play, and you can do so for hours with infinite replayability.

As far as I'm concerned, Deadly Shadows is to the Thief series what Invisible War is to Deus Ex, and I don't mean that in a bad way, because I enjoyed both. I mean this in terms of, it's using the same engine with similar system requirements, and suffers from similar problems.
Let's start with what was added. The visuals are great, and even if they lack color, the pristine detail of nearly every model makes it look a generation ahead of its time. A lockpicking mechanic introduces gameplay more complex than "hold F to unlock". The city now serves as a hub, allowing the player to sell loot and buy equipment, and explore for extra challenges in an open-world environment. Even backtracking doesn't seem very tedious, due to the presence of hostile who roam the streets. A faction system allows the player to make friends or enemies with the Hammerites and Pagans, who in turn can provide backup in combat and freedom to explore their respective domains.
However, a few things were removed. Rope and vine arrows are gone, replaced with gloves that allow Garrett to climb some walls. Also not present is the ability to swim. While Deus Ex: Invisible War dealt with this by simply removing water, Deadly Shadows has the player die in it, which just makes it seem like a tease. Moving the equipment purchases to shops means that, to restock, a player can no longer buy just before a mission. It goes hand-in-hand with the depth of city exploration, sure, but it makes a significant chunk of gameplay time just restocking. On a side note, the prices of these goods is far lower than that of the previous titles, so I don't find myself running into the same problem I had with Thief 2 (running out of useful items) as often here.
The biggest problem with the game, though, is the inefficient and somewhat clunky (modified) Unreal Engine 2, which, as I stated earlier, was also used in Invisible War. The small areas are handled considerably better here than they are in IW. Enemy patrols and depth of level design are well done, but the level transitions between these smaller levels is a sword that cuts both ways. On one hand, it provides a quick, if unfair escape from pursuit. On the other hand, enemies are left in the exact same spot and alert level when doing so, and going back to the area will lead to a pummelling.
Handling also feels a little awkward. The hit detection isn't all that great, and I frequently found myself falling from places against my will because the ledge detection is so awful. My most common problem was with the jumping glitch, where Garrett will appear to be floating just above the ground, with no ability to jump or crouch.
Overall, it's a good Thief game, a good stealth game, and a good game in general. Apart from the occasional crash and the removal of some perfectly functional mechanics from the previous games, this one successfully experiments and improves on a few of the other gameplay aspects.

if you are looking for victorian settings in gaming then i can safely say this is the best i've seen so far, better yet! its one of my favorite stealth games as well, not to say it doesn't have flaws...
thief games constantly get the credit they deserve for how they demonstrate the victorian period of history, how pretty and detailed the architecture, the vestiment, and even the licanthropy and fiction the games showcase, so many years after release and it still holds a strong impression of how life was like during that era, the illustration of this concept becomes memorable thanks to music, the design of the city and the way it foreshadows its progression as you explore the city, most common examples of this are the cradle, the hammerite level and the one in a mansion, outside of the city itself, in fact it seems as though this is a running theme on the series and shows the hard work that was put into these games. even if the actual illusion gets broken from time to time by the clunky, mechanical AI, i'd like to comment on how i enjoy this in an ironical sense. i like seeing it as a victorian city, fillied with animatronics. conceptually epic, but it detracts from the experience due to how lifeless it actually feels.

if you've ever played an elder scrolls game, then you know what you're getting into with this game, as its part of that trio of games, that are basically TES, but more polished but without the Open Worlds bethesda puts into their games. want better combat? then dark messiah! better magic? arx fatalis...(morrowind)
but again, while its more polished in some aspects, it still suffers from most of the issues the elder scrolls suffers from, that includes garbage, lifeless AI, clunky mechanics, occational crashing and bugs. but the reason people love these games is because, somewhere hidden under all these technical issues, there's a fun. innovative game that still holds up to this game, if any of these things bother you then you can always mod these games because PC master race. (that's just the way it is around here)

If you can get past how often this game screams to you "Old!!get the new one insteadXDDD"
then you'll find a replayable game with fun mechanics and a strong sense of design, if the victorian setting interests you then give it a shot. for stealth game fans this is a must, and if you played a stealth class in the elder scrolls you'll feel at home as its basically a glorified thieves guild.

Which im sure a lot of people would have at first, after reading recent comments.  I played a few weeks on the official website to post this here to fellow steam users.
So here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
-Hack and slash action rpg, much like Dungeon Fighter but much more graphic. (This is a pro. if you like these type of games since the description doesn't say much)
-Not pay to win, unless you really want to PvP I don't think you want to spend as much as they have for upgrading. In time, you can earn/make the same upgrades.
-The fatigue system in this game isn't as bad as dungeon fighter online. Although, that makes me wonder how they're going to combat the botters when they eventually flood the market.Those not familiar with the fatigue system, it's just how they limit your exp and grind by either lowering exp/item gain or putting a stamina bar on your dungeon runs that do not replenish over time but reset daily.
-Hotkeys can be changed to whatever you want, except the gaming mouse buttons for some reason. It's a bit limited, perhaps mine is just not supported.
-Progression is failry easy. Just do quests and grind  dungeons.
-Mechanics are very fluid in terms of your skills and abilities no matter what class you play.
Cons:
-Too graphic. Remember I said this in retrospec to a pro.? Well, it may not bother most but I wanted to throw this in anyway. Females in this game are overly sexualized. Everything from playable characters to NPC's, they all show cleavage and skin in intimate areas. Npc's constantly remind you to keep your eyes on their face. It's funny because their faces don't match their body. Just a word  of caution.
-You will need to play with people end game as the dungeons get a lot harder. This isn't much of a con but more of caution as early on it's failry easy to level up. After you reach max level there's not much to do except pvp against cash shop users with better equip.
-The tutorial is all over the place and makes things harder for a beginner to remember it all. The UI is also a bit messed up but takes time getting used to.
-Not much customization available at this time.
-Steam client crashes this game very often. If you don't want constant crashing, play on official website on any server and you'll notice a big difference. Or try to tweak it yourself until you find a fix for your issue while using steam client  Your account is saved on both platforms.

Let me start out by stating that I hated
, which looks and feels like your basic low-level Unity crud.  It's filled with several typos and quite a few bugs that range from instantly having access to the final battle in arcade mode to falling through a platform near the end of one of the canyon race stages (which has a tiny strip of land before some rising spikes).
The story is poor.  It's about a tournament taking place to see who can obtain the throne and rule over the animal kingdom through a series of minigames.  These minigames include a time trial/race, a collecting contest, a block breaking contest, and a catching contest before partaking in an event where you have to stun all characters on the screen by throwing boxes at them while they punch you (in almost all minigames, computer units can punch you to insta-stun you...you cannot punch back).
The biggest crime I have seen this game commit is its control scheme which cannot be changed.  To move, you must use the arrow keys.  The other controls are the 5, 1, 2, 3 keys on your number pad.  This means that all your fingers are going to be bunched into one tiny little corner of your keyboard, leading to an awkward and uncomfortable experience.  That said, I didn't have fun.
Although I can say that I didn't like this game, I will say that the after-arcade CGs were somewhat decent.  The artist behind them did quite well with them.  It's only a shame that they're part of a game that I have to dismiss as trash.  The actual graphics in-game are what you would expect to come from Unity titles.
So...to recap:
PROS:
+ Decent CG artwork.
CONS:
- Poor controls (which cannot be changed)
- Buggy stages

Yes. Spoilers below.
++Incredible, immersive, "get lost and just drive" world of Hong Kong
++The most comfy game in existence at night and in the rain
++Looks so good it hurts, with or without the "HD" texture pack
++Top-of-the-line production values across the board with very few exceptions
++Loads of collectibles which is perfect for autistic completionists like me
++Good story with loads of actually-memorable characters
++♥♥♥♥ing with random NPCs is fun, which is something I look for in my open-world crime games
++World actually feels alive and the simple act of walking and looking is highly enjoyable
--Chase missions (car or on foot) are entirely scripted, to the point there is literally no reason to try to win, catch, or kill the target because it will either A) break the mission forcing a restart, or B) not work. Just follow along until the scripts fire.
--Random police chases are also impossible to win due to exaggerated rubber banding. You can have the supercar DLC, but the cops will overtake you in minivans. Just go 10mph and ram the cops until you "get away."
--Races in general are awful because of the rubber banding
--A lot of the DLC is overpowered and wrecks enjoyment. I found the cash envelopes fine because I wanted to buy all the cars, but the XP DLCs destroy what little RPG leveling there is
--Some things are unfinished, or at least feel that way. For example, there are a handful of "girlfriends" you can have, but they serve no purpose except unlocking minimap helpers. One is voiced by Emma Stone, but she is only in the game for around ten minutes (real time, including playing). Others act like you've been in a lengthy relationship and accuse you of cheating after doing another girl's mission, but either I missed something entirely or that section of the game was cut. Likewise, there's a fairly decent karaoke minigame that goes with the girlfriend system, but there's just no point to it
--The first True Crime game allowed you to stop, frisk, and arrest random pedestrians anytime you wanted. It was the best part of playing a "straight cop" that put it above other games like it; here, the police missions are boring and most of the time force you to do the same things you would do as a criminal
--In going with the unfinished complaint: it seems as though there was supposed to be a two-prong narrative at times through the game, but for whatever reason you'll always end up being a criminal.
--Winston died way too soon. I just started warming up to him (the errands mission with his fiance was great), and then he was ♥♥♥♥ing dead. Such a waste.
--While the main characters and a good number of the side ones are spectacular and will stick with you, there are also a bunch of people who are injected into the narrative with false importance. For example, in one of the police missions I found a serial killer had been knocking off gang members, at which time Wei Shen found a burnt body of...somebody he knew well. The game acted like we were close, but I couldn't remember his name at all. Later in the game, when you're in control of your gang, you have sidekicks that apparently are crucial, but I couldn't begin to explain why. In my opinion problems like this are a result of too many writers working without a clear vision, or maybe a direction change mid-development. Sad!
--Missions will almost always take away your car or gun. I understand Sleeping Dogs is supposed to be part homage to kung fu movies and guns are not a central theme, but later in the game I really started to like shooting people instead of beating them to death. Likewise I had enough money to bring supercars along, and I wanted to use those things in the missions. Too bad, sonny jim, because you will be using this ancient fish truck with only your fists. Just like the scripting and rubber banding, the actual missions are highly linear with zero (and I mean ZERO) room for improvisation.
TL;DR could and should have been a 10/10 goat; another year in development would have made something legendary. Still, this one's worth buying if only to experience Hong Kong in a way no other game has done. A solid story with good fisticuffs make the 15-ish hour main story worth the asking price.

Stacking is another rather unique game from Double Fine.  It is essentially a puzzle game starring nothing but Russian stacking dolls where you try to solve problems by stacking into certain dolls and using their wacky special abilities.  It sounds simple, but the levels are large and there's a lot of dolls to choose from, so it can be quite difficult to determine which dolls will work for a given situation.  There are always multiple solutions and only one is required to progress through the story, but the game has a way of making you want to find them all.  It would actually be quite frustrating if it weren't for the hint system, which provides 3 increasingly obvious hints (the last one actually tells you exactly how to solve it) for each puzzle solution.
The game is made in the style of a silent movie slathered with Double Fine's signature style, with all aspects of the game fitting together so well.  Doll abilities range from farting to charging, punching, and even firing a gun and other dolls will react in ridiculous ways.  They even look shocked when you stack into another doll, since you seem to be the only person with that ability.  It even fun just watching the dolls react to you when you're going about your business solving puzzles.
As an additional note, this game is locked to 30 fps.  It is the only game I've played that I feel has an actual reason to do so, given its silent movie style, but it still makes the game feel choppy and I would prefer being able to run it at a higher framerate.
So, Stacking is great fun.  If you like any of Double Fine's other games or just want a silly fun game to play, Stacking is a great choice.

I'm amazed with this game... I really am. I had my eye on this game due to its peculiar art direction with the whole matryoshka theme. And, being from Double Fine, it should be good! Although I haven't really heard much about it, which now surprises me.
I'm yet to play Psychonauts, but so far, this is their finnest! (...)
On to the game. Stacking is a third person Adventure/Puzzle game, in which you play Charlie, the smallest doll of all. The game is set in the industrial revolution era, a place where there's a tyrannical Baron who exploits workers and/or children. Your brothers and sister and taken by him during a workers' strike, and so you're on your newly found quest to rescue them, and find your father, who disappeared to pay off the family's debts.
Presentation
The art direction in this game is amazing! Everything shows character and is highly polished. In this regard, I can't find any flaws, really. The screenshots don't do it justice, but you get the feel of it. The cutscenes are done in an old movie style, without any speech and then added text, with fitting music.
Despite the dolls' shape, their animation gives each of them a very unique feel, even in the way they walk and talk, which isn't something anyone could pull off.
The music fits every scene really well, with handpicked classical pieces, which contributes to the very unique atmosphere of this game. Even if you're not a fan of classical music, I'm sure you'll find it in its right place here.
As for me, this might have given me the will to explore classical music a bit more. It's one of the game's spotlights for me.
Presentantion is simply excelent! I'm surprised with how they've managed to do it so perfectly, I really am. From the animation, to the cutscenes, the music... everything is just awesome and you'll find yourself just stop progressing and look around for the sake of it.
Gameplay
This is where this game is truly inovative, it blends mechanics with the world it's set it, gameplay and the artstyle just fit perfectly.
Due to your size, no one pays much attention to you. This is where the main mechanic comes in. You can Stack into other dolls that are one size bigger than you, and those can stack into others that are one size bigger than them, and so on.
There are Unique Dolls, with a name and a backstory, and a very personal feel to them. Then there are types of dolls, mainly a satirical depiction of their "class", I'd say.
Every unique/type of doll has its own special ability that will help you solve puzzles or just interact with other dolls to simply have fun with the game!
In the main game you have 4 main areas (one of which is like the Hub area, which gets more quests as you progress) in which you rescue your family, solve puzzles and just joke around, each with a theme to it. Another area and sidestory is added in the DLC.
Each area the main quest, divided into smaller puzzles. To every puzzle you have from 3 to 6 different solutions, which are accomplished by stacking with the right dolls and using their abilities accordingly. You only need to solve them once to progress in the story, but replayability is highly encouraged in this game, for various reasons. Every solution is very creative and actually pretty fun, so I'd encourage you to try to get to every solution even after finishing the game, as you can go back to every area at will. The in-game hint system is actually very good, giving you little hints that will definitely help you solve some of the puzzles without spoiling it all for you!
Aside from the main quests, you have Hi-Jinks. These are essentially challenges to your creativity with the different dolls and interacting with each other to comical effect. Each area has a bunch of them, and I can't stress enough that you should definitely try them all, every side objective in this game rewards you.
In the main area of the game, you have the friend you meet at the start of the game, and he essentially keeps track of your progress, and creates dolls, wall paintings and puzzle pieces for each solution and unique doll found. In the end of the game, it's awesome to go meet him and see the whole cast of characters and locations in a sort of secret exposition.
This is a reason to do the sidequests and challenges, but do them for the sake of it, because every single one of them is very fun to do!
Story
The story is pretty straightforward, but it actually has many nuances to it and follows the world hand in hand, leading with some serious issues in a very casual and humorous way.  It's not something I'd examine very carefully, but I like that it's there, and it helps you understand the characters and the world better.
Conclusion
As if what I wrote was not enough, this was a truly brilliant game, in my opinion!
Everything fits, the world feels alive and is just eye-candy. While I'm not much of a puzzle game fan, this one pulled me in and made me keep playing until I've absolutely finished everything there was to finish in it!
If you're intrigued by it in any way, go ahead and buy it. I'm sure you haven't experienced anything like it so far, and it's great to see some developers doing something they like and being inovative... and succeeding!
From the music to the artstyle and game mechanics, the writing... I can't find anything worth complaining about. The only problem one might have with it is the fact that it's a puzzle game, but the fact that it has several solutions makes at least one of them fairly easy to get, even if a couple of them were a bit hard to get if you hadn't talked to the right people.
Enough of this chatter. Buy this game if you haven't already, it's awesome!

I thought I liked this game, but it managed to suprised me with how shallow and quickly stagnating an experience it is. You may be saying, "Well you only played like 3 hours" and I will tell you that it took only that long for me to be bored enough to quit playing and angry enough to write a review about my experience.
If you don't already know, Battle Brothers is a game where you captain a mercenary squad in a dark/norse style fantasy world. You move your little chess piece looking guy around the map from town to town picking up contracts for gold which you will need to cover your squad's expenses(pay, food, repairs, meds) as well as purchase recruits and upgrade equipment. These contracts range from, going to a graveyard to beat up some badguys(graverobbers!), to going to a graveyard to beat up some badguys(but hey its not graverobbers this time around!) In the time i spent with the game i completed around 10 contracts, 2 delieveries, 4 graveyards, 2 monster hunts and 2 item recoveries. There may of been another contract where I had to go to a *not* graveyard to kill some bandits. At that point i had enough gold to recruit enough people to fill the shoes of the people who died getting me the gold and stock up on food and tools to prevent the not dead ones from starving and their weapons and armor from breaking. Yes, perma death is a big part of the game, and unless you are save scumming constantly to avoid losses you are going to lose people. And its pretty easy for characters to die(no bleed out phase when hp is gone, just dead), especially if all they are wearing for armor is a cloth sack, but armor costs money, lots of money, so i better go find another village with a graveyard that is full of bandits/ghouls/skeletons for me to kill and get money from.
If you havent figured it out yet, what I'm trying to say is that the game is a grind, a big monotonous one. And frankly, unless you absolutely love the combat, which i wasn't impressed with at all (if anything it frustrated me), then I don't see anything really redeeming about this game.  I won't say its a bad game and that people won't like it, but for me it was boring, repetitive and ultimately unengaging.
This game, is amazing, one of the best remakes i have ever had the pleasure playing and it always will be one of my all time favorite games, i hope it wins.

There are quite a few things I don't like about this game, but my overall experience was still very positive. They really did a good job with the graphics and audio, and the atmosphere in this game is great, which I think is very important in a point and click adventure. My best memories of adventure games comes from sucking in the incredible atmosphere of brilliantly portrayed locations like Stark in The Longest Journey or the Land of the Dead in Grim Fandango, and I definitely did get a similar experience on several occations in Lost Horizon. That really was the main driving point for me to complete the game, because the puzzles were too easy and rarely interesting, and I don't think the story was especially impressive either. Still, if you are looking for a calmer, more atmospheric experience than what modern QTE adventure games offer, I heartily recommend this game.

First off, I am recommending this game only for diehard fans of A Song of Ice and Fire, or anyone that wants an entertaining way of exploring the history of Westeros.  Obviously, this isn't the HBO branded Game of Thrones you might be used to so the art or characters may look a little bit different.
The way you play this game is a very dumbed down version of any RTS you may think of, build units, take towns and castles, kill your enemy.  The way any single player vs AI or multiplayer game works is in two parts: Peace time, where you build alliances and build up your power undertaking various actions either directly or indirectly against the rival houses and the method for taking towns and castles is using non-combat units.  Once war breaks out in the seven kingdoms, you must now rely solely on your combat units to take the remaining towns and castles.  The first house or houses to reach the required honor score wins.  Each house will have their own special ancestral home which cannot be taken.  The way you build units is a bit silly, allowing only one to be built at a time but you can queue up to 5, if funds and food allow.  Gold and Food are the two forms of commerce, gold to buy mercenary units, non-combat units, and upgrades and food for your professional standing armies.  The game uses an upkeep system so you must ensure you have an adequate supply of food to maintain your armies after they are built.  Various non-combat units will give you bonuses to gold production and your peasants will level up with experience if you can manage to protect them and keep them alive, thus making them more efficient at harvesting.  Each house has a unique unit that provides a special ability or skill but nothing spectacular, like a maester that can heal units for the Tyrells, or a direwolf bodyguard-type unit for the Starks.  All houses have the same types of combat units available to them, so don't expect the Targaryens to throw dragons at you.  The time period for the House vs House mode of play is right before the events leading up to Robert's rebellion.
The campaign, while not too expansive, is a semi-enjoyable experience taking place from the landing of Nymeria in Dorne to the Night's Watch defending the wall from Mance and the united free folk.  The variety of missions you will play is obviously limited to the somehwat limited features of the gameplay itself, but it can still offer some fresh experiences other than escort unit A to point C.
All said and done, pick up this title at a heavily discounted price and for what it offers if you feel you get your money's worth then you've won.

Did you ever have one of those three dimensional puzzle toys growing up?  Sometimes they're plastic, sometimes they're wooden, maybe even metal, and they usually have a lot of pieces that interlock in strange ways that, depending on your mood, can vary from perplexing to outright frustrating.  Please, Don't Touch Anything is one of those puzzles in digital format, maybe with a little bit of Sudoku thrown in for all of the numerical hints and pads they tossed in.
A lot of people seem to want to draw parallels between this game and Papers, Please.  It might be the Eastern European influences, or the greyscale 2D desk work, but the tonality of the two games fall on complete opposite ends of the spectrum.  Where Papers, Please makes you worry about how your choices will effect you and the characters around you, PDTA approaches the consequences of your actions with a lot more comedy and general lack of seriousness, a few endings aside.  There's also plenty of pop culture references dashed into some of the potential endings you can get by fussing around with the machine, cultured science fiction fans will be satisfied with all of the "oh I get it!" head nodding they'll be doing.
Also, maybe we should talk about the endings?  There are 25 in total as of this writing, and if I recall correctly the developers have patched in at least two batches of new endings/easter eggs since launch.  There's even a Papers, Please crossover tucked into one of the endings!  These patches have, again, also "to date", all been free, and I love it when a developer continues to support a title for free after release with extra content.
The game itself runs a little short, especially if you use a strategy guide for some of the more obscure endings (I'm guilty, I wanted to see what I had missed!).  There's plenty to play around with though, especially if you're a fan of puzzles, scavenger hunts, or modern-day ARG-style vague-hintery, and that's like three hyphenated words in a row, so it must be pretty legit.

Sleeping Dogs achieves what most games fail to grasp when chasing the goal of “cinematic” and does so through action packed gameplay, dramatic story, and an immersive open world. It was refreshing to play in an unfamiliar environment and United Front's recreation of Hong Kong is stunning. You grow to care for the characters you deal with and feel the stress of protagonist Wei Shen as he tries to balance his duty as a cop with the loyalty earned with the Triads.
Some areas of the game feel as if they had more planned but for one reason or another were cut short and some missions required frustratingly precise strategies to earn the best rank, but these issues are soon forgotten once you return to the main flow of the game.
Finishing Sleeping Dogs felt like coming to the end of your favourite TV show; it's sad to leave the characters and world once you complete everything but they'll be there again when you return. I highly recommend picking up Sleeping Dogs as a new player, and to visit again if you already own it. Easily worth the price and at discount it's a steal.

This is an entertaining puzzle adventure game. You play as Charlie, the tiniest wooden stacking doll. You can stack into other dolls, thus changing your size and what abilities you can use. In order to solve puzzles, you must find which doll to use in which circumstance.
You can also combo abilities. For instance, I lit a flame with one doll, but the fire needed to be bigger. Hmm, what fuel could I add to the fire? I found a stinky doll and used his "Flatulate" ability near the flame and it made a huge, satisfying inferno. Apparently I could alternatively have used a doll that spilled oil on the floor, but the farting was much more amusing. *giggle*
While you're playing the game, you naturally have to solve puzzles in order to progress. But for each of these puzzles, there is usually around three different solutions. You only need to find one solution in order to continue the story, but if you're a completionist, you can explore the area more thoroughly and find all of the solutions. You can do this as you go along, or you can return to the area later, even after you have completed the storyline.
While using different characters with different abilities to bypass obstacles is by no means a new concept, the implementation of it in Stacking makes it feel fresh and fun. The art style is adorable, and the cutscenes are designed to look like old silent films. I enjoyed this game quite a lot.

Bastion is an isometric action-RPG taking place in a world on the brink of destruction from an event known as the calamity.
The story and atmosphere really shine here, mostly because of the narrator. With the just the events that take place as you're playing, the story could seem barebones, but the information given by the narrator really gives a sense of history to it and elevates the narrative. He also foreshadows and brings a sense of impending drama to the events (something that is much more noticable on NG+!) and when you combine that with beautiful handdrawn visuals and a great soundtrack it really immerses the player in its atmosphere.
The gameplay itself is mostly moving through short levels to collect certain items, fighting the creatures that impede this. The combat is decent and fun, though not groundbreaking. It's mostly hack/slack or kite, which mostly will depend on your playstyle and the difficultly level. The variety of weapons and skills keep it interesting, and way they use a 'higher-risk = higher-reward system' for the difficulty will keep it challenging for any level of gamer without frustration.
I think Bastion is  mostly for those who love great story and worldbuilding, though I would also reccomend this to anyone look for a fun action-RPG.

I've been meaning to make a review of this gem for some time, though I must make it clear that my Steam play time bears no indication as to the amount of time I’ve actually spent on it; my experience deriving from the physical copy of the game.
Insofar as the WWII era and the Tibetan locations upon which the game is set, Lost Horizon is roughly based on James Hilton's novel of the same name though here represented by Fenton Paddock - a former British military officer who's been tasked with investigating the disappearance of a British detachment originally posted within the Tibetan wilderness as a means of repelling the Nazi German advance.
Very soon thereafter the journey takes the player around the globe, admiring the sights of such locations as Hong Kong, Morocco and even the heart of Germany itself.
: By today's standards the graphics are nothing special, though I should point out that they have a certain charm and vibrancy about them that adds to the uniqueness as well as the ‘buoyancy’ of the game (something I’ll extrapolate on later).
: The ambient sounds and music are adequate while the voice acting is for the most part acceptable. There's nothing that really makes the game stand out in this department however.
: While Lost Horizon uses typical point and click mechanics, the puzzles can be said to lean more toward the ‘mainstream’ player in that they are not very taxing and are generally very easy. This is further compounded by a distinct lack of depth with regards to the player’s ability (or rather inability in this case) to interact with many things throughout the various scenes.
: This is where the game really excels, in that it has created its very own take based upon James Hilton's original narrative template. What initially appears to be a clichéd WWII adventure offering, eventually culminates with an adventure game whose ending is worthy enough that even James Hilton himself would have been proud to have been associated. Indeed it's this clichéd setting that enables Animation Arts to flash their own creative muscle via personal artistic license, that seals the deal for me personally.
In conclusion then, Lost Horizon is a fun little gem of a game that uses established clichés in an intelligent way, by creating its very own story upon which Tibetan mysticism (which exists even today) runs central. This together with the buoyancy of its aesthetic offering makes it, much like a flower in bloom, an experience to truly savour.

I would recommend Lost Horizon to anyone a fan of the genre. You get exactly what is being sold to you in the trailer.

Even though the game took just shy of 12 hours to complete, the gameplay itself is not very complex. The game itself plays in a very cinematic way, with quite a few cutscenes with the ingame engine, a movie-like story and lots of dialogue. Luckily, all the dialogue and the cutscenes are skippable, if you wish to do so. I really enjoyed the very linear story and also linear puzzles, which make this game feel like an interactive Indiana Jones movie. Just be aware that there are absolutely no choices to make which send the game in a different direction.
The gameplay consists mostly of the typical point and click one, which boils down to inspecting items, storing some in your inventory and combining them when necessary. During the whole game, there were only two exceptions which did not involve those ‘take a look at A and combine with B’ puzzles. Occasionally you take control of two characters to solve some puzzles. I really liked how, despite the cinematic direction, you could take as much time as you wanted for each puzzle. There is no dexterity or speed required. Even in a car-chasing scene! This helped with not getting frustrated, if you couldn’t figure out which items apply to which ones. Generally, there is no way to die in this game, which I really appreciated. Instead of letting you do actions that would get you killed and thus waste your time, were simply not allowed and instead just commented by the main actor in a humorous way. In general, the logic behind the puzzles was quite solid and generally solvable on its own.
I extremely appreciated that all interactable items in a game scene can be highlighted with the click of a button! So there is absolutely no ‘pixel hunting’ in this games. More devs should have this in their adventure games! Without this highlighting, I might have not completed the game.
However, I had to resort to a walkthrough a few times, because I missed an item. As all the puzzles are extremely linear, every item has to be applied to the others in a certain order. So, missing just one item would make the whole puzzle unsolvable. I think this is my biggest grip with the game. I didn’t mind having linear puzzles. I felt they were very fitting considering the whole style of the game. I wish there were some hint system, as the only thing coming close to a hint would be vague comments by the character, which were not enough for me. I often ended up just randomly trying and clicking on things when stuck. What I liked is that the game at least showed if items could be interacted with just by hovering with the mouse or with another item over them, so they would spare me at least the clicking part. However, the items you need are often only a screen away and almost all things you can interact with will be needed to progress. There are no false trails. If you try any solution that does not work, it will simply not be carried out and dismissed by a short comment, which minimizes the wrong solutions you could be misled by. Occasionally backtracking was needed and I really appreciated that the transitions from screen to screen were short and that the walking times were even shorter! The wasted time is very minimal, good job devs!
A few technical things: the game runs extremely well, however there are a few bugs. What threw me really off was not that many small items would not be rendered at all, which would lead to characters exchanging or looking at invisible items. No, it was the occasional graphical glitch, where characters would clip behind pieces of the background and suddenly become invisible. The game runs in a letterbox, so it does not utilize the full width of the widescreen. Slightly annoyingly the cursor is not constraint to one monitor in a multi monitor setup. The quality of animations is quite good, overall.
I loved the setting of this game! It is heavily Indiana Jones inspired and takes you to all kind of exotic and exciting locations all over the world in hunt for a secret artifact. These range from the scorching hot Morocco to the ice-cold glaciers of Tibet. A game scene usually consists of an absolutely stunning, hand-drawn backdrop, with added 3D interactable items, which were a bit crudely drawn. The unbelievably gorgeous, detailed and very historically accurate backgrounds were supported by unobtrusive, atmospheric and fitting background music.
The humor in this game is amusing in the typical action hero manner. I often smirked about the humor and did not grow tired of it over the whole 12 hours of the game. Yes it's the weakest of the first three Thief games but with mods it's quite a good game, and in a few respects the best of the Thief games. It has the best storytelling by far. The new mechanics are a mix of good and bad. The shadow system is more accurate but the blackjacking is terribly clunky and requires you to line up shot directly from behind which will fail and probably ruin your plan if the target pivots at the last second. On the other hand the ability to switch into third-person perspective gives things a more realistic feel and is tactically useful (although rather cheap because it lets you see around corners). The leaning is useless.
The levels are not bad. By my count three of them are mediocre and six of them are good to outstanding. Many people think one of them is the best Thief level of all time.
I think the real problem, after you mod out the loading zones, is with the hub city. Often it's good and adds a lot of nice (though completely unnecessary) mini side-quests. But at other times it's just a nuisance having to go through two or three transitions and avoid a handful of patrolling guards just to get to your next mission. It also never feels like a real world. It's too small and the NPCs are too obviously just spawned NPCs.  On balance the formula of the original Thief games worked better. All missions with no filler.
Anyway the reason I'm writing this review is because I think this game has an undeservedly low reputation. It rounds out the trilogy well and should have been the basis for a much better 3D Thief game.

I fondly remember this game which was the first stealth based one I played. There are especially two scenes I remember for their uniqueness when compared to other gaming experiences I had up to that time.
The first one was in Shalebridge Cradle. I entered this old decaying building in the middle of the night. On my path to the uppermost level of the cradle I was crawling up that long and wide circular stairs, when the athmosphere and the sound of the scenery won: I could't bear the tension and closed the game. The next day, in bright sunlight, I tried it again - and failed after seconds. Too vivid were the horrors I imagined lurking in the halls beyond.
So I got reinforcements and brought a friend who - unlike me - had played and loved the first two titles of the series. That actually helped and - slowly - I made my way up the stairs. I can't remember the exact place, but soon  afterwards I looked at the crossing of two hallways. So many directions the evil that must be lurking in this building could come from! Cautiously I approached the crossing, listening for treacherous sounds, when I suddenly saw something moving in the dark. My heart rate increased when I went to investigate it. But I couldn't find anything in any direction. Then - you know what's coming! - I turned around, only to find myself eye to eye wuth the first of the gruesome remnants of this cursed place. I screamed like a little girl and ran! Then my friend and me had a good laugh.
In the other scene I remember I was lurking atop some walkway which was built at noticable height to allow good overwatch. I believe this was when I made contact with the pagans, but don't know for sure. However, I saw some female guard on patrol right below me with no one else in sight. I braced myself and jumped down, expecting to hurt myself. Instead I landed gracefully right behind the guard who, to my excitement, screamed in surprise without turning around - paralysed be the shock. Once I understood what had just happend I took advantage of it and landed a clean hit with my trusty blackjack before the scream ended to knock out the poor guard. Amazing!

Game of Thrones - Genesis is an interesting game to review.
It explores some really neat features that I have not seen before and I wish other games would implement them.  It also gets some of the more basic things not as.... right...
If you are going into this expecting a typical rts, turn back,  the skirmish mode for this (which I'd argue is the best part of this mode) is more like a political simulator that hopefully finishes before being blasted into War (combat in this game isn't really... satisfying).
The campaign gives some interesting backstory to the universe and shows you some of the ropes of the features in the game but had a lot of scenarios that fall flat either relying on the worst aspects of this game (combat) or feeling like less well done arcade scenarios from starcraft.
So the good, which will specifically focus on skirmish modes:
In peace time, it captures the political intrigue of game of thrones to a T, with a system that has a lot of depth, and a lot of counters to strategies.
To give a barebones example, to get gold, you need to send emissaries to form an alliance with towns.  You'll notice merchants pop up and your gold income per minute SHOULD increase (note this).
Here are the options (and some counters) that your enemy has to break the alliance.
Your enemy can send his envoy to your town to cause the town to break their alliance, unless you send/have your envoy in the town to kick him out.
Your enemy can send an assasin to kill your envoy and send his own to break their alliance.  You can counter this by having guards guard the envoy who will then capture and imprison the assasin.
Your enemy can send a spy to establish a secret alliance, which gives you 0 income and them half the income, you can counter this by inspecting the town to make sure no secret alliance was had, or having a noble marry into the town to form a blood alliance which is immune to this tactic.
Your enemy can send a rogue who can start a rebellion in the town, (which also spreads) making the income of the town to 0.  This can be countered with guards guarding the town.
There are ways to counter the above counters as well, forming a myriad of complex and satisfyingly interesting choices.
The Bad:
Combat is displayed weakly and while there is a rock paper scissor mechanic to it, typically the bigger blob will win.    When War begins the above diplomatic and underhanded options are no longer possible so it becomes a, who has the bigger army.
Verdict:
While I don't think the game is a must buy (and should be avoided by those looking for a typical rts with a GOT skin), it should be a try for those looking for an rts with a lot of diplomacy and intrigue options.  Playing with friends can be super fun as they slowly realize you've infiltrated their house and formed many secret alliances.  War however again is quite weak, but the game goes off of a prestige point system which can be won wihout the War phase.
I don't think this game deserves a Mostly Negative standing.  Mixed or Slightly Positive would be more accurate I think.

A somewhat sandboxy Thief game with side activities you can do in town when you're not on a mission. Specific activities however are activated from finding notes and eavesdropping on chatter which you can also do on your own time or within the time given.
Something that was pretty much shown on screenshots of the game is Garrett himself in third person; the option to go into this perspective feels weird at first since the first two games were strictly first person though it may not take too long to get used to. This function can prove useful and makes the implemented lean function relatively obsolete.
There won't be anymore swimming either for anyone as in no one, not even Garrett, can swim now; people simply die from dropping into big bodies of water.
When trying to climb over walls or obstacles or whatever it doesn't seem to always work, which can be very problematic when making quick climbs while a guard is very close. The game would think you just jumped or dropped from a small height which would make a sound for anyone close to hear.
Another big change is the lockpicking. Instead of having to manually select a specific lockpick to pick a lock and then select another to finish the job you go through a more involved way of lockpicking. This time you go through a small & simple lockpicking minigame that's a little more realistic and can be a lot faster the more you get used to it.
Like the first two games directions aren't straightforward though your compass is now implemented on to the UI. For a number of missions you'd have to find a map for said location you'd have to go to if you're seeking any form of directional help though it isn't mandatory. Also many of the things you find that progresses a mission are pointed out a lot more. The mission levels themselves feel a little smaller and somewhat more linear as in there's not too much to walk through and not too many additional ways to reach objectives.
This time around, after you think you've stolen enough loot or completed a mission, you have to actually go find a fence to sell the loot you stole for gold and travel to another shop to buy equipment.
Side note: The game would crash for me every time I finished the tutorial level without downloading a sort of patch.

Now that Starbound is finally out it is time for a proper review. Starbound is a good game, but not a great game. Everything feels a bit shallow. It feels like there were much bigger plans but the devs ended up bitting off more than they could handle.
The missions are shallow and are (to me) a dissapointment. They never truely made me feel like I was part of a story. Unlocking the missions is a tedious and uninspired chore of moving from one random planet to another hoping that you get lucky and find what you need. The characters in the missions are never given time to develop into anything more than a source of exposition.
The planets are numerous and are truely massive. While this means there are pleanty of places to explore, this also means that there are large tracts of land that have nothing to see. No matter how much the enviroment varies, large empty areas are just boring to trek through. I can't help but feel like there was going to be a lot more content that would have filled these areas...
In the end, starbound has a excellent framework that COULD be developed into something amazing but comes across as somewhat shallow. If you want to build an amazing looking 2D sci-fi colony, this is for you, If you want an adventure, look elsewhere.
Make sure this is something you truely will enjoy before you buy it.

If you like puzzle games that don't explain much about themselves and make you figure everything out as you go, then I'm pretty sure you might just like this game as I did. Just do yourself a favor and stay off the walkthroughs, you'll thank yourself for it and will feel genuinely smarter in the end.
The story is as follows; you're put into the position of covering for another employee that went off for a short break and you're left with a large, unfamiliar, empty console in front of you, save for one big red button and an image of a city on the monitor. You have only one instruction from your fellow employee: don't touch anything! Feeling like you've been handed the history eraser button, you're left alone with the temptation staring you in the face. The start of the game does not tell you how to play and instead leaves you clueless and confused, just like you normally would be in a sitiuation such as this.
Please, Don't Touch Anything is not a long game in retrospect, but it does require a lot of out of the box thinking and tinkering to achieve all the various referencial endings that it has. The pixel visual style, though simple, works pretty well in illustrating all you need to see and the awesome soundtrack reflects your actions and thier eventual inevitability.
Honestly, saying much more about the game would be doing a disservice to it. My advice? Look closely at every detail, every pixel and do some research on specific clues. This game can be deceptive.

I, obviously, give this game a benefit of doubt because of it being in early access; the game's incompletion may be greatly improved by time it's full release. Some of what I'll state are of personal bias, and in terms of visuals and opinion on gameplay is subjective. Yes, I have to point this out because people become upset by reading criticisms. Why? No clue, but if you're upset by reading something in which people discuss about their feelings/opinions on a subject, you should probably turn the other way considering you're going to read things that don't suit your beliefs. You have been warned!
: Gameplay's simplistic-- throughout the game, you complete different quests and gain loot; cards which vary of 'Guildians' and their characteristics/levels (as in bards, knights, clerics, etc) to cards which multiplies gold made, along with chests which provide resources such as gems and gold. What you do with said gems and gold are to (and respectively) purchase chests and upgrade quests' stats and army spawn time/capacity.
~~~~~~
: Not too shabby. I'm not exactly a fan of these kinds of games (given that I easily bore), but it seems to be like every other incremental game (fancy-schmancy word for click-games). So with that being said, repetition becomes... repetitive. Because of how simplistic and non-challenging it is (except testing your patience) you become bored fairly quick, then you eventually just leave it idling moreso out of disinterest than as idle-farming. I know many people who enjoy these type of games regardless, but given that I tire easily as it is along with this game not bringing me any reason to come back for more it's not of my interest. From what I've seen it's fair, but that's the most I can comment on it.
Opinion on Visuals: Visuals are fairly crude; not exactly pleasing or considered of high-quality aesthetic. Especially given even in Fantastic mode (quality over performance) it's quite bland. I understand the art going for that route of simplicity (or at least what I assume) but it's slight saturation kills the aesthetic. It's contrast with, for example, the taskbar being purple but yet seeing the map's saturated warm-like colors makes the aesthetic awkward and it grabs your attention of rather as an obstacle over interest of said color choice/palette. Fair note I'm no professional artist, however as a hobbyist I notice some artists do this which kills the simplistic yet charming palette. I recommend as a solution to use less saturated colors in details which expects color to be involved-- good example would be investing in vibrance of boss quest buildings colors-- this especially applies to quest level bars and bars which shows spawn production/army capacity to match the theme given.
I may or may not touch on soundtrack, and anything else truly necessary will be updated as expected. Thank you for reading!

Underwhelming is the only word needed to describe this game as of 1.0
I have ~100 hours in this game, and 80 of them are just screwing around in multiplayer pretending to have fun.  The only reason I didn't stop at 30 hours was because I got a few friends on a server and I enjoyed hanging with them. We weren't playing the game, Starbound was just the chat platform we used.
The story is against the very nature of Starbound. It forces you to be the good guy. Ontop of that, it's literally just 5 repeated "go fetch this to fight boss" quests that ends up in a game-ending boss that's stupid hard to solo but a walk in the park for 2 players.
The ships are too different. Novakid' ship has (personal opinion) the coolest design, but it's probably the smallest one even after it's fully upgraded. The developers said there would be different advantages for the different races, but so far, the literally only advantage one race has over all the others is that it glows in the dark. But actually, all races glow in the dark, for some reason. There's no reason to choose any 1 race over another. Adding game-changing advantages to each race would allow for 7 different replays, right now there's just 1 playthrough, and after that, you've seen all the game has to offer.
The enemies are incredibly boring and generic. Every enemy is a reskin of another enemy. There are basically 2 enemies in the game: flying, and not flying. Everything that flies just dashes into you from the air to deal damage. Everything not flying runs into you to deal damage from either side.
Every planet is the same under the surface. The dungeons are boring. The celestial system makes no sense. You can find ice planets in close orbits around "Fiery stars" but around the very same star, there's a magma ocean way further out. It makes 0 sense.
Do not be fooled by the "Procedual generation" everyone is talking about. The universe is the same to everyone. It may have been generated originally, but if you start over with a new charachter, it's the exact same universe. If you go online to a server, you'll find the exact same planets at the exact same coords and each tile is placed exactly the same.
Basebuilding is pointless because you can have everything in your ship. Engineer crewmembers are overpowered to the point where it's not even funny. I have 1 single engineer, and he's upgraded my ship so much without me doing anything that I can fly from one star to another without using a single unit of fuel. It's horrible to see this game next rated so low that it almost reaches the kind of treatment Ride to Hell or No Man's Sky receaved.
WHILE IT IS ACTUALLY A PRETTY ADVANCED GAME.
Not only that. But it is filled with conent and had so much work behind making it.
So let's start with the basics.
This is not an RTS.
At least it shouldn'T really be considered one.
Because while it happens in real time the game it self focuses more around managing your alliances than actual fighting or tactics.
The recipie for basics is the following:
So send a diplomat to a town/village/castle and he makes an alliance over time.
You send your spy to hostile towns to make secret agreemnts which your enemy won'T know about.
You can defend your own towns with Diplomats from hostile diplomats.
And your spies can reveal enemy spies and your mercs will take shot work of them.
Now this is the basic of the politics system. There is much more dpet to it but I'm not going to further explain. The game works like a super advanced combination of Malefic and Risk.
Where you have to defend your settlements against enemy ainfluence while simultaniously conquering new ones.
The battles are extremely boring on the other hand and there is not much to talk about them.
So let's talk about everything else in the game:
Graphics : Pretty avareage for its time not nice but not horrible either. It didn't make me womith so in my opinion it is alright. I think if the game would have a similar design as Eu4 or CK2 it would look nicer because the artwork in this game is actually really good.
Music and Sounds: For the music part again pretty mediocre. For voice acting I think it is good.
You could argue though. I haven't heard all voices in the game so far but the normal units sound alright. Other sounds in the game are not annoying either.
Story: since it is based on the historical backstory of the The Song of Ice and Fire there is nothing innovative or stunning about it. It basicly tells the story how it is.
SO should you buy it?
Is it on sale?
Are you in love with the game of thrones games and have read ALL books including documentraies and spinoffs?
Do you like slow pased games?
Do you want something different in terms of strategy?
If 3 of the 4 answers are yes then YES you should.
Otherwise pass. You won't like it since there is nothing particulary interesting about the game. I think that's why it's failed.

I am only interested in the story campaign so I am probably a bit unusual for this type of game.  One of the major reasons I am not recommending it because that aspect of the game is lacking.  The story consists of one paragraph to read per mission.  Nothing else.  The objectives are not particularly fun either.  Every mission is divided into three types of objectives: bronze, silver and gold.  Bronze is required to win and you get more rewards for completing each objective type you complete.  Once earned they never go away so they are very helpful, maybe even necessary to completing the harder missions later.  It was all a bit too much of a formula and too dry for me.
For the battles themselves, it is a real RTS even though the graphics may imply it's not.  It is a bit simpler though.  You can only build one building at a time with no queuing (or if there was I couldn't figure out how to do it).  I found this very, very annoying.  Having to consitently go back to base to build 1 build is just no fun.  It takes away from the fighting that you should be concentrating on, in my opinion.  Also starting a 2nd base is quite hard as you can only build in a certain radius around your other buildings, so you have to build a chain of buildings to the new location.  Usually it just isn't worth it.  There is a nice variety of units and some synergies and counters but nothing that hasn't been done before and better.  Due to the build speed and building requirements I found myself just throwing large groups at other large groups most of the time.  Not exactly my ideal RTS.  They pretty much all have this but this one if much worse in that respect.
Still a bit of fun and most missions aren't too difficult (with some major exceptions) so not a bad game to pass some time on though but there are better options out there.

A fine twin stick action game, interesting RPG mechanics and a really painful story make an excellent debut for Supergiant. Many things have been said about the story, so I'd like to focus on its' unique perspective on its' progression.
Its' a little bugbear I have with a lot of RPGs and shooters and stuff to have different equipment that's basically just number adjustments and a new model. It makes me wonder why they just don't have the same type of weapon and just escalate the difficulty through means other than number adjustments. The progression in this game really scratches that itch for me. Each weapon has a different function, and a different feel. Then there's the upgrading for those weapons. They mostly add a bunch of new mechanics. I'll use my favorites, the scrap musket and the carbine as examples. Each upgrade tier has 2 choices that are generally contrasted with each other. More AOE, less range and vice versa for the musket, for example, or more damage, slower aiming and vice versa for the carbine.
The way your character progresses is also quite interesting. All levelling up actually does for you is allow you to equip more drinks at a time, which basically give you interesting buffs. More health potions carried at a time. massive crit rate at >30% health, and you can swap each of these out to suit your playstyle. There's the shrines where you can pray to increase the difficulty in certain ways. More damage, or faster enemies, or enemies dropping explosives when they die, etc. In exchange, you get more xp and currency.
Finally, there's the training fields which are a nice little feature. Each weapon has a training field where you have to complete a bronze silver gold challenge only using that weapon that usually nets you a nice little upgrade or special move for that weapon at each tier, and the fields' challenges are unique to that weapon. The repeater has you shooting as many targets as possible on a course that falls down behind you. The bow has you trying to shoot all the targets with as few shots as possible, the hammer has you wrecking a bunch of scenery as fast as possible. They acclimate you with these weapons, and also provide a nice bit of variety to the gameplay.
Each bit of progression is a new tool in your set, which makes it stand apart from so many others in these genres, and it really needs more praise in that respect.

It is basically Mount and blade + Xcom + Darkest Dungeon and it is very well made.
Edit: For those that question the similiarities:
Similarities to M&B:
Overworld with factions all interacting.
Cities you can visit to buy equipment and find quests.
Faction leaders with which you can improve relations with.
Raising your own warband and levelling them up.
Medieval setting.
Dynamic trade.
Destroyable cities and trade lines.
Same resource system in which you have to pay and feed your members.
Similarities to Darkest Dungeon:
Both roguelikes with random generation.
Stress mechanics.
Random event mechanics.
Use of morale in combat.
Dark fantasy elements.
Characters with different traits and quirks.
Characters that interact with each other during gameplay and events.
Permanent wounds and traumas.
Similarities to Xcom:

I don't like to post reviews of Early Access games, but I promise to come back after a few Updates to change it if necessary. But I think it'll be unlikely that I'll ever recommend this game, simply because its fundamentals are about things I don't like.
Pretty much the whole design is based on time-pressure on the levels just like Spelunky. The levels are very chaotic, however, and the constant enemy respawning everywhere (including the shop!) makes the exploration feel aimless. The level also has traps, but they are mostly just VERY annoying and contribute to this overall clunky and contradictory rhythm.
The combat is based on circle-strafing and all-powerful abilities that pretty much clear the screen when used, like in bullet-hell games.
Overall it's a combination of interesting elements that just don't fit well for me. I get very annoyed playing this game, wishing it was something it isn't.
If time pressure + constantly respawning enemies + circle-strafing combat sounds good to you, you'll probably like this game. If, like me, this combination annoys you deeply, consider yourself warned.
Also, I got killed instantly by a spike trap when spawning... twice . Hope that's very high on the to-do list before release.
Other things that will probably be fixed in future updates but you should be aware of before you buy into early access:
- One low-quality music through the entire game. I recommend shutting it off to preserve your sanity.
- All traps are annoying and their placement is terrible
- Special mention goes to the world's worst "floor spike" trap. In Dungeon Souls they are a real pain and break the flow of the game as you have to carefully time your way past them every. single. time.
- Visuals are cluttered and dark already, but when loot starts dropping it gets much worse. It takes a lot of time to get used to it, expect to be constantly hit by enemies and traps that you couldn't even notice because of the lack of visual clarity
- "Easy" mode could serve as an introduction/tutorial to players, providing them with more time to read the item descriptions and to explore at a more careful pace. Instead, it is the same pushy time-pressure that you get from normal, only with less damage (and less XP, for whatever reason)

I'm not going to sit here and lie to you: I am still going to play this game even though I think it's very flawed. Why?
This may be just my completionist talking, but the game is, without a doubt, a decent game. The game is fun and if you like these game styles, it'll likely be for you, as it coincides with other games like Terraria and Minecraft. The problem is, there's no game like that that I think is actually that fun or enjoyable after a few hundred hours of gameplay. Both of those games are terribly flawed, and this game is no different to them.
Now I'm not going to complain too much about things that are insignificant that most reviews here state, like the obvious crap that all games of this genre suffer from such as pointless and boring, or sometimes insulting progression levels, because to be frank, these are issues that people who like these games don't really care about and play the games anyway, similar to how I do, because half the negative reviews, albeit having good points, still don't understand that these issues are consistent with every exploration game suffers from, and aren't exclusive to Starbound, even when they claim they are.
The game generally is flawed from the fact that the story is boring. It's REALLY boring. The dungeons are  cool-looking but generally make me bored to tears, nevermind the fetch quest crap that the game suffers from. Having to walk around every planet and finding races to talk to them so I can go fight some either stupidly-hard bosses (that don't have clear times to attack.) and go through some boring maze that has some "secrets" that aren't really worth finding. The story itself is fine, the idea of getting artifacts from each race to defeat the entity that destroyed your homeworld is great in concept, but the way they handled it was laughably terrible to the point where if there wasn't an achievement for doing it, or the promise of some great reward, there would be no reason or reccomendation in my mind for you to do it.
The issue I have with the story is that the fetch quests are terribly handled, you have to find a certain planet to go to a certain structure where you collect facts for a person that should obviously know stuff, and sometimes the areas you find don't even have everything you need, forcing you to find another place to collect facts from. This would be worth it if the dungeons were fun. They are usually just "fight a couple of enemies and fight a boss that does way too much damage if you don't fight it the way the game wants you to". You won't find much enjoyment.
Also, the fact that the game constantly begs for you to explore the way they want you to generally leaves you feeling unsatisfied. The game locks you out of areas if you don't wear the certain back-slot item, which means that you are locked out of ores until you follow the games suit, which could be seen to avoid difficulty spikes, but there's only 1 or 2 biomes that is consistently (at least in my findings) locked behind these worlds, while the rest are usually just found normally anyway. For example, you may be too cold to enter an ice world around a frozen star, but the problem is the ice world is the exact same as other ice worlds that don't require you to find something to warm yourself up with. It generally gets bland and stale, and the only reason you'd really want to do this is for the two exclusive worlds, as when the game suggests that I need to find racial colonies in areas, they can usually be found outside of those areas just fine without much trouble, but they may be a bit rarer. Nontheless, this generally just feels like a pointless feature to either halt exploration for the player, not trusting the player's intuition to see if an area is too difficult for them to enter yet.
The game generally suffers a lot from other issues that I really don't care to talk about in this review, but you get the gist. Buy the game if you like these types of games, but if you're an outsider who doesn't like games like Terraria or Minecraft, these won't be too different to you.

I really enjoyed this game. It's a tad clunky, not as polished as it could have been, but a ton of fun. The story is amazingly interesting. The unique setting is enjoyably more realist than past entries in the series, it has a touch of steampunk and a touch of fantasy but neither is overpowering. The game takes place in one big city, which is littered with lore, loot, sidequests, and main missions. Exploring the city, instead of simply being transported from mission to mission (as in previous thief games), makes the experience feel more cohesive. Furthermore, this extension of the atmosphere conveys the place of the hammers, the keepers, and the pagans more clearly. Sadly, some of the items (like the rope arrow, invisibility potion, speed and slowfall potions) from the previous games did not make an appearance. The maps are a bit cumbersome to use because your current position is never indicated, forcing you to navigate by compass; luckily levels are, generally, simply laid out...but still assuredly interesting. Great atmospheric music! The mission 'Robbing the Cradle' is spookier than most horror games and the highlight of this game IMO. Unfortunately melee combat is a bit of a joke, and load times are a bit long. Despite this game's few unpolished aspects, I think its overall game design is fantastic and its gameplay undeniably fun. It's mysterious, suspensful, and satisfying. Good game, great Thief... highly recommended for stealth fans!

Having recently finished
(it's awesome, go play it), I was really looking forward to trying out another game with a similar play style where I could mess around with a strange device and gleefully revel in seeing how everything on it reacted. Rediscovering this in my Library and loving its premise and presentation, I couldn't wait to get stuck in and unravel its mysteries. But, sadly, it fell pretty short of expectations.
Presented with a large console adorned with a single, big, red button in its centre and a small restart switch at the bottom, you're left alone with it and given one simple instruction - don't touch anything. So, naturally, you immediately start hammering the sh*t out of the big, red button. Various kinds of interactions with it reveal an array of different switches and levers and buttons and even a mini game or two as you find out all the many ways in which you show why you can't have nice things as you completely ruin everything. For each sequence of button presses and such that you complete, you're presented with its consequence on a screen above the console, most of which are very brief little pop culture references or tips of the hat to things the makers clearly love or were inspired by (inevitably including a nod most notably toward Papers, Please which feels like a big influence on its look). And that's basically the name of the game for the hour or two it should take for you to see everything. I enjoyed my first 20 or 30 minutes of this, but the fun dried up pretty quickly after that.
Of the 22 different "endings" you can get, I think I worked my way through the first half or so pretty quickly just by naturally following my curiosity and trying to pick up on the clues around me. But from then on it was a real slog as the hints became increasingly obscure and my trial and error approach yielded diminishing returns. Eventually I had to resort to a guide to get to the bottom of the final few endings as the solutions seemed to become ever more convoluted (having to Google the Fibonacci sequence was a particular low point). But while it isn't really the game's fault if I'm too stupid to figure out what's mostly in front of me, the biggest problem I really had with it was the repetition. Many of the puzzles require multiple steps, maybe about six or seven on average, but the trouble is, for quite a few of these, the first three or four of these steps, or maybe even more, will be exactly the same process, just with a slightly different finish. It made me lose interest pretty quickly as it felt like it was running out of new things to do except present me with a moderately entertaining pay-off as reward, quite a few of which seemed like they were completely unconnected to the puzzle that unlocked them.
As much as I love the idea, and do actually hope there's a sequel with a greater variety of entirely new and separate things to do with a more cohesive, connected logic to all the actions and their rewards, I just couldn't bring myself to sustain the joy of that initial wonder and potential it suggested from its start. I'm sure many will enjoy briefly dipping their toes into this and get a quick kick out of all the references they know and love, but for me, it all ended up being far too unsubstantial for me to meaningfully latch onto, and not really fun enough for me to be able to recommend.
