A little buggy here and there, but for an early access game I am absolutely stunned.
For me, the game ultimately comes down to the sense of isolation you feel. You are literally all alone out here. With only the sun on your back and the tools that you can find or build, you must survive hunger, thirst, sickness... and the sharks.
No hoards of bloodthirsty players looking to shoot you and steal your equipment.
No equaly bloodthirsty hoards of zombies ready to chase you down and chew you up at a moments notice.
This is literally You against both Nature and the Clock.
At times this can be immensely relaxing, and at others it can be frustrating as hell, but either way I found an experience something unlike any other recent survival game that Ive come across.
It left me with a smile.
Bugs (That I've noticed);
-When you row about halfway out to a different island, your raft has a high chance of disappearing and leaving you to swim either the rest of the way there or back.
-When carying a makeshift raft infront of you and you walk into it, you can end up levitating into the sky for as long as you hold down the W key. The resulting fall is not advised.
-Players shadow is invisible.
-Occasional load freezing.
...And for now, that's about it. Aside from a few other odd animation bugs, this is a remarkably clean game for something so recently released into early access!
Kudos to the developers, and I hope heartily that they continue to work out the kinks in this game (and perhaps add some more advanced building options), and make it into something truly astounding!

A fine twin stick action game, interesting RPG mechanics and a really painful story make an excellent debut for Supergiant. Many things have been said about the story, so I'd like to focus on its' unique perspective on its' progression.
Its' a little bugbear I have with a lot of RPGs and shooters and stuff to have different equipment that's basically just number adjustments and a new model. It makes me wonder why they just don't have the same type of weapon and just escalate the difficulty through means other than number adjustments. The progression in this game really scratches that itch for me. Each weapon has a different function, and a different feel. Then there's the upgrading for those weapons. They mostly add a bunch of new mechanics. I'll use my favorites, the scrap musket and the carbine as examples. Each upgrade tier has 2 choices that are generally contrasted with each other. More AOE, less range and vice versa for the musket, for example, or more damage, slower aiming and vice versa for the carbine.
The way your character progresses is also quite interesting. All levelling up actually does for you is allow you to equip more drinks at a time, which basically give you interesting buffs. More health potions carried at a time. massive crit rate at >30% health, and you can swap each of these out to suit your playstyle. There's the shrines where you can pray to increase the difficulty in certain ways. More damage, or faster enemies, or enemies dropping explosives when they die, etc. In exchange, you get more xp and currency.
Finally, there's the training fields which are a nice little feature. Each weapon has a training field where you have to complete a bronze silver gold challenge only using that weapon that usually nets you a nice little upgrade or special move for that weapon at each tier, and the fields' challenges are unique to that weapon. The repeater has you shooting as many targets as possible on a course that falls down behind you. The bow has you trying to shoot all the targets with as few shots as possible, the hammer has you wrecking a bunch of scenery as fast as possible. They acclimate you with these weapons, and also provide a nice bit of variety to the gameplay.
Each bit of progression is a new tool in your set, which makes it stand apart from so many others in these genres, and it really needs more praise in that respect.

I never played the board game but I have been a bit curious about it for some time.  I'm really glad that I picked up the computer version.  The game seems to be one of those elegant games that are easy to learn, but tough to master.
The idea is that you collect gems that you can use to purchase cards.  Cards give you bonuses towards purchasing other cards, but also can give you victory points.  To be fair to the person who goes last, the game ends at the end of the round whenever a person accumulates 15 victory points.
You also can earn 3 victory points by gaining a noble -- whenever your total bonus matches the numbers on a displayed noble, you earn that noble (assuming no one else has beaten you to him).  Earning a noble also gives you a gold gem, which is like a wild card.
The game is certainly casual and light, as strategy games go.  But it's fun.  If you want a strategy game that you can spend 15 minutes or so playing, to kill some time now and again, but will still satisfy your brain, then I highly recommend it.

Splendor is a European-style card game. It's a pretty good one at that.
Gameplay, to be simple in explaining, is picking the cards and then playing the best you can. All luck is based upon card draw, which is just like having dice (no matter how much European gamers insist otherwise). There's no online mode to square off against real, live players with different strategies. So you only get AI opponents, and they pick one of three ways to play. That's a minus overall, though to be honest the people who do play these type of games competitvely online tend to be fast, non-talkative and cut throat, which is kind of strange for a game over cards. But the randomness and good AI make up for that limitation.
I got this on a sale price on Steam, but I like this sort of thing and probably would pay full price for it. It's certainly cheaper than really buying the cards and having to convince someone to play. It's easiness and short game play are a plus, and the computer takes care of the card set up and scoring points for you.
All in all, I'd recommend it if it sounds interesting to you and is on any sale, and wholeheatedly even at full price if you're a fan of European-style board games.

Although the game takes some getting used to in terms of animation, lack of lip synchronization (at least for the English version), slow progress of actions (though primarily in the first few chapters), and mediocre voice acting, the plot is very involving and develops with some nice twists leading up to the end of the storyline. Heavily inspired by Indiana Jones - seen in the main character, fonts, music, locations, the opposing Nazi force (the bad guys of the game), and numerous verbal references - the game also exhibits elements of the mysticism, legends, and historical/"archaeological" backgrounds as typically flesh out the
series. For me, those were some of the best moments, providing the game with a sense of discovery, mystery, and conspiracy that I so enjoyed with the aforementioned series. The ending
, which in a way was a bit disappointing, yet didn't reduce the overall experience of the game, as it takes a novel approach to the concept.
Gameplay itself is excellent, with very few truly complicated puzzles yet, simultaneously, is challenging enough to remain fun. What really helps towards this is that your inventory is cleared for each new chapter, reducing the amount of combinations of objects you need to try when stuck. As there are also no ridiculous combinations between objects as in some other adventure games, all that is typically needed to progress is some time to logically think something out, or search for a possibly overlooked item. Hence, advances in the challenge of the game don't come from an inventory that grows full or becomes increasingly filled with more and more illogical items, but rather is based on an increase in the challenges of tasks you need to perform in order to progress. This culminates at the ending of the game
. Mini-games can also be played at two levels of difficulty, making the game easy to progress in, yet at your own level of difficulty.
The game includes bonus features
.
Overall, though I completed the game quite rapidly (in about 13 hours), I very much enjoyed playing it. If you like the Lucas Arts adventure game series - including the likes of

series, and are a fan of Indiana Jones, this is definitely a game to add to your collection!

EDIT: after playing more, I feel like editing my review.
I wish there was a neutral button, but I will settle for negative because the game doesn't deserve the absolute praise it gets. If it was the other way, I would score it positive to balance. Battle Brothers has some very good things and some fatal flaws. It is one of those RNG-heavy, grind-heavy games like Darkest Dungeon. I prefer my games to be deterministic, but in all fairness the RNG can be mitigated a bit in this one (taking spears, surrounding the enemy): nevertheless, there will be a time when the enemy marksman will score a critical hit and kill your archer outright. That would not be a problem, if training a replacement wasn't so slow and tedious.
Basically, the whole thing goes like this: take a contract, fight a battle, take some losses that may or may not be your fault, then recruit other mercenaries and build them up fighting other battles, till you lose them too and the process starts again. There is very little in the way of permanent perks for you warband, so when you lose people you're basically back to square one. Money is hard to come by even on the middle-tier difficulty, equipment is expensive and you lose it if you retreat leaving people on the ground. A nasty defeat just adds hours of grind to your campaign. You can partially counter that by playing on the lower difficulty level, but that's simply too easy for a veteran strategy player. The higher ones, I don't even think they are more difficult: they are just more tedious and inflict more busywork on you.
The turn-based combat system, on the other hand, is very good and has a lot of nuances, and can keep you entertained for a long time. The gritty atmosphere is great, the variation in weapons interesting, so if you don't mind grinding (but be advised, it is really over the top) you'll find this fun. I find this fun occasionally. But I want games to respect my free time and don't force me into loops of repetitive actions because of bad dice rolls.

Battle Brothers is a high-stakes tactical turn-based RPG for high-stakes gamers.  In this game, you carefully craft a team of ruthless sellswords out of a rabble of farmers, cripples and gravediggers and set out to become the most renowned mercenary company in the land.  Carefully craft your team with an enormous variety of skills, weapons and armor.  Name them, love them, and watch them die.  The game features a wide array of enemies to face, from bandits to orcs to undead and more.  Each enemy type has certain strengths and weaknesses and you must ensure that your brothers are versatile enough to handle anything that might come their way.
This is a game where the best made plans are laid to waste.  Sooner or later, your enemies will land that fatal blow that sends your poor mercenary's head flying across the battlefield.  This is not a game for people who frustrate easily;  while you can play by saving before each encounter and reloading until you like the outcome, the game was intended to be played in Ironman mode, where the game saves automatically and you cannot save scum.
Battle Brothers will have you shouting for joy, cursing at your monitor, and sadly shaking your head at the screen, and you will keep coming back for more punishment.

I have been playing Starbound since it first came out on Early Access, having been an pre-EA backer. I have seen all the changes and directions the game has taken since then, and I still love Starbound. While I do have my criticisms, which I will go into, I would recommend the purchase to those who have the right mindset. However, I also feel that is a problem among its userbase; a widespread misunderstanding of what Starbound is.
I have heard throughout the game's development that it's "Terraria in space." I find this to be absurd, because it's inaccurate. It is not meant to be like Terraria and never was. If I was to make a comparison, I would say it's "2D Minecraft in space." It has far more in common with Minecraft than it does Terraria, despite what similarities might be skimmed from the surface in relation to Terraria.
Terraria is, at it's core, not necessarily about exploration and creativity. Those are fairly secondary; instead, its main focuses are about combat (especially bosses and events) and progression. You gear up to face your first boss, defeat it, gear up for the second one, defeat it, gear up for the third one, etc. That's its real strength. That's not what Starboud is really about.
Minecraft, on the other hand, is absolutely about exploration and creativity. It's (for the sake of argument) an infinite world with infinite resources. A huge open map to play with, and in Starbound you have an infinite universe to explore full of planets both large and small. The very nature of Starbound is about exploration, even moreso than in Minecraft. You have to explore your first planet to get off of it. You have to explore  your first planetary system to reach a new system. You have to explore those new systems to further explore other systems.
Exploration is priority in Starbound and that is the kind of mindset you have to approach it with. On top of that,  you should have a creative approach to it. Yes, you can use your ship as your base, and never need to build a structure on the surface of a planet, but if that's how you're coming at the game, I feel you may be making a mistake. This is a game where you should approach it with the sense of "wanting" to build, or at the very least, wanting to decorate your ship in unique styles and decorations. Simply put, it has greater emphasis on the "sandbox" part, like Minecraft, over the other stuff, which is what Terraria is more interested in.
Now, as I said, I do recommend the game. I feel it's current price of $15 USD is reasonable. However, it does have issues that leave me with a fair amount of criticism.
- The most of the tech upgrades are fairly situational and, quite frankly, you may not get much use out of them. While some are improvements over previous techs that didn't make the final cut, I feel some of those on the chopping block would have made for better inclusion with some tweaking. As it stands, I typically only use spike sphere (aqua if on an ocean planet), sprint, and pulse jump.
- Pets are, unfortunately, rather underwhelming, at least from what experience I've had with them. While I appreciate the idea that their stats are tied to the armor you're wearing, they still often feel too weak and vulnerable. Furthermore, you're unable to heal them if they are defeat until considerably later, when you can finally build a Pet Station and are able to make a Pet Healing Station from it, in spite of the fact you can get capture pods as early as the Erchius Mining Facility.
- Pet collars and EPP augments are, quite frustratingly, not swappable. If you try to change a collar or augment, it actually deletes the old one, instead of returning it to your inventory. That is quite ridiculous. Furthermore, the EPP only ever has one slot for augments, despite having a fair variety of them. This severely restricts their usefulness, which is compounded by the previous problem. And considering the EPP is absolutely necessary beyond Temperate stars, this also restricts the usefulness of your lighting gear, such as the Lantern Stick or Miner's Helmet, meaning they're used more as vanity than utility devices.
- A smaller issue for me. I support the idea of the Erchius Ghost, an unkillable enemy that makes gathering fuel from any moon a potentially dangerous venture. It used to be you could dig down into a moon, and farm not only enouogh fuel to fill your tank, but enough reserve fuel to fill up all of its spare slots as well. While the Erchius Ghost is there to offset that, I feel it could use some balancing, and perhaps a way to defend against it in late-game, since as long as you're careful and don't get greedy between trips, it's more of an annoyance than a genuine threat.
- Hoverbikes are... meh. They don't really climb up hills well, they get stuck a lot, you can't really go through buildings with them. If I want to travel across a planet, it feels like I'm constantly stopping to pack it up, then dropping it down again to go a short distance before I have to rinse-repeat. It's almost better just to go on foot.
- Sadly, the racial weapons were removed. I had heard it was due to how they reworked the way sprites were adapted into the game, which would've meant having to redo a fairly hefty amount of weapons, and I certainly hope they make their return in the future, but the fact they're gone is sad.
Now, this is all not to say there hasn't been any improvements, mind you. While I would like to see a bit more inventory space per tab, there only used to be three tabs instead of five, so that's an improvement. Although, being able to put an item directly into any tab would be nice instead of the game forcing it into a specific one. The hotbar was considerably improved, if you ask me. The way the codex is organized is much cleaner than before, where all the entries were just one big old list. There are more types of planets than back in the early days, and the planets now have sub-biomes to them. You can now just scan objects to register them into the 3D Printer, when it used to be you had to collect it and let SAIL destroy it to "scan" it. The Separator, Manipulator, and Accelerator are now addons to the Replicator, whereas before they were each their own unique crafting table. Weapons now have special abilities.
So, there has been improvements, and there has been some stuff I feel are setbacks that I hope they improve on. Overall though, I would still recommend the game if you treat it more like Minecraft than Terraria, like I said. And, again, as I said earlier, $15 USD is a fair price. So if you're interesting in exploring and bulding over combat, give it a go.
Also, it has the most wonderfully soothing title theme I think I've ever heard.

I've been playing Kritika since the SEA version, so my Steam play time doesn't reflect my actual play time, which is probably around 150 hours by now, I think. This Kritika Online is published by En Masse and they can only maintain US and EU.
is probably the best Dungeon Crawler MMO I've played to date. I have played a lot of them and this just feels better.
is super fast-paced and destroying the enemies is satisfying. Insane difficulty dungeons can be a fair challenge, but once you beat an encounter, it creates a nice feeling of accomplishment. Enemy hitboxes have so far been fine, I have not come across enemies, where you should've been hitting and didn't. You also have crowd control abilities and can dodge out of the way, if you feel like you're about to get overwhelmed.
Unique to this game (as far as I know. Never seen it in other games of this type) is the fact, that they promote playing multiple characters. You get passive boosts for having more than one character active, and these bonuses can also just help you level alts faster. I love to create one of most of a game's classes in MMOs to play through, but this game actually rewards you for doing just that.
is a subjective matter in the Dungeon Crawler genre. This game is no different in the sense, that content does get repetitive, when you play a lot of it, but it hasn't bothered me in most Dungeon Crawlers, and neither does it bother me here. I think it helps, that here bosses do different things, so you have to play differently, when going against them (Although some of the bosses can be stunlocked, so I guess with those bosses you don't have to really make up tactics)
are released on a regular basis. Hopefully that will continue in the future. It's always nice to see developers actually care and support their game, which isn't all that common in MMOs, especially P2P. So far I have also not had any issues with updates at all.
I think that sums it up for now. The game performs well, feels great, is supported, and for Dungeon Crawler fans is probably the best option (That's of course an opinion).

Stacking is another game that won me over with its gameplay, while also having enough visual charm to stand out from the crowd.  I'm a pretty big fan of Double Fine games such as Psychonauts and Costume Quest, but I wasn't sure what to expect out of Stacking.  Thankfully, the game keeps the quirky humor behind Schafer's other games while introducing a mechanic I've yet to see in any other game.  I suppose the mechanic of using NPC abilities for your own purpose has been used before, but not while combining it with Russian matryoshka dolls!  This gives a different layer of puzzles as you can only stack into dolls one size larger than you, and sometimes you need to be sure to stack into several particular dolls so you can use their abilities one after another.  Overall, Stacking is not too difficult unless you intentionally decide to seek out the extra challenges, and the narrative is pretty cheesy and unmemorable (which was a disappointment after Psychonauts).  The charm and the unique gameplay won me over though!

There are some REALLY glaring oversights that make the game not worth playing in its current iteration, which is somewhat understandable for an Early Access Game. Although, why would you bother going to Early Access if your game isn't fun to play yet?!
Most disturbing is the lack of mouse support on the main menu. Without mouse support, the main menu becomes a puzzle in its own right. Arrow keys? No. Press Enter? NOPE. Try the mouse again? Nothing.
You have to use ASWD on the menu. WTF?! But how do you select options, you ask, if it's not enter. With SPACEBAR of course.
After picking from one of three characters (more can be unlocked, to be implemented later I take it), you're dropped into a great pixelated dungeon, usually right on top of enemies. You'll be taking damage from the second you start playing, and it doesn't stop until you die. I mean that. It never stops. Want to spend the point you earned from leveling up? No time. The character sheet nor inventory pause the game. Basically, if you bother to read anything or attempt to understand any nuance of the game, you'll die. Why on God's green earth was this deemed a good idea? I'm not even playing a multiplayer game. I just want a damn second to read what my abilities do. But you don't have a second. Read, and you die. That's the moral of this game.
Also, it lacks controller support. It's a twin stick shooter... that lacks controller support. Let that soak in. I mean, did everyone forget that twin stick shooters were born in the arcade?! That the WHOLE point was to have independent control of movement and shooting via two separate analog joysticks? Hence, twin stick. Why wasn't this game built from the ground up to support controllers? Do they have any hope of releasing to other platforms? They should! Because the design, aesthetic, art are otherwise fantastic. It just suffers from some REALLY bad production decisions.
This game is in VERY early access. It has great potential though. Wait for release, otherwise we're sending developers the wrong message. That message being, "Yes, yes I will pay for your proof of concept."

This fairly recent mobile port by developer Days of Wonder is a direct translation of the competitive multiplayer strategy card game from designer Marc André and publisher Space Cowboys.
Players assume the role of Renaissance era merchants as they seek to secure cards that represent the various mines, cargo ships and bazaars responsible for the acquisition and distribution of their valuable gem stones.
The first thing that strikes you about Splendor - other than its rather fantastic artwork - is just how simple it is for a novice to jump into the game. It's fast to learn and the equally swift pace of play gives it an addictive 'one more go' sensation that's hard to resist.
Despite its inherent simplicity, there are some interesting layers of strategy bubbling beneath the surface and although it might take you 5 minutes to pick up the basics, it will likely take another 5 hours before you'll really begin appreciating the most efficient paths towards victory.
Like most "Euro" style board games, Splendor features very rigidly defined mechanics at the expense of theme, but what helps it succeed is the variety of strategies that you employ from session to session.
Specializing in a specific type of gem, or "buying all the greens" for example, could be a legitimate approach should the initial setup feature several high-scoring cards with a suitably steep emerald cost.
Alternatively you might decide to downplay the importance of the expensive tier 3 cards entirely and balance out your purchases as equally as possible in order to attract the lucrative noble cards into your tableau.
It's even possible to play an opportunist role; collecting as many gem and gold tokens as the limit allows whilst waiting for the other players to reveal the cheaper bonus cards that will allow you to maximize your profit margin.
You won't ever get into the feeling of being an actual gem dealer, as Splendor is more a game of numbers than anything else, but the wonderful artwork from artist Pascal Quidault certainly does a good job of making each card evocative of its period setting.
Reputedly inspired by Anglo-saxon artists, Quidault effortlessly breathes life into what could easily have been a very sterile game with his various illustrations of appraisers, expeditions and Renaissance settlements giving the production a certain level of authenticity and class.
Much of what I've said above translates into the Steam version very well. The high definition UI and card graphics successfully remain true to the original game and there's some added value in the form of crafty AI opponents, achievements and a handful of single player challenge packs.
Similar to chess puzzles, the themed challenges in this digital version are an interesting addition that task a player with striving towards a particular goal such as earning a set amount of points in a limited number of turns or collecting a combination of cards without the assistance of added gem tokens.
Whilst the difficult challenges in this sense do provide a satisfyingly "thinky" experience, it has to be said that there's really not enough of them.
The easy challenges by comparison - which sadly represent the bulk of the pack - are too often dull and repetitive affairs that sometimes don't even present you with a failure condition; usually meaning that you simply need to collect points aimlessly until reaching a preset amount.
Some of the nuance in Splendor's flow of play is also lost when playing against AI opponents. I haven't played the original board game itself, but I can easily see the potential that exists for blocking competing players.
This is not a game of direct interaction, but the competition over resources is sorely missed in the digital version as AI players mostly seem to ignore your efforts in favour of building their own point-accumulating engine.
There's no online mutliplayer included in the digital rendition either, although there is a hotseat multiplayer mode for up to four players as well as leaderboards for those players who are willing to register an account at the publisher's website.
Perhaps the most jarring facets of the Steam version though are the rough edges brought about by its port over from mobile devices.
Some of these gripes are minor, like the multiplayer section which is still named "pass and play" (instead of the more traditional "hotseat") and the menu dialog which asks you if you wish to "exit the app" instead of "exit the game".
Other problems are more severe however, like the fuzzy or sometimes missing text on the challenge menus, the overly repetitive music and the lack of difficulty settings for the AI players.
The Steam store page is also inundated with customers reporting crash-to-desktop errors and I can attest to experiencing a dreaded CTD once myself when trying to start a new game from the main menu.
These problems certainly make this Steam version a disappointment at times, but I don't feel that they're serious enough to deter from the strength of the original game's design as it's that strong on the basis of its own merits.

This game rocks.  You command a company of murderhobos going across the land trying to get paid by killing things.   You fight in a turn-based system on a hex grid, and between battles you wander on the world map looking for clients or foes.  The context is a well fleshed-out low-magic late medieval/early renaissance setting.
The battles in this game are intense.  The AI is pretty relentless, and the odds are often not in your favor.  You fight a variety of foes, including bandits, orcs, goblins, and the undead.  The major factions are all well-developed and each fight in a distinctive style: mindless Wiederganger zombies shamble at your men without pause, while crafty goblins harass you with hit-and-run tactics with their bows, poison, and nets.  Every moment counts because if you are unlucky your men can drop from perfect health to dead or nearly so in the flash of an eye.  You can and will lose men, especially if you're playing on Ironman.  You need to manage the fatigue system to make sure your advances don't run out of steam.  The morale system also provides a cool way of modeling the tide of battle turning.
You manage the general business of the company, giving you a pause from the intensity of battle.  You have to make sure your men are paid, fed, and well-supplied.  You also customize your company by buying equipment upgrades (or loot and repair them from your fallen foes) and leveling up your men as they accumulate experience.  This consists of increasing basic attributes as well as choosing special perks from a tree.  An example is 'Pathfinder', which reduces the movement cost of uneven terrain.  I will note that the attributes aren't quite made equal; for instance, most Brothers need increases to their Melee Skill, Melee Defense, and maximum Fatigue, whereas increased Initiative rarely seems comparably worthwhile.
The game is not a sandbox per se, but has many similarities.  You are occasionally pursued on the road by wandering raiders, but the vast majority of battles will be chosen by the player via the contracts system.  For instance, this allows you to take your time with a hopefully sedate courier or caravan mission while your company is repairing its equipment and healing the temporary injuries suffered in battle.  The game has an ambition system giving you medium-term goals for building up your company.  The game until recently had an open-ended endgame (enemy groups get increasingly dangerous), but the developers recently implemented a late-game crisis system, introducing one of three possible world-changing events to deal with.  These can be disabled, however, if you prefer more of a sandbox.
This game was made by a small team, but does very well on the art front given their constraints.  The unit sprites don't seem impressive at first, until you start to pay attention to details.  Armor shows damage as it's degraded, and injured brothers start to look increasingly beat-up.  There is distinct music for various enemy factions, and the sound effects do a chillingly good job of making battle feel visceral and brutal.  Every contract includes little vignettes of the interactions, and the game also has random events.  In both of these cases the writing does a good job evoking a grim, unforgiving world.
I picked up the game late in the Early Access period, and during that time the developers have been actively supporting the game with bugfixes and balance tweaks.  I hope the sales provide them with the ability to continue to give support and possibly even to add more content.
All in all, this game does an excellent job of making you tell yourself 'OK, just one more contract' again and again.  The combat and leveling systems are deep enough to make winning against the odds feel thrilling, and due to the lethality of battle every clean victory is met with a sigh of relief.  A single campaign is easily dozens of hours, and the procedural nature of the world means that if the game clicks for you the replayability is nearly endless.

This is a real hidden gem of a traditional point and click adventure. On seeing the title screen it becomes obvious how much care has gone into every aspect of this game.
The plot and cinematic style of Lost Horizon  are a homage to adventure films of an 'Indiana Jones' type. It's all about a reluctant hero saving the world from Nazis who are after powerful mystical secrets and has everything you'd expect: biplane fights, secret mystical locations all over the world, ridiculous car chases and cutscenes of implausible fights on Nazi trucks.  Oh, of course, the spunky irritating sidekick/love interest - I suppose nothing's perfect.
If you have played the LucasArts classic  'Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis,' you'd probably find this is really similar in writing, plot depth and gameplay style and there are other things that will make you think the writers were trying to bring back the old Lucas Arts classics. For those who haven't...
The best bits
-The plot is daft but fun and interesting with lots of mystery, pseudoscience and silly cutscene action.
- This is a properly long game. Really good value for money.  12-15 hours gameplay I'd say.
-The puzzles are mostly combining inventory items together or with objects in the environment. These are (with a few glaring exceptions) very logical.
- The visuals are gorgeous.
-The voice acting is excellent.
-The music was good though not hugely memorable.
-The interface was easy to use with one exception (see below)
Bad points
-Some of the puzzles cannot be solved until you've examined an object to death because your player character is a fool that needs everything spleed out to him.
-There seems to be a minor bug where when you try to solve a puzzle correctly  with an object, the game doesn't recognise which object you're trying to use. It always works by the third attempt.
- The two cursor interface can make some puzzles a bit easy.
Highly recommended, particularly if you like inventory based point and clicks with engaging plots.

You can tell a lot about the game by its ending, or - more precisely - by the feeling you get when you've reached it. If you feel like "at last! my suffering is over", or "and that's it?!", or "wtf was that?!", it means the game probably did not deserve to be finished at all. If you forgot where you are or who you are and it was you who was that guy who kissed the girl in the end - that is the sign of a great game. But when it comes to _good_ games, one can always be recognised when you feel sad that it's over. And that's exactly how I felt when I finished Lost Horizon.
The game is safe from anything edgy or grandious to be an outstanding title, and that's probably why I have completely missed it when it came out. But with its beautiful art, solid feel, enjoyable puzzles, super easy mechanics and pretty good voice acting, it's far from being a waste of time. I'm sad it's over not because I'm disappointed, but because I enjoyed the process of playing it. It was not an epic rollercoaster ride, but a journey equally pleasant all way through. With this game you get the kick in playing it, not in getting it finished.
Influenced heavily by adventure films and games of the past, but not making a direct adaptation of the Lost Horizon novel, developers played safe to avoid a disappointment. It feels as if they are saying: "We are not making revolutions here, we are just following the great tradition". Lost Horizon will not shock you, will not turn your world upside down, will not break the grounds, but if you like the classic feel of adventure titles, you will enjoy it. It will not insult your intellect, or upset your ear with speech impedimented voice actors. It will please your eye with the striking beauty of its backgrounds and sometimes will give you a chuckle or two with a clever joke. The idea of hand-drawn backgrounds and 3D-animated characters seems to be the perfect approach. The only thing that stops this game from being great is that developers did not have a megalomaniac urge to make the best game in the world. They just did a good game, and that's what it is. And I think, it is better to make a good game and succeed at that, than try making a great game and fail to deliver.
So, if you like old Indiana Jones games, or the Broken Sword series, you will most likely enjoy this one. Just don't expect much - and you'll be pleasantly surprised on every corner. I was!

The last game in the Thief series, before its reboot, and I just can't play it. I have played all three of the games in order, without ever having played any of them before. To make matters short, at least at the front of this review, the only game I like out of the three is Thief II, though I only really enjoyed about 60% of that game and found the rest of it rather lackluster.
As my other reviews say, the first Thief was good in virtually everything except for the level design, which killed it for me. The second game continued with all of the proper mechanics and had much better levels, at least for 60% of the game (as said above). This game, however, has much more issues with it than just the levels.
Firstly, the game is terribly optimized with a horrible engine. From the start of the game, I had this weird stuttering issue where the camera would essentially shake as I looked around, bugging my eyes. Even with patches and such, the problem still occurred, though eventually it vanished for some weird reason. Regardless, that ended up just foreshadowing everything else I would have problems with in the game.
The game even just crashed multiple times for me, for what reasons I could never tell. I never had either of the first two games crash or freeze (nor did System Shock 2).
The levels themselves take a relatively long time to load. Now, I'm not an impatient person, and I understand if the level is initially loading up for the first time, but even just reloading a save I made 10 seconds ago will end up taking nearly 1 minute or more to load. The game first just goes to a black screen for about 20 seconds, then it will go to a loading screen, and finally get back to the level. But the weird thing is, about 50% of the time I would load a save or a new area would start up, the game would do a weird "freeze." The level would render but there would be no sound, and I couldn't move, attack, look around, jump, or do anything at all. What is odd is that the level would "start" in a halfway manner. For instance, at the beginning of the second mission, I could see subtitles of the guards talking outside, but the sound wouldn't play. Then about 20 seconds or more later, I could finally move and the sound would start, in the middle of their conversation. This happened in any place that I would load or enter.
In terms of the controls, nothing is smooth. Just walking straight would have the game become choppy occasionally, but not because of a frame-rate drop. Getting near walls, even several inches away, would sometimes cause me to stop moving properly at the same speed. Leaning left and right is terribly slow and choppy. Jumping feels like you are disconnecting and reconnecting yourself via a chain to the ground. The third person isn't really anything well done. And of course, I ended up no-clipping through some walls in a few places and dying.
Even attacking isn't proper. The very first guy I went up to in the second mission, I tried to use the blackjack on him. I was standing exactly behind him and never moved, and it took FIVE times for the blackjack to connect and knock him out. The first four times it just swung and nothing happened. I didn't bother moving, nor did I look at a different angle. I just stood exactly still and it missed four times, while neither of us moved.
Further, just in the second mission, the game made me lose my controls multiple times as well. I don't know what made it occur, but twice when I was walking around, the game suddenly disabled my ability to creep, crouch, jump, or press against the walls. I could still walk and run, and I could still swing weapons or shoot arrows, but anything that required me to change my stature or get off the ground wouldn't work and I had to reload.
In terms of looks, the graphics are somewhat better drawn, but they look more dull and less life-like. They don't render properly either, often flickering or disappearing throughout the level. The compass and visibility marker at the bottom is ugly; the menus are worse in design, and it is silly that things like options aren't available unless you quit the game. Big shining objects and doors are annoying.
The game is missing some interesting items such as the Rope Arrow. The lockpicking is really nothing better than before. I thought it was better at first, because it was more interactive instead of just waiting, but in reality, you just twirl the mouse while clicking over and over. The only thing remotely better is the inventory as you can see the items as you swap through them, instead of trying to remember where a given item is in the list.
Then you have the AI which is dumber than the first two games. I saw multiple guards walking into walls repeatedly. One even got onto a set of stairs, then went down 3 steps, back up, then back down, over and over in circles. Even more funny, in the City Hub, I knocked out random civilians and people just walked by them as if nothing was there.
That's another thing... the City Hub. I thought it was going to be an interesting addition, but in fact, it isn't really. The areas I explored weren't that big, and there's only like 5 doors you can go into at a given time anyway. Essentially, it seems it only exists to add more roadblocks between you and your next mission, including having to repeatedly return to sell loot and buy new items (though I understand that more so). But really, it is a boring stopping point between missions.
Now, despite my complaints with the first two Thief games, as I said, I thought Thief II was the best (which seems the general consensus) and I really enjoy the story and world atmosphere. However, I think the interior of the games actually ruin those things, for the most part. I didn't even get far enough into this game to see where the story was going, because of all of the above issues; but I finished both of the first two Thief games, even though I nearly hated the first one because of its levels.
This game was easily the worst of the three overall, and I just can't put myself through anymore of it. Next, I will try my luck with the Thief reboot, though I already hear many people hate it. Here is hoping there are some better things done with it in comparison to Deadly Shadows.

I'm excited that KO finally came to Steam, so hopefully that helps with player numbers.
Yet as for KO itself, it is a genuinely good game. It may not be the best but it stands out in comparison to others I've played and I've had quite a fun time for the past month. While I do enjoy the game, I'll try not to be biased.
Pros:
- Decent to good graphics, framerate holds up well in most stressed situations.
- Soundtrack to me is quite well done, its a nice mix of rock and orchestra. Somewhat generic but at least it helps fit the game and the gameplay.
- The gameplay itself and combat is fast-paced but not hard to get used to. Early game is relatively easy and it helps you ease into your first character or a class thats different than what you normally like. It basically offers a fair chance.
- Combat once more, is satisfying. When you get your skills together and learn how to use them appropriately, its not only fun but you actually feel like you're hurting the enemy. Especially since some classes are slow but hard, hard hitters, or opportunistic strikers, or even bombarding with constant attacks. Now the speed is relative but you get a feel for it when you play more classes.
- Partial voice acting. While not entirely voice-acted, the player characters have many voice lines during their gameplay that helps give a personality. Some npcs are as well, but its mostly just greeting messages, or random babble. Better than nothing and helps give atmosphere.
- Dungeons, enemies, and bosses are at the least decently structured and planned. Dungeon running is normally fast where it only takes a few minutes for longer dungeons with a full party or an adept player going solo. Most bosses up to the level cap have neglectable mechanics, but some can give you a hard time, which is good. It all can't be easy.
- Endgame content does exist and its not entirely singular. It is also decently populated and finding groups isn't too hard.
- The guild system is nice as of this moment, you can hold a lot of players within higher level guilds and there's many nice little benefits. Like a free title you can ask for and stuff to buy with guild coins.
- Various jobs to choose from even if there are only 4 classes as of the base release (more will come later such as Eclair/Psion later October 2017). Most feel different from each other and offer unique approaches to how you attack and rotate skills.
- Besides Endgame content, there's much other content you can do without being at level cap. Such as Letter Runs during dungeons that give a bit more nice loot, the Arena which is a floor-based boss rush, and daily dungeons.
Cons:
- While its obvious every game has its glitches, bugs and whatnot, it kinda shows more in this game. While none are horribly game breaking, some are odd and hard to ignore such as standing on invisible walls in PvP with certain classes and skills, going outside of a certain PvP map, and some Arena problems and other PvE boss quirks. Hopefully these will be ironed out soon.
- Lower population. While endgame does have a population, the road to level cap can be a bit iffy on players. Some areas are dead, some are low, and some may be populated but the problem with such areas is that they have a level split. For example, an area called Deeprock Mines has 17-25~ content while also having 58-60~ content. While some people may help lower levels, they have their own goals of course and it creates an odd atmosphere. Hopefully this problem goes away after Steam release or if it grows more popular.
- As of the time of this review, meta-classes are more pronounced in KO than some others I've played. Of course most if not all games have "the best set of classes" but here its almost night and day as to what they are. Obviously any class is good if you play it well and some people can really even it out, but sometimes its hard to ignore that the "lesser" classes do often have numbers that keep them just a bit behind the wave.
- Not much character creation is available, on top of the gender-locked classes. While some may not care about gender-locking, others do and it can be seen as a problem. While a good array of outfits and styles are free, some are only paid for. Game has to make money somehow at least.
- The game is a little grindy, while not as bad as others, it does add up time and effort especially if you have alts, which funny enough this game encourages in many ways.
- Story is uhh... lackluster. Easily skippable. Some may find it interesting, maybe more when there's additional content, but as of now its not a good detail.
Other points:
- There is a bit of sexualization in this game. You grow to not care after a bit or you're just not bothered beforehand. Yet I can understand for others its a deterrence. Really its easy to ignore when the game's real focus is its great combat.
- From my perspective and opinion, the game isn't terribly pay-to-win. You can reach high Combat Rating, or your fighting prowess, by not spending a dime to achieve it. At least one person I talked about it with got to a high cr, enough to stomp most endgame content, without spending real life currency.
- As mentioned, there are a nice array of free-to-get costumes and styles. You just need to put your time in, which in the process you're nicely rewarded.
As of writing this review, thats most of what I can think of. There may be other pros and cons, but you can either find them yourself by playing or look at more reviews, or even talk to regular KO players. Especially regarding PvP, as I only do PvP dailies and for those, no one actually tries. You can just let each other win.

World of castle is a medieval castle builder sandbox, which will feature action strategy/RPG combat, already in its earliest stages the game looks promising, as of this review will be of the currently implemented features.
Unlimited sandbox build mode
Flag customization tool
Marshal skill tree and equipment tool
While the finished game will include both PvE and PVP modes, right now the combat is not implemented so that will not be discussed at this point, however, I can say based on the quality of whats already in-game, the upcoming combat and siege based mechanics will be well planned and implemented.
In the current unlimited sandbox mode you can build to your hearts content, much like other games creative modes this gives you a chance to sample all of the parts currently in-game and create some truly majestic structures, I felt like a kid again, building a castle made out of lego for an upcoming epic battle, I can only imagine the thrill when the combat is added of defending my castle from others!
The addition of the upcoming prestige mechanics which allow unlocking of better parts by exp and victories will only enhance the feeling of childlike wonder for more hardcore gamers while allowing those who simply wish to build the creative mode to enjoy.
The flag customization tool is surprisingly in-depth for an early access title, I was able to create a stylish version of my own welsh flag in minutes, the graphics for the flags and banners are very well made and look fantastic on shields also.
The marshal system while not fully fleshed out at this point allows a good range of custom armoring from peasant chic to the French heavy knight, items from different sets can be mixed and matches also to allow a unique look.
While the current price of £22.99 is too high for whats here currently, you must understand that price includes cost of all the features we have yet to receive, once everything that is planned is manifested in-game the price will be a complete bargain, do not let the current early versions dissuade you from this purchase, the devs have already created a quality title that has surprisingly good fps for an alpha version and shows the love and dedication they have for the project, and with time it will only improve to something even better.

A different take on simplistic platformer with some interesting level mechanics.  Good, fast paced, active level designs make me dissapointed that I ran into a bug that severely undercut the tight controls that should be expected in any platformer.
The setup is simple: you can jump, double jump (more of an air dash), stick to walls, and wall jump.  Each level is an enclosed space with obstacles ranging from a wave of projectiles firing straight across the stage to laser guided turrets and death zones.  It is an engaging, albeit somewhat easy and short platformer in campaign mode.  The multiplayer mode does not interest me personally, but with how frantic that game can be I'm sure it makes a good multiplayer experience for the people looking for it.
Something I personally don't like about the core gameplay is that platforms and walls react differently to the player depending on if a flat surface or a corner of your playable square contact the platform/wall, but you are not given a way to manually rotate the square AND when you jump you cannot be sure if you will be rotating in the air at all, making anticipating your landings impossible.
As of the time of writing, the game is in early access and buggy.  There is at least one bug pertaining to platforming controls, specifically walljumping when in "simple" graphics mode which made some later stages artificially difficult.  There are also many bugs with the boss levels, either visual bugs so you are missing very important information about what the boss is doing, or flat out soft-locks.  The game is still in early access so bugs are somewhat to be expected, but as I said the walljump bug crippled my ability to play.
That being said my original review was based on the walljump bug being an intended mechanic, and the dev was quick to reach out and help me band-aid the bug by using different graphics setting and it seems they will look into fixing the bug outright, so as far as development of an early access game goes it looks promising.
I have edited my original review that was based on a bug that I thought was intended, and changed my recommendation from "No" to "Yes" based on developer response (and assumed future fix) to the bug in question.

I played Starbound for a while pre-release, coming back every few months or years (yes, the development period was THAT LONG) to see what was new.
Over all that time, the game hasn't really changed much. Actually, if anything, it is more flimsy, buggy, and grindy than it was before.
The story is simply stupid, boring, and uninteresting. Chucklefish scrapped the opportunity for varied character backgrounds and railroaded every race and every character into the same opening sequence and plotline crammed with weak dialogue and annoying fetch quests. Most of the game is spent running around to different planets hunting down race-specific settlements so you can scan their funiture and then occasionally go do a dungeon with a boss that is way easier than the rest of the dungeon you just came through.
As a sandbox game, there is yet more railroading. There is nothing to do but grind for resources, so you can upgrade your stuff, so you can grind for resources, so you can upgrade; and onwards. You can make settlements, but your settlers don't DO anything. The game makes it hard to be a bad guy, since all non-hostile NPCs are invincible and the only way to MAKE them hostile is to break their houses and steal their blocks (or accidentally "steal" their blocks when a weather event breaks their buildings). The side quests are all the same boring, vapid fetch quests, escort quests, kill quests.
The only fun thing I've done is run around on high level planets with low-level gear, doing "big game hunting." That can get exciting, especially if you up the stakes on hardcore mode or are carrying a bunch of rare stuff with you. Oh, by the way, you can't change difficulty after you start. Because... reasons.
PvP would be a nice addition. I'm thinking in the vein of Dark Souls or even Ultima/Eve Online, where you git gud or die. Could add some excitement.
There is some solace to be had in building things, if you're into that. And perhaps more mods will come to fix these problems and add cool stories. But right now Starbound is dull. Put it on the backburner, maybe torrent it if you really want to try it (the devs themselves had recommended that course of action, actually). Otherwise, remember it as an example of what a project looks like with no direction and no deadline discipline.

Frantic, tense gameplay mixed with beautiful music, pixel art, and RPG elements – Dungeon Souls is a hectic, punishing ride I love to take.
An indie roguelike RPG with a heavy focus on its gameplay, Dungeon Souls won’t be foreign to those familiar with Hammerwatch or the Binding of Isaac, as the player is pitted into a cruel world where absolutely everything wants to murder you. To survive, the player must run, kill, level up, gather items, master skills, and run and kill some more.
It’s set in a fantasy world where after choosing one of several available character classes, such as the Barbarian, Archer, and Thief, the player must fight their way through hordes of mobs and bosses, gaining powers and facing tougher fights with each floor. Each level is also procedurally generated, making every playthrough unique and vastly more enjoyable had it not been.
One of the greatest strengths of Dungeon Souls is the balance among the character classes. The Barbarian is tough and meant to be tossed into the fray. It deals decent enough damage, but is slower compared to its long-range counterparts. The Thief is light-footed, can deal decent ranged attacks and has the highest critical-hit damage. But, the HP is quite low, along with its defense. Even though they’re vastly different, neither of the classes felt imbalanced, but rather only changed how I approached my game.
The only downside I saw was the lack of co-op. As of now the game is still in Early Access, and the developers state the full version will feature multiplayer. Given that, I do have to knock it down a point for what I played myself at this time. When multiplayer gets up and running I’ll gladly revisit this and adjust accordingly.

Bastion is a isometric action rpg with heaps of charm.
The plot is simple, someone or something blew up a massive chunk of the world and now most of it is floating around in space, you meet an old man with a voice like molasses coated gravel who is also the narrator. He tells you to help him fix the bastion, a device that can apparently fix everything. It gets deeper and more complex a little later on, but no spoilers.
Gameplay is pretty easy to understand, throughout the game you get your hands on a arsenal of weapons to choose from, but can only bring two of into any mission, along with a single ability. Each one handles very differently from each other and has a very specific function. For example, the hammer is slow but hits hard, but the machete is quick and good for quick amounts of lighter damage, the pistols are for steady mid range damage while the rifle is for long range high damage, etc. You can either dodge attacks or block them with your shield, sometimes deflecting attacks right back if you time it right. Abilities vary greatly, and its really down to taste as to which one you prefer the most.
If the game is too easy for you, a little later on you unlock modifers for combat, which can make the game much harder, you can have any combination, or all of them activated at once, turning a relatively chilled experience into a fight to the death with every enemy. Its a way for players who want to push themselves for better rewards. You also get tonics which can help you change up combat even more by adding buffs to yourself, such as a large health increase, or damaging anything that melee hits you.
visually the game is wonderful, nothing extremely stunning, but its still a pretty game to look at overall. The soundtrack however is the star of the show. Every track is unique and is truly the most stand out thing of this title. I would recommend the game based on the soundtrack alone.
Overall, Bastion is a good game for beginners of the isometric style of games to jump onto, its a great game for lovers of game sountracks, a wonderful experience if your looking for a challenge that you yourself can set the rules for, and an overall just a game worth anyones time.

No, the answer is no, you should not buy Starbound.
The reasons are multitudinous, but let's start with what they get right. The game looks nice and sounds nice, the soundtrack is pretty boss and I never had a track there that I disliked.
That's it, that's all they get right.
The main storyline is bad, the lore isn't bad, but perversely going v1.0 involved deleting all of the MUCH better lore present in the beta(I think one or two books survived, but that's it), both hugely reducing the volume of lore present, and rewriting a ton of stuff to have a much more serious tone which the game just can't support.
The main storyline consists of six missions which steadily get lazier and less detailed as you go along, until it's literally just a flat plain where you kill enemies for ten minutes until you get a boss that has only a single attack pattern. Still, the pre-made dungeons for the main storyline are still better than the actual planets...
Because there's nothing interesting on the planets, at all. Each planet has(or, well, most...), one dungeon, one village, and one or two minidungeons lying around that just contain a structure and a chest. Everything else on the planet is dull filler full of really annoying monsters, and getting around the planet is more annoying than in the beta because they removed some techs that made travelling much faster and less painful.
Also, "most planets," because several planet types(magma, frigid ocean and toxic) contain nothing. Literally nothing. Not even dungeons or minidungeons. And they don't even have any special resources to mine for that the other planets don't have.
The combat is also pretty bad, because 90% of the weapons you get are useless, and the remaining 10% completely trivialize combat. There's a literal ONE useful secondary function for weapons(assault rifles with grenade launchers), and all the rest are an absolute waste of your energy. Melee weapons are thoroughly pointless, they have no advantage over ranged weapons unless your hand-eye coordination is too poor to know how to aim.
Crafting suffers from having way too many crafting stations and way too many crafting ingredients, especially because the game still only pulls ingredients from your inventory, not nearby containers. Crafting weapons and armor has, what, 50-ish ingredients to keep track of? If you add in food-crafting, you're easily at around 150, if it stops there. So have fun keeping track of where you put all those ingredients, or even just which ones you have in storage.
Speaking of crafting food. Food in your inventory decays, so it benefits you to eat the closest to decaying first. However, there's no option to sort your food tab by "decay level." So you have to mouse-over each unit of food in your inventory to figure out which ones you should eat. Also, speaking of sorting, you can sort your own inventory tabs, but not currently-opened containers, so your storage will ALWAYS be a mess.
I remember they said they were going to add it in, but NPC's still don't give a damn if you rummage through all their sock drawers and steal all their♥♥♥♥♥♥ Also doing this is so lucrative that you often won't need to mine at all, since random villagers nebulously have piles of rare ores lying around their bedroom or attic most of the time. The rest of the time you get manipulator parts or tech cards.
Manipulator parts are nice because they take the mining/building parts of the game from "suicide-inducingly slow" to "frustratingly slow." Tech cards are worthless since there are four upgrades for each tech, but they're sidegrades, not linear upgrades, so you're really only going to want to pick one upgrade for each tech(the only one I actually used outside of main quest dungeons was the double jump, too). This will cost you 16 tech cards total, but the game just keeps pouring them on you. It feels like they were originally meant to have more of a point.
Speaking of things that don't have a point, the Outpost, AKA the only place in the game with merchants you'll ever care about, starts out not being fully staffed, gaining open shops as the main quest progresses. However, once the main quest is over, there's literally nothing left in the game. So the outpost will only be fully staffed by the time you no longer care if it is or not.
Also, on the main quest again. 50% of the main quest involves looking for randomly generating items, with no idea whether they're present or not before landing on a planet. It's slow and tedious. To be more precise, you need to scan certain items, of a certain species' construction. There's a stage for each species for this, and only that species' items count during that stage. So if, say, you find a place with all the Apex items you need to scan during the Floran stage... too bad, hope you remember where that planet was by the time the Apex stage rolls around.
The game also has terrible performance, so any time there's more than three enemies and/or an atmospheric effect on screen, it'll slow to a near-crawl and half the time ignore your keypresses. Logically, the final boss fight them involves constantly spawning large amounts of tiny enemies. This does make it the only challenging boss fight in the game, though, because sometimes the game will ignore a keypress when you use a healing item and almost condemn you to play it again. It's not a bad boss fight outside of that, it's just waaaaaaaaaaaaaay too much of the same thing over and over again. Either reduce the final boss' health bar by, like, half, or add some more stages to him to shake things up a bit.
The rest of the game's bosses are defeated by finding a staff with the [Element] Portal spell and placing it on top of them while you dodge their projectiles(Erchius Horror excepted, but that's only the very first boss, you probably don't have a staff by then).
I probably missed SOMETHING else that was bad about the game, but it ultimately amounts to "pretty much everything, except for one piece of fluff(Ironbeak) and the music. Oh and also all those other pieces of fluff that they inexplicably deleted, but I guess they don't really count, do they?"
EDIT: Forgot that they also, inexplicably, decided to make asteroid fields pointless, they used to have resources and facilities, now they have literally NOTHING. Moons got emptied out as well, for basically just a pointless fuel collecting minigame. Barren planets got added, and, again, they're a type of planet with NOTHING on them, not even trees.

Splendor is an excellent adaptation of the board/card game of the same name.  The visuals are very nice, the music is appropriately "Renaissance-esque", and the play is fairly fast paced, with a match able to be completed in anywhere from 20-30 minutes, or perhaps a little longer if the players need to think about a particular action.  As a game, it's fairly light due to this, what many groups would call a "beer and pretzels" game, something to warm the group up for a proper, all-night kind of board game.  Despite that, it remains very fun and entertaining, if a little light.
The downside to this digital version is the poor AI.  Once you've wet your feet on them, you're really going to want to move on to multiplayer with your own group.  Being only about 30 minutes per match, it's perfect for laughing, chatting, and passing the time until your entire group is on, and players are obviously going to be a much greater challenge.  The AI doesn't truly understand how to counter-play an opponent by taking gems he will need in the future, or how to hold on to valuable gems, and generally just goes for the highest point cards they can, when they can, or take "freebie" cards if they're available.  Their poor play will leave you itching for a real contest.
The other downside is NO online play, it is against AI or local hotseat only, which I don't feel the need to go into further detail here.  TRAGICALLY missed opportunity there.
That aside, everything else about the game is pretty much flawless: if you've played the real card game, the digital version basically just removes all the tedious counting out your gems, depositing them back in the bank, reaching over the table to grab from the gem pile, etc, i.e. the administration stuff, and leaves you with the actual fun part of the game, playing it! And at $5 bucks, it's a steal.  No online play means you really don't need to buy copies of it for your friends, since they have to come over to play anyway.
Overall, a great digital adaptation and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for something small and light (not to mention light on the bank account!) to fill in time until you can start some heavier gaming for an evening!
TL;DR version:
Visuals: 8/10 - Slick, polished, glittery, and makes you really feel like a Renaissance gem merchant!  Wish the card backgrounds had a little more tie-in with their gem bonus, but hey, the actual game has that too.
Sound: 7.5/10 - Fairly generic "card swish" sound when you play cards, or "plinking" sound when you turn in gems.  The Renaissance-era music in the background is heavy on the harps and lutes, and it's nice for a while but eventually I turned it off, as it does get to be pretty repetitive after some time.
Mechanics: 9/10 - Works flawlessly without any bugs or glitches, which is of course a bare minimum, and is exactly representative of the real card game.  I wish you could turn off the animations though, after a while, the slow-ish speed of the cards moving around gets to be a bit grating, but hey, it could be worse: you could be dealing with your sweaty friend sitting at the table next to you reaching over you to grab cards!  That said, the hotseat only nature of it means you may have to deal with your sweaty friend anyway :/
AI: 5/10 - Very poor AI, with them making some plays that left me scratching my head.  They don't really watch for their opponents' plays, and instead play pretty much solitaire-ish.  This leaves them very open to exploitation by a decent, or even newer player.  They will go for nobles, when they have the chance, but don't have much of a game plan past that.
Overall:
Singleplayer: 7.5/10
Multiplayer: 7/10 - The game plays out like the real card game, minus all the real card game fuss and mess.  Excellent work here!  My only regret is that it is local play ONLY, no online capabilities, which was a real missed opportunity, seriously, what kinds of game DON'T have online play these days?

About me: I love adventures, especially the old Lucas Arts games.

Conclusion: I enjoyed most of it, but really hated some of it.

Battle Brothers is a turn-based tactics game, set in a low-fantasy medieval world. It bears heavy influences of titles like classic Darklands, Jagged Alliance, with a strategic layer very reminiscent of Mount&Blade. It is a great game, an example of Early Access done right, showing how developers with clear vision can make a polished game that delivers exactly what was promised
Positives:
- The tactical layer is fun to play, every weapon comes with own set of skills, the interconnected systems make you take into account positioning, fatigue, terrain, elevation, etc. Battles can be very hectic, especially at higher difficulties
- Game features varied set of enemies that are not just a reskins with shuffled stats. Fighting Goblins is totally different to facing Orcs, Skeletons or Nachzehrers (ghouls)
- It is a breath of fresh air, that it is not yet another generic fantasy/medieval, but instead a dark, gothic darklandsesque world of evil lurking in black forests. Many of its aspects have unique twist, my favourite being the Ancient Dead, Undead based off Roman Legions in place of your generic skeletons
- The presentation, considering we are talking a smaller indie dev is really astonishing. A proof there are other ways than expensive 3d photorealism, or the omnipresent pixelart trend to make your game look good
- RPG elements are reasonably fleshed out, your mercenaries can have many traits affecting their effectiveness, skills are varied and are impactful gameplaywise
Negatives, but depends on what kind of player You are:
- The game is repetitive, you get contracts, fight battles, and try to make money and develop your company, rince and repeat. There is barely any story, little premade scenarios. Both tactical battles and management side are well made, but ultimately they are the only things that you will be doing during the game
- Some battles can drag on, especially in marshes and ESPECIALLY against zombies. It is not a prevalent problem but sometimes the fights feel like hassle, they take a lot of time, while not posing a challenge
All in all it is a great game, if you are into tactical turn-based games, if you want Jagged Alliance going medieval, I couldn't recommend it more.

First game I bouth in Early Access, and although this is usually not smart, I did not regret it with battlebrothers.
It is not for everybody though. So I will just list what I like about the game, not a full review. Check other reviews for that.
You feel like a leader of a mercenary gang. The game gives you meaningful choices, decide what the men should wear, their weaponry, armor usables ect. You have to recruit raw recruits most of the time and trim them into soldiers. It offers great possibilities for RP-players, as you can change the name and the look of each character.
Men only gain experience in combat, so you have to send your recruits to battle eventually. Sure you could keep them out of the frontline and in the back, but you will need every hand to fight, at least in the beginning.
The KI has a variety of tactics and takes into account if they have the higher ground, if they are lead by an officer or if they have archer superiority. So you cannot just set up defences and wait for them to come, if they have more archers. They will just wait an pepper you with arrows.
After several battles your men grow on you. You start to like them, and they develop relationships with each other (although this is not that well depicted yet). Loosing a high leveled soldier feels terrible. But you will lose men inevitably, especially on higher difficulty levels. Get used to the fact that everybody can die. And just one mistake, one tactical misconception can ♥♥♥♥ up your entire team and you will hate yourself for sacrificing your men for nothing.
The Devs are also really cool. It is an Indy developer, but they are very realiable and responsive. Certainly one of the best indy teams out there. Early Access done right!
So in short: buy it!

Great third addition to the Thief series. Instead of simply going on to the next mission after completing one, you go back to the city. Here you can do everything from purchasing arrows and equipment, to stealing from the citizens, to picking on the guards.
Plus, the story is a bit more open. Not sure if this is a spoiler or not, but
Instead of a sword, you have a dagger. Makes backstabbing much easier.
No rope arrows, but you can eventually purchase climbing gloves. These are AWESOME, if you can figure out how to use them. :D
Oil vials. Can be ignited to make a temporary, impassible wall of flame, or can be used to make guards slip, slide, and fall down elevator shafts, if you know what you're doing. Awesome.
The ability to go 3rd Person in the game is interesting -- at first it detracted from what I was used to in the Thief series, but I quickly got over it.
You also now have the ability to press up against a wall, suck in your gut, and thus become almost invisible in a dark hallway. Reeeeaaaally creepy putting this to the test for the first couple times.
Lockpicking is a little more immersive and realistic, as well.
Needs some tweaking to make it work on newer machines (opening cutscene is an instant crash for me). One thing that sucks is loading screens within missions. But all of these issues are easily fixed. Just look up some mods for Thief: Deadly Shadows and you'll be set for an amazing time! :)
