With Flat Heroes you have it nice and simple, without the game ever coming off as incomplete. So why the Early Access label? Well, I have to appreciate a developer which constantly struggles to improve a game, which many others would have released and already stop supporting. But that’s the beauty of Steam and the ever growing indie game scene hosted here. You have plenty of creative and ambitious folks, which do their best to tip the scale in their favor and wash some of that sour taste left by the equally numerous lazy and cash-grabbing bunch of “devs” out there. Now, as you may have noticed, I did write a con revealing the current Flat Heroes price tag as “slightly overpriced”. I consider it so, but perhaps time will prove me wrong once the game gets released in its final form. The artificial intelligence in the Battle section is savage, to say the least. I wasn’t left wanting, that’s for sure.
Being mostly a single player kind of gamer, I did enjoy the fact that the entire game can be played by yourself without feeling like you’re missing out on a lot. The objectives are straightforward: blast your opponents into oblivion by smashing into them. Obviously in a game about squares, violence isn’t far off, right? Some aggression in arcade titles isn’t necessarily bad. Breaking the mold never is. Wave section feels more natural for the genre. Mixing both platforming and quick reflexes, its levels have you dodging obstacles while also avoiding or fighting off other Human players in co-op. And survival ain’t that easy when you also have to avoid homing missiles (another example of good AI). The beauty of it is that even in single player mode, Wave offers plenty of challenge. Co-op is indeed, optional. Flat Heroes doesn’t become boring fast, a syndrome frequently found in arcade titles.
Unity Engine says it all. It’s pretty, in the right hands and it offers such a large spectrum of artistic expression. Minimal style being among my favorites, it wasn’t hard for the dev team to add even some degree of player-controlled customization. If you don’t like the color choice of either the squares or the background, you have several chromatic alternatives. Sounds selection isn’t the best, but this genre doesn’t need much to get by. Despite warning that the game is best played on a controller, the keyboard layout felt very responsive. Perhaps pitting human players against each other, might increase the odds for the one using a controller. Still, don’t underestimate the AI.
+ Fun to play in either SP or MP mode
+ The AI offers enough challenge when you play by yourself
+ Minimalist arcade design
- Slightly overpriced Early Access title
- No Steam Achievements or Trading Cards
I was only slightly bothered by the price tag (in regards to my readers and potential buyers of this game) but other than that, Flat Heroes doesn’t fail to deliver a consistent and entertaining arcade experience. Near flawless as far as I’m concerned. You just have to like this genre, I guess. Grab it while on a seasonal Steam Sale or when bundled and you won’t regret it.

I don't normally spend time writing game reviews (I normally spend it playing) but I'll make this just one exception as it is such a wonderfully polished, minimallistic, delicately balanced, challenging, and overall fun game that I just couldn't resist.
The game starts off with zero tutorials, and the player needs to discover the controls, what they do, how they respond, etc. After that, levels start going at you one after another as you struggle to complete the objective (which you discover on-the-fly so to speak, just as you jump to the next level)
You plough through the roughly first ten levels learning the basic mechanics so that you can finally confront the epic boss. On your way you learn about the arrows, the bomb arrows, the lasers, etc. all moving dynamic obstacles that you, as the player, must avoid. After you've completed your "rite of passage" you get to the boss.
And now, the bosses, oh man, you're in for a kick (in the teeth). Much like the entire game, they are designed as geometrical figures, and their behavior is quite intelligent. It is very hard to take them down by just jumping or impacting on them, you need a specific, often non-obvious, strategy. Here the real fun begins, because it becomes a great challenge of trying to find the boss's soft spot, or its patterns, (even it's lack of), and by repeatedly playing the level discover what it's actual Achilles' heel is. After you defeat a boss you move on to the next area and from the on its rinse and repeat in a crazy, very fun, loop.
This, of course, you can do on your own or by your loyal squires (aka friends) because it's got up to 4-player coop! So imagine trying to beat those whacky bosses with someone else.
The game has been translated to every language on earth, I think only Esperanto and Elvish aren't there, and there are other gameplay modes you unlock that I won't spoil for you.
Overall a very fun experience, highly recommended.

Thief: Deadly Shadows is definitely the weakest addition to the Thief series, as it catered for the broadened player base as part of it’s developed for the Xbox console, making it nowhere near the level of its predecessor, but still a solid stealth game and probably one of the lasts of its genre. Despite that, the developers have put in an effort into recreating the world of Thief.
It takes what was best from Dark Project and adds a new layer of surreal horror to it that results in one of the most widely playable games yet. The setting is familiar to the first instalment and the story becomes similarly weird and mysterious. The controls have improved over Metal Age and enable a flawless exploration of the world. The story is what really tops the two previous titles.
However, the dated graphics engine means that loading screens are plentiful and levels are small. It's been streamlined for the Xbox crowd and the consoles limitations and features a bunch of nonsensical elements which were not present in previous Thief games. Getting wedged in the scenery is not a rare event and the rag-doll physics are lazy and unnatural compared to what they should have gone with - good animations. The game now uses a ‘City-hub’ rather than the assumed natural progression between missions as seen in the previous titles. Deadly Shadows is a lot more linear, and suddenly rope/vine arrows and scouting orbs don't exist, and Garrett has forgotten the ability to swim as he dies the instant he touches water. The combat system as expected is not one of the Thief’s strong points, and it would be safer altogether, to just avoid an enemy in the first place.
Die-hards fans might consider it a disgrace to the Thief series, and as a whole, it simply does not live up to the legacy, but despite all of this, the game does deserve credit for maintaining the Thief atmosphere and keeping the series going.

As a fan of the original NES Mega Man games, I cannot recommend this.  The graphics are cute, sure, and many of the enemies have a Mega Man feel to them, but overall the package is just lacking.
The music is lackluster, the level design is atrocious (the 3 I tried all felt like variations on Shadow Man's Revisit stage in MM3, which is not a flattering comparison), and while the "soft-death" features sounds good on paper, the level design seems to be based around you dying to something you didn't know about instead of allowing you to decipher what to do as you progress.  Other minor nitpicks was that I was unable to fire single shots with the 360 controller (pressing the shoot button fired a 3-round burst which prevented me from shooting again until some shots impacted an enemy or left the screen) and that the control was way too floaty for the amount of precision expected.
The one boss fight I made it to was...okay...at best.  She didn't have a pattern in the typical Mega Man styling.
I'm not sure what the intent was here.  In terms of difficulty, METAGAL doesn't do the Dark Souls "Git Gud" concept well enough for the deaths to feel fair, but it also feels like if you take away the really, really weird difficulty that the game would have almost no content.  If you really want to play Mega Man style games, the Mega Man Legacy Collection or Shovel Knight will serve you much better than this game.

This is a great game, even early access. The characters are interesting, with varied backgrounds, flaws and boons and leveling leaves the player with just enough decision making to customize mercs without bogging the game down. Early on I found that I often hired mercs as fodder, fully intending for them to die, but as most reached level 4 or 5 I purchased better armor and have been able to keep them alive for a while. Overall the progression is very well balanced and the game has several elements (e.g. major injuries, armor being destroyed on merc death) that keep it challenging. I'm really enjoying this game as something of a successor to Darkest Dungeon and can't wait for the additional features to be unlocked at release, highly recommend!

This is a classic game. It's not perfect and in terms of graphics and sound it shows it's age. However, the story is compelling if you allow yourself to see past the game engines limits. This is most likely a love it - hate it game due to it's age. I played this when it was new so the ability to replay the game was special. The "Orphanage" area is still completely creepy and honestly scary at times. The game improves as the story unfolds so continuing to play will be rewarded.
The basic mechanic of "Stealth" is what makes this game. You are Garrett, a master thief. You are not a fighter, you are a shadow. You do best when you knock out guards or, better yet, sneak past and continue. When you're deep in a Mansion and you snatch that special loot ... you realize that you haven't completed anything, now you must escape into the night with your prize.
To me, this is the only game in the Thief series that is worth playing and it shouldn't be confused with the other installments. This really is a stand-alone game.
This game does suffer from some NPC issues where they will behave in a frustrating manner. You will need to adjust your gamma and brightness at different times so you can "see" the shadows in which you can crouch undetectable.
It's difficult for me to rate this game so I will give it 2 ratings.
For the ability to be Garrett in an excellent story with an expansive world I'll rate this 8 out of 10.
Compared to the expectations of modern gamers ... I must give this a 6 out of 10.

Almost since this game came out, I have been constantly playing it. The unique combat system which mainly revolves around hand to combat is such a joy to experience. (Though I don't mind going around with the Wheels Of Fury car from the DLC and shooting down all of the civilians and police alike).
My own repetition aside (sorry!), I still find myself coming back to this game even with more graphically enhanced games out on the market. I've played GTA 5 and Watchdogs 2, and while each of those had their own unique points a little something just kept dragging me back here.
Sadly, this game will never see a sequel as United Front Games shut down earlier this year (Not before a few beta copies of Sleeping Dogs 2 were sent out). I urge for everyone to at least take the time to play this game as you won't regret it.

This game was not what I was expecting at all. It was more like a fast paced board game than the sort of resource management and strategy game I thought it would be. I can't fault it for not being like the Total War games, which I was thinking it was, but I can fault it for not being particularly fun. As far as I can see from playing the tutorial and the first level, you basically run around with envoys and spies trying to keep alliances with towns while your opponents ruin your alliances and make their own. It can get a little hectic keeping up with all of that going on, while also trying to get some food or money together to make an army.
You don't build structures in this game, they already exist on the map. What you do is build units, which will carry out certain tasks like assassinations and spying. The goal is to build alliances with nearby towns and castles to keep yourself stronger and richer than your enemies. You do this to collect prestige points, which determine the winner of the map. The combat in this game is not at all exciting, since your armies will consist of around 8 little guys that will hack at the other side's armies until one team is dead. You don't really want to declare war too often anyway, since it will cost you prestige points. So you want to convince the other guy to declare war, and then spend some time chasing around his units to destroy them, all while chasing his envoys with yours so that you can keep them from stealing your alliances.
The graphics are decent but not particularly impressive. The music is standard fantasy fare. Not memorable, but not bad either.
It's just not as impressives as I was hoping for, and I think I only gave it the time I did because of the GoT license. It does go back a ways to give you a taste of some of the origins of the great houses of Westeros, but I felt like the license was not important to the gameplay. It was like playing a licensed version of Monopoly, wherein the lore of GoT only ran skin deep. Overall I could not recommend this title.

Much of what I origionally didn't like has been changed or fixed etc.
It's basically a Fantasy Nuclear Throne with crazy abilities. It's advanced quite a bit from my first review.
Notable Changes:
-Melee Classes are no longer as awful as before, infact maxing your Q as the barbarian and just forever doing spin attacks is great.
-Attack speeds of the enemies feels slower, so you have more time to dodge, however I do find some of the Skeleton King's blasts to be undodgeable.
-The 50% chance potions are nice, although I've yet to see the second effect of a potion happen? (For instance the potion of rage, I've 100% of the time gotten Beserk in my past 4 playthroughs of the game, never a damage down.)
-The new skills system is odd, but I do like it, it's a fun RPG Fantasy element =)
-Designs are still wicked awesome!
Things I dislike:
-I cannot progress past the sewers yet again, though this time my game crashes towarsds the end of the second sewers floor, or during the boss fight.
-Ranged classes having lower cooldowns than the Melee classes, though I guess the health discrepency helps balance out the cooldowns?
-Ranged classes still feel overall better at clearing the game, unless you're Barbarian and just smashing Q + LMB
-Death Spikes being One-Hit to disable, though I did hate them a lot origionally because they ruined everything, I feel they've been over nerfed given that an Archer just one shots it out of commision. I'd hope it could take more something around 15-20 damage before breaking.
Class Specific:
-Necromancer feels WAY too overpowered. The Skeleton's healing for 20% of your health, and being able to have three at a time is like giving the class reusable potions every 15-25 seconds. I rarely was low on health until of course I crashed and that just obliterated anything.
-The Wizard feels weird, because I find myself relying more on the first ability, rather than even the normal attacks. It has a larger field of damage that requires EVERY level up in your first few floors to truly clear out marks and groups of enemies as at just level 1 it can sometimes maybe half health a bat?
Otherwise my previous likes stand. It's fun with lovely pixelly design, and I now can definately recommend playing it considering they've done away with instant death spikes of evil.

A good example of how Early Access should work. The devs have gathered opinions and playing data during the production, and the progress towards a finished game has been quite easy to follow. Great work by Overhype Studios.
The game itself is also fun. Level-based RPG with nice strategic and tactical features. Graphics are polished but, as you can see in the screenshots, of a simplistic nature. There are events and your interaction with the world matters. Great music and good sounds as well.
On to my complaints. First and foremost, battle is based on a punishing RNG. Random map configuration can cause your doom. Missing shots with 75% or better chance to hit feels common. Losing veterans due to bad luck is highly frustrating, because (complaint number 2) it takes a lot of grinding to get your mercs somewhat skilled.
So if you don't mind having your balls in a RNG-powered vice, I highly recommend this one.

One of my favourite games of all time. Solid mechanics and fun interactions together with a semi-predictable new dungeon every time you play makes this game what it is. You start off being horribly murdered by anything and everything, but as you learn from your mistakes the game becomes an intense risk vs reward struggle. Experience and knowledge about the games floors and items is your greatest strength.
With the multiple characters and game modes, especially with the addition of the Afterbirth expansion, it provides many, mant hours of quality game time, which then is increased even more by the auto generated maps.
The setting and story is fantastic in its own, revolting way. Ever wanted walking ♥♥♥♥♥♥s shoot period lasers at you? Yeah, this game's got you covered...no pun intended.
It is also a solid upgrade from the first Binding of Isaac game, mostly because of it running on a better engine and having more interactions between items. Some just plain overrule others, but not nrealy as often as in the previous game, which is a huge plus.
Score, you say? If you insist; 8/10. Very solid game, might be the best in its genre.

Beyond that, it's a strategy game akin to Heroes of Might and Magic, but without the town-building aspect and little resource management.  You'll spend most of your time seducing enemy towns to your side or neutrality or ferreting out spies.  In my opinion, it has very little to recommend it, and the gameplay is more frustrating than engaging.  Many mechanics of it are clunky, frustrating, and certainly not what I'd expect from a modern title. Save yourself some time and frustration.  Don't buy this game.  If you're interested in the history of the Song of Ice and Fire world, go find GRR Martin's source books.  If you really want to play a game based on Game of Thrones, you'll have more fun with the RPG.

A very odd game that I'm not sure if it's anything or everything.
The game mostly involves exploring areas and trying to touch every object in them to discover them... no, it's try to complete the tutorial that takes a couple hours.  No wait, it's just a sandbox to mess around with.
Actually Everything is all those things and none.  It's an odd game, reminding me almost of Katamari Damacy in a few ways, however it doesn't exactly have a "gameplay" loop.  You explore the world, experience lots of stuff, and then either shrink or grow out of that world.  You have the option of doing either and you do it through your own control rather than hitting a size limit.
While you play the game you listen to fantastic lectures by Alan Watts and let's just say he's a bit out their on what he's talking about but it works perfectly for the game.   It's relaxing and different and beautiful
Is it good?  Well first watch the video, most things in the game don't animate well, or at all, but it's kind of endearing with how the game works.   Graphics are acceptable when you realize how much you can see in the game, and you aren't given a mission after the tutorials, mostly just "listen to Alan Watts speak and explore the world".  And from that.... well honestly that's the game, you can do what you want, try to capture everything, explore everything, or just let the game autoplay itself for a while, and honestly none of those are the wrong way to play the game.
Is it worth 15 bucks? Depends, it's an odd game, I left it on for a day, and was surprised to find it's actually earning achievements for me while I'm not there.   I mean... it's just an odd relaxing zen like game, and for that.... it works well.  I like the game for what it is but it's really a game that you have to experience to decide if you like it or not.
However I will give the game this, there's a LOT in this game, in two or three hours I think I only saw about 5 percent of all the objects in the game. There's a lot of stuff to explore discover and experience, and honestly I'm rather happy to have it in my library.  I recommend this game, but just realize the term "game" as it's more just a relaxation program.  Excellently well done, interesting but lacking the goals that most people feel games should have.

The game is a fun little time waster where you think you know how to handle the enemies till you get bored and stop paying attention...and then you get eaten by a frog...I'm not kidding, this is my favorite way to die in this game, I was about to change my gear because I thought I cleared the room and picked up some loot...always look for moving shadows, that's my advice for you! ;-)
There have been multiple updates to the game since release which added nice effects and new enemy behavior.
Boss fights are fun but sometimes a bit too easy, but the difficulty increases with every dungeon you finish.
Duo to the recommendation of a high-score mechanic by many on Greenlight, including me, the developer implemented such a feature which gives the achievement hunters in us a reason to go on.
There are some really cool features in the game, like when there is a bonfire, you can shoot your arrows through the fire and it becomes a burning arrow which does additional damage to enemies. Also, enemies don't hit you by touching, they rather all have an attack animation which must clip with your character to hurt you.
There are a few issues with the inventory system and the enemy AI gets stuck from time to time, but for a low budget title from a new developer, it is a lot of fun, especially when you got friends to compare score with!
Over all, this game might be a bit behind of what it could have been, and you see potential in every corner, but I believe it's worth to pick up for the price to support the developer, this might be his first Steam entry, but it shows that there might be coming better games by him in the future!

Weakensses

The idea of the game is great -- play a platform game where your character starts at the end credits and travels back through time through the game while not creating any time paradoxes as you revert the game environment back to its pristine shape before your character played through.  For example, as you play the game from the end credits back in time toward the start of the game your character must avoid the coins that were missed, "un-get" the coins that were collected, leave the monsters still alive, and jump on the monsters that are squashed (bringing them back to their pre-squashed selves)...
The lesser problem is simply the controls.  On the plus side, the controls are simple as there's only two things your character can ever do -- jump or "action".  But jumping, good grief, your character is so floaty!   It just seems to be at an unnaturally slow speed, making any quick reaction jumps impossible.
since the jump action is so slow and floaty you can't quickly react to anything like bullets that suddenly appear or aliens that suddenly change direction.  At best you have a sliver of time in which to react, but in many cases,
It just feels like cheating on the developers part trying to make for a "challenge".
This takes any skill or ability out of the game.  It's "challenging" solely because it's impossible to react to something that hasn't happened yet on screen!
Thankfully the game is short.
Another 6-8 minutes to wrap up the 4th bonus world and complete a few more achievements.

Interaction in the game is pretty limited as of now, but I respect the concept.
Unique game that makes you wonder, every now and then.
8/10
Hope the potential takes off soon.

Starbound is a tricky beast to nail down. It's not Terraria, it's not as simple as saying that it's got a world where you kill progressively nastier bosses and work your way through crazier and crazier biomes, because it's much wider than that. The best way I can describe it is as "Sci fi fantasy : The game", it has a lot of different activities, all of which can be explored to a reasonable depth, and all of which complement each other to a decent enough extent that regardless of HOW you want to approach Starbound, you're going to find something to like in it. Want to go on a pokemon style pet battle hunt through the galaxy? Starbound has that. Want to become an iron chef and cook up all kinds of alien cuisine? Got that too. Want to go spelunking through alien ruins for phat loot? In spades. Want a reasonably okay story that gives you a reason to go exploring the big wide universe? It even has that.
You can even build a massive colony and become an administrator of a planet, with your own vendors, NPC quests, income, housing, all that jazz. There's so many ways to play Starbound that frankly you're almost lost for choice, to the point some people are going to get turned off. The overarching quest I mentioned is the thing that probably will keep most people playing for a while, but past that you really need to supply the imagination and the goals as to what you want to achieve and get out of Starbound. This doesn't even count the mod scene, which thanks to Chucklefish having the foresight to build in -really- good mod support, is likely to become a very long term and integrated part of the Starbound scene.
There's lots of content here, especially if you add in a few key mods like Frackin' Universe, you're going to need to go out there and take a peek though, spend some time getting around and figuring out just what parts of it you want to invest into. When you -do- find something that hooks you though, it's almost Minecraft levels of addictive, you'll blow past the tens of hours and easily into the hundreds. Starbound is that kind of a game. As a value proposition, it's unmatched. There's questing, there's exploration, crafting, pets, crew, colonies, cooking, farming, vehicles, the list goes on and on and on.
Each individual area isn't *stupidly* deep, but because it covers such a wide number of activities, it doesn't need to, they're all executed competently enough that they all work together and form something that's greater than the sum of it's parts. That's pleasing, the whole game feels cohesive, and everything from the music to the lighting to the artwork just "fits".
This could have, and perhaps should have been the next Duke Nukem Forever, another object lesson of what happens when a game gets trapped in development hell, but Chucklefish has proved damn near everyone wrong, including me. That makes me happy, because it proves that sometimes being cynical and jaded isn't a guarantee of being right, instead Chucklefish put their heads down, got the development up to a phenomenal speed and created something that is truly worthy of a 1.0 release, even if *nothing* more was added by the official developers, they've created a platform for modders to paint their own ideas onto a wonderful galaxy, and one I'm more than happy to call home. If you have any interest in Terraria, Minecraft or similar games, Starbound should already be in your library. Even if you're not, this is one of those few games where you definitely should go and check it out.

Bastion is an interesting take on an isometric hack and slash where everything everywhere is floating, and therefore, almost everywhere is a pit.
The art is good, the narrator is good, the animations aren't bad...
I like isometric hack and slash.
Thankfully the dev added 'windbag ranch' near the beginning so I can stop playing, write this review, and delete the game.
Your character has tiny little arms and legs, so he moves like an anthropomorphic turtle.
In order to move faster, you must roll... but rolling is hard to control.
Did I mention pits?
Windbag ranch is an arena for learning the 4th weapon of the game - a sword.
The arena is surrounded by monster spawners and turrets, the only weapon you can use is the sword.
Three turrets are floating outside the arena.
You must kill all the monsters within 60 seconds.
The monsters can fly, and half of them
You can't kill them without throwing your sword at them (unless there's some way to fly coming later on.  I doubt that)
Throwing your sword takes about 1-2 seconds, and of course it's a slow projectile... so it typically misses at range.
Add to this that you have to aim for the enemy's shadow to hit their body.
Add to this that you are slower than they are.
Add to this that it's not always clear whether you can walk on a spot or fall ...
and did I mention that there are three spawners for these monsters?
If you kill the spawners the monsters will have time to scatter - you'll never kill them all in 3 minutes if this happens.
If you don't kill the spawners... the monsters never stop spawning...
I can understand super frustrating end game challenges like chocobo racing to obtain the best sword in FF10.
This is a XP grind / training arena, and everytime I fail it I must
- shuffle over to the reset button
>confirm reset<
- watch the entire training area intro animations...
One of the levels is made almost entirely of falling platforms - there was an area I couldn't get to because as soon as went the wrong direction I couldn't go back.
This is the model for the entire game - pits and resets.
I haven't even heard enough of the story to know why I'm gathering crystals...
I'm glad the developer put windbag ranch in the game early - It probably saved me a few hours attempting to play this game.
Bastion is perhaps a very good game.
I can't stand it. Playing it is frustrating and slow for reasons I hate.

I really wanted to like this game, I've been looking forward to its release for quite a while. I have played in early beta and soon after they added the Outpost. But I just feel the progression is too slow and too linear. In past versions of the game you could be out exploring the galaxy pretty soon into the game, but now you have to do a lengthy series of mundane quests  involving scanning objects and getting to the end of a tedious handcrafted dungeon.
The game is hampered with a boring main quest about Earth being destroyed by a giant space monster. Even if you are a native of another planet, it starts you off as a graduate on an Earth academy, This means you character is not a blank slate but is instead an Earthling most likely. Even if you skip the tutorial you have to sit through a long cutscene once you have reached the outpost where an old lady tells you about the fate of Earth (I don't care about Earth, I'm a beep boop alien robot for the Creator's sake!).
The game shows you everything you can craft so far, even if you don't have the materials. This is pretty good, plus mining and exploring the planet is fun, even though the lack of randomly generated monsters does hamper the sense of danger and caution when exploring a planet. However, movement abilities are pretty weak, you get a dash after you give the Outpost tech-guy 10 copper bars, however this dash is barely a metre in distance and has a long cooldown. You can upgrade this dash to an air dash but this is also pretty weak in comparison to other platforming game's movement options.
It took me a very long time to repair the FTL, which requires the completion of the linear dungeon I mentioned earlier. I am still gathering resources to be able to breathe on the moon, so I can mine it for FTL fuel to actually use the FTL. This progression is really slow and I don't like being stuck on the starting planet for that long, I have already explored all of its surface and the mine area. To get the best gear you have to complete these scanning quests to populate the Outpost with more NPCs, these scanning quests require traversing the galaxy hoping to find items of that race, you then repeat this for every race and call it the main quest.
Overall I can't really recommend it as a game you open up, sit down and explore,craft and mine in. The open end sandbox of the game comes after an extremely long series of quests and you will be stuck on your starting planet for a while, so you better like mountainous green planets because you will have to stay for a while.

In Spoiler Alert, you play your Chili Pepper hero, and you must undo all your actions while avoiding time paradoxes. That is to say, revive your enemies, put back the coins, don't kill anything, don't pick up anything. All while running backwards, right to left.
It's certainly a creative concept, but it also means any errors you make require you to restart the level. Fortunately, the levels are short and simple, but I question whether this affected the game length. I 100%'d this game in just short of an hour, although I did not try the speedrunning mode, where you play the whole game in one go.
Overall, enjoyable, but I wouldn't expect to get too much time out of it.

I do think the sequel is a better game, albeit only slightly. There are still many reasons to play the original game instead nowadays, even though on paper Left 4 Dead 2 is everything the first game is and more.
1. Left 4 Dead 2 lacks almost all survival maps from the first game including my favorite Last Stand/Lighthouse, which was clearly designed just for survival mode letting all the best parts about it shine. Most other maps are about knowing the "meta spot" and camping in that place as hard as possible to get gold whereas Last Stand pretty much forces you to fight on top of the lighthouse punishing you really hard if you let the tank get on top as the player that will get knocked down from the tower with a solid punch from the tank will probably die in an instant - fighting on such height gives a sense of danger that makes it super exciting. I know there is an unofficial workshop mod allowing you to download this map in Left 4 Dead 2 and maybe there are similar things for other survival maps of the original game, but the lack of official support for this one and many more is just sad given it is pretty much all this mode is about.
2. Left 4 Dead 2 added a huge amount of variety in arsenal, which is of course good, but many of those things just make it often too easy. Sure, in the sequel there is Realism Mode, which is great at raising difficulty, because it doesn't have respawn, but there are also defibrillators, which resurrect you anyway, so... You have melee weapons of which I'm a big fan of as they're fun to use, but they pretty much act like shove that you can use while holding a ranged weapon (the best option for short range defense in original Left 4 Dead) except without any cooldown on use AND killing the infected in an instant - compare this to shove which does no damage. You have incendiary and explosive ammo for weapons, which when equipped make getting through hordes of enemies a cakewalk. You have a grenade launcher which, like explosive ammo, punishes you for using it incorrectly, but otherwise wreaks absolute havoc with little effort. There are more examples, but all of it comes down to that all those additions make Left 4 Dead 2 a completely different game.
3. Despite its limited options for survival, this game still is tons of fun and actually its simplicity compared to the sequel may be the greatest reason for it. It has everything essential that also makes Left 4 Dead 2 great - while barebones, the gameplay has everything that it needs for a satisfying Left 4 Dead experience as it focuses on those basic skills of players, which still leave huge amounts of room to improve on. Even though I've played over 200 hours of this game and have all the achievements, I still don't feel like I have mastered it and I can jump in a game any day knowing I'll still really enjoy it.

This game reminds me of True Crime Streets of LA, and the other one True Crime New York, which I haven't played yet. I guess I can say this is probably the spiritual successor of that series. If you've played those, the gameplay would be similar to them, if not - I hope you've at least played some sort of open world roam game, like the GTA series or SR series...
But if not, gameplay is similar to those other open world games, but combat is mainly focused on melee and fist fights, rather than guns and bullets that those other games are more inclined to. There are QTEs too, that makes the combat system interesting, because you gotta be ready to press the button that shows on the screen to counter that blow or to K.O. that guy.... As with those open world games, you able to drive and hijack cars for joy rides or what have you... Can ⓟⓘⓢⓢ the cops off too if you want to have fun.... Unfortunately, this game only has 4 levels of heat, so no millitary like guys(with hummers that have a 50 cal mounted minigun or tanks with 100mm cannon(or in combination with a 20mm machine gun) coming at ya...) will come after you, and no those swat guys don't count...heh... And no, no helicopters either.....would have been fun too to hijack them and ⓕⓤⓒⓚ the cops with...
Anyways, there's a skill tree system to that's implemented, one for cop persona, one for triad personal and one just for melee combat. For the cop one, you need to be a cop and not steal things or kill innocents whilst on the mission and stuff. For triad, you do the opposite of course.... And for the melee upgrades, you collect jade statues I believe or and open these lockboxes I think.....and then you go to the dojo and select your melee upgrade after putting away that jade statue for the master.
There's a leaderboard too! You can compare your stats with your friends, see who's got the longest cop chase or the most points in this particular mission! Which I thought was interesting...
So yeah, if you're a perfectionist, you'll want to be on the top of the leaderboard against ALL your friends...
Oh yeah, just wanna add here that you can also togggle between a global leaderboard and friends one.... I checked out the global one, and was surprised to wonder how the actual ⓕⓤⓒⓚ did they get 1 million points in this mission and that!? Surely they probably hacked their way....but if that's the case what's the point of having a leaderboard if you get hacked scores??! Ok, epeen, I understand, but still....
The sound mix is pretty good actually! No ⓑⓤⓛⓛⓢⓗⓘt low quality audio that I could hear, unlike SR2............but I think that was the fault of the porter, so blame CD Projekt as apparently they failed in the port.... :P Game uses 5.1 discrete channels, so enjoy playing this in your home theater system, or your 5.1 headset - though that's not really how your should *truly* experience surround sound....but whatever, some people just prefer to play with crappy gimmiky surround headsets and what not or have good reasons *not* to, like they live with others and they can't bare the noise that you will be making whilst playing this game...
Music/song tracks are pretty good....never heard of any of them before, but they do seem to fit the game right.
Can't turn off the radio in vehicles...when I just feel like I wanna cruise in silence...the only car that doesn't have a radio are the police ones....but I don't wanna cruise in them....not unless I'm doing cop jobs... Would have been nice if there was some sort of inventory system for weapons, like how you have for the pistol, except that you don't get to keep it with you through out the entire game, assuming if you're not used it once and still have full clips and everything(which means, as long as you haven't died, from the time you got the first gun, till the end game, you should still have the gun present in your sheath or whever it is you put it in). But I guess, this game isn't really weapon oriented in terms of combat gameplay so I guess it's just a minor complaint...
Also would be nice if I could drive the cars with manual transmission and shift gears when I feel like it, and not on auto...I think I saw a car or two or a few that had the actual gear stick for manual transmission but yet when driven, it's automatic....and no, I don't see the main character using the other hand to control the gear stick...
Um, what else - oh yes; the social hub to replay missions - unfortunately you can't replay the dating ones so I can get that screenshot I want.... TT_TT
Anywho, as I did enjoy my 52 hrs of game time in this, I can say for certain I recommend this to anyone who likes open world type games, asian culture or and melee combat!

Metagal isn't everything I had hoped for, but what it offers is still quite fun. Does that make sense? Because I literally sat here and spent about six minutes trying to figure out how to begin this.
So. Straight out of the gate. is Metagal worth a buy? Yes. Is Metagal the shining successor to Mega Man? No. But it's still fun.
I feel bad for Metagal because it journeys into the ever dangerous territory of "Clone". It's a Mega Man clone, through and through, but it still does enough on its own to merit its own accolades. But because it's a clone, the Mega Man fanbase will sink their claws into this and tear it apart. Follow me now...
Metagal's story is classic Mega Man: scientist makes robots, bad guy repurposes them. Metagal is the only bot in town to save the day! There's some ProtoMan flavored subplots thrown in, but it's all just whatever. You shoot bad bots. That's all you need.
At it's core, Metagal works. You jump. You shoot. You use special attacks to defeat enemies and traverse the stages. Cool. Just like MM. Nearly everything about the game is a direct lifting from MM: level design, ladder climbing, doors opening, enemy design, using certain weapons against bosses due to their weaknesses, etc. There are some differences, though: Metagal fires in three shot bursts. No single shots, no charges. Just bursts. Different, a little weird here and there, but pleasantly different. Instead of finite weapon ammo, Metagal gets an ever recharging gauge. This adds a nice touch to the tried and true gameplay we know from MM, so I welcomed it. There are only four bosses to gain special weapons from, two of which are incredibly useful, so not having to worry about finding ammo power-ups was a nice change of pace.
Here's a big deal: you have infinite lives. You have. Infinite. LIVES. For anyone that writes this game a negative review because it's "too hard" or because "Fortress Area 3 is too hard", please remember that you have infinite lives. You do. Granted, you respawn back at every check point you pass, and you can techinically earn lives (Rebirths) that respawn you at the exact room you died in, but listen: infinite lives, infinite continues. For anyone who grew up playing OG action games, you'll know what that actually means.
And really, Metagal isn't that hard. I beat it in a single two hour sitting, even collecting all of the hidden power-ups. Died a few times here and there, took me a while to figure out to beat the final boss' first form, but I did it. It's doable. The graphics were colorful and the music not terrible. so it was a pleasant ride. If you can find this on sale, give it a whirl. While it's no Mega Man 6 (my personal favorite), it's certainly a playable and enjoyable action platformer in its own right.

I've been enjoying and appreciating this game so much that I highly recommend it to any gamer who likes mercenary company management, squad-sized turn-based tactical combat, and a low fantasy medieval setting. The game's great qualities are a superb combat system and an excellent character background and development system.
The game features several scenarios and an open world campaign mode with 25+ different enemies, 280+ items, 49 character perks and thousands of procedurally generated mercenaries for hire.
Your mercenary company can have up to 20 mercenaries of which 12 can participate in combat (wounded mercenaries need time to heal). Each mercenary can "equip" a wardog that can join a combat at the mercenary's discretion, whereupon the A.I. controls the wardog for the remainder of the combat.
Mercenaries have an experience level between 1 and 11. All hireable mercenaries have a background profession which may give them permanent stat modifiers and may determine the equipment that they come with.
Combat takes place on a hex grid. Combatants have their turn determined by an Initiative queue, and combatants can delay their turn. Actions consume APs (action points) and Fatigue Points.
Blunt weapons are capable of stunning opponents for 1 round. Slashing weapons are capable of causing opponents to bleed for a few rounds. Axes are capable of damaging and/or destroying shields. Mercenaries wielding shields are capable of setting shieldwalls. Mercenaries wielding spears are capable of setting spearwalls.
There are 3 types of armour: body armour, head armour, and shields. Each of these types of armour can be destroyed if they take enough damage equal to or greater than their Armour Rating.
Opponents include humans (including bandits and knights), orcs (including berserkers and warlords), goblins (including shamen), direwolves, undead (including ghouls, geists, and fallen heroes), necromancers, necrosavants, ancient priests, and ancient honor guards.
Combat is brutally lethal. Expect some of your mercenaries to die, especially early on in the game when your mercenaries have very poor armour.
You can choose to play the game as good mercenaries who kill bandits and monsters, or you can choose to play the game as evil mercenaries who attack trade caravans (in which case, expect to eventually be hunted down by the regional lord's soldiers and knights).
I have been playing this game in Ironman mode and I am loving the experience so much.
If you do play this game, then I strongly recommend that you play the game on the easiest difficulty setting because I first played this game on the middle (Veteran) difficulty setting and my mercenary company was wiped out by an orc raiding party.
I expect that this game will be a huge time-sink in my life.
The game is currently priced at US$20 but the price will increase to US$30 when the game is released on March 24.

Please, Don't Touch Anything is a puzzle game, and a very interesting little curiosity. You're asked to watch over this box with a large, red button, and asked not to touch anything. The magic begins when you press the button, and more controls open up. Doing certain things opens up more controls and more ways to interact with the box, and your goal is to get each of the possible endings by performing specific tasks.
The problem is that the things that need to be done are not at all straightforward. You'll have to use your puzzle-solving skills and your curiosity to see all of the content. You'll have to hunt for clues and find out what to do with them.
I enjoyed this game, but I don't think it's for everyone. If you don't have the patience to work through riddles, this game probably isn't for you, but if you do, then it's probably worth the $5. I'd definitely recommend avoiding walkthroughs until you're really stuck... there are some pretty tough ones, though, and some of the clues are difficult to find.
As for the soundtrack, I think I'd recommend playing the game before making that decision. The tracks are nice, but most of the game's music is fairly ambient. With full hindsight, I probably wouldn't have spent money on it, but that's because it doesn't appeal to my tastes... your mileage may vary.

Let's cut right to the chase; everything is decent up until fortress 3. The level design is a little uneven, the dialogue is clearly written by somebody whose first or even second language is not English, but the challenge of the game is on par with most normal Mega Man games as are the controls. Originally you'll think that the game is a fun, if short little romp into something we've all been begging for; more Mega Man (but with mostly female characters for flavor). However, once you hit fortress 3, everything goes out the window and it becomes apparent that the person or people who made this stage hates your guts.
The first section isn't that horrible, it's a bunch of moving platforms and if you stick to the top then everything will be fine... but if you do fall then you're in for a world of instant death pits, spikes and tricky jumps. The next section is delicious cake and perhaps the only small mercy you will ever see in this place, it's just simple timed dashing. Then the next part is where the stage first lost me; blind jumps onto spikes, having to abuse the fire dash special ability to pass over multiple spike floors, water that will send you head first into more spikes with enemies whose respawn is beyond anything Mega Man had seen, and then another section of more blind jumps with spikes with a gravity gimmick over instant death pits. Oh, and none of this has a checkpoint, so you need to do this all in one life.
When you do finally get a checkpoint it's just cruel sugar coating to the horror that the stage is half done; now comes instant death lava below you, sheets of timed screen filling instant death lava from above (which wasn't bad in the original stage you first saw them) and you have to use a property of a weapon never once explained to you to enhance your jumps to ensure that you can outrace a stage gimmick that has gone from fun to a waking nightmare. Then once the lava is done you get more spikes and fast instant death flamethrowers that never actually deactivate (see also Quick Man's instant death beams from Mega Man 2) that require more use of the weapon property nobody told you about and reflexes of a god which, even if you were a deity, would be tired by this point as you've died about 30 times from the horrible instant death nightmare.
Once that's done, however, you get an insulting easy boss, as if to pat you on the head for not throwing your PC out of a window in a fit of anger from the horrors you just experienced.
Fortress 3 is draining mentally and is out to crush your will to ever finish the game. It is there not to challenge you, but to torment you, to beat you down and try to break you. There is no fun in this, only mind numbing tedium, the kind of thing you find in I Wanna Be The Guy, only jacked up just a little more. Somebody wanted to outdo them and claim the title of worst possible stage design from Mega Man X6... and they did.
This game goes from scratching an itch you so desperately need to crushing your will to live within a few hours, and I am sadly beyond the point where I can get a refund. I cannot in good conscious condone this sort of thing, where the designer of this stage missed the point of Nintendo Hard so much that they went into territory that even the most horrid of ultra hard nonsense fan hacks (collectively called kaizo even though the meaning of the way has no inherent inclinations toward soul murdering difficulty spikes) would be jealous of. Do not, for the love of all that has ever existed, subject yourself to this unless you are masochistic enough to enjoy these sorts of things.

It has been a long time since I had last played a game like this. The type of game you'd label "A Shameless Cash in."
With the fourth season of Game of Thrones hitting the air, you might feel inspired to do your own bit of dynastic warfare. I am here to stop you. Whatever you do; you don't want to spend a penny on this pile of refuse. Game of Thrones Genesis is a broken and convoluted mess. It has some nice ideas, but pretty much everything stop it from working as it should.
Game of Thrones Genesis is a Real Time Strategy game, but it has a twist. Instead of building units and testing your tactics against your opponents you are now in the business of building alliances and brokering treaties between the many colourful houses of Westeros. The goal is out out-prestiege your opponent. You achieve this by earning money, maintaining alliances with towns and castles, eliminating prominent enemy units, uncovering your enemies' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sons, and upholding the faith. To accomplish this you employ the services of assassins, envoys, rouges, spies and even your own daughters to break or make allegiences. If you think that this sounds pretty cool then you are sadly mistaken. The system is a micromanagement nightmare. It is impossible to see what you need to do, because each unit is highly specialised. Even your random highwayman can't just be told to kill the enemy envoy. You need another unit for that. To make matters worse, everything is tiny. Even my HD screen is too small to even give me a remote chance to properly click on the one unit I need.
When all else fails you can always resort to war. War is an utter joke. Declaring war will deduct points from your prestige, so you need to trick your enemy into declaring war on you. What AI that cannot even walk from end of the map to the other without burrowing through a mountain is going to take your bait? War cannot be waged with your regular security units. Oh no, you need armies; special units that need food to function. Food is a resource that is advertised in the game as much as Sarin gas is advertised as a nice party trick on children's tv programming. You need to put peasants to work the field. However, both the peasants and the fields are hidden in the horrible interface and the unsightly map textures respectively. The army units then are supposed to work with a rock-paper-scissors system, but it doesn't. You're lucky if your army even goes to where you ask it to go.
Just when you thought you had seen it all the crapshoot AI comes in. The campaign is joke. It tells the origin story of Westeros and the Iron Throne. You begin as the Martells and shortly after you play as the Targaryans to subjugate the entire continent. Only to lose it the inevitable alliance of Stark, Lannister and Baratheon in the endgame, followed by a little bit of 'What if' up at the wall. The problem is the crapshoot AI. The moment you start the stage the AI makes it move and beats you. The only way to win is by trial and error. Find out what the AI does, counter it in the first minute, and move from there. The AI will just keep on trying to do what it was going to do, but will fail forever. It is both lame and boring. What's the point of playing a Game of Thrones if there isn't even a real game to play.
Don't buy this game. Avoid it like the plague. Put it in chains, drag it up to the wall, send it north, dump a couldron of gold on it, bury it in soft peat and finally recycle it as firelighters to burn the box it came in.

In Fairy Tale Mysteries: The Puppet Thief you're hired by the Grimm Brothers to discover why the children in their town keep on disappearing. This game follows the exact same formula every Artifex Mundi game uses and combines grim and fairy tales as usual as well.

Overall this HOG is short and easy, which makes it perfect for people new to the genre.
The average HOG player might be disappointed by this, but it's a good game nonetheless.

Average HOG from Artifex, You’re a detective in 1818 sent by the Grimm brothers (!) to investigate the disappearance of kids. The game is dark, all during the night, a bit creepy; perfect for Halloween.  The graphics are rather washed out, dark and a bit blurry, the game could use a graphic lifting with a bit of colors and contrasts. There’s also a bit of distortion probably due to converting the game on to 16/9 format.  The search screens are cluttered and not very pretty, it’s hard to distinguish the items which are generally almost blended into the background, or half hidden behind other objects! So the game looks and feels old with those distorted and cluttered screens.  But the music is good and the gameplay is top notch, closer to an adventure game than ever. The puzzle/mini games are as usual for Artifex short but of good quality, except for the bonus part  where they were really awful. I rather liked the main story, the puppets theme never gets old. Bonus chapter is however bleh and totally unrelated to the main story; yes for once the bonus chapter is really a bonus, not a part of the main story that was ripped off from the game to sell a collector edition version! But it was totally bland and the search screens were even more ugly and cluttered. Bonus lasted one hour and wasn’t really enjoyable, it felt so lackluster and subpar compared to the main game that it makes me wonder if it’s the same studio that made the main game that did it.
All in all the main game is vey classic and old school but it’s rather enjoyable. It lasted a total of 3 hours (including the bonus chapter!), which is VERY short! I find myself on a green planet, much like Earth. Right now, I'm an orca in the ocean, swimming around alone. I see a landmass up ahead -- a rocky, mountainous continent. With almost no effort, I become it. Then I focus in and descend into myself. Now I'm a bighorn sheep rolling around with the rest of my herd. Life as a bighorn sheep isn't that interesting, so I expand my focus outward. Very soon, I am everything at once: the herd of sheep, a pack of wolves, the forest, the rocks on the ground, the birds in the sky, two log cabins, a campfire, all of it rolling and sprouting and flying across the landscape in a honking, barking, chirping, rumbling riot. Then, on a whim, I press a few buttons and everything, all of it, turns into multi-colored gummy bears.
"Everything" is silly, beautiful, and one-of-a-kind. You play as a consciousness inhabiting an infinite world that can possess and transform objects and living beings at will. This isn't a sim, though. Once you possess something, there's not much else you can do besides move around, make noise, and transform into other things. However, Everything still manages to be fun and addictive due to the sheer range of things you can become and manipulate. Moving around a cityscape as a delivery truck, versus a factory, versus a black ant, is a totally different experience. Moving around a cityscape when you've turned all the buildings into flowers and all the cars into tropical fish is something else entirely. There are so many possibilities that it becomes very difficult to tear yourself away from the game.
The game definitely won't "click" with everyone. If you are very objective-oriented and don't like sandbox or exploration games without win conditions, you probably won't like Everything. The closest thing Everything has to a goal is to discover everything there is to be and fill out your "catalog." As a completionist, I'm really enjoying this goal. It feels like a cosmic scavenger hunt. However, I I know it won't appeal to everyone. If you enjoy just exploring a massive universe, taking in the sights, and making absurd things happen, Everything is definitely for you.
Personally, I'm so glad this game exists! Just talking about it makes me want to get back to plunging the universe into sweet, candy-colored chaos \o/

So close.  So close to being a real gem here.  They need to really polish it up.  The graphics look great, the animations are fantastic, and the concept is amazing.  Everything seems to work, it does have random dungeons, and they are all very unique.  The inventory system works well, the stat levelling up appears to be functional, and thank F$^%K you don't run out of arrows with the bow.  Also, the music is great.
The game's issues are ones which can be fixed.  They can adjust the movement speeds of the bats to be a little bit more reasonable, make the bosses run slower, make the zombies run faster, etc.  Fix the typos.  It's HIGHLIGHTED, not Highlited, and you even put "reccomended" and "completeing" in the store page description -- let's use spell check when trying to sell something!  Oh I found another one, you wrote "expreince" instead of "experience" on one of your signs in the front area but it was written correctly a few words previously.  Go take every word of dialog in this game and triple check them.
But the main issue is the melee weaponry.  Developer: go play Zelda: A Link To The Past.  Notice how far the sword swings, how quickly, and how smooth it is.  You would never swing a sword in that game and have time to turn around mid-swing, but more often than not I don't have time to finish a swing in Dungeons Are Random.  It's like the swords are wet pool noodles.  It's basically unplayable like this.  You have bats that can run at almost the same speed as you and you have to stop, turn around, swing your sword and just hope it hits.  Thankfully you can run around and run away before the weapon strikes.  It's actually one of the weirdest things I've seen.  The bow and arrow is perfect, however.  Does just as much damage, infinite ammo, and can reach them from far away.  I was not able to figure out how to use spells, the signs were not immediately clear.
You require a login and password, set up externally through your website to track high scores.  Why?  Steam leaderboards would be the professional way of doing things, and it sounds like the way you are doing is harder to achieve.
When you level up and are assigning your strength, agility, and whatnot...  It isn't clear what does what.  Only later I realized that I had to memorize the sign at the front.  Why not display a hint when you are levelling up?  Also, you start off with 1 point in each stat.  When you level up, you get an additional 10 points.  I put all 10 in strength to have a total of 11 there..  But it didn't seem to make any difference?
Minor complaint, when reading the controls, you have to read the sentence several times to understand it.  "When using a controller A, RB, X, B and Select buttons are for attacking, blocking, using item, pickup and opening inventory."  Maybe you might want to make that more clear.  Just show a picture of a controller and point to the buttons or something.
And lastly I will add that the block system is entirely broken.  You seem to state that while holding a shield it will reduce the damage taken by a set amount.  Well, if you are not holding a shield, you block 100% damage.  With a shield it is the same thing.  So you can just stand there and have 3-4 enemies attacking you for 20 minutes straight and you will not be hurt.  That's when I turned the game off.  Go finish your game!  It needs a lot of work, but I am very impressed at what I see so far.

Uncover mysteries, upgrade your equipment, and face believable antagonists in your touching quest to find survivors and restore hope to a small part of the world.
In Bastion, you explore once-populated lands and upgrade your equipment to face the enemies they contain.  A narrator follows your actions and explains the backstory.  After every mission, you return to a home base where you can customize your difficulty in interesting ways and pick the weapons you want to take on your next mission.  The upgrades are numerous enough that you will not get them all on the first playthough, providing incentive to play new game plus.  My first playthough took about twenty hours, with another nine hours to play through new game plus the first time.
+ superb narration
+ excellent artwork
+ great music
+ compelling story, with sympathetic antagonists
+ incremental upgrades that are not permanent (tune the weapon for the mission)
+ unique choose-your-own-difficulty mechanic which provides small benefits for increasing the difficulty in very specific ways, encouraging you to play at the edge of your abilities
+ sensible new game plus mode works well with the above difficulty mechanic
- It's not always clear when going down a path will result in permanently leaving the area

It's basically GTA in the city of Hong Kong.
You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop, who was tasked with infiltrating the Sun on Yee, one of the big triads in HK. Wei Shen recently returned to HK from the States and tasked with gaining access to the Sun on Yee, he returns to his old ties and his good friend Jackie who is a lackey of the Sun on Yee. You play both sides, completing missions from the triads and the cops. The main story will progress with Wei climbing the ladder in the Sun on Yee and each passing mission shows how he is maintaining the balance between his two identities. On the side, there are the many aspects of GTA such you can race, buy cars/clothes/customize, kill, and raise wanted levels ("level of heat" in this game). Unique features that differ from GTA is the karaoke and DLC clothing sets let you adapt the fighting style so if you equip Shaolin set, you fight like one.
Story is good, but a bit short. Would've liked if they had added more missions that went into the other gangs.
Excellent and funny AI dialogue; the best phrase is from Pork Bun guy : "A man who never eats pork bun is never a whole man"
Slow-motion shooting, kung-fu fighting, vaulting/parkour, wide range of Asian brand cars/bikes/clothing.
BONUS: if you understand Catonese, the game is even better and funnier because of the cursing and slangs, otherwise, there's a translation provided in the subtitles.
Overall, funny and well-made game. This version of the game isn't available anymore so get the Definitive.

It's been a long time since I enjoyed an RTS! I never played 8-Bit Armies so I don't have a comparison, but 8-Bit Hordes has a lot going for it. It's been reminding me of the old CnC games and Total Annihilation, which is one of my all-time favorites. The tech trees are basic and let you focus on tactics, and running a match doesn't take five hours, which I like a lot.
So far it's been really easy to pick up and understand. I went straight into the campaign to do the tutorial mission and went through the next couple missions without any issues. Everything has been straight forward plus the music is great and the art, effects, and animations add a lot of character. Controls are easy peasy and the game runs smooth too.
Skirmish mode is fun, plus community maps? Hell yes. I did run into a small bug where after the map was downloaded I had to cancel/start again, for some reason it didn't continue after it finished but that's hardly anything to turn my nose up at, especially on launch.
Coop is even more fun doing set missions with a buddy, and if only playing with one other friend isn't your speed then you can get a lot more of your pals into a multiplayer match to wreak havoc.
I'll update this review as I get more experience in it but so far it's been great! I can already tell it's well worth the money, I'm seriously surprised it released at such a low price point.

I don't usually write reviews for the videogames I've played, but I felt that this one deserved one. I have completed the game and now I try to improve my records on every stage, which means I have a good overview of the game. The game takes most of its elements from the Megaman videogame series but the point is that it improves a lot of these elements further. It provides a challenge without being devilishly difficult (+supports the player) and has a lot of great gameplay mechanics which vary among the stages (and a lot of clever level-design ideas too). Fortunately, you won't actually meet the cheap deathtraps that overwhelm the Megaman stages. I also liked the fact that the abilities you earn aren't just variations of your buster but completely different gadgets and "augumentations" that evolve your character's actions. Lastly, I loved the soundtrack of the game (it's just amazingly crafted) and the artwork during some of the cutscenes. The only minor negative I noticed were some small glitches here and there, but you may hardly find them during playing the game. Some may feel that there should be more stages, but I believe that the total duration of the game is fairly good given it's price. It's been quite a while since I had so much fun fighting epic bosses and shooting my way through a 2D action platformer (and I played "Megaman and Bass" last month). As a closing comment: those of you who can't stand the high difficulty of the Megaman videogames but would love to play something very close to the series' gameplay, this is just the game worth spending your money on.

The actual battle gameplay of this game is a godsend for turn based RNG games, but the real time overland map is super frustrating and has no tactical choices. The pause and go style is a horrible choice here.
For this game to become truely perfect, the overland map needs more turn based and RNG factors. The transistion from overland map to battlefield is very disconnected right now.
Ideally this game needs a skillset for the mercenary leader that add these elements. Like increased overland map movement, better tracking and vision. Also a "stealth" skill to better avoid overland battles or have a tactical preparation phase when going into battle, so you can choose you're starting terrain.
(A similar game, Expeditions: Conquistador has a skillset for the player, handling resources and overland travel. Very disappointed BB doesn't have something similar.)
When playing expert ironman, the overland map quickly becomes a frustration, your survival depends on avoiding battles and retreating often - which means you have to pause and go constantly, some times run in circles to avoid enemy bands and the manual battlefield retreat is horribly boring to do over and over.

Just a warning ahead:
The game is HARD. Don't get attached to your mercenaries, because many of them will die a very horrible death. Combat is brutal, a hit that penetrates armor (if you're lucky enough to have anything worth the name) is likely to cause persistent wounds.
So that warning out of the way, is the game worth buying? ABSOLUTELY!
It is one of the few RPG/Tactical Fantasy Wargames where the individual weapons truly matter.
Just some stuff the game considers:
Shields give a big defense boost. A battle line using a shield wall is hard to penetrate. A fighter with a shield can easily block arrows and strikes from swords. But flails ignore shield bonuses and axes can be use to destroy shields. Each weapons has different stats for armor penetration and damage to armor.
Troop morale matters. A lot. Soldiers seeing their comrades die will lose morale and eventually run. On both sides. Do you take out the strong enemy first? Or maybe it is better to quickly finish off the weak, so overall morale goes down? It's a question worth asking in every encounter (except, of course, against Undead).
Armor matters. A lot. Armor effectively gives the wearer a different set of hitpoint which is reduced before health damage occurs (though weapons do a % of penetrating damage). So vs highly armored enemies, hammers are a good weapon because they're designed to do more armor damage than other weapons. But heavy armor slows your soldiers down, they get fatigued more quickly and then cannot use their attack maneuvers.
The whole combat is rounded off with some RPG elements in that you can level your troops, increase their stats and unlock "perks" - special skills or maneuvers that may well make the difference for survival.
There are also some light fantasy elements. There are undead, monsters and orcs and goblins. But no mages throwing fireballs and stuff. And no healing spells either. This is a brutal, gritty flesh and blood type of battle that immerses you in small scale conflicts in the middle ages. It's also well written.
So if you like complex but still easy to understand small unit tactics in a medieval like setting and are not easily frustrated, but instead welcome the challenge: Buy it!

(Sigh)...Where to begin...
I mainly played on the 360 controller, which wasn't too bad if a bit rigid. So overall the controls weren't too bad, as most of the movement was relegated to the D-pad which considering it is how a game like this is supposed to be played. There was a few issues with getting the controller to work, but that was due to a HID (Human Interface Devices) issue and is entirely on my PC setup.
Along with the decent controls, the handling of the player avatar is pretty spot on with what you'd expect from a game in this genre. The jumping and movement are decent approximations of the older platformers in this genre of games, even the inclusion of a dash is quite nice to extend jumps and push through obstacles. It definitely channels the old Mega Man games well, but that's where that comparison ends.
Now on to the really bad parts of the game and the stuff that made me start this review in the first place. The Level Design is possibly the worst offender in deaths and cheap moments in this game, but that's not to say that the theming and the atmosphere of the levels are bad, on the contrary they each have their distinct feel which is actually good.  However, when it comes to the construction of the levels and overall enemy placement it is clearly so far flung from what a good game is that it creates it's own level of hell for all involved to stew in.
Let's back up a bit, the concpet of a decent level should have some Hazard Foresight/Telegraphing, where the player is put into a situation where they encounter dangers in a relatively solitary environment, then later on be thrust into a much more dangerous environment with multiple dangers coming at once. MetaGal does none of this, it basically throws caution and decent level design to the wind which results in a multitude of situations where the player is thrown into a situation where death is the only recourse for no misstep of their own.
This poor hazard telegraphing goes hand-in-hand with the amount of instant death pits and spike traps, the latter of which reminds me of a LEGO crazed six year-olds bedroom. It's nearly impossible to get around or through the levels when death is looming below numerous fall away and moving platforms. The worst part is all the levels are like this and make traversing them to the Boss room harder than the bosses themselves.
Along with these death traps, the enemies are a constant source of frustration and death which along with all the previously mentioned issues only ramp the problems up further. The basic enemies in MetaGal sponge up way too many shots and are so numerous that sometimes the screen scroll IS your worst enemy (Ex. Warp's Stage). Not to mention the placement of such enemies are often in front of instant death zones or in areas where a single hit can knock you into said death zone.
Overall, I don't recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the genre or even looking for an alternative from other games (i.e. Mighty No. 9). This game falls so flat on what makes a platformer good and memorable that I regret adding this game to my library.

I loved this game, I found it to be a very philosophical and interesting experience. Anybody who is interested in philosophy and enjoys quiter and more contemplative experiences will love this game. I had never heard of Alan Watts before or been exposed to that much eastern-inspired philospohy, so that aspect was particularly enjoyable. This is one of the more deep and thematically interesting games I've encountered.
That said, this game not for everyone. In fact I would say this is less a game and more of an interactive conceptual art piece, and some people aren't looking for that. I loved it, like I said, and would strongly recommend it to the right person, but if you get bored easily, or want cutting edge graphics, or want lots of action and a concrete plot and objectives, or aren't interested in philosophy, this game is not for you.

Fairy Tale Mysteries: The Puppet Thief [CE*], is a HOPA* game, developed by The House of Fables; Gogii Games and published by Artifex Mundi.
This is the first installment of the series. The next installment of the series is 'The Beanstalk.'
*CE - Collector's Edition
*HOPA - Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure.
Since this is an collector's edition game, it comes with some extra features, that aren't available in the regular edition game.
I want to mentioned that the visuals for this game is nicely done. The visuals can be adjusted in the option menu.
I want to mentioned that the audio for this game is well done even if it's simplistic and somewhat repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the option menu as well.
There are only three difficulty game modes to choose from: Casual,  Hard and Expert.
Diary Notebook it keeps track off all game's objectives and notes.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates there are tasks that needs to be done at certain locations. But it isn't immediately given at the start of the game.
All of the hidden object scenes consists of traditional word list with little or no interaction.
Most of the game's puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them.
There are seventeen different achievements that can be unlocked from playing the game. Each of these achievements do has some requirement before they can be unlocked.
There's a bonus chapter, but it can be access, only after the main portion of the game is fully completed. This bonus chapter is the direct sequel to the main story.
There are total of five different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, I've found this game enjoyable to certain extend. The replay value for this game is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

You would think that after years in development during a protracted early access phase with the benefit of feedback from players Chucklefish would produce something worthwhile, but Starbound falls significantly short of the mark, resulting in a confused, directionless game.
Starbound's locales are largely uninteresting and either populated with soulless procedurally generated quest givers or outright empty. The universe of Starbound feels like a lifeless husk.
In a misguided attempt to add traditional content to Starbound, Chucklefish shoehorned story and MMORPG-like quest progression into the game. Often you may even be given the same quest to visit the same landmark and perform the same task by several different questgivers from the same hub. Instanced dungeons defeat the purpose of sandbox-style gameplay and are clearly not designed to accomodate multiplayer when loot is not distributed to players in shared instances.
Combat is inexcusable; weapons are designed to hit in front of you and enemies are designed to run into you in a place where your weapons cannot hit--dealing with enemies quickly becomes a chore and the game would be actively improved by removing combat outright. The vast majority of mobs behave the same with a handful of exceptions that only serve to make combat even more tedious.
Crop growth times are
long, artificially inflating the playtime of the game and making farming-related quests utterly unreasonable.
is your grand vision for what Starbound is supposed to be, Chucklefish?
is the result of three years of iteration; each phase changing progression is increasingly nonsensical ways?
