Stacking is an interesting puzzle game where you have to stack yourself inside of other Matryoshka dolls and use their special abilities to solve the problems.
Let me give you an example, you need to clear out a party in a nearby room, so you find the doll that cuts nasty farts, and lay a stinker right into the vent that supplies that room with air; puzzle solved.
The game maintains that humor style throughout.  The visual style of the cut scenes is done in a style similiar to a silent movie and it works for this game.  The level design is very polished and everything meshes for this particular art style.
The only drawback of this game, is that each problem has multiple solutions.  It's good from the aspect that the game never forces you to solve a problem in any particular way; you're free to choose your solution.  However the game encourages you to solve the problem by exploring every solution.  This was fun for awhile, but the levels are massive and movement around them is not very fast.  So you figure out the second solution, and remember that the doll you need is all the way across the level.  Many puzzles have four or five soutions.  After you make this trek a few times it gets monotonous, even if the cut scenes are funny.  I got part way through this game and then let it sit for awhile exactly for this reason.  However I picked it back up and played it out to the end, just solving each puzzle once, and I'm glad I did as the ending was enjoyable with a quite a few hearty laughs on the way.
A good game for adults and kids alike, even though it delves into toilet humor territory, it still keeps it clean.

Not too sure what to write here so here's a recipe for Pancakes instead:
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it:
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

This is a quality 2004 stealth game. You are Garrett and you have to find out what the Prophecies of the Keepers are. Because you are a Master Thief, the keepers use your abilities to steal certain items which involves the prophecy.
The game is a first/third person stealth game where you can roam around the city. Steal from houses, pickpocket random people on the street and do whatever you can to get money, between missions. It all feels quite alive in all the small areas of the city and it's always fun to find new routes or hiding places from the guards as you bag all them precious stuff.
The people talk to each other, saying Good evening or bugger off as they walk by. Making it feel like a should be.
Missions are done in special areas where you can't get in when you are just roaming though.
However, I said hiding. Though in this game you can hide from a guard who spotted you in a shadow that is about 1 meter away. The AI isn't the smartest around. Once a guard killed a, what I think was a bandit, and when he walked passed it 15 seconds later, he wondered how there could be a corpse on the ground and directly want to scan the place for enemies.
Which in most cases, is the player because well...nothing is as suspiscious as wearing a black hood.
But even in missions, I once had an AI regularly walking and suddenly fall to her death, alerting everyone in the area.
I think that has to be the worst and maybe the only real problem of this game as the other thing that springs into my mind, is how awfully bad the physics system is. Bad but a good kind of bad. Everytime you will be amazed at how bodies go there way in this game.
But other than that, this game is a wonderful game. The story is interesting, the difficulty gradually gets higher as the game goes and the level design is just wonderful. Especially props to 1 certain level which could've been a stand alone horror game. *Shivers*
All in all, I recommend this game for it's story, gameplay and level design. The game looks a little old and it's best to download a FOVPatch from the internet, but the value of this game is certainly worth it.

Just a warning ahead:
The game is HARD. Don't get attached to your mercenaries, because many of them will die a very horrible death. Combat is brutal, a hit that penetrates armor (if you're lucky enough to have anything worth the name) is likely to cause persistent wounds.
So that warning out of the way, is the game worth buying? ABSOLUTELY!
It is one of the few RPG/Tactical Fantasy Wargames where the individual weapons truly matter.
Just some stuff the game considers:
Shields give a big defense boost. A battle line using a shield wall is hard to penetrate. A fighter with a shield can easily block arrows and strikes from swords. But flails ignore shield bonuses and axes can be use to destroy shields. Each weapons has different stats for armor penetration and damage to armor.
Troop morale matters. A lot. Soldiers seeing their comrades die will lose morale and eventually run. On both sides. Do you take out the strong enemy first? Or maybe it is better to quickly finish off the weak, so overall morale goes down? It's a question worth asking in every encounter (except, of course, against Undead).
Armor matters. A lot. Armor effectively gives the wearer a different set of hitpoint which is reduced before health damage occurs (though weapons do a % of penetrating damage). So vs highly armored enemies, hammers are a good weapon because they're designed to do more armor damage than other weapons. But heavy armor slows your soldiers down, they get fatigued more quickly and then cannot use their attack maneuvers.
The whole combat is rounded off with some RPG elements in that you can level your troops, increase their stats and unlock "perks" - special skills or maneuvers that may well make the difference for survival.
There are also some light fantasy elements. There are undead, monsters and orcs and goblins. But no mages throwing fireballs and stuff. And no healing spells either. This is a brutal, gritty flesh and blood type of battle that immerses you in small scale conflicts in the middle ages. It's also well written.
So if you like complex but still easy to understand small unit tactics in a medieval like setting and are not easily frustrated, but instead welcome the challenge: Buy it!

You already know what you're in for when looking at this, right? Like Legend of Dark Witch (another highly recommended Mega Man-like Run n' Gun for super cheap) this is a basically a gender swapped Mega Man. It's a retro-style run n' gun platformer pitting your mechanized heroine against a bunch of Android "Gals" vs. Mega Man's various dude Robot Masters (excluding MM9's Splash Woman).  Unlike Dark Witch, which adds in it's own ideas (like a Gradius style upgrade bar) this one sticks to the MM formula pretty much exclusively. But it does pretty well!
Visually it looks fantastic; the pixel art here and the color palette used is as good as, or better than, genuine SNES/Genesis/Amiga quality. The chibi character art really evoke cute, Japanese sidescrollers from the era. The quality of the chiptunes is great too. Controls are absolutely on point. They're super responsive and tight; it feels great with a 360 controller. The levels are very well designed, with areas being themed around various classic MM stage hazards like timed drop platforms, flame throwers and conveyor belt sections. Once you defeat the four main Gals and move onto the levels beyond, they even start making great use of your powers! See a wall you seemingly can't get passed? Fire the black hole-thing at an enemy on the other side to switch places and warp over there! See a gap that's too large for a dash jump? Jump anyway, then use Magma Gal's Flame Dash to cross to the other side! A ladder you can't reach? Shoot out your Mines, then jump on them to use the explosion to give you a boost! It gets REALLY GOOD once you have all these powers; the levels know that, and are designed thusly.
Meanwhile, enemies are positioned in ways and combinations that almost resemble an "action puzzle"; they'll shoot bouncing projectiles to get you to move to certain safe spots or you'll be able to perfectly take them out one-at-a-time from certain vantage points. It's just like the good old days! Speaking of, the difficulty is tuned to be "NES Hard"; really difficult, but never impossible and rewarding when conquered (and able to be more speedily conquered after you get it down). Sit there and watch patterns, try different weapon & ability combinations, or die and learn from failures when you try again: you WILL make progress... most of the time.
There are *some* issues that affect the difficulty. The timing windows on some of this stuff is absolutely brutal (particularly the fullscreen flame throwers in the second half of Magma Gal's stage and the explosive, timed platforms on Buster Gal's stage), enemies respawn THE SECOND you leave their "screen" (there's definitely places you can stand still that will cause them to continuously fly in from the edge of the screen, one after the other. Kind of good for grinding, but awful for combat where you have to maneuver in the air while jumping).
EDIT: The developer is doing a good job currently of patching and otherwise updating this game constantly. Issues I had a week ago (I previously mentioned no way to change the controller config here) are no longer here! Meanwhile, the balance on things seem to be constantly tweaked for the better. I definitely have to give a shout-out to the devs for continually polishing this up!
In the end, I just have a tiny issue with everything. Namely, the music compositions are a little repetitive (they all seem to be variants of the same song to me). But this game is $4 so I know its petty to bring up. What's here sounds good, but it bares mentioning anyway.
That's it. Every other little issue I had is now gone :D
--
Overall, it's definitely recommended if you're looking for a cheap Mega Man style run-n'-gun retro action game. This is an extremely well-crafted little game and definitely provides the fun and challenge you're looking for. This title could absolutely go for $10 and it would put some other games in that price range to shame. RetroRevolution has a quality game here for the price of a sandwich at Burger King. I hope this isn't the last we see of Meta Gal :)

I wish these guys every success because this game has me very exciteed to see what they do next.

Fairy Tale Mysteries is painfully short even for a hidden object game. It tries to hide its mediocrity behind a plethora of cinematics, but in the end it can be safely skipped in favour of its
Artifex Mundi is one of the best hidden object game developers, but as a publisher, they made some interesting choices—including this game.
The main problem with Fairy Tale Mysteries: The Puppet Thief is that it relies on its cut-scenes and barely anything else: the handful of places have very little to offer in terms of content. On top of all, the hidden object scenes not only feel like something made in 2008, but they repeat a lot.

I've recently played through Crystals of Time, which was my first hidden object game experience. Overall, I liked it, but I did not enjoy the shallow story and its fairly minimalistic realization that much. Fairy Tale Mysteries: The Puppet Thief exceeds the aforementioned game in these aspects, making it an ideal choice for the lovers of hidden object games (even though by reading other reviews, it seems there are better ones out there).
According to the story we've been asked to investigate the mysterious disappearances of local children of the fictional town of Arbourshire, by none others than the Grimm brothers (who were German aouthor and collectors of folk tales, but nevermind). Apparently an evil sorcerer, called the Puppet Thief is kidnapping the children and uses them as puppets.
The premise seems exciting and spooky enough, but after having finished the game many unanswered quetions remain. Why did the sorcerer did this? Why did he need the souls of children? What happened to the other children (we get to release only one), especially to the daughter of the Silver Magician for example? It seems it's been put together in a hurry and feels rushed, even though it successfully manages to keep up the scary atmosphere all the way till the end.
I liked the relatively frequent cutscenes (usually after achieving something important) that added a lot to the interactiveness and also strengthened the adventure factor of the game. Speaking of interactiveness, I don't know how ordinary it is in hidden object games, but there were some unusual occurrences (the mob setting the wagon ablaze while we are in a shop) that created some new sources from which we were able to acquire items needed for progress. Unfortunately these events were scarce. Item and inventory management isn't overcomplicated, so be warned: it is still far from the complexity and depth of a classic adventure game.
The hidden object scenes are nicely done, it's not too hard to find any of the required items (with the exception of one towards the end). The problem here was also present in Crystals of Time: you'll have to backtrack and reuse the exact same hidden object scene a second or third time to find something. So if you play on expert difficulty and get stuck, make sure to check back on previously visited hidden object scenes. The minigames were enjoyable and often tricky to solve, wish there were more of these.
I realize this game was originally designed for tablets and smart phones, so the graphic design should be judged accordingly. The game has nice, stylish graphics with moderate effects (sparks and lighting), but the quality of the cutscenes isn't that great since they are basically still images with dynamic elements zooming in and out.
The music is conventionally good, with mysterious tunes along with sound effects that are perfectly good for these kinds of games, that creates the necessary mysterious atmosphere.
The game also contains a bonus chapter (that's why it's marked as collector's edition), the Bella Island Adventure which is a pretty good additional adventure and is the continuation of the main game, where the player has to discover a mysterious island and free a young witch who has also been cursed by the Puppet Thief. It prolongs the 4-5 hours long playthrough of the main story with another 1.
Fairy Tale Mysteries: The Puppet Thief is solid, well made hidden object game which I would recommend to anyone who likes or wishes to try this genre despite its plotholes and minor faults.
PROS
+ not so hard hidden object challenges with very good minigames
+ stylish graphics, relatively many cutscenes
+ good atmosphere
CONS
- flaws in the story, despite the possibilites
- too few minigames
RATING
6.5/10

This game shows great potential, and with the right development could end up one of the most memorable survival games in the history of the genre. As one might expect, it's a bit bare-bones at the minute, but I have very high hopes.
Naturally, this being an alpha build, there are a number of bugs which need solving, but it seems that the developers are well aware of them. I do, however, have some suggestions as to how the game might be improved:
1. There ought to be larger islands with mammals that can be hunted.
2. A craftable bow and arrow should be introduced.
3. Resources ought to take much, much longer to replenish. Yucca and potato plants are so bountiful as to entirely mitigate the possibility of starvation/running out of rope.
4. Cooked food ought to have a noticeably different appearance in-game, such that one can differentiate between raw and cooked fish, for example.
5. Lighting a fire should be a difficult process, no more infinite lighter, please.
6. Shelter currently serves no apparent purpose, 'exposure' should be introduced as a feature in order to make the building of shelter an essential survival task, whereby prolonged spells in rainstorms rapidly accelerates the depletion of the hunger bar, eventually causing the player to become ill.
7. Fatigue should be introduced as a requirement much in the same way hunger and thirst currently are; sleep refills the fatigue bar to a greater or lesser degree depending on the quality of the shelter in which the player sleeps.
I'm excited as to what the future holds for this game!

This game ended up being surprisingly stale, they cut a massive amount of functioning content that made the game more entertaining, leaving the game with little to stand on compared to it's predecessor or other games in it's genre.
-The weapons are overbalanced and stratified (Magic is a joke, swords can attack in a combo but they get a huge delay afterwards if you do, all melee weapons are around the same level of slow etc.)
-All the interesting flying and movement options are removed, the morphball is the only surviving relic of this stuff, but its useless and is never necessary out of dungeons, and because it lacks any special abilities all you do is move through tiny holes with it. Like how hard would it have been to make it drop a little energy bomb to solve switch puzzles or something?
-The main questline requires you just running through same styled planets and clicking on furniture until you luck out enough to be able to play a dungeon. This could happen on your first try, or only be possible after around 5 hours of gameplay going through towns and planets per quest.
The worst part of this is, the game USED to have interesting and fun content, there used to be more than one reason to go to a moon, there used to be fun flying techs and movement modifications. Weapons used to attack in reasonably diverse ways, and actually good ones used to exist. But all this functional and fun stuff that people enjoyed from early access was taken out.
The only reason I could see, seeing as how all the stuff worked and was finished, is that they wanted these things to "fit" in the game. Like they wanted the morph ball to be useful, so they designed dungeons and levels with holes small enough to require it. But if say, someone had a jetpack, then any dungeon with a jumping puzzle would be trivialized. Thing is, they still have jumping techs in the game, because the "meat" of the game is still exploration, so you still can cheat at jumping puzzles, just not to the same extent. So in addition to failing there, this also means that you will never really be able to explore as easily as you want to, because the "meat" of the game is crippled by the devs inability to work around flight mechanics when designing pointless single item drop puzzle rooms.
This game's skeleton is still a metroidvania, and do you know what metroidvania's AREN'T beloved for, platforming and balanced combat. Few people played Castlevania Symphony of the Night and then commented "Wow I hate the crissaegrim, magic, and being a bat, climbing this tower while fighting the 800 medusa heads that spawned should have been WAY more tedious for me."
The changes made seem to reflect the dev's desire to make the game feel "whole" on release, no loose or frayed ends, and with mechanics at least "loosely" fitting in with what they've done, but the aspects of the gameplay they sought to preserve by removing content are the least palatable parts of the game, and now were stuck in a crippled snoozefest.
In summary, the devs goofed with their decisionmaking and the game has suffered for it.
Its a space game, throw in black hole guns, giant orbital beam cannons, jetpacks, lazer swords that can attack rapidly and in huge arcs, put in nukes that can unexist whole planets, either yielding huge mineral rewards or releashing eldritch terrors I need to fight with my ship. Throw in short range blink teleportation that doesnt suck. Make light not be an Issue for god sakes, I know the monster hunter logic of "the more we cripple the player the more mechanics we can have to uncripple them" and that makes sense for that game, but were in space for christ's sake, ALL suits would have A light on them, and there's enough other things going on that this wouldn't be missed. Put in high gravity planets, put in planets with poisonous food so you need to stock up. Throw in floating sky cities that hover on high density gas planets(real scientific possibilty for venus colonization). Or at the very least just put BACK in some of the fun that was removed.
The game as it stands is you double jumping around samey rocks while swinging a sword one time a second and clicking alien pots to get to the next dungeon. All other content is either nigh pointless or removed, and what's left is boring.

For example you can play as DeathSworn(Orcs) and vs Renegades(Basic C&C army). The art style is very simple and the gameplay is also very simple making it an easy pickup game. Anyways lets go into the pros and cons.

This stand-alone expansion type thing to Petroglyph's 8-Bit Armies is quite a solid game. It features two factions, both basic archetypes of fantasy-good and fantasy-evil similar to the original Warcrafts, simple uncomplicated RTS gameplay, and a cute aesthetic that reminds me of old browser based LEGO real time strategy games.
If you want the full experience, I would recommend getting this game along with its twin 8-Bit armies, so that you can mix and match the four factions from the two games together in multiplayer and skirmish. The campaigns for each faction are a bit lackluster, with no real story, voice acting, or cutscenes, just a series of skirmish maps (beautifully designed skirmish maps, mind you) with different scenarios to play through. However I feel that the core gameplay is fast and tense enough that doesn't matter so much, even if it is little more than a fantasy reskin of 8-Bit Armies.

This is a fun little game with two notable problems.
Metagal is a Mega Man homage and unashamed of it. It is a 2d run and gun platformer with a health bar, boss gates, stage select and the other trappings you find in any good game staring a blue robot. Little new ground has been broken but the engine feels more like a late GBA game than the familar NES classics and fangames.
The visuals, sound, and controls all meet expectations. The backgrounds are rich and vibrant while enemy designs are consistent and charming. The songs have strong melodies and good instrumentation. The controls are responsive and tight. Sometimes the shots can feel a bit delayed but it seems to be more a matter of projectile speed and animation than input delay.
The game has two significant failings: text and dash.
Text- The developers clearly do not use english as their first language -and I support game development all over the world- but if they want to market the game  as professionals they need to hire an editor to check their spelling and grammar. Thankfully the story is not the main attraction of the game and the tutorial conveys enough meaning to teach you.
Dash- To dash in the game tou need to double-tap forward. There is no other option. No ability to bind to a button. No ability to bind down + jump.  Every controller that supports this game has enough buttons to bind an additional but the option is absent. Some may find this to be inconsequential but I see it as a clumsy barrier tangling gameplay. (EDIT: they are already working on the dash button patch)
All things considered it is still a functional and cheap game that should be worth picking up if you are a mega fan running out of fangames.

Please note that although the game is still in Early Access the official release is just around the corner and so I'm reviewing the game in what will be its form upon release aside from a few tweeks here and there (especially since I'm opted in to play the latest beta updates).
My affair with Battle Brothers began when a friend of mine casually said to me "hey this game looks like it might appeal to you", and after lazily checking out the Battle Brothers store page I replied with, "yeah it looks alright. Might as well give it a try." Well it wasn't long until I was regailing him with epic tales of victory, tragic stories of defeat, and amusing little incidents that had taken place. He soon became worn down and bought the game himself, and here we are a few months and over two hundred hours of gameplay later, both hopelessly addicted and daring each other to play on "Veteran" difficulty now that the developers have renamed "Normal" difficulty to "Beginner" again, thus making us feel like cowards for choosing the latter. Well played, Overhype Studios. I know that you're deliberately taunting us.
As the recent tagline says, Battle Brothers is "a turn-based, tactical RPG". Imagine a game set in a gritty, low fantasy world with the campaign map of Mount and Blade and the tactical combat of XCOM. That's Battle Brothers. However I don't mean those comparisons to be as reductive as they may sound—they're merely comparisons. Battle Brothers is very much its own beast.
The world of Battle Brothers reminds me of Warcraft: Orcs and Humans from back in 1994, and I'd be prepared to swear in a court of law that some of the battle music was inspired by the orc tracks in that game. But this is a good thing. Like that original Warcraft game, Battle Brothers is set in a decidedly low fantasy, psuedo-medieval world. There are supernatural entities like the undead, there are orcs and goblins, and there's even magic, but it's all very grittily portrayed and relatively low-key. Think Robert E. Howard, not J. R. R. Tolkien. I personally really enjoy this approach more than I would a purely psuedo-medieval one and especially more than I would a tired, generic high fantasy interpretation.
In Battle Brothers you're tasked with leading a band of up to twenty men (twelve of whom can participate in battle at once) to glory, whatever that might mean to you. Your primary tasks will be recruiting said men (from a start of just three), making sure that they're always well supplied with money, food, tools, and medical supplies, settling any disputes and personal issues that might arise among them, leading them to settlements around the world to find contracts, and guiding their development as they gain experience, level-up, and acquire new skills.
The men that you'll be recruiting come from a variety of backgrounds and have their own traits which will influence how they behave and how they interact with everyone else in your band. Why just yesterday a monk that I had recruited from some destitute village convinced my flagellant that self-harm was not of God. That flagellant was brutally beheaded in battle not long after, but my monk can be proud that he brought the man to repentance before he met his Maker. The death of a brother, like so many things, affects the morale of your men, so you've got to be sure to keep their spirits up, sometimes with actual spirit (alcohol, not supernatural being) if that's what it takes. Oh, and you can name your company and each man in it anything that you like, and you can also choose a banner for them.
The destiny of your band is in your own hands. Perhaps you're just surviving until the great orc or undead invasion where you intend to prove your worth to the whole world. Perhaps you want to get cozy with one of the noble houses so that when war inevitably breaks out among them you'll be there to stack the odds and profit from the horror. Perhaps you're guided by some higher principle and want to seek out like minded men that can help you survive in a hostile world. Or perhaps you'll linger by the roadside like a stench, waiting for vulnerable peasants and their heavy-laden caravans to pass so that you can strike at them for some cheap gains and well deserved infamy. But the game doesn't leave you without direction—you'll be asked to choose one ambition from several to fulfil, which you can either go along with or ignore entirely. The choice is yours.
What I really love about Battle Brothers is just how important every last item is, especially the weapons. You know how in most role-playing games there's always that junk lying around that you'll never ever have a reason to use? There's no such thing in Battle Brothers. When your brothers find that pickaxe among the corpses of their fallen enemies, they don't see a rusty and worthless old tool—they see a wieldable ally with a proficiency in armour piercing, and that tatty old hood can mean the difference between a concussion and permanant brain damage. Yes, your brothers will incur injuries, and if they fall in battle but survive, it'll be a permanant injury of some kind. I'm not ashamed to send my brothers into battle wearing straw hats if necessary; better to look foolish than to end up dead. When you first play the game you'll be trying to discern whether it's best to have more, less well equipped brothers, or fewer, better equipped brothers.
The combat in this game is some of the most satisfying you can find. Every blow is visceral and you'll find yourself jerking forward in front of your keyboard as you click the mouse in an attempt to crack someone's skull with a warhammer before they get a chance to kill one of your more beloved brothers. The violence has weight and each death is a serious matter, as well as being an emotional one if the departed soul happens to have been a long time companion that you perhaps named after a close friend of yours. Having said that, I once named a brother that I'd assigned as my starting archer after a friend of mine, but he proved to be so utterly incompetent that I disbanded him and refused to pay him any compensation for doing so. Hey, I've got a heart, but I'm also trying to run a business here. Sort of.
I guess I should warn you that Battle Brothers is by far the most addictive game that I've ever played, and considering that I began my life of near daily gaming on the Commodore 64, that's no small claim. It's one of those games where you can get beaten so badly that you'll quit the game and be furious for a few minutes, and then have the urge to get right back to it, because deep down you know that as hard as the game is, failure mostly comes as a result of your own mistakes. When things are going well you can begin to get careless, and this game is not merciful to the careless. One wrong move can turn your merry band into the sorriest mercenaries who ever lived. Battle Brothers is hard, especially with Iron Man mode enabled, and I love it.
Battle Brothers is a fantastic game and the only thing more interesting than the game as it currently exists is just how much potential there is to expand upon it. The main strength of all games like Battle Brothers is the emergent gameplay and the ability to help shape the game world in a way that you've never seen before. With every new element that gets added, that world becomes so much richer and the possibilities increase tenfold. I very rarely feel the urge to spend time writing a review for any game, but I'm having so much fun with Battle Brothers that I just had to sing its praises.
So you've read my review (or skipped down to the final paragraph to see a summary that I intentionally don't provide), and it's possible that even now you're not convinced that you should buy this utterly compelling and endlessly replayable game called Battle Brothers. And that's okay. There's no shame in it at all. No-one is judging you. I mean, not everyone is manly enough for this kind of game.

I've only played two hidden object games thus far, but if the general quality of those two is in any way indicative of the genre in general, I may be better off stopping at two. I received a roughly a hundred of these for about three fifty from one of those ever present online bundles, and it seemed like a good time to try the genre out as I have someone missed out on them up to this point. And while I might not know much about hidden object games, I can still tell that Fairy Tale Mysteries: The Puppet Thief isn't a very good one.
This is a hidden object game, so it makes sense that the core gameplay feature is hidden object scenes. Between the main game and extra quest, there are over thirty of these scenes in total. The game will present you with a cluttered collection of objects, which tells you both that it's time to find some stuff and that the game may have a pretty serious hoarding problem. Each scene gives you nine different things to find (with some objects appearing more than once in the scene) and you need to scour the scene to find them, or give up and use some of the copious hints the game gives you if you really like hidden object games but hate hidden objects for some reason.
The scenes themselves are fine. Thirty in total is a decent amount (especially in comparison to the paultry amount offered in the sequel to this game), but it feels like another ten to twenty were needed for the price they're charging. The scenes themselves are fairly bland and while the objects themselves are fairly well hidden, the overall scenes are simply uninteresting. Furthermore, the game doesn't really integrate these into the gameplay very well, and they just sort of pop up every once in a while when the game gets bored. They also reuse the same scene frequently, and after you clear a scene the first time, about half of the time you need to come back later in the game to do the very same scene with some new objects to find. Not only does this just seem lazy, it requires pointless backtracking and if you ever get stuck, the solution usually is to poke around all your old hidden object scenes and find out which on is open for business again.
Beyond the hidden objects, the rest of the game is flat out bad. There are a handful of logic puzzles, but there isn't a single one that is even mildly clever. The very best can only be described as "mildly annoying" requiring you to rotate things to get them in the right order, while the most are so simple it takes all of ten seconds to figure them out. "Match the colors" or "figure out the simple pattern" isn't a logic puzzle - that's something you do to make sure you're ready to pass the first grade.
And the story is just absurdly bad. It has an interesting and spooky premise, with some evil force kidnapping kids and cramming their souls into puppets. How terrifying does that sound? How does this game manage to make that concept so boring? They really deserve a reward for making the terrifying mundane, because this level of botching a story really needs to be recognized for how acceptional it is. It could be that the visuals are laughably bad, but it really is more than that. There is no development, no real world building or anything like that. Sure, this is just a silly little hidden object game, but why put in a story if you aren't going to try and make it entertaining then?
So the hidden object scenes are only "okay" and everything else is terrible. This may find some appeal if you are an absolute, die hard hidden object game fan, and have already played every other single hidden object game. Beyond that demographic though, this simply isn't worth the price. Maybe if you find it in a bundle. But, hey, I found it in a bundle and wish something else had been bundled with the rest of the games instead. Like a rock or a root canal.

Metagal ended up being exactly what I hoped it would be.  I was looking for a game that paid homage to the old Megaman games of old.  Metagal does this in its own way but retains the feel (and difficulty) of those games.
It's not perfect.  There are some bugs and some issues with grammer.  I did feel like the controls are a bit sluggish.  Shooting while jumping felt a bit off, as did dash jumping.  It felt like it could be me but I noticed a few others mentioned it so it might need to be tweaked.  I didn't run into any gamebreaking bugs.  Just some minor ones but they were there.
That said they nail most everything else that matters.  The weapons are integrated pretty well into the gameplay.  There are plenty of secrets to find.  The stages and the bosses are diffcult but actually fair.  I got plenty frustrated doing each one over and over but at the same time I learned more about each fight and by the end knew exactly what I needed to do.  The look of the game might as well have come right out of the past.  The overarching feel of the game was great.  It's a great deal at the price as well.
I believe it's worth the price ($3.99) at the moment if you are looking for a good Megaman type game.  It does more than enough right to overlook the current issues in my estimation.  If you're not sure check back again after a patch or two and try it then.  It's certainly worth giving a shot.

This game ended up being surprisingly stale, they cut a massive amount of functioning content that made the game more entertaining, leaving the game with little to stand on compared to it's predecessor or other games in it's genre.
-The weapons are overbalanced and stratified (Magic is a joke, swords can attack in a combo but they get a huge delay afterwards if you do, all melee weapons are around the same level of slow etc.)
-All the interesting flying and movement options are removed, the morphball is the only surviving relic of this stuff, but its useless and is never necessary out of dungeons, and because it lacks any special abilities all you do is move through tiny holes with it. Like how hard would it have been to make it drop a little energy bomb to solve switch puzzles or something?
-The main questline requires you just running through same styled planets and clicking on furniture until you luck out enough to be able to play a dungeon. This could happen on your first try, or only be possible after around 5 hours of gameplay going through towns and planets per quest.
The worst part of this is, the game USED to have interesting and fun content, there used to be more than one reason to go to a moon, there used to be fun flying techs and movement modifications. Weapons used to attack in reasonably diverse ways, and actually good ones used to exist. But all this functional and fun stuff that people enjoyed from early access was taken out.
The only reason I could see, seeing as how all the stuff worked and was finished, is that they wanted these things to "fit" in the game. Like they wanted the morph ball to be useful, so they designed dungeons and levels with holes small enough to require it. But if say, someone had a jetpack, then any dungeon with a jumping puzzle would be trivialized. Thing is, they still have jumping techs in the game, because the "meat" of the game is still exploration, so you still can cheat at jumping puzzles, just not to the same extent. So in addition to failing there, this also means that you will never really be able to explore as easily as you want to, because the "meat" of the game is crippled by the devs inability to work around flight mechanics when designing pointless single item drop puzzle rooms.
This game's skeleton is still a metroidvania, and do you know what metroidvania's AREN'T beloved for, platforming and balanced combat. Few people played Castlevania Symphony of the Night and then commented "Wow I hate the crissaegrim, magic, and being a bat, climbing this tower while fighting the 800 medusa heads that spawned should have been WAY more tedious for me."
The changes made seem to reflect the dev's desire to make the game feel "whole" on release, no loose or frayed ends, and with mechanics at least "loosely" fitting in with what they've done, but the aspects of the gameplay they sought to preserve by removing content are the least palatable parts of the game, and now were stuck in a crippled snoozefest.
In summary, the devs goofed with their decisionmaking and the game has suffered for it.
Its a space game, throw in black hole guns, giant orbital beam cannons, jetpacks, lazer swords that can attack rapidly and in huge arcs, put in nukes that can unexist whole planets, either yielding huge mineral rewards or releashing eldritch terrors I need to fight with my ship. Throw in short range blink teleportation that doesnt suck. Make light not be an Issue for god sakes, I know the monster hunter logic of "the more we cripple the player the more mechanics we can have to uncripple them" and that makes sense for that game, but were in space for christ's sake, ALL suits would have A light on them, and there's enough other things going on that this wouldn't be missed. Put in high gravity planets, put in planets with poisonous food so you need to stock up. Throw in floating sky cities that hover on high density gas planets(real scientific possibilty for venus colonization). Or at the very least just put BACK in some of the fun that was removed.
The game as it stands is you double jumping around samey rocks while swinging a sword one time a second and clicking alien pots to get to the next dungeon. All other content is either nigh pointless or removed, and what's left is boring.

Your journeys will take you alll over the continent, from the sprawling ruins of the City, to the jungles of the Wild Unknown, and even to the far east, in the snowy lands of the Ura, a race of tunneling folk who once maintained a tenuous peace with Caelondia, but are now quite mad at you for reasons you will discover later.

Mount and Blade mixed with XCOM is the easiest way to describe this, but Battle Brothers is so much more.
At it's core, this is a tactical strategy game. Players control up to 12 units in battle and will fight a myriad of enemies from nobles to orcs to undead, all with their own strengths and weaknesses. More importantly, every hostile army feels truly unique. Orcs aggressively ram your troops while trying to overpower you. Human parties will defend their elite marksmen, forcing you to flee or go on the attack. Ancient undead legions use their shields to play a game that forces you to win before your men become too exhausted to fight. There is no one size fits all tactic in Battle Brothers, and that's honestly pretty rare.
The RPG element comes from leveling up your mercenary brothers, hiring new ones, completing quests for towns and nobles, exploring the procedurally generated map, and buying/finding new equipment. There's a lot of immersion to be had from quests that generate based on nobles' personalities and local threats. Well written events happen every so often to slowly flesh out your characters. Eventually, an endgame scenario arises that will challenge the player. Afterward, it can be played more like a neverending sandbox or the player can start again in a brand new world.
It is still in Early Access so it's not perfect yet. The pros and cons are as of today's patch.
Pros:
+ Thoughtful and varied tactical strategy
+ Procedurally generated worlds feel unique yet familiar
+ Tons of backgrounds, traits, and events to provide emergent gameplay opportunities
+ Permadeath will keep you on your toes
+ Large roster of potential brothers (12 active, 8 reserve) to create unique compositions and ease the pain of permadeath
+ Challenging difficulties (Veteran, Expert) for those who want it and Beginner difficulty for those who don't
+ Excellent pacing leading up to the endgame crises
+ Developers are on the ball with updates
+ Combat feels accurately representative of medieval warfare without being too nuanced
Cons:
- Events occur too infrequently to grow too attached to characters
- Some perks still feel too weak and some traits feel odd
- Achievements aren't particularly exciting (feels more like things you'll just get from playing rather than goals to shoot for)
- Game has crashed while autosaving, corrupting my ironman save so I don't play true ironman anymore (even after Avast fix)
Neutral:
- RNG. It's not bad in this game. I find it much more reasonable and easier to mitigate than in XCOM. But if you'll go ballistic because an arrow one shots your leather wearing brother then you better not play this. You'll miss 80% shots just like you'll hit 20% shots. Random happens but I've always felt that if a battle went poorly, it has been my fault.
EDIT: I reviewed this in Early Access shortly before launch. Looking it over, I only had to change a couple of things. I really hope quantity and frequency of events to build up the Battle Brothers squad get a look as it is (IMO) the only thing missing from a complete experience.

A Game of Thrones - Genesis is a "boardgame" style strategy game with real-time-strategy elements. It's a simple concept: you begin with a "home base" and slowly expand your empire. But that is where simplicity ends: expanding your empire is accomplished principally by winning the loyalty of neighboring towns and castles with diplomatic envoys. The more towns that are loyal to you, the more income you have, and income will help you produce more units.
Then, you will need to create some spy rings in enemy cities, subdue spies in your own cities, assassinate nobles, and other nefarious acts in order to succeed. You can even have the enemy create and command units that he thinks are working for him, but are actually working for you. It is the most layered, deep espionage system I have ever seen in a game (think Civ4 times 15). That being said, I also feel that the game is too deep for an RTS, playing strategically requires a bit of deep thought and I felt intimidated about having to think faster than my opponent, rather than being able to take my time and press "end turn" like in Civilization or Master of Orion.
Here is most of the game's complexity in a nutshell: envoys create alliances, spies ruin alliances, nobles create blood alliances, assassins ruin blood alliances, guards block towns from assassins, spies and assassins working together can circumvent guards. Spies can reveal hidden enemy units, because about 90% of the units in the game are visible only to the player who controls them. They are on a generous "stealth timer" when in enemy territory.
* Great interface, smooth controls.
* A game so deep that it could never be released on anything but PC.
* The game is very well suited for multiplayer matches with a friend.
* It is kind of fun to learn, but I assume you cannot truly appreciate it until you have mastered the basics (which I was never able to do.)
* Lots of achievements to unlock.
* High skill ceiling.
* Long load times
* Expensive pricetag, the game would be a fair buy at $10, but not $20.
* Very little connection to the A Game of Thrones series that we know and love, except for the Lannisters are all jerks and killed me in my first match.
* The game might be too complex for many people. I don't want you to confuse "complex" with "strategic." There are times when things are needlessly complex.
* Some small problems with the tutorial. It will direct you to "look at the map in the lower right corner," when the map is actually in the lower left. Also, the "back" button does absolutely nothing in the tutorial's dialogue boxes.
* High-learning curve.
* The game is not friendly to colorblind players. The fog of war is just a b&w version of the map, but it's very difficult to differentiate between the colored (visible) parts of the map and the b&w (fog of war) parts of the map, especially in snowy areas. If you are colorblind, you will go mad if you try to play as the Starks.
* The battle animations are, well, terrible - but I'd rather have bad animations than bugs. Additionally, although war is a large aspect of the game, 90% of the game is the espionage that happens before the war.
* Uses TAGES DRM. (5 machine installation limit).
If you are looking for an ultra-deep strategy game, pick this up. If you are new to 4X games, I would suggest waiting for it to go on sale for >49%, as the game is really hard to appreciate if you aren't already intimately familiar with its genre.

I don't get as much time to play games nowadays as I used to, so a game which packs the most punch into the shortest time is the one which'll grab my attention nowadays.  Also I've shied away from the "retro-looking" games for the most part:  Just because I liked the games back then, doesn't mean I want to play them again.  Let's move on!
So, why did I play PDTA?     Because while this is very retro-looking, it's a brand new twist on the point-and-click genre.
So, the point of the game seems to be to find all the ways to blow up, squash, terrorise, vaporise, or imprison the inhabitants of a city, using an enigmatic "machine".   Alternatively, the intro makes me think that it's a set-up, and I'm being surreptitiously "tested" for my intelligence and tenacity...
This is where the full, FMV cutscenes of other games, spend millions in acting and rendering to establish a plot, while this game achieves exactly the same with about a dozen lines of text.   Testament to the genius of some developers and artists, imho, versus the big corporate machine.
I rattled my way through about 3/4 of PDTA without any real difficulty.  The game is almost fully self-contained clue-wise, and a cup of tea and a digestive are usually the right brain-food, while also taking the right amount of time for you to sit back, think it over, and hit on the solution.
There do come some points, though, where you just hit a total brick wall.  There's one "Diamond" puzzle which (to me) seems woefully incomplete in the clue department, and I ended up giving up (after many many hours of trying to puzzle it out), and reading a walkthrough.  This, I suspect, is how most people will solve the last few puzzles in PDTA.
I found about 80% of the time I spent playing PDTA immensely satisfying, and I got the same feeling I get when I'm doing a Sudoku, or a crossword... That deep intense "me vs. the puzzle".    For that, I'd happily recommend this to any one of my friends.
It's a relatively short game, unless you're a massive completist (like me).   I don't think I'll go for the perfectionist badge, though... I don't trust my clicking skills that much, haha..

Everything is an unusual game, it's actually more like a documentary. It presents philosophical questions like "What exactly is a thing?", "What happens when we die?", "What are we?", "Why do we live?" and so on... These questions may sound cheesy when you look at them but when you are inside the game they seem interesting, because the ones answering will be Oak Trees, Squirrels, Spiral Galaxies, Hydrogen atoms, everything really. (And Alan Watts)
So if you can bear the first 20 minutes of confusion, you will be out for one hell of a ride.

Hello, all. It's been a long time since I've played Bastion, but I think I can remember it well enough to post a review. Let's get started, eh?
*****************************************
*Name: Bastion
*Developer: Supergiant Games
*Publisher: Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment
*Year:2011
*Platforms:Windows, Mac OSX, Linux, Xbox 360, iOS, Playstation 4, Playstation Veta.
*****************************************
+Pros
+Well, first thing that comes to mind when I think of Bastion is the music. It was delightful to listen to while slaying enemies, and while doing most tasks. I still listen to it regularly today, even though I played the game in, around early 2015.
+The Narrorator. His voice is very nice, to say the least. I enjoyed the storytelling through him and not so much the main character, as I tend to in most of the media that I consume.
+The weapon variation. I can't remember exactly how many weapons were in the game, but each one had its own style of play, and you can carry two weapons with you going out into your missions. The ones that come to the top of my head are the hammer, rifle, and the bow. Another thing that spices up the customization of the game is the abilities. You can pick up black potions (the in-game name escapes me at the moment), to use a secondary ability, such as summoning squirts, or other such things that I won't spoil.
+The Visuals. I heavily enjoyed the aesthetic of the game, the paths building themselves as you walk onto them. Very pretty indeed.
+It has New Game+, which is always a good thing
-Cons
-Well, it's hard for me to think of cons for Bastion, if I'm honest. I'm sure they're there, but it's been so long since I've played Bastion that I can't really remember anything that truely annoyed me. So yes, I would recommend this game.

Bastion is my favorite game of all time. It provides a great experience from a gameplay, visual, narrative and (of course) auditory perspective.
From a gameplay perspective, it's a typical action ARPG. Nothing new, but Bastion really polishes the isometric action ARPG formula to the point that everything you do feels good. Interacting with the environment, while only in simple ways, is accomplished at the press of a button. The controls are of course tuned for combat, and feel really intuituitive, to the point that you don't eevn think about them while performing complex manouvers in combat. Again, something we've come to be used to with games these days, but Bastion does it really well.
From a visual perspective, Bastion displays it's overall tone before a single word is said by the narrator. A semi - wild west setting that at first seems colorful until the sense of desolation sets in.
From a narrative perspective, Bastion is a simple, yet hard - hitting and meaningful experience. (Without spoiling too much) the plot follows a small group of survivors, surviving in the wake of a catastrophic apocalyptic event. Honestly though, the larger plot most of the time takes the backseat to the lore of the game. You see, the narrator, one of the NPC survivors, has something to say for almost everything you do or find. By finding objects within the missions of the game, and honestly just playing the game regularly, the lore of the land before the apocalypse, and the events leading up to said apocalypse are revealed. Learning so much about the land, and knowing that none of it matters anymore gives a unique melancholy that is leagues apart from the "cue cutscene, awww I'm sad now" scenes of the mainstream.
From an auditory standpoint, Bastion is absolutely amazing. It's soundtrack is so good, it's almost as hard to describe as it's genre. The closest anyone's come is the actual creators of it, offerning "Frontier acoustic trip hop." Again, hard to explain. It plays almost as important a part in the game as the plot and the gameplay, maybe even more so. It casts the mood as much as the visuals, and well it's just amazing. Of course, there's also what most people associate Bastion with, the narration. Like I said in Narrative, he's just integral to the plot, but from an auditory perspective, it's just as great. Logan Cunningham performs amazingly as Rucks, with a rough, grating, world weary, but  ultimately wise voice, complete with soft western accent. Very well done.
HOLY GIANT WALL OF TEXT BATMAN!! OK, I had no idea I wrote so much, sorry. TL;DR: It's a great experience gameplay, visual, narrative, and audio - wise, and you should totally pick it up.

As someone who has spent over 200 hours in Mount&Blade, I love the idea of running a mercenary company, so I immediately took notice to Battle Brothers. It might still be in early access, but I found it to be more polished than most games upon release. Haven't experienced any crashes and the only bug I encountered was when an enemy failed to act during his turn, forcing me to restart the battle (happened twice in 30+hours).
The thing I love the most is how well Battle Brothers immerses you in the world. You are going to care about your fighters and you're gonna be sad when one of them gets his head chopped off. Perhaps not "oh no, I only have one week left to live" kind of sad, but more like "oh no, they ran out of bagels and I really wanted a bagel" kind of sad. And your mercenaries are gonna die quite often.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥his pants while surrounded - death. Trying to take on an orc warrior one on one - most likely death. Being eaten by a Nachsehrer while the rest of the party is retreating - death. Yeah, there are a lot of ways to die, each being more gruesome than the last. But that's what makes it fun.
Then there's customization. Of course you get a large variety of perks to choose from when leveling up (the new system is MUCH better than the last one) and you can also equip each brother with weapons, armor and accessories. There are different types of weapons, each with its own attacks, strengths and weaknesses. Spears can form a shield wall but don't deal that much damage, swords are great against unarmored targets but aren't that good against armor, axes can make quick work out of shields, flails have a change to stun...  Each brother also has its own backstory, profession, attributes and passive characteristics, making him unique in a way and giving you a good way to separate them from each other (or identify what's left of the bodies). Oh, and since one of the recent updates, you (and enemies) can also get injured. You really have to plan your lineup later on, because you'll be facing stronger and stronger threats.
I would also like to cover the enemies. There are quite a lot of different types, including orcs, goblins, skeletons, bandits and more. Each has their own tactics and style, forcing you to adapt according to your opponent. I found the AI really good too and they act like how you would expect them to. Mindless zombies are going to charge brain first into your shield wall, while bandits will try to avoid it. Support units are going to stay back and try to avoid close combat, while the others will do their best to protect them. I've also discovered that archers and ghosts sometimes act a bit funny, moving a square back and forth instead of shooting. One thing I'd really like to see in the future is an even larger enemy variety and I am looking forward to discovering what the developers have in store for us. It's an early access game, after all, and a lot of things can still be added or changed.
As the last thing - world map. You travel on it in real time, visit towns to restock and get a profitable contract (you are a mercenary company, after all). After you're happy with the pay, you will usually have to fight an enemy group. What else is there to do on the world map? Not much. You can of course explore and fight on your own, there are even named items to find in the uncivilized part of the world, encouraging exploration. But besides from that, there really isn't much to do. The recently added fast forward option does help a bit, but I would still like to see more things to do. Oh, and one more thing that is almost necessary - animation speed. The default movement speed during battles is quite slow and while there is an option to turn animations off, it can get confusing, since it's harder to keep track, where everybody has moved. Besides from that, I really don't have any issues with the game. Of course, things could be improved, but I find it really fun and well made already. One thing I'd like to see in the future is mod support.
So, what do I have to say about Battle Brothers? I love it. It's a great tactical turn based strategy game that is easy to play, but hard to master. It is also a bit luck dependent, but that's the case with every game of this type. The AI is surely one of the best I've seen in this kind of games and the variety is good enough to keep you going. I highly recommend that you try Battle Brothers out, especially if you're a fan of Mount and Blade.

Being a massive fan of the book series and television show, I bought this game the day it was released. It has gone down in history as one of my most regretted gaming purchases. Cyanide's A Game of Thrones - Genesis is a messily designed, technically janky game that I wouldn't recommend to any besides the die-hard fan, who isn't reading this review anyway.
The game is essentially a virtual board game, in which you send one of a few kinds of units around a map in order to maintain control of them. It's largely tedious and frustrating. You can do this in a story campaign, which gives you small maps and half-thematic objectives. I didn't make it far into this story and wouldn't recommend you do so. Much more tolerable if not actually enjoyable is the multiplayer mode, in which you select a larger portion of Westeros to fight over with computer or human opponents. Though I very much doubt you will find human opponents online at this point. The gameplay in the multiplayer mode is slightly more interesting, with a few more kinds of units and actions you can take.
To be frank, Genesis seems like a game designed with bullet points in mind. Marketing materials might say you can marry off your noble daughter to an enemy to cement an uneasy alliance, or send an agent to infiltrate the enemy AS an enemy agent, and then turn him when the enemy thinks he's hurting you with that double agent. Both of these are true, but these mechanics are very shallow and there are only a few of them.
In the end Genesis will likely leave you wanting, as a fan of Martin's world. I might recommend instead the actual board game from Fantasy Flight Games, or the Crusader Kings 2 conversion mod. Sadly, an amateur game modification is vastly superior and better supported than this official game.

If you love turn based RPGs, its like a dream come true. You start off in a randomly generated world with a bunch of towns which are all different (have different buildings, charge different prices, etc) The game has initial direction (sort of like a tutorial mission and tips) and after that its up to you what you want to accomplish with your mercenary band. Just my opinion, but I would start by playing the game on easy to learn. Then once you learn the game, veteran ironman before taking on legendary ironman. Ironman can be frustrating but once you've played it, its hard to go back.
The say that they will come out with end of game events, sort of like endings, in order to give the game some closure. If you just like fighting turn based RPG style battles, it's not really needed IMO. The best part about the game is your freedom to choose. You can just go on reking stuff for a long time before your company reaches GOD status.
I've had the game for about a year (maybe more) now and am just getting around to writing the review.
PROS:
- Simple to learn. Gameplay and UI make it easy. Going from menu to menu is probably the best aspect of the UI. In some games, it wont let you access your inventory or see your party status without exiting certain screens but this game doesn't have that. It makes high frequency transactions easier to deal with. IE: selling, recruiting
- The art is pretty cool. Characters will change appearence based on the armor/weapons equipped as well as status (will look injured or bloody) The world map isnt fantastic from a terrain perspective, but its not a big deal.
- Replayability is fairly high. You can't really go on autopilot when you play this game. Again, I play on legendary/ironman nowadays and if you take a bad mission things can escalate very quickly. Especially in the mid - late game. Even on veteran/ironman, you can't really lose focus or you'll end up losing a character or 2 every now and then.
- Every battle has terrain and opposition nuances which make every battle a challenge. Makes tactical choices more interesting and important. Its easy to lose track of time just hopping from one contract to another.
- Different weapons and fighting styles make the game interesting and have their own unique skils which means you can customize how you want to fight. For instance, spears can set up a spear wall. Swords have riposte. Axes can break shields. You can choose a two handed weapon with no shield, etc.
- Hero customization is pretty cool. Can change appearence, give em nicknames, etc. Makes it hard when they die though. They also come with a set of pre-exisiting personality attributes which you can't change. You just have to use skill points to get around it. For example, being tiny decreases your melee attk but increases your def. Craven lowers their resolve, etc.
CONS:
- Like all turn based RPGs, the RNG can drive you completely nuts. It helps a little bit if you learn adaptation and level up your heroes, but when you miss several 70%+ attks in a row, it can get pretty annoying. Worst I've missed is I think a 91-92. But in the beginning, when your guys aren't that strong, you have to just play a bit more defensively and plan on missing the majority of your attacks.
- Losing people is awful and can be completely demoralizing. You get attached and you have to either pay alot for more advanced recruits or start off with a lvl 1 person. OR if you're not on ironman, reload from a savepoint. In the midgame, this process is completely brutal and can sometimes lead to the whole company getting rekt if you have too many low lvl people and take a bad contract.
- Can't see enemy movement possibilities. Some games have this, some games don't. But you can't see where the enemy can move to. After you play for awhile, you'll sort of know. But I have almost 100 hours on the game and eneimes can still surprise me and move into a hex I didn't think they could reach.
- I wish they had battle classes. There are no healers and no magic. Its more of a gritty fantasy based game. True, you could just skill characters up to sort of mirror classes. (IE: train weapon mastery) and before they are recruited they come with previous jobs which give them pre-exisiting attributes. (IE: farmhands have more fatigue and HP) but it would still be cool to make someone a knight or a lancer, etc. Best you can do is just give them bad a$$ armor and weapons, then rename them to "SIR" or add "THE LANCER".
- Game has been in early access for awhile and I would play more but I'm just waiting for this final patch to go through which is taking forever. I understand that they want to get it right but the game has been in early access for about 2 years now and its time to finish it up.
CONCLUSION:
Would definitely recommend this game, especially now. Its almost complete and there's not much fine tuning left. As I stated, if you love turn based RPGs, this is a great game. If you don't, you won't get as much out of it as I have. It doesn't have the art and animation of an Xcom but the gameplay is engaging and challenging. Anything they add in the final update will just be a cherry on top. I can't swear that any final changes they put in will NOT totally break the game, but look for posts after the final update goes in to make sure.

I understand that Valve ported the entirety of this game into the sequel, but I feel that if you want to play the original how it was meant to be played, you should buy this masterpiece as well. The original is zombie survival horror in its purest form. You've got guns, three other players, and the occasional healing item; it's up to you and your friends to figure out how to make it work.
That being said, it does lack some of the features found in its sequel. Melee weapons are nowhere to be found, your weapon selection is a bit slimmer, and you will encounter only three types of special infected. However, there are smaller details present in the original that can't be found in the second. Survivors collapse and are affected by physics upon death, and any playable character has legs. The lighting is nicer than in the second game, and there are subtle changes in character animation that aren't featured in the second game. All of these things do wonders for creating a more authentic and absorbing experience.
If you've played the second game and aren't willing to sacrifice more content for immersion, I can't say that I can recommend buying this game. But for those of you that can look past it and see this game for what it really is, this is a game that you'll genuinely enjoy.
After 300+ hours, there is one thing that I can say for sure: Left for Dead is an a timeless classic and a one of a kind experience that you'll find yourself coming back to again and again.

I was so excited to finish this game, the first time ever to get all the way through a game.  I was excited to play another hidden object game published by Artifex Mundi.  The story had a great premise and built well on the scare factor.  I enjoyed the flow of discovery and unfolding of the story through the use of the letters from the Brother’s Grimm.  The graphics were less dramatic than previous works and I found at times during the hidden object scenes that a couple of items I found quite difficult to make out at all.  There seemed to be a grainy quality to the scenes that at times hindered discovery.  I found myself using the hint option more than I have previously and the skip came into play quite a few times when it came to the mini games, which disappointed me.  The Puppeteer character was well thought out and used to great effect and the Brother’s Grimm was  fantastic addition.
I feel this game almost feels like an initial phase of a franchise and with the sequel already being available on the Steam platform goes someway to proving that.  I believe that there are so many aspects that could have been built on further.  For instance how did you become connected to the Brothers Grimm?  How did the Puppeteer become evil?  Where were the children’s souls held?  What happened to the angry mob? What is the story of the wizard with the crystals?  I found it handy to check your journal for progress and hints when I couldn’t figure out my next move.  I enjoyed this game and was proud to have completed it I just feel it could be built on to be better.
I would recommend Fairy Tale Mysteries: The Puppet Thief to casual gamers who want to spend a couple of hours playing through a hidden object game with minigames and a connective story.

Most people see the $15 (USD) price tag as a turn-off. "I could buy
, a real game, with that money". Well here's why I disagree. Think of how much it costs for a movie ticket. You buy a movie ticket for about $8, maybe even $15 for 3-D. You get about 1-2 hours of enjoyment, and the memory of the experience. It's usually a one-time thing, and then it's over. With this game, and many other atmospheric games like this, you're given so much more than a movie. You can play for hours and hours, every minute feeling new and exciting. You can see all these different things and places, and feel like you're truly there and interact with them. In
, you can be everything. Think of any item you see in a city, or any plant you see in a forest, or any body you see in space, or any bacteria you see in a microscope. You're given free control to shift your Perspective through any item in the universe, and beyond. Along with this unique gameplay, you have a wonderful soundtrack, beautiful audio sounds, and a thoughfully engaging speech seminar from Dallas in 1965. It's such an enriching experience that I reccomend anyone who has a couple hours to spare, and an open mind, to purchase, and become

I've tried this game twice and both times I just didn't like it.
The first time I played for a couple hours and just kept having less and less interest in starting it up again.
I tried it again this week, and I am pretty sure I'm not going to bother with it again in the future.
For a GTA-style game there feels like so few options...in stores, with weapons, etc. The driving feels AWFUL. Cars handle worse than their real world equivalent. That just baffles me. It's a @#$%ing game. It is fine for cars to handle too well, to take less damage, and to accelerate too quickly.
Combat is terrible, too. Wait for enemy to glow red and press E. Hit them a few times. Repeat. There's an unnecessary number of combos, but really they are superfluous. The game gives you no reason to mix up your attacks.
Racing is stupid. Your opponents drive incredibly slow when you are behind and then have warp speed if you ever take the lead.
A lot of places seem bizarrely unforgiving of very minor errors. End a section with low health and you have no choice but to move to the next area and die the first time you get hit. Take a turn a little off while driving and suffer the lack of acceleration, maneuverability, and torque for 15 seconds while you get yourself out of the stupid corner you are wedged into. And so on.
There are no checkpoints. Lose against the last guy in the last wave of fight club? You get nothing and have to start over from the very beginning. Lose in part 4 of some mission? Back to square one with you!
The trailer for this game was sensational, but the gameplay feels nothing like it. Very disappointing. C- overall.

Everything is something, and somewhere everything is everything.
This isn't a game: it's a philosophy seminar. A way of life, a manner of thinking. I picked up this game just to see what all the fuss was about since the graphics didn't look that exciting and the way creatures moved was unrealistic...but then after I found my first seminar extract/narration I understood why this game was so captivating.
Each section of narration delved deeper into the philosophical thought that what we perceive as reality is in fact our own universe talking to itself. Seriously, this game makes you think deeper than it needed to, and I find that fascinating.
Everyone will take something from everything differently, the experiences we have are all the same but it is how we perceive those experiences that is truely unique.
Honestly I would have been perfectly happy if this seminar was just played over footage of a goat rolling around in circles.

is a quirky, experimental game. You move around the world and take control of different objects. There are 6 categories of objects which are sorted by size. Those objects range from planck lengths to galaxies with a great deal in between. My personal favourites were a construction crane and a set of ancient ruins.
These mechanics are meant to tie in with the ideas of Alan Watts; a pop philosopher who helped popularise a particular strain of Buddhist thought in the West. Excerpts  of Watts' talks are unlocked gradually as you move through the game. It is enjoyable to listen to Watts talk and the sort of notions he clumsily gestures at broadly tie in nicely with the game's mechanics but they do not offer anything but the most superficial insight. Watts is a good orator but his theories are of no philosophical value and they are not taken at all seriously in academia. His work is hopelessly vague and marked by what Daniel Dennett calls 'deepities'; claims which are on one reading obviously true but boring and on another they are bold but obviously false. 'Deepities' create the impression of profunding by trading on the ambiguity between their two possible readings.
As a result some who play Everything may be irked, finding it pretentious. Others may play it and get frustrated, worried that they are not smart enough to 'get it'. But if you opt not to take the game too seriously, if you avoid looking for any earthshattering wisdom, then there's a lot of fun to be had in this game. It's impossible not to get some joy from a game that has you rolling around the desert as 5 camels one minute then flying through the void of space as a spiral galaxy the next.

Dungeon Souls is one of those special gems of a game in the sea of bad indie games. Let me start this off by saying: The dev definitely listens to the players and takes their opinions into full consideration. I see replies to questions and bugs on the discussions page and it really makes me happy. I have a feeling that this game will go far.
Now, with that out of the way... The review, shall we?
Dungeon Souls has to be some of the most fun I've had in a long while. The game only came out a few days ago and it's got a solid start. There's not a whole lot there, but the stuff that is there is pretty dang fun. There's plenty of items, all of which are passive (except potions). There are also orbital items, also passive, that are very useful. Each of the 6 characters (Barbarian, Archer, Thief, Warrior, Wizard, Cleric) has their own skillset. Each one feels and plays differently than the next, which is great. Each dungeon floor is randomly generated. There are different "tile sets" for the dungeon, which is usually switched every 3-4 floors (I haven't counted, but I think that's close). There are also different enemies for each tile set. The bosses are decent, however there isn't much strategy involved as it's mostly spamming your attack, your skills, and potions while dodging projectiles. I hope to see more work on that aspect. There also isn't much enemy variety, which may get repetitive.
However, I do believe the developer will address these issues soon. I mean, the game just released on Steam (pretty successfully, if I do say!), so I can't rip on it too much.
There are some kinks to work out, yes. There is plenty of work for the developer to do.
I would strongly recommend purchasing this game ASAP. Support the developer!

Stacking is another unique Double Fine 3D adventure and puzzle game that revolves around, surprise, stacking - more precisely the stacking of russian Matryoshka dolls.
There are dozens of different dolls in different sizes, each with its own ability that you have to use in order to solve the numerous puzzles and challenges. In the later stages, abilities of different dolls even can be combined to progress further.
Visually, the game is set sometime in the industrial era of the 1920's or 1930's, which is a very nice and welcome change from all the generic modern-themed games these days. A lot of detail has been put into the 5 different chapters to make it even more authentic.
While the game's story isn't exactly award-winning, the presentation and the cutscenes in stage performance and silent film manner are really well done.
With the additional Lost Hobo King DLC, the game offers a solid 8-9 hours of challenging puzzles and solid fun, so make sure to give it a try!
