Starbound is a game I really wanted to enjoy. Terraria had some good ideas, taking the Minecraft Genre 2D, but its implementation for some things felt a bit rushed-- because they were. I won't go into that here, but things were rushed out the door. Starbound was taking its time, and that made me hopeful.
If this was the game it was a year ago, I would recommend it. Heck, if this was the game it was when it first entered early access I'd recommend it!
Back then, the progression was fun. It didn't force a story on you with unskippable cutscenes that have text so small I have to squint to read it. It didn't have frustrating dungeons you can't build in when building is a core mechanic of the game. You didn't need to collect lots and lots of powerups to dig better, because you could just make a drill. The bosses were fun, and progression was quick. You could actually start the game, find coal, and instantly go to another world! How cool is that compared to this?
The game was great when it felt like it was embracing being a multi world Terraria. Then it added very finicky combat that made me long for Terraria's simplicity, and made you need to go through one of the most frustrating dungeons I've played to be able to get past the first world.
The 50 hours I spent on earlier versions was well spent.
I cannot recommend it anymore.

Good stealth games are hard to come by, at least the hardcore ones, but this one does not disappoint.
The plot is really well presented, you don't know much of it at the start, but as you play it the more engaged in it you get. It starts with a faction asking you for help (not willingly) to retrieve a certain artifact from a church of the religious Hammerites. At first Garrett, the main character, not wanting to get involved in any political game refuses, but then thinks of all the good stuff he could "borrow" while he's there... What starts simple, gets a little more complicated later on. Not spoiling anything, let's just say that it is somewhat unexpected (but in a good way!) and surpsisingly scary sometimes (yes "The Cradle", I'm talking to you).
The game encourages you to really sneak around and not be detected, since a confrontation doesn't end well for the player in most cases. But don't think that this is an unforgiving game, as the game provides the player with a good variety of tools to make all the sneaking around possible. For instance, there is the Blackjack that can be used to knock enemies out silently, there's the Water Arrow which is used to extinguish fire based light sources from a distance creating areas of darkness, the Moss Arrow that is used to create a grassy spot where it isn't noisy to walk on, or the option to simply grab something fom the environment and throw them to lure enemies away. And if you screw things up, there are also the "escape" tools as well, like the Flashbang, that blinds the enemy giving you time to hide again, the Oil Flasks in which the enemies can be slowed down in case of pursuit by sliping on them (or to be set on fire if shot with a Fire Arrow, creating a true firewall), and so on. And if you really need to fight, you have your bow (which can kill the enemy instantly, but only if he/she is not aware of your presence) and dagger (you can also backstab unaware enemies with it), which is possible to guess, isn't very effective in a direct assault on armored sword wielding angry guards (but possible to beat with the help of some Health Potions)
With all of the tools in the game, it is even possible to beat the game without a single confrontation, lethal or non-lethal. These items give you a nice balance in the game, making every mission possible to be approached a different number of ways.
The game can be played in a first person perspective, which is more immersive but a little more problematic, or in a thid person perspective, that makes the game easier since you can take a peek at corners without moving for instance.
As I stated before, the first person perspective can be a little frustrating, a good example of this is when you lean: the purpose of this is to be able to look from the safety of the shadows without compromising yourself too much, in previous installments of the series, this manouver was one of the most important of those games, it was easy and quick to use, in this game however instead of the character just leaning his head out of cover like it was implied by the movement of the camera in the other games (there was no third person perspective in those), here the character literally places himself to the side really slowly, which compromises you instead of giving you an edge on the enemies.
In fact, it can be dangerous to use sometimes, as it can make you fall from a ledge if you're trying to lean near one for instance. So this kinda forces you to use the third person perspective a lot more than you could wish for.
But this isn't something that can take you away from the game, it's a minor inconvenience that doesn't break the game. You can face a wall and then put your back on it if you think an enemy is going to walk by TOO close to you (can be a life saver) and the movement modes give you more strategy options: you can run, walk crouch, and sneak, each one presents a different speed and noise, so choosing carefully how to approach a place or enemy is always a good plan.
The AI can be unforgiving, or just plain stupid. Sometimes it will chase you relentlessly for a long time, and sometimes it will give up at the first corner. At least it is good to be surprised sometimes and have to adapt to a certain situation. It is just weird (but necessary in a certain way in this genre) that the enemies see you and may even engage in combat, but later forget that you were there when you hide ("It was probably just my imagination").
The game takes place in The City (that's the name presented by the game), and it is kind of a free opened world. "Kind of" because of the engine limits, since the game can't handle large areas, there are a lot of transition places which requires the game to stop and load content, breaking the pace of the game, and making it really annoying when you are just trying to explore. The missions take place in separate places of the city, and can only be accessed once, so you can't visit the mission areas prior to reaching them in the story.
Graphically, the game looks really good for its time, great particle effects lighting effects and shadow projections (which you can use to see the enemy coming or the opposite). There are a few problems with colision detection and you can get stuck sometimes requiring you to reload the game in a previous save slot, but thankfully, that's really rare (unless you want to climb everywhere).
The sound in this game is great, the musics, the ambient and the voice acting are terrific (and comical sometimes as intended). People talk about you in the streets, or think out loud that they must be seeing ghosts and so on, and that's all very convincing.
The game is pretty long, without taking consideration the times you will reload and try again going through a certain spot or the load times themselves, so it provides a good ammount of time of entertainment.
In the end, even lacking a few things that made its antecessors great (like the Rope Arrow), Thief Deadly Shadows still greatly succeeds in delivering a solid stealth gameplay and at the same time gives the player liberty to approach the tasks at hand many ways differently (but that doesn't mean without a little punishment) giving the game a good replay value. And with its lenghty campaign, it will certainly have you immersed in its world of intrigues and surprises for a good (really good by the way) time.

For the hardcore strategist or tabletop gamer ONLY.
The gameplay is slow without being sluggish, and is in-depth enough to provide a frustrating learning curve.  Features are poorly-documented and the gameplay itself is immensely complex.
These are all reasons that I enjoy this game.
I never got along well with the speed-clicking featured in Blizzard's RTS games.   They're great, polished, and well-balanced, but at the end of the day they're about who can churn out the most orcs in the shortest amount of time.
AGoT: Genesis is the polar opposite.  It is a game clearly designed around a desire to recreate political tension and betrayal in a multiplayer scenario.  Hire assassins to kill lords, send spies to forge secret alliances, and train armies to march on your enemies and claim the throne.
A warning: This game is not single-player friendly!  The campaign plays like Ben Stein teaching a class in Westeros History.  The characters are lifeless and the scenarios drag on and on.

I like this game quite a bit.  You fight bandits, undead, goblins, and orcs in your quest to run a successful mercenary company.  The campaign map and equip management is kind of mount and blade style, but the combat is  turn-based tactical on a hex grid.
The actual combat system is pretty good too, with different weapons having strengths and weaknesses, along with special abilities.  Spears are high accuracy, and can keep enemies at bay.  Axes are high damage, and can split shields.  Maces can stun, warhammers can heavily damage armor, and so on and so forth.
Overall, it is a lot of fun.  I am looking forward to seeing what the developers keep doing with it.

If you enjoy tower defense games, this game will be perfect for you. Kingdom Rush represents what this type of genre has to offer.
- A huge map, with multiple levels to discover and beat.
- A big array of heroes that you can upgrade and exchange between levels to better suit your strategy.
- 3 level tier of towers which one with its own abilities and power that truly change the course of a fight.
- Increasing dificulty of enemy types.
- Great animation.
- The actually need of strategy like using your soldier to box the enemies into a killzone where you can maximize your output damage.
- Each enemy has a set of advantages that you can use and build towers to counter those effects.
- Many many movie and game references built into the actual game, where you can click somewhere on the map and something happens just for the player.
Poor storyline!
Kingdom Rush represents what the best tower defense games are all about. Tower and Hero customization, destroying hordes of adapting enemies. Its a must buy for the die hard fan. The easter eggs are the icing on this well put and beautiful game but it could benefit from a Storyline. I give it a 9 out of 10, making it a necessary buy.

Basically thought it was an OK game. I had a lot of fun with a whole lot of mods. UNTIL I accidentally laid my hands on Fallout 3, I finally cannot torlerate Bethesda practice anymore.
So what's the problem? I'm just going to spit out what I thought of. SPOILERS!!!
First I found out that this Fallout 4 is just copy from Fallout 3 but downgraded.
- Music in the radio is almost the same as FO3 (I didn't stop and listen to all of them)
- Sentry bots and power armors are better than FO3 but fewer kinds of power armors left in FO4.
- Fewer kinds of weapons with a lot of stupid mistakes such as they name light machine guns "assault rifle" and you can hear a bullet shell drop on the floor when Kellog shot your wife with a revolver and so on. And all the weapons in FO4 are UGLY!
- Most of the weapons in FO3 have their bolts on the right side of the gun. You want it in FO4? Good luck searching for mods.
- In FO3 you can holster your weapon on your back. Want it in FO4? Good luck searching for mods.
- In FO3 interior lighting is very dark and immersive. Want it in FO4? Good luck searching for mods.
- So on
OK then what's new about this Fallout 4?
First of all art design. I saw a lot of awesome concept arts before and after the release. Apparently Bethesda didn't adopt any of them. Instead they abuse some cheap resusable ugly buildings, outfits, faces and everything else. That's why this game looks so pale and empty. And why Deathclaws look like Diablo? In general FO3 has more details in every frame even with much lower resolutions. And the landscape dosen't look all the same like FO4.
Cut contents. Lets count how many settlements are there in FO4. By SETTLEMENT I mean a place where there are more than 5 civilian NPCs from whom you can recieve more than one mission which is not a recycling faction mission such as killing raiders dwelling miles away or rescue hostages. I can only count 4: Diamond CIty, Goodneighbor Bunker Hill and Covenant. And if you don't like fascisum and want to save a poor robot girl Covenant has to be destroyed. Then how many settlements you can find in FO3? Figure it out yourselves. That's why you find there is nothing to do after the main story is finished. There is basically not so many NPCs and side missions! Guess in order to rush out the game in time Bethesda decided that it's OK that players find out what to do in the wasteland themselves and speaking of wasteland this land is really wasted. Do keep in mind I'm not comparing FO4 with Skyrim. One of Skyrim DLCs has almost as much content as FO4 main game.
Short missions. Since I just mentioned about recycling faction missions. Do you know how boring and short these facion missions are? If you are willing to do all the recycling missions congrats! You will have to literally help every single settlement (not the kind of settlement I defined) and call it infinite mission if you want cos all you do is teleprot to settlers, talk to them, teleport to somewhere else, kill everything inside, teleport back to the settlers, teleport to Preston, get a new mission. If you don't want to do this you can finish the main story in like 5 hours. With DLCs you can finish it in 7 hours and a half if you choose minutemen route, destroy Far Harbor and "Open season".
Wasted companions. Before that many people told me FO4 has a DYNAMIC companion system. I don't know where they learnt this fancy word but what I see is a wasted NPC following algorithm. What do companions do? Blocking your way, blocking your shot, messing up your stealth, judging what you do. So yeah while you're on the way saving your family you still have to figure out how to please your companions. Good idea. Companions will try to step in your conversations with other NPCs but actually no f**ks given to them cos the conversation usually won't change with or without the companion. And really no one is giving a f**k if I bring Hancock to Diamon city or if I bring Strong to that Prydwen. When I brought Valentine to Railroad HQ Desdemona asked me "do you know about synths". When I brought Hancock to kill his brother he didn't give any reaction other than a short comment like "so he is a synth after all". I'm very interested in Hancock and Valentine but Bethesda didn't care to give any depth to their stories. What should be happening? Preston should go back to Quincy to have his revenge, Cait should go back to destroy that huge slavery system she's talking about all the time, Hancock should take out his brother himself, Piper should go uncover mayor's conspiracy and Valentine should let go of all those holotapes cos my god that mission is a wreck.
Ridiculous DLCs. Speaking of huge slavery systems, in FO3 what do you get for these DLCs? You can go to The Pitt to save all those slaves, you can go you fight Chinese army and you can even go to space! What can you get for FO4 DLC? Work bench upgrade and anoher work bench uprade and another work bench upgrade! Then you get some more boring short missions in which you kill more ridiculously dressing clowns and get rewarded with 3 more kinds of ugly weapons with special ammo type that you can't find in main game.
Buuuuuuuugs! How long has it been released? Till now I still suffer from all the bugs I suffer at the beginning. Today the subtitle for your first conversation with Sturges is still bugging. NPCs still walk away from you when they talk to you. There are still invisible walls everywhere through which you can see your enemies but you can't shoot them. Leaver action rifle reload animation is still a joke. Companions still can be stuck in some corner and stay there forever. Sometimes it takes 20 years for you to switch your vallina guns. Corpses in the water is still tapping the water like crazy. Sometimes there are still mysterious flying limbs and other debris frozen in the air and so on. So what have Bethesda been doing these days? Oh Creation Club! Marvelous!
Finally junks. I remember when The Witcher 3 came out people all agree that Skyrim is better. One of the reasons is that in Skyrim you can pick up any junk laying around. So Besthesda was like "Oh players like picking junks? OK lets make a game in which they HAVE TO pick up junks." And here we are, saving the world and picking junks. Actually it makes sence that you need all resources you can find to survive the wasteland but really? You build your city by searching trash and your settlers come up to you and say "mayor our happiness is droping please find more trash so thant you can build a clinic". And Bethesda took advantage of the picking junk system to boost play time. If you don't bother salvaging you'll find that every dungeon is very small and decorated with very few enemies. Good job done Bethesda.

Once in a while a game will come along that not only manages to be great, but even pulls off being perfect. Bastion is easily this game.
Perfect doesn't mean it does everything, at least not in my definition, but rather it does exactly what it sets out to do.
In the game you assume the role as 'The Kid', the story itself narrated with pitch-perfect charm by Rucks. I won't touch the story, I wouldn't want to spoil a second of it, but I can safely say that like most everything else, it is compelling, elegant, and sublime. The only thing I will spoil are that along the way The Kid meets others, and they bring their own tales to the narrative that mange to enrich the story rather than make things feeling convoluted.
The game play takes place in various areas where the stage actually spawns up around the player as you move. It can feel very trippy the first time seeing it happen, and is a unique and clever take on discovery and exploration. The stages themselves are a great mix of wastelands, aerial complexes, swamps, mines, snow lands, and a few things I'm not even sure how to describe.
Combat is executed very well, the controls are tight and responsive. I used a game pad and found no issue moving, rolling, aiming, or deflecting. The game takes a small amount of getting used to, but once I had the hang of things I could readily see both my mistakes and areas where I could improve. In other words this is a game of skill, and practice really pays off. Not super hard by any stretch, but the game really gives as good as you play. If I lost I knew it was my fault, period.
The Bastion itself is a hub where The Kid can customize everything from additional special abilities such as added damaged dealt with reflecting shots back at enemies, modding The Kid's arsenal of weapons to suit the players preferences, experiencing side stages called Dreams that are entirely optional, or even choosing Idols in the Shrine that mix up the game's difficulty and can make even the most skilled player tread extra careful in the wilds. There are other things happening at the Bastion, again I will leave it to the player to discover what unfolds, but I will say they add just the right elements of customization, challenge, and side-quests to keep thing interesting without feeling bloated.
Visually this game is a stunner! The artists really poured a lot into bringing the world to life in vivid colors and stylized artwork that gives things a very hand painted look. The audio and visual components work well together, to the point that even the level spawning has a very subtle but effective sound that cues what is happening in a way that is not at all distracting, but rather strengthens the immersion. I loved the monster designs; some of it was just odd but at the same time wondrous, even funny. Much of the artwork was just terrific to. Everything here screams polish; nothing shiny or 'big studio', just well crafted artwork that perfectly fits the overall tone of the game.
The music in this game is beautiful! From twangy folk to rock beats, and Zia's dreamy ballad, this is one of the most unforgettable soundtracks I've ever heard, video game or otherwise. The sound effects were also suitably beefy, strange, punchy, and fantastical.
I could go on about the voice acting in this game especially Rucks, but you have to hear him to get how well-delivered his lines are. Listening to him narrate the story is like listening to Ron Perlman telling campfire tales. The voice actor the chose for the role is awesome! I loved listening to him talk about areas, give back-story, even describe items in the game. His delivery was equal parts charming and witty. A huge nod to him for his work here
I also want to offer my respects to the writers for their great work here as well.
Time Attack and Score Attack only had me coming back for more. The best part is that as I did I found myself only getting better, faster, and sharper. The truest mark of a great game is one that allows me to perfect my skill and rewards this with added challenge, all the better that I could do so on my own terms thanks to The Shrine, Idols, and harder modes of play. Again, difficulty is very customizable here.
A game that delivers on everything it sets out to do; this is easily one of the best video games I've ever played.

An excellent staple of the Stealth Genre, Thief: Deadly Shadows is a game wherein you play Garett, an experienced thief who makes his fortune off of the work of others. The game has robust and intriguing characters, a reactive environment and surprisingly realistic stealth, and an overall enjoyable thrill of thievery and sneaking around.
There are some things, however, that make this game awful. First is mostly a technical issue of screen problems and spontaneous lag, although this can be fixed with patches or some tweaking of the files. Not a dealbreaker.
The combat's sluggish and unappealing; it doesn't flow well at all. Which, to be fair, it's not supposed to (stealth game, and all, that dagger's a last resort), but even when forced into combat, Garett really can't do much.
And then there's the issue of your game completely wiping your save files when you try to save. No warning or reason, it will crash on the save screen and wipe your current saves. That being said, you can download save files from the internet and continue as you wish, but honestly, doing a lot of hard, sneaking work, going through the first few chapters and getting the game down, and then it wipes your saves?
Do not buy this game. It's one of the few fun games in existence, yes, but with the technical issues stated above, it's clearly not worth the buy. Unfortunate.

Got this on steam sale for $2.50 and was worth that price for the entertainment for this evening, but I'd struggle justifying a ton more than that.
All in all if you like trial and error setups / brain teasers then you'll like this. Dont get me wrong its not all just pushing random buttons until you find a combination that works because at the end of the day all the hints and clues are there, Some more obvious than others and some are more prone to accidentally entering the correct sequence without actually knowing where the sequence or hint actually came from.
After tinkering with it for about an hour and a half I was able to navagate and locate most of the pieces you would use and was able to achieve most endings (all but about 6-7) of which I opted to look up the solutions online and was plesently surprised that atleast half of those I was on the right track to and probably would've gotten it had I stuck with it, but my frustration levels peaked. To be honest some of the most annoying parts of the game wasn't just solving the clues or finding how to unlock the controls but rather figuring out which control should be used to enter what clue. Sometimes I would spend a great deal of time trying to figure out how to force a code I solved in the clues into a control only to later find that it was supposed to be entered in a differ control.
Ultimately the only hints I will give you to help ease your frustration is to try and pay attention to when you start inputing a sequence into a set of buttons. They almost always show a number of blanks/used key strokes on the monitor. If you have a 4 key number/sequence and you see 6 spots for entry when you start entering, then just skip that sequence as it goes somewhere else. And take note of everything, hints are nicely crafted into just about everything, so if it seems like something it trying to tell you something then it probably is.
8/10 its a good time killer but ultimately once you solve the problems then its essentially unplayable for you, and while I suppose you could take days/months to solve the couple more difficult puzzles if you wanted to do them without help/walkthroughs, Well I just can't see that being continued fun beyond the first few hours since you'd litterally spend days just repeating the same old cycles trying to figure out what you're missing. For me, spending 2 hours or so solving most the puzzles on my own and then going over the harder solutions with a walkthrough was satisfying enough for my needs. I'll probably just let my friends tinker with this game now to see how well they do, other than that its probably going to be uninstalled =P

When PC games were young there were a run of games on the PC and Amiga where you would travel across a randomly generated land using WASD to try and build an army to defeat some great enemy and free the kingdom. They used ASCII for the terrain and you simply had numbers for your army size, food and equipment. Battle Brothers is the modern epitome of these classic games, and when finished, based on how it is going so far, has the potential to sit along side epic games like FTL in that, no matter how many times you have played them, you will occasionally dust it off once again and have another game to see what happens and where it goes.
So far I haven't quite figured out what the end goal of Battle Brothers is or even if it does in fact have one, the story line is very thin leaving you with a lot of autonomy to do your own thing.  What I do know however is that I have had more fun playing this game, running quests and kitting out my mercs to fit my preferred fighting style than I have had with many mainstream games that cost 3 times the price.
As for the actual game, it's a little like a medieval X-Com, you don't build a base (or a least I don't think so), or have a scripted story line  (or a least I don't think so), but you build up your little mercenary company from almost nothing taking contracts to get better gear (either from battlefield loot or from merchants in town) taking on greater and greater challenges and occasionally going your own way to raid a stronghold or ancient burial ground just because you can.
Combat is brutal and vicious and bloody, and often you lose some of your finest mercs with your best gear and take two steps back for one step forward. This isn't a game where you leave every fight with your team alive.  Also recently added, merchants and tailors and other pre-merc skills of your band can help if you add them to your camp or battle line, opening additional quest lines or getting bargains on special items etc.
Overall this is a fantastic game, and if you like strategy games using small squads on a hex map, this is a must have game for your collection.  Don't let the funky chess piece like graphics put you off, what the game lacks in graphics, it makes up for in strategy and complexity with weapons and combat skills that are integrated and really well balanced.

Ok, so as an early access game, even an early Aplha Stranded Deep is a very well done piece of work. Ill get into detail below :D
The Good :
First: The graphics for an alpha are great, some small adjustments are missing in the options menu but overall the look and feel of the game are what you would expect from a carribiean island. The underwater trips are a whole other beast.
The sound design is great, especially underwater where noise is muffled and blurred. Vision isnt the greatest and An imporvement would be having blurred vision underwater without say improvised goggles or found divers masks.
Second : the wildlife though sparse at the moment is varied enough to keep you occupied especially while diving and encountering a Tiger Shark or Great White (sadly havent went far out into deep enough waters to see them yet)
Sharks behave like a real shark would, they circle and look curious, The more stressed you have your character the more provoked they are to attack you. Otherwise they could just bump you without biting and swim away. Or they could drag you deep and eat you.
Third : The Crafting system. Ill admit the crafting system is a tad infuriating if you dont know what to do, basically you are crafting in the real world no boxes like minecraft or h1z1 etc. You literally drop your items say two sticks, a lashing (rope) and rock shard and you can make a spear. Or five sticks to make a fire. Its quite a cool crafting system all together even if a tad clunky. Stranded Deep is early access.
Fourth : The world is infinatly generated meaning there is no end. New islands pop up in the distance, same with ship wreakage some can be close to shore others further in the deepest black waters where more dangers may lie. Its possible to build a shelter but at the moment No way to backtrack to the shelter.
Now for the bad (which isnt all that bad)
First: Stranded Deep is Early Access Alpha, so some things are missing and this isnt a full game. While there are plenty of things to do and be done, there isnt much to craft, farm, grow, etc yet. There are only two shark types, Great White and Tiger, others will be added later.
Second : There will and are bugs, one includes occasionally falling out of your rubber life raft while paddling if you arent careful which with a shark around can be quite scary even for a game :D
In general keep in mind you are buying into a early access title but, one with a ton of promise and active developers and support for being released only a few days ago at the time of this writing.

You start off initially with three characters (this used to be different, but I think it's better this way) that are sort of unique. However, one character, the barbarian, is a melee character. Melee in Dungeon Souls is almost kind neglected in a way. In the earliest versions, melee was considered to be the better of the classes, besides of the wizard of course. After several updates, melee was outsourced to ranged. The issue here is that melee takes too much damage going in for the hit. Buffing the health or starting with more defense to counter this would better balance the classes.
Also in terms of game balance is there is no exact way to know how to counter an enemy. I feel adding an enemy database after killing a certain amount should unlock background information about the enemy including base hp, base dmg, scaling for the former items, some general information, weaknesses and strengths. Killing more of the same enemy adds more information, simple.
Bosses are a toughy here. They are all lumbering tanks that for the most part are kind of unique. The voice-acting done on some of them are sub-par, one of them I remember being better than the rest but I don't want to spoil anything for those who have not touched it yet. Each stage has it's own unique boss which I feel is very wrong. They are essentially uber-versions of normal enemies that are beefed up with special attacks, size, health, and damage. If that's the approach, I would think a neccessity would be multiple bosses per stage so it doesn't get as repetitive as quickly grinding for coins and resources for the forge.
Also, characters are not even fleshed out. We know them by their class, but being able to distinguish more than that, such as more background information that I suggested about enemies, possibly when you rank up the character. Speaking of character development, I feel like there is a lack thereof in terms of continuation of upgrades to them. We have our basic stuff during the dungeon such as temporary skill upgrades and stat upgrades. Outside we only have stat upgrades the provide miniscule amounts to our stats in the dungeon. There's also the forge but I'm going to ignore that for the time being because it needs to be fleshed out A LOT more and the UI cleaned up very much. It also needs more of an explanation.
The music in Dungeon Souls is a very vibrant EDM genre (that I won't attempt to name because hardcore EDM enthusists will strike me down because I'm probably wrong) I feel the tracks fit the game very well. Though in spite of this, it loops terribly and there isn't enough variety for each dungeon level. On several occasions I could tell when it would loop because there is a small void of sound when it does. One way to counter this is to create loop points in the code that send the timeline of music to a specific point, and upon reaching the boss of the stage, it skips and fades to the boss music by constantly asking the game if the player has reached the boss stage in the current dungeon level.
Despite all my negative things to say about the game, this is all constructive criticism. I really recommend it. It's a fantastic dungeon crawler with roguelike elements. It's not for the faint of heart as it requires skill to make it further in the game, knowledge about items, and so forth. If and when the game goes on sale, buy it immediately because it is in fact worth the money if not already at $12.99.

Dungeon Souls a great game that has some great inspiration, and this game is coming along quite nicely. My only real critiques are below:
-As said to death, melee is way outclassed. the weapon size on barbarian is way to small. It's impossible to hit a melee enemy without getting hit. Warrior is manageable, but you have to rely on his ranged ability. Give these classes bigger weapons to balance. Barbarian should be warrior size, and warrior should be a size larger.
-Number on enemies can be ridiculous, especially early game. Wizard handles them with multishot and Cleric does the same, but other classes have trouble with this. I understand preferred playstyle, but compare it to Risk of Rain. Enemies become stronger and more frequent over time. The current system has lead to me watching larger stuff spawn while I deal with crowds of enemies on the first floor.
-Leveling is a pain. You get one statpoint per level, and as far as I've experienced, about one level per floor. Leveling is not a fast process, and should be rewarded more largely. Vice versa, leveling reward could be the same, but leveling could be faster.
-Bosses. I read this in an earlier review and must say that bosses are not impossible, but are one of the greater annoyances in the game. An enemy with 1500 health I'm dealing 7 damage to at a time is tedious. Add constant enemies spawning as I kill them off and attempt to attack the boss is more than most players can handle. Clearly one must be of a higher level to defeat the boss, but as I stated previously, leveling is not properly scaled. Beating a boss right now is the most rewarding feeling in game while overpowered. The statement for bosses is also true in the current version of the game for floors following them. I always feel underleveled when entering floors after a boss, and it usually shows by a swift death.
-Not currently in the game, but there should be some form of tutorial. I know what I'm doing now, but a tutorial would have made the learning curve infinitely easire.
Should I have any other critiques, they will be added, but these are things I would like to see improved right now.

Start at the end of the story and traverse past level after level killing enemies that were previously killed and collecting coins previously collected all the while avoiding the ones that weren't hit and thus also dodging pesky time paradoxes in the process (because those are never good for time travel...right?). Along the way you'll also re-collect a unique power every world that was lost through a death (because hey...none of us are perfect, right? ;) ) like shooting fireballs, chucking hammers (Hammer Bros, anyone?) or rolling up in a ball to get through tight spaces.
Long story short I definitely recommend it if you can pick it up in a bundle or during a sale. There just isn't an awful lot to do after finishing the story mode which is why I recommend a lower price point. There's an extra set of 10 "Mariachi" levels and a speed run mode unlocked after story, besides these and a level editor for custom levels (if that's your sort of thing) there isn't anything else to do unfortunately. That said the only real downside honestly was that the short story just left me wanting more now...but I suppose there could be worse problems.

It's fun enough as idle/clicker type games go. An interesting thing to keep in the background. The pay walls and the way they're worked into the game is more than a little greedy, but who doesn't do that these days. Hard to recommend at present though for one reason: There isn't a mass buy.
Leave it running on it's own for a few days without opening, come back to an astronomical amount of money and rather be able to click a single button to communicate your intention to max out upgrades on individual things, you have to hold down a purchase button. The pace that this 'fast' purchase leaves you sometimes spending chunks of time anytime you open the game to actually spend the money you've earned.
At one point I had spent 15 minutes trying to spend gold, only to crash to a fatal error and be shunted back through several minutes of progress through the inane task of actually holding down the button, and if I wanted something I had to pay this much attention to, I'd not be looking for something to run in the background.
Fun enough concept, charming in it's own right, very aggressively monetized for how early in development it is and not terribly user friendly. Certainly things that could be developed on as per expectation with an 'Early Access' title, but with other, similar titles offering more usability with less gouging, it's hard to think that this will be one for the history books regardless.

The concept of the Zombie Apocalypse has been fodder for many movies and video games, and this most recent one draws from several inspirations to create a wonderful and very fun experience. Through four campaigns made up of five maps each, you'll guide four survivors to be rescued from an onslaught of hundreds of Infected. The survivors that you control can include Bill, a Vietnam veteran; Zoey, a photojournalist; Louis, an office worker, and Francis, a biker.
These zombies (known in groups as the Horde) seem to have more in common with the creatures which humans became from the movie 28 Days Later instead of traditional slow zombies; these that we face now are super fast and very ravenous. There are also four special types of Infected: the Hunter, the Boomer, the Smoker, and the Witch, which inflict special damage on your team, and which spice up the action as you attempt to hide and/or fight the relentless Horde. Several times throughout each campaign, you'll also face a fifth special boss Infected, known as the Tank, which can both deliver and take a massive amount of damage and requires your whole team to bring down. At the end of each campaign, you must use a radio to call for help, and hold your ground for an extended period while awaiting evacuation.
There is a special design element hidden within the game known as the Director, which autonomously varies the amount and type of Infected that are thrown at you based on your movements and skill level, so no two games are ever the same.
The game uses the Source engine for very realistic and well-performing graphics, and the voice acting in the game, mostly performed by the Survivors, is appropriately cheesy for the subject matter, and evokes that same B-movie feel which the rest of the game does. In fact, the whole presentation is modeled after an old-time zombie-slasher movie, complete with film grain effect and mockup movie posters for the loading screens. Of course, the standard we've come to expect from Valve for high quality first-person shooting action remains intact.
I give this game a 10 across the board.

This game is very distinct from every other that I've played.
It's got a little bit of everything, there's that cozy overworld feeling like in Mount&Blade, if you've read the Chronicles of the Black Company the  game just reinforces and adds onto how you'd imagine a medieval mercenary company to be. Dark fantasy is there which serves to reinforce your feeling as a member of the company trying to survive and even abandon your honour and contract for the lives of your men. The gameplay is great too, if a bit repetitive at times.
+
Different weapons serve different purposes, so there is no one meta weapon you want to equip your men with. Having various weapons mixed into the shieldwall is a smart way to go. You want axes against Undead Cohorts and their shields, for Orcs a good spearwall is your best bet. When it comes to zombies you want something that cut decapitate and fighting skeletons is dumb if you have piercing weapons like crossbows/bows/spears.
Better armor means heavier armor, heavier armor means your men are going to get tired quickly. So no, donning your archers with the best armor isn't really a good thing.
Small things like being able to rename your party members, change their appearance,get a war dog or a falcon etc
Different enemies use different tactics. Orcs love to rush in and try to stun and overwhelm you. Humans use various tactics including skirmishing, sitting in a shield wall and trying to flank you. Goblins are outright annoying with their poison arrows and running away, also throwing spiky bolas and nets to try to hamper your frontline. The undead are generally stupid, but what they lack in brains they make up for sheer numbers. You won't have to use amazing tactics against undead, but their sheer numbers and ability to reanimate after death can easily tire out your men, and if they've got a necromancer backing them up you're in for some fun times. With ghouls you might think they're pushovers, but little did you know they can devour corpses and grow bigger, with the tier 3 ghoul being able to swallow one of your men aside from being much more tankier.
Your men WILL die, the RNG isn't much of a factor as are your tactics and equipment. If you go barely armored against an Orc Warrior expect heads to literally fly all over the place.
And much more.
-
Some "choose your own story" events would be nice. We already got an objective to pick and follow it through for renown, but this is just a "get 10k gold" or "burn 4 orc camps" which gets boring after a time. Maybe if these objectives had their own little stories or events it would be much more fun to pursue them.
The game gets a bit repetitive after a while. Main problem is that the battlefields are somewhat samey. Some ruins/castles/encampments with their own little natural hazards/barricades etc would be nice.
The random events seem somewhat rare, and when they do happen it's just a bit of flavour and they as well might have never happened.
Generally the main thing that the game lacks is more interaction in the overworld. You can't interact with peasants, mercenary companies, militia etc. A few options where you ask them if they saw some enemies, latest rumours and so on would make it more fun. Also relationship with other merc companies, maybe actually having them take the same contract as you and trying to do it faster. Or getting angry if you finish it just under their nose. Maybe them attacking you in the wilderness to hijack a contract etc. Or another company popping out from nowhere and backing you up in a battle because you helped them before.
TL;DR - The game is great, if you like turn based combat and a somewhat dark fantasy setting definitely go for it. While there are some minor issues that might or might not get ironed out, it's already very good even in it's current state.

People have said it, but yes, Thief: Deadly Shadows is one of the best stealth games ever to be made. When it came out, the general consensus was that it wasn't as good as the first two Thief games, but I felt it rightly earned its place within the saga.
What stands out the most about Deadly Shadows is its immersion. From the beginning I found myself intrigued with the world presented in the game, and the rich lore that serves as the backdrop. Taking place in a dark, Dickensian fantasy world, Deadly Shadows pits the new world order of the steampunk "Hammerites" against the ancient and magically luddite-like "Pagans". With different factions vying for power and for the services of the main character, Garret, the stage is set for plots, intruige, double-crosses, and a whole lot of sneaking. The story grabbed hold and sunk its (Sometimes terrifying) teeth in deep.
I can only hope that the next game in the series, simply titled "Thief", will live up to its predecessors; like Deadly Shadows did.

For a game that is supposed to be the spiritual successor to the True Crime titles I was expecting at least a good-cop/bad-cop mechanic, but nothing you do matters to the story or characters. It's essentially 5 types of mini-games strung together with a movie.
Many pieces of Sleeping Dogs are good, but an overall "game" is missing - it's just a linear story. You can't fail a mission because you keep replaying until you pass. Everything you need is (eventually) marked on your map so there's little point to exploring the beautifully crafted city. You can't make any decisions that change the story or the game or your character. Talking your way past a guard or cop consists of pressing 'Y'. There's only one ending. Basically - there's no player choice.
The Good:
- Environment / Visuals
- Voice acting
- Soundtrack
- Hand-to-hand combat - thought it gets repetitive toward the end
- Dialog
The Middle:
- Open-world map - starts off fun but eventually becomes annoying running around looking for a taxi to fast travel.
- Characters - Wei and a couple of the supporting characters are well developed but for the most part the other characters, like the Triad bosses, exist for one mission.
- Driving physics - ok for a non-driving game
- Skill tree progression - Fun but you eventually get everything, so all you're picking (sort of) is the order you get skills
- The story - interesting but somewhat predictible
The Bad:
- Romantic relationships - it's like they were written by an alien observing the human species
- Pathfinding/GPS - doesn't handle overpasses correctly
- Interaction with objects - if you're too close to something you can't interact with it. If you're not standing still you carjack a taxi instead of hire it.
- Player impact on anything - You can't save characters thar are going to die. Some you go to great lengths to save just to have them killed a few cut scenes later. You can't decide to take sides in a dispute. You can even decide if you're a good cop or a bad cop. The only thing you can control is the amount of skill tree XP you get for completeing a mission. You eventually get all the skills, so you're not even choosing to specialize the main character. True Crime LA had two endings. True Crime NY had 3 endings plus rogue status. Sleeping Dogs (supposedly True Crime: HK) has one ending.
I picked this up on sale for $6 and I don't feel ripped off, but I wish I would have spent the time I spent playing this game to the end (20h) playing something else instead. I kept waiting for the event where I got to make a decision about something but it never came.

I have owned Battle Brothers for quite some now, played over 200 hours, and with the title in final beta, readying for release, the time has come to write a review:
Had the Brothers Grimm created a fantasy RPG instead of writing dark fairy tales, Battles Brothers would likely have been the result.  Fitting, actually, as the Battle Brothers dev team, as did the Grimm brothers, hail from Germany.   Battle Brothers takes you inside medieval life and shows you both the good and bad of living by your sword.
In Battle Brothers, you lead your troop of up to 20 mercanaries (only 12 can fight at a time) back and forth across a beautifully hand rendered map, seeking employment by local nobles and businessmen in a time honored exchange of services:  your swords for their money.  Side elements allow small amounts of speculative trading of goods.
You start the game with 3 men.  Most towns and villages you encounter have several men for hire.  Backgrounds of recruits vary, affecting both their initial capabilites and impacting what events may randomly occur as the game progresses.  It isn't every game that makes you WANT to find a cripple for hire because you need a few men for cheap.
In Battle Brothers, the thrill of combat is real.  So is the pain and suffering it can impose upon the unskilled or unlucky. The joy of gaining experience and levelling one of your mercenaries is countered in one fell swoop of an enemy axe, permanently blinding one of your men and forcing you to make a huge - and heartfelt -  decison:  do I accept the lowered combat ability inflicted by the loss of his eye or do I cast aside his loyalty to the troop and previous prowess in combat, set him adrift, and hire a potentially more capable fighter in his stead?  The answer may seem obvious - you kick him to the dirt curb and hire a bettter man - but after he has been in your troop for days, saved your butt 4-5 times, and from time to time produces a sweet leather armor out of direwolf pelts, you may well find yourself succumbing to sentiment and retaining him. Such is the power of the game to immerse you beyond a facade of pixelated warriors into a realm of YOUR men; sweating, fighting, cursing, laughing, bleeding,..dying at your side.
As your sometimes merry, sometimes POd, and sometimes apathetic band of men travel from job to job, they gain experience (if they live long enough), allowing you to assign them new skills and abilities as they grow.  Classes, per se, do not exist.  Any merc can perform any function on the team, but that doesn't mean they should.  The skill, ability, ands equipment choices you make have a huge impact on how your men fight both individually and as a unit.
Now, I know most rpg type games say this even though the truth is choices in many games impact how you play very little.   Choices in Battle Brothers definitely make their presence known!  Weapons have unique abilites and applications.  Specific skills change what you can and can not do efficiently.
Weapon choices make a difference, skill choices make a difference, tactical choices make a difference.  Try to fight Goblins the same way you fight Bandits and you will find yourself hiring a bunch of new men. Some opponents are best played sitting back and sniping with your ranged troops before engaging.  Other oppoenents will carve their initials in your armor as you fall unless you rush to close with them as soon as the battle begins. Others are so mobile, you just hope you can adjust as they shift around the battelfield.   Get cocky and take on Greenskins (Orcs) before you are ready and you will find yourself starting a new game.
Battle Brothers never lets you get comfortable with your men.  It demands you keep some flexibility on your team.  Orient it too far in one direction and fate will demand payment for your poor leadsership skills.
And just when you think  you have the game figured out, in comes a curveball, messing with your mind.  You can choose to rip off your employer.   You can go rogue and fight peasants or caravans.  You can flaunt your power and pick off patrols.  But beware, local nobles will not appreciate mercs out there stomping on their serfs, trade goods, and security forces.    You might want to think twice before enraging the only noble who has kennels on his lands; those war dogs can be great force multipliers!
I haven't even mentioned the need to maintain adequate supplies of money, food, arrows, bolts, and medical supplies.  Logistics are a light but important facet; one you must constantly watch and address if you wish to succeed.
I have seen some reviewers struggle to find another game this compares to; a failed quest, as Battle Brothers is a unique endeavor.  Were I pressed hard on the issue, I would say Battle Brothers most closely reminds me of Mount & Blade with a fantasy side and no horses.  They are closely enough aligned that if you liked Mount & Blades, you will most likely enjoy the heck out of Battle Brothers, as well.
But Battle Brothers is more what Mount & Blade would be after a demented Court Jester took it deep into the donjon for a few hours of torture.   The polish would remain albeit now coupled with a luster of dark humor, non-politcally correct content (for example, you can place wagers on your war dogs in dog fights), and language and events that skillfully teeter on the edge of going a bit too far for a family approved game without ever crossing the line.
And that, I think, it why this game succeeds so well.  It acknowledges the brutality of combat and hardness of life in medieval times without ever becoming too overbearing.  It is a game for people who don't like participation awards.  It makes you earn your rewards.  The artwork is outstanding, the stories are fantastic, and the gameplay is solid, challenging, and varied enough to keep you logged in for one more battle hours after you should have gone to bed.
I definitely recommend you buy this game.  But as you begin to play for the first time, remember, just as in a fairy tale from the Grimm Brothers, in Battle Brothers, things are not always as they seem and the price for making bad decisions is often brutal.

Bought it not expecting much and was pleasantly surprised. It's a good game despite being early access and is already very solid. Previously I would crash often and enemies would get stuck in walls but that seems to have been fixed. I haven't crashed in awhile.
The classes, despite being classic fantasy fare, are fairly unique in their playstyle. Melee classes can destory projectiles with their attacks, but still feel fairly weak compared to ranged ones, even with the recent buffs. My favorite is the Thief I think. His invisibility is incredibly powerful.
The gameplay is reminiscent of Nuclear Throne and Binding of Isaac but still feels unique enough to stand out. You level up and upgrade your abilities and get items that remind me of Risk of Rain. Each floor of the dungeon has you activate a number of marks, each of which spawns enemies, to open the door to the next floor. Every third floor, is a boss fight with a total of four bosses in the game right now. Once you beat the fourth boss, the game loops and gets harder.
Right now there is the Dungeon, Sewer, Tundra, and Castle(?). The balance of these areas doesn't seem quite right and doesn't scale in difficulty well. The Dungeon, being the begining, isn't too difficult but can still be deadly as you start out. The boss, the Skeleton King, isn't too difficult.
The Sewer is by far the most difficult area despite being the second one. The difficulty seems to spike upwards and you'll feel like you're taking way more damage immediately. It also has a collection of very annoying enemies, many of which are hard to hit. The boss, a giant slime, is also the second hardest (right behind the last boss).
If you make it past the Sewers, it's really unlikely that you will die in the Tundra. The boss, a giant crystal, can slow you but isn't very threatening. I mean, you made it through the Sewers, you can handle anything.
Except for the last boss. His large health pool and seemingly undodgable attacks make this fight seem like a test to see if you picked up the right items. At some points it's a bullet hell, he spawns a room full of demons, and he will frequently teleport to you and attack you in melee, which seems like unavoidable damage and is really going to be your downfall. I've gotten to this boss several times and I have yet to beat him. I think he should be very difficult, but right now the seemingly unavoidable damage feels unfair, especially when he can do the teleport melee attack several times in a row, easily doing damage faster than you can heal with health potions.
Recent patches have definitely improved the game by buffing melee classes (they almost feel viable), adding items, a new class, improving the HUD, and changing how leveling up works. At this point in the game, however, it can be frustrating as sometimes you simply don't get any items that increase your damage which makes it unlikely you get past the second area. This feels more common and detrimental than similar games.
I'd like to be able to see what items I've picked up during a run. You can see them once you die, but I'd like to be able to see them somehow during the game.
TLDR: Very solid core that is very enjoyable right now. The gameplay is good, and the game can only get better.

I have had enough time to play each of the characters at least once, and to get through the game on easy a single time.
There is plenty of content here to enjoy. This game is *highly* inspired by RIsk of Rain. They use a very similar upgrade system, where the upgrades can stack if you end up getting the same thing twice. For example, there is a rotating shield upgrade, which causes a shield to spawn, and slowly rotate around the character. If you get a second rotating shield, you will end up getting two of them revolving around you.
The game is split up into separate areas. Each area contains two floors, followed by a boss floor. The bosses appear to be fixed, rather than random. The boss of the first area was always the same for me. I think I recall counting four areas, but immediately after exiting the fourth boss room, the game crashed, so I can only assume that they plan on adding more.
The regular areas which you spend most of your time in consist of randomly generated floors with enemies spawning every few seconds. Each floor consists of a locked staircase to the next floor. To unlock the staircase, you must search the floor for the five "glyphs", and defeat the enemies that spawn around it.
After clearing a floor, enemies continue spawning, but to prevent the player from grinding out levels, the "Redeemer" spawns, slowly draining your health until you die. I never had the redeemer spawn before clearing all five glyphs, so I'm not sure if there's a mechanic to prevent grinding out a floor before getting the glyphs.
Regardless, the leveling up part doesn't seem to make nearly as big of an impact as the upgrades do, and you'll get plenty of them. Each boss drops a handful of these upgrades, and they are also scattered around in chests throughout the floors, and they can even drop as loot from champion monsters.
In addition to that, you can also acquire upgrades from the shops. Each floor has a shop, and the shop contain three items for sale. Currently, the only use for money in-game is these shops, and since each shop only lets you buy one of three items for sale, you will most certainly never need to worry about your money.
The other user for money is permanent character upgrades which happen at the character selection screen. When you die, the money you didn't spend is saved, and you can purchase character class upgrades with that money. Each run will start you with no money, so it doesn't roll-over into your next run.
As this is a brand-new early access game, it does have it's bugs. But the gameplay is absolutely amazing. They really nailed the combat aspect, and there are quite a few classes to play at the moment.
This is one of those games that will get more and more fun as the developers begin adding more of the random upgrades to collect, so that players can create more unique builds.
Since the only influence you have towards your upgrades is the shop, which lets you choose one of three items, you don't have that much control over your build. I would certainly like to see more places where the player can spend their in-game money and better control the direction your character is going.
I can already tell that this game is going to make it's way into the ranks of Risk of Rain, Binding of Isaac, etcetera. Have fun!

I only recommend this game under one caveat:  Get it on deep sale, a dollar or less.  And that's counting the larger version, with the extra content.  That's really all the content it's worth.  As of writing this, I have managed to get gold in every level, the bonus items, and the extra challenge on one stage for the final trophy - at 63 minutes in, before there was even a single Steam card drop.  There is not enough content here to justify spending more than that.
The concept is neat.  You are unplaying a game.  But that ends up meaning that the execution is fairly standard puzzle fare, just with a different coat of paint.  You need to hit certain enemies or coins, and miss others.  The game rates how well you do on a stage based on how many times you die.. but it's a simple matter of restarting the stage to set it back to 0 in order to get gold every time.  They also play the backwards bit strangely, you have to "catch" fireballs and the like, bosses receive health from attacks (though they don't always line up properly, for example the world 1 boss regains health by FIRING a missile rather than getting hit by it at one point).  But it means that the game, by itself, would be getting easier and easier as you play, rather than have the hard stages (or parts of the boss fights) come first as you play backwards.
It's a cute idea that is half-executed, and would almost make for a better free flash game than a commercial product.  BUT, if it's on sale and cheap enough, and a simplistic puzzle game sounds interesting, by all means pick it up.  Just remember that the game is painfully short.
The bonus does include the original version - which I played.  It's much shorter, more a proof of concept, and it has a few things I like better (actually having to shoot the fireballs, keeping a count of how many coins left to uncollect, lives in the final boss fight).  It makes for a good bonus.

You are Garrett, you are a thief. You steal for a living. This incredible skill you have, will make your life quite complicated. This is the third game in the series.
First off. Don't let the hours I spent on this game fool you. I have played this game so many times, countless of hours. I just have not owned it on steam until recently. I bought it again, because I think it is that great. Let's see when I have more time to return to it..... Just to make it clear, I am a great fan of thief. I have played all the games, and countless of fan-made missions. I am eagerly awaiting the new game (even though I am also a little bit worried about it). I have also played the entire dishonored game plus all DLCs, which I consider to be the best spiritual successor of the thief games up to date. I love stealth games, and I consider Deus Ex (and mark of the ninja) to be great titles as well, which I have all completed.
So, the game:
There was one thing that this game did really well: atmosphere. I love the other thief games, but I think this game was outstanding in this area, and in a way, that is what thief is all about.
At the beginning, this game was not too well recieved. I think that is because of two things:
It was made with a console in mind, and it was compared to one of the greatest PC games of all time: thief 2. Trying to be as good as that game, is no easy task. But it actually think it did rather well in my mind. (Also, it was made by an entirely different game studio because "looking glass" went bust...)
The other problem was that consoles in those days had quite limited resources, so areas could not be very large, making the game feel small with many loading screens. Now the PC did not have that problem, but the game was designed for the console, so....
But there the problems end in my mind. Because the rest of the game is really very good. And if this title would not be compared to its predecessors, I think everbody would agree it is a great game in its on right. There where some changes, but I think the essential "thief" was still in this game, and it was well made.
Graphically, it was quite a thing when it came out. It was one of the first games to use dynamic shadows, and it required quite a PC to run well. Today that won't be a problem, but the game still looks and feels great, because the atmoshpere and design is that good. It serves the purpose very well even though you don't have the most amazing latest graphics. For example, Deus ex (invisible war) was made with the same engine, and that game has not aged well. I think it is because the art and the vision was so much better in thief than deus ex, so you forgive the graphics in thief - they are not in your way as much. But in deus ex the graphics turn you off a bit. A great examples that it is not always about the technical stuff, but how that media is used, and in thief it is used well.
It used to be a problem to run on modern PCs, but I find that this steam version works well, and there is also a lot of patches and support from the community that makes this games run better. There is an update that makes the game look better for example.
But what the game did even better was sound. You had to listen. Where are the enemies? Do I sound too much myself?
The music is sparse but just perfect. The sounds from the environment creates a great atmosphere. And sometimes the void of sounds was creppy too. Also the chattering that the NPS are making are fun to listen too. The original thief perhaps was better in this sense, but this game still kept some of that humor very well.
The story and levels in this game is also very good. And long, really long. You won't complete this game quickly.
The game is also one of the most scary games I have ever played. Not because of the monsters, or cheap scares, but because the atmosphere is that good, and because of the "uknown". Thers is one level in this game I think should go to history as the most atmospheric level ever in a game. If you have played this game I think you know what I am talking about. The first time I played that level... I have never enjoyed and suffered so much at the same time, playing any game - I wanted to go on, and quit at the same time...
You can play this game in third person if you like, but that is just wrong. This game should be played in first person, or it is just broken and less immersive. This is a game where you need patience, perception and wits. Feeling vulnerable is half the charm of the game, waiting in a shadowed corner hoping the "whatever" won't discover you. (this game was also new in a way that the NPCs could carry light sources, lighting up areas that previously were dark, making the games more interesting)
This is not a fighting game, you are a thief hiding in the shadows, where you are quite powerful. I miss games like these. Let's hope the new thief game is ok. But the 3 thief games that exist are still alive and worth it, with tons of modding and fan-made missions. And there is also dihonored of course...
This is one of those games you should complete if you considerd yourself a PC-gamer.

-Suspenseful stealth action game, the classic series-
A lot of people just hate this game because 1&2 were beloved classics but the third part is still similar enough and a good game on its own. I think it's still brilliant (also own it off-steam) to play.
Setting is a fantasy city with a bit of steampunk for good measure. You play as a thief mostly avoiding combat and try to find the valuables in the level while checking the mission goals. To that end you want to stay in the shadows or walk on carpet as enemies can see or hear you. You can club guards from behind and hide their bodies from the patrol routes of other guards. You have a limited set of tools like flashbombs, water arrows to extinguish torches or moss arrows to place "carpet". Levels are mostly open like in Deus Ex and it's fun to find the way around the guards and play hide and seek with them. Also there are a lot of hidden treasures or secret doors to discover. And there are really scary parts too.
Can recommend to anyone who likes stealth maybe not for too casual players.

Starbound 1.0 is a solid game I found very fun but left me hoping for a lot more. There are some spoilers ahead so please be alerted.
I had just emerged from a very intense couple of weeks of Terraria when Starbound 1.0 came out. In all fairness the well stewed Terraria is a tough act to follow. Competing with Minecraft on a sandbox-level: even tougher.
Starbound seems to have amazing sandbox potential that seems a bit dulled by some of the decisions that went into the 1.0 release. All traditional gaming conventions such as combat, leveling, loot, mobs, and bosses, felt poorly implemented in Starbound to the point where I would have preferred most of them not to exist at all. By adding these traditional gaming elements, including dialogue boxes and a story line, the sandbox itself was made utterly tiny and almost childish. A space game with this many planets should not be coming across as miniscule. Visiting new planets in Starbound becomes blatantly predictable even though certain elements have been genereated procedurally.
Starbound does certain things extremely well. Audio and artistic value are excellent. The music is excellent and does not suffer the repetition-problem that seemed to quickly arise in Terraria's great but limited music score. I am somewhat attached to the (human) character I created in Starbound. Cute AF, and they've given some facial expressions that are controlled by the arrow keys.
The building side-of-things seems completely phenominal. I made some basic electronics but clearly there is a deep world of crafting to explore. This would be far more attractive if the product took itself a bit more seriously. Starbound somehow comes across as very "cutesy" in areas where Terraria is truly terrifying. How is it that Terraria with its more-finite world still seems so much bigger?
I wrote this review because I feel Starbound has an incredible future ahead of it. I'd like to see the product be far more difficult. Limitless teleporting to other players, while convenient, is immersion-breaking. It makes the ship itself seem almost meaningless. The hosting of the game itself turned into a problem; what we need is for the worlds to be hosted on beefy servers so they can be persistent. Everyone was connecting to my game, so when I was not online my friends could not access their works made in my world. The planets could use a serious increase in size. In Starbound you can completely run around a planet in a short amount of time. I'd prefer planets to be so large that it would be impossible to run totally around one. In contrast my Expert mode character in Terraria, Bob, can barely leave the house without running into serious challenges. Just getting to the ocean is an adventure.
To wrap this up I'd say go ahead and play this game. Expert gamers can wrap up the story stuff in well under 100 hours. Sandboxers have a ton of content to enjoy. More amateur gamers seeking a slower experience with great art and music should be perfectly aligned with this 1.0 release. Overall a big thumbs up and a lot of fun.

Stranded Deep is yet another survival based game that has been released in Early Access. While there are many more survival games out there, something about Stranded Deep sets it aside from all the others I have played (Minecraft, DayZ Standalone, DayZ Mod, Rust Classic, Updated Rust, and H1Z1). There is an element of actual survival, immersion and beauty to this game that the games I mentioned prior simply do not have. So far, Stranded Deep is the only game where I actually felt like I was surviving.
Stranded Deep creates this immersive survival experience by taking away the UI based crafting method and instead forces you to actually look at the materials you are crafting in real time. If you want to make a stone axe then throw some sticks, twine and rocks on the ground and make it. Don't drag and drop icons, drag the actual object on the actual ground damnit!
As I mentioned before, the game is pretty gorgeous, though to be fair it isn't hard to turn a tropical island surrounded by ocean water into something beautiful during a sunset.
The gameplay is immersive. You can craft a hut, a fire pit some tools and a spear and go kill a shark, or row endlessly from island to island trying to survive off the land, scavenging ship wrecks as you go.
The problem is that there isn't much else to the game. You craft, you scavenge, you cut down a palm tree and kill 20 sharks, and you've done it all. It took me about 4 hours.
Now here is what I am going to say about this game. The potential is massive. The fact that it isn't multiplayer is a positive, besides multiplayer mode can always be introduced later on (which also has some interesting potential) but the lack of multiplayer at this stage is currently what makes the games a short run. There is no direct reward for your hours spent crafting and gathering. If you were genuinely stranded (deep) finding an actual axe would be the best thing ever. Not so much in a videogame though.
Given how much I enjoyed this game, I'll reccommend it with the hopes that the game continues to grow. Hopefully I don't regret it.

Where to start with this game... This is a fantastic game, do not get me wrong. But it is very buggy and needs some fixes (Remember though, this game is in Alpha right now). I have played a couple times and had to restart a few times (for fun and for not so fun). Instead of just making some god awful long statement about it, I am going to make it into bullet points.
1) Glitches, oh dear lord the glitches. My most recent game has had as many as I can find. First of all, I will start with what I have taken to calling the "Sand Shark Dilemma". What this is, is a problem with the Tiger Sharks, where they can somehow swim into the island and become "Sand Sharks". They can't kill you which is awesome and the game knows it's not supposed to be there (evidenced by being launched 100 feet into the air and falling back to my island no problem) but in a game where you throw your stuff on the ground to craft, Sand Sharks are a nightmare. I had gathered many materials and placed them all together when all of a sudden a saw the tree next to me shivering. All of a sudden it flew, a long with other materials, out into the ocean where I had to pray I could retrieve them.
1.5 Glitches... I had to start my most recent game due to the fact that I was investigating a boat that wasn't completely submerged. When I went into the hold which was underwater I got trapped, I could not get out because the ledge was too high and I couldn't jump out. I had no choice but to restart.
1.9 Glitches... Again... I went to a different island as I found myself out of rocks and I needed some to continue working on my home. When I returned home I found that some of my stuff had fallen through the holes of the foundation which was raised (See Sand Shark Dilemma). I couldn't get them back... I lost my hammer, my pocket knife and my bottled water. So I am now faced with the idea of do I put stuff on the ground where the Sand Sharks can play ping pong with it? Or do I put it on a foundation and hope it doesn't fall through.
2. This game desperately needs a way to modify your inventory. If you could carry more then stacks of 4 that would make me happy. If you could make a backpack or find one, that would make me happy. The current inventory system is so limited it makes the game a massive hinderance, especially with the distance between islands. I thought I could outsmart the game and when I went to a different Island I cut down a tree, broke it down into logs, and threw it onto my raft. It stayed for a bit, but when I arrived at my home island it was gone, fallen into the ocean.
3. This game, more than anything, needs some sort of navigation. I restarted games because I went out to a different island to get materials, got caught in the fog trying to return home, and could never find my island again. This♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off to no end, I had worked so hard on my home, had been diligent in leaving (That is I only rowed straight there and I thought I rowed straight back). I don't feel adding at least a compass would be too much of a stretch, I get the game is survival, but I mean the dude has a watch that tells the weather, temperature, time and can detect how hungry, thirsty and healthy I am. A compass should be the first reason he bought the damned "Survival Watch"
4. A bit more to do with your stuff, more diversity in items and a bit of simplification.
4.1 First of all, I would like to make note I realize this game is an Alpha, that is why diversity in items and more crafting is something I can happily wait for. I mean, the game has a lot going for it already and is an awesome game. It will be nice to see the way it grows, I just wanted to add that it does need to grow. BUT.
4.2 Crafting needs to be more comprehensible, the "Tutorial" in the beggining left me clueless. I figured it out after a bit but I'm still trying to figure things out like cooking. I have tried throwing crabs on the fire, tried holding them on the end of a spear over it and none of it has worked. It's frustrating not having any clue what to do with stuff.
This game is awesome for being in alpha stages, in honest the reason I went so in depth is because it's in alpha and I wanted to give the creators a bit to read so that they could get the perspective of someone activley playing. If you like survival games, this is the game for you, it is so much damn fun and an actual challenge. It just has a bit of work to do before it can be considered the perfect game.
