is an indie action RPG with roguelike elements. In this game, you play as one of six adventurers, including a Barbarian, Archer, and more. You must activate Marks along the dungeon floor in order to advance deeper into the depths in search of the Soul Orb, the only way to regain your soul. Every few levels, you'll come across a deadly boss who will drop epic loot if you can defeat them. You'll need powerful items and your own skills to survive and succeed.
The game draws inspiration from games like
,
,
,
and
. The gameplay is easy to learn but tough to master. There are three main elements: an autoattack and two special skills with some cooldowns. Items gained can passively increase your characters stats or add special procs to your attacks. Killing enemies yields EXP points to level up and increase your base stats and gems for purchasing items from shops. There's a good amount of variety among the items and enemies that can be found, and the boss battles are frenetic and challenging. In true roguelike fashion, the game is definitely hard, no matter what difficulty level you choose. However, it isn't as RNG-dependent as most other games are, and it definitely rewards skillful play. There is also permadeath, so you can't save progress between runs. However, money that you accumulate is kept and can be used to permanently upgrade your favorite characters, which balances some of the difficulty you can have when starting fresh.
At the time that this review was posted, the game is still in Early Access. Though the game is fully playable and is totally fun and enjoyable, it isn't a perfect release. Some of the elements are very unbalanced, such as traps and the melee classes. Playing as either one of them can almost guarantee a swift death as they are ridiculously underpowered compared to the other characters. Traps like sliding spike-balls and triggered boulders can quickly end a run. Though I've never experienced any, players in the forums have reported some game-breaking bugs or can't even run/download the game.
Still, the developer, Mike Studios, is dedicated and is constantly tweaking the game. Before release on Steam, Dungeon Souls has gained a notable fan-following on other gaming sites, such as
,
, and
. All in all, the game is good in its current state and is definitely worth buying now if you're a fan of hack n' slash, roguelites, and dungeon crawlers.

PROS
-Gunplay vastly superior to the clunky "tile" feeling mechanics of Fallout 3 and NV
-Graphics are decent. Some people hate the graphics, mostly the chracter models, and while I agree some of it looks pretty terrible, the environments and lighting are actually very good.
-Basebuilding/Settlements are a neat idea and distraction, even if they aren't very useful or fleshed out.
NEGATIVES (Oh boy)
-Dialogue system was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ No choices, stupid dialogue, cringeworthy lines. Literally everything you say to someone is a yes, sarcastic yes, or no (which is yes).
-Voiced protagonist. The worst sin of this unholy abomination. First off, the voice actor for the male character does a very poor job at convincing he gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥about anything, including his missing infant son. Second of all, where the hell is the roleplay in having a voiced protagonist? To put it bluntly, it's impossible to roleplay in this game and feel like a unique chracter as you'll always have to be the "concerned father looking for his son".
-No skill points. Why, just why? Take out a major RPG element out of what's supposed to be an RPG. This isn't an RPG. Hell, this isn't even an open world shooter with RPG elements. It's an open world shooter with ability upgrades much akin to Far Cry 3.
-The Plot. Extremely boring and meaningless. So the premise is that you're looking for your son, which is already pretty boring since it's just the opposite of what you already did in Fallout 3. Then you get to choose which of the major factions you end up helping. The only two factions that are interesting are the Brotherhood of Steel, and the Institute. The Minutemen and The Railroad are forgettable. You feel as if you are not interacting with the world and its inhabitants throughout the game, like any choices you make dont make any difference, unlike in New Vegas for example. I'm actually having trouble even thinking about what to write for this part of the review, The story is THAT uninispired.
-Lack of originality. As said above, the plot is just a reversal of Fallout 3s. It also seems like Bethesda couldn't come up with an original idea that hasn't been seen in other Fallouts to save their lives. For example, I thought East Coast supermutants in Fallout 3 were pretty stupid to be included. I felt like instead of reusing existing ideas to remind you that you're playing a Fallout game, they should have instead used their imagination of what could be in their interpretation of the universe. But my god, they included supermutants in Fallout 4, and you know what's the kicker? THEY'RE NOT EVEN RELATED TO THE ONES FEATURED IN 3. That's right, there are now THREE goddamn versions of these things, all because Bethesda knows they couldn't make anything interesting by themselfs, so they resort to rehashing rehashed ideas. This is just one of many examples of Bethesda being lazy.
CONCLUSION
This game is pretty terrible. It's a damn shame since it could have been so much more. The Creation engine, while not being great by any means, was much improved over the Gamebryo. Bethesda had unbelievable amounts of potential with this game, but they just♥♥♥♥♥♥out a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥product and knew the hype surrounding it would guaruntee that their pockets are filled with green.
TL;DR Play New Vegas instead (Or 3)

Not a bad game, but has aged terribly and there are far more rewarding alternatives out there.
This game has a lot in common with Deus Ex: Invisible War, which was made by the same developers and is based on the same engine. It's really not suited to open-ended environments and it shows in this game. About half your computer's power is spent trying to draw shadows and as a result, the levels themselves are too small and 'boxed in' to give this game the free-roaming sandbox feel that it's trying to achieve.
I can't fault the atmosphere in this game. It's very dark and eerie, right down to Garrett's growling voice and background ambience when reading books. There are subtle prods towards cults and witchcraft and you find yourself in some very unfriendly places as the game progresses. It comes to a climax with 'the Cradle', the penultimate level of this game which is deemed to be one of the spookiest levels in a game, ever.
However, the core gameplay is flawed. Moving about the world is a clunky experience. I like how you can look down and see your body, and that you can pull yourself up onto things, but I still felt disjointed and distant from the world. It just doesn't feel quite right. This extends to the combat, lockpicking and every bit of this game.
There are occasional flashes of brilliance, like when I discovered another thief who I found breaking into the place I was sneaking about in. Running away from guards / black figures (COUGH Cradle) is a nerve-wracking experience and discovering hidden treasure makes me happier than I should be.
This game is a very odd relic, stuck in an awkward transition period between old and new-style games. At the time, you could consider it a quirk of the game or assume that you were doing something wrong. Sadly, it just isn't worth playing today. Play Dishonored instead while you're waiting for Thief 4 to be released.

The concept for the game is really good, but the execution is awful:
- Hitboxes and Sprites don't seem to match up too well.
- Only one music track per world, which constantly loops throughout the world.
- The Entire Game, including the Deluxe Content (only 10 levels), can be beat in 37 minutes. The only reason to replay is to get Gold on each level.
The level design is also fairly shoddy, IMO; one level that sticks out in my memory involved jumping, bouncing on a rolling enemy, and practically nothing else. It sounds easy to do, but the jump had to have perfect timing, or else you'd die. You also had to know that the rolling enemy only detects collision inside of the enemy.
The idea of playing a game in reverse is a novel one, but Spoiler Alert is a product that fails this idea entirely. If you really need to play this for some reason, please buy the normal version; the deluxe edition only has 10 extra levels (each 20 seconds long) and a level editor.

There is a difference between a challenging puzzle and an unintuitive puzzle. This is a distinction that Please, Don't Touch Anything fails to grasp. It's a shame because the concept of "console with one button that hides more" is simple enough to provide a framework for a series of interesting puzzles to solve. Instead, the player is required to make random observations and can be cut off from significant portions of the game by failing to do so. There is also no hint system, giving the player no other options but to simply look up solutions - something I had to start doing after about an hour of trying to figure puzzles out and getting nowhere.
This poor puzzle design combined with minimal rewards for finding the game's different endings ("another animation of the city being transformed - oh joy") made this an unrewarding experience that I would only recommend to puzzle solvers with a high tolerance for puzzles that are designed by their creator with an attitude of "there's no way they'll figure it out."

This is a short little Platforming game with an interesting hook - you play the entire thing backwards, undoing everything you've done (and only what you've done - so touching a coin you didn't collect originally or killing an enemy you didn't kill the first time through causes a paradox and level restart) as you undo the whole game.  The concept was done better in Retro/Grade, but that's a rhythm shooter game, where this is a platform game.  And it's moderately fun, definitely tricky.  I finished all 100 levels in about 40 minutes, but that's because I didn't go back and try to gold star every level (I gold starred about a third the first time through).  There are some other bonuses and stuff in the game if you want to spend more time, but it's basically a short creative concept that doesn't overstay its welcome.

I think this game receives too much flak, people bandwagoning on a hate train created by popular Youtubers. Sure, it is not perfect, but nothing truly is. I see this to be like another Bubsy 3D, a gem that is simply thrown into the trash by people with unrealistic standards. Not everyone can create a Triple A budget title, and have to make do with the tools available to them. And in this regard, I see Day One: Garry's Incident as a rather fine title. If I were to change only one thing, it would be  to have multiple areas which would load separately, so not to stress the system too much. This simple fix could turn this B- game into an A for me.
Don't fall victim to this blackhole of negativity. This is hardly one of the worst games ever, like so many claim. I mean, if it were that bad, it'd have been taken off Steam by now, like so many other titles. Such as Ride to Hell and War Z.
To conclude my report, this game is a fine deal for the low price it is at. Just do not expect it to be on par with something like the Nathan Drake series, which I feel this is very comparable to in terms of setting, themes, and characters.
Thank you for reading, and I hope anyone who decides to purchase this title will see the positives to it. Such as a nice variety of weapons, a crafting system, and survival mode which I feel surpasses that of Rust, Garry's other project.

First off, let me just mention that I loved Terraria back when it was released. A two-dimensional minecraft with tons more unique creatures and biomes, not to mention unique bosses for different sections of the world.
Now we see this beautiful casual gaming masterpiece we know as Starbound; much like Terraria, but on a much, MUCH larger scale. It may not have as many pre-designed creatures, and the procedurally generated ones may not be much to talk about either, but when combined with the variation of the different worlds' landscapes and scenery, procedurally generated or not, they fit in very nicely with the worlds around you. There are many more block types, most of which share a theme with other blocks. If put together correctly, you could even create a style completely different from that of the rest of the game. The bosses are okay. In a way, they feel like your average boss in Terraria; quite tough when you get to it, possibly even inspiring during your first time fighting it, but once you beat them once, it's like riding a bicycle.
And although the gameplay is solid, addictive, and most importantly FUN, I will admit that what really caught my attention when I started playing this game was the character customization, whether it be via the character creator, cosmetic items found in-game, or a combination of the two. And this leads in to another topic of discussion: roleplay. I'm quite into it, and believe me when I say that this game is bursting with potential in terms of roleplay. The game has a linear storyline with non-linear gameplay, allowing the player to complete the game at their own pace, or simply choose not to complete the game at all. With this in mind, the player may choose to complete the game in order to get it out of the way or simply not do anything and stop tracking Esther's quests if that furthers their concentration on whatever activities they may be pursuing, such as roleplay, building a colony, exploring, or any combination of those.
Now if you'll excuse me, I have an appointment to kick Big Ape's @$$ in about half an hour, so enjoy the game and its future updates. This game is definitely recommended by me and earns my seal of approval (which doesn't really mean much and is only meant to emphasise my fondness for this game)

Double Fine seems to have an intrinsic knowledge of how to make a charming game and, as a result, "Stacking" is a joy to play. Every little detail of the miniaturized world has been lovingly crafted out of marbles, matchsticks, and bits of string, setting the stage for an old-timey story of heroism, child slavery, hobos, and matryoshka dolls. Alongside this are puzzle mechanics that echo vaguely of the adventure games of old, complete with a few puzzles that have you wracking your brain for the solutions. All of these elements are combined into a completely unique, positively delightful, and absolutely charming adventure, making "Stacking" a game that everyone should take time to enjoy.

Every puzzle has many possible solutions. Finding first is a matter of minutes, finding all soltions often requires more lateral thinking. What I really loved about this game, apart from sense of humour and natural usage of concept, was art. Game is beautifully designed and has a great vibe to it. Alright, to start off the review, there will be spoilers, my own opinions, and all that jazz. Another sidenote, I didn't actually beat the game, but my friend told me the ending and what you get and I've played enough to give this a solid review.
First things first, the gameplay.
While it did take things from other games that I liked, a lot for me stemming from Terraria, it still felt like a pretty original experience. The space element I really liked, uh, I liked the fact that you didn't have to have different tools to break blocks and other enviromental items. I mean, that's about it for the positive stuff, just because this game was so lack-luster. Seriously, if I were to make a game where the beta had so much great features then remove most of what the fun was, I would really contemplate my life and why I would even do that. There were mechs, specie weapons, real combat, and even more that they removed for no reason at all. That's probably what threw me off the most about this game, the lack of content. Other stuff about the gameplay is even if you choose Survival, it's still pretty hard, actually, not hard, straight up annoying. You would have to cook items and eat them in order to live, which for me, is pretty ridiculous, since you would probably have to worry about that more than anything else, you would drop your items that may have taken a very long and tedious time to even recieve, and on top of all of it, on top of all the stuff I already ranted about, the mode itself didn't do anything to the game really, but to me emotionally. I swear, I have never been more anxious to grab my 800 copper and silver that took literal hours to get, and in the end, wouldn't even get them because I would KEEP DYING.
Next up, story.
It sucked. Period. I saw this in one review, but I might as well repeat it. All you do is talk to an old woman, go to a bunch of planets, where you have to waste resources to get to, suffer dying, dying, and more dying, until you find a village, in which you scan stupid posters and furniture, go back to the woman, do some cooky dungeon then beat either a really easy boss or a really hard boss, and in turn, do the same thing like 6 more times. Seriously, and in the end, you get 25,000 pixels, which I will say is the only good thing, some upgrade modules and manipulator modules, which I might add, won't do anything, and a Thank-You Card. A Thank-You Card. No legendary weapon that destroys planets, no clothing or ship additive that makes the game more fun, a flipping Thank-You Card. How lousey is that, to finish a, might I mind you, A SANDBOX GAME, AND NOT GET ANYTHING TO ENHANCE THE EXPERIENCE. Overall, it sucked.
Finally, everything else.
Since I've already expressed how I felt, it also sucked too. Weapons, don't really enhance anything, since there's a very small select few that are actually good, clothing and armor, which again, do nothing to benefit, and your crew mates and companions don't really even help that much. Seriously, it was really useless in the end.
Final Review: 3.5/10

So i originally reviewed this back in 2013, stating the game was fun for a while but was overall to linear with nothing to really mix up gameplay, currently its pretty much exactly the same, except some things have gotten worse aswell.
So first of all, the main complaint with the previous iterations of the game was a lack of story, this game has addressed the problem with an actual story with quests and so on, the problem is is that this story is incredibly repetetive and incredibly linear still. Gonna leave spoilers out but it basically copies the same main quest 5 times with some smaller stuff thrown in, all main quests ending with a final boss. So while there is an actual story mode, its pretty much the same old game with some hack of a story thrown in. The lore and story related atmosphere of the game has also been ruined. The older, intricate and detailed lore has been redone and is all the more bland and generic (check the wiki's removed content to see yourself) and the atmosphere of towns has been removed. The apex had a whole 1984 aspect going on, but now its just 1984 styled with barely of the actual atmosphere.
Gameplay was i'd say its gotten less diverse, which for a game like this is pretty bad. Enemies scale in such a way to where a player will never really end up feeling strong at all, even with some of the rarest weapons in the game. Generation has to do with a lot of the negatives of the game, planets no longer feel truely unique. Basically out of 5 tiers of planets there are only about 4 or 5 indivudal planet types per system, and all of these planets feel copy and pasted. All underground regions feel the same as well. Monsters are also the same type between planets depending on what biome you're in. Weapon variety has also been cut down since all weapons fall under like 10 categories.
So essentially, the only main positives this game had before: generation and combat, are now gone.
Do i regret spending the 15 dollars i did on this game? Not really, becase i got my time out of it. But i wouldn't recommened you give this company your money as even with some friends it isn't good at all. Its only gotten worse since its early versions.

The game would be an okay game without the glitches, worth a look in that case. With that said there are plenty of glitches. I know this is early access and all, but the glitches are pretty big, not really glitches you can toss aside and say whatever the games still fun. (In fact, I don't think there's any small glitches, or I have yet to discover them). The glitches I've encountered so far ar as follows:
There are boats located all over the place in the game (old rusty ones) in which you can find supplies, which is all well and good if you find it in the ocean, but on land if you drop down the hatch, you are stuck there for the remainder of the game. (I guess some boats end up on islands I'm not even really sure how they get there).
The rest of the glitches I've found are all about the life raft. 1: While trying to jump onto the life raft either you or your life raft will spontaneously fly high and far into the air, only to fall into/ontop of (what is most likely) the ocean, where you will find a fair amount of shark inbetween you and the nearest island. 2: while trying to get to another island my raft dissapeared, and I (somehow) fell as if I was in the air to the bottom of the ocean. I can then swim back up to find my raft, and try to climb onto it. Only problem is as soon as you touch the raft it dissapears. There is a ladder on the raft, once touched, as aforementioned, dissapeared. Yet you may still climb up the nonexistent ladder only to tumble right back into the ocean. Raft problems happen nearly everytime using the raft, I've only successfully reached 1 island on the raft without glitching out and having to restart to my last save point.
Although this is a problem of its own, it stems from raft glitching issues. Every island in the game is small with limited resources on each, so when you start the game you quickly find that you need to go to another island if you wish to progress at all in the game, which isn't really possible because your raft will probably glitch. So basically, I can't play the game until these major glitches are fixed.

Let me get this out of the way, and it hurts me a lot to say it. This game is a huge dissapointment to all of us Bethesda fans. To me, Bethesda has been going downhill since a little bit before the release when I was finding rumors of the creation club idea. So for me, this game was going to be one last epic title in memory of how great bethesda was, one with adventure! One with fun quests! One with *intuitive* settlement building! One  with characters that you had to read and find out more about! Yeah... I wish that was what we got.
In the famous words of Codsworth, "Ehh you've simply changed, sir. And not in a good way." Those words accurately described what a let down this game was. We wanted adventure and well, we did get it! In the form of DLC which took you to far harbor and Nuka World which were expensive as all hell.  "What if you don't buy the DLC?" You may ask. Well, you get to explore the bland map of the commonwealth! With the only cool parts being the irradiated zone to the south east of the map, or the sunken stuff in the ocean.
We wanted quests right? Well we got them! Infinite quests even! Given by Preston Garvey himself. What are these quests you may ask? Go to a settlement, kill a raider or two, come back, and what's your reward? Preston Garvey's thanks of course! Ahhh and the settlment building. Originally it sounded like a great idea! But then they added Garvey, and made it so the settlers couldn't do♥♥♥♥♥♥no matter how many giant rocket machines you sorrounded them with or how many corn seeds you left in a trunk. No. You had to come and go, come and go, come and go, every two damn seconds! You may think that this has some exciting and inspiring reward for all this tedious♥♥♥♥♥♥right? Nah. An achievement. That's all.
About the characters, they're really bland and a dime a dozen. The only interesting ones are probably Kellog or Curie, and maybe Cait. But that's just my opiniond and my I really didn't find anyone else interesting. About those "interesting" few however, you never get the chance to find more about them due to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ little dialouge system with four choices which are practically just yes, no, why, maybe. You also got a terribly voiced protagonist (which im not sure why bethesda gave us? The old dialouge system was so much fun)
This, and many more reasons are why you should just go back to NV or 3, maybe try some of the older ones if you want. Just please, don't play this game. It will massacre your respect for Bethesda.

I've been following Battle Brothers since before it received the GreenLight in October 2014. Man, that's quite some time. At that time I was looking for some sandboxy type of game that allowed us to grab some medieval weapons and fight our way through hordes of enemies in a turn based game, with management features and some sort of procedural story telling.
Guess what: that's precisely what Battle Brothers is!
So I've found this game on
and thought: "Nah, it's too good to be true, there's no way they would manage to release that". But, disregarding my predictions (and also to my delight), they're now just a few weeks from releasing the full version while managing to keep almost all the features they've promised. Not all, unfortunately, because of the tight budget they had to deal with (things like battles inside dungeons, ruins, sieges, etc., were left for a later moment, for example). Even so, it has been very rewarding for me to watch the Battle Brothers' development through the blog posts, which I started following some time before the Public Pre-Alpha Combat Demo release way back, and see the game coming to life little by little.
For anyone wanting to try a Sandbox Turn Based RPG with a medieval theme, deep tactics, procedural events and the harsh atmosphere of a mercenary life (which's something Battle Brothers captures really well), I assure you that this is your type of game, which is also made by one of the most transparent and communicative devs I've ever seen.

Seven days. That doesn't seem like a long time, but seven days ago Hilderich was a founder of the Poor Sods mercenary company, an axe weiding terror who once beheaded three men in one battle, but this morning, he's a rotting corpse with his skull split down the middle. Anton the Brave, he's now Anton the deceased. Good ol' Bjarne, a beggar who signed on for a chance at something better was gutted and bled out as he begged for just one more breath. Steinar fared no better, his blonde head was cleaved from his sturdy farmhand shoulders. That's a lot of blood for one week.
Who knows, maybe the dead are the lucky ones. The rest of us knit our busted bones and stitch severed muscles nearly starving on a gray paste of grain and water. Of course some wounds can't be fixed with bandages and a bowl of gruel, poor Robert the Juggler took a pick to the head that scrambled his eggs and hasn't been the same since.
Yes, we have a a juggler on our fighting line. As I write that, I realize that we're barely a mercenary company at all. We've only two soldiers in the whole group. The rest: a brain-damaged juggler, a gravedigger drunkard, a fisherman, an apprentice of questionable loyalty and a cripple with no ears. Our gear is the broken bits we scavenge from the bodies of our enemies, or post-mortem hand me downs from our own fallen brothers.
But despite our dearth of battle-ready fighters and our rummage sale gear, we've somehow got another contract. Another benefactor with clean skin and white clothes who'll pay our rusty asses 400 crowns to murder some nearby inconvenient thugs.
My share of the 400 isn't enough to get me out, but maybe they've a cache of gold to loot, or captured princess to rescue. You know, with just a few more contracts and a few lucky breaks; I could turn this bunch over to Niels or Rumar, buy Robert a new set of juggling balls and retire somewhere green and quiet.
Poor Sods form up!
We're off to battle.

Oh what a game.
So Mortal Kombat is known for it's absolutely vicious gameplay and totally overly violence.  In the SNES/Genesis era, it was the game with a blood code (Genesis only) when Street fighter was relatively tame.  It had Fatalities.
Well Mortal Kombat (really Mortal Kombat 9) has continued that march of progress.  While it's not it's ultimate form (Seriously, Mortal Kombat X takes everything 9 did and makes it almost disgusting... ok actually disgusting.)   Mortal Kombat 9 has a special charm in it's self.
The main game play (besides online, which I only dip my toe into because... I really don't have the time to dedicate myself to all the fighting games I play) seems like it's a story mode.  Which is 16 chapters each four fights each.  And while the story is decent, it's never that deep.  Basically unless you REALLY know the lore, (and as such you wouldn't need to read a review) the story is... acceptable but there's a lot of mysticism that's their for super fans of the series.   It's good enough to play through though.  But there is a REALLY painful fight just over half way through the story mode to watch out for (Liu Kang vs Shao Khan).
However there's another mode.  Challenge Tower which contains 300 levels, and I have to say that's the real killer experience.   This is similar to star mode in Injustice.  The player fights through 300 different matches with different rules and a lot of variety.  You'll play as every character (or almost all of them) and each gets used for about 10 levels.  But the variety in these levels are some of the best in the game.  There are matches where the player is headless, or armless, or throws arms at the opponent, or only is limited to one move.  The fact is there's at least 100 matches that don't feel like a normal match, and I absolutely love this mode.
There's also Arcade modes, which each character has an individual ending as well.
And there's more, there's now a tag mode in some matches, that can be applied to arcade mode as well, there's a number of Tests you can take (unlocked from progressing through challenge tower) and of course Online.
Overall there's a LOT to do in this game, the fighting is the typical Mortal Kombat fair (Super moves, combos, throws, and blocking) but honestly the wealth of content really shines, and it works great for hard core fans of the series (the guys who will go online after taking down the expert mode difficulty) and the novices of the series.
Just realize, this is a game that revels in the blood and violence.  It's incredible just how brutal they keep making the game and upping the ante, and Mortal Kombat 9 is a perfect blend of the old and the ultra violent.    In fact they added a new attack in this game called the x-ray.  All I can say about them are they are somehow almost as brutal as the classic fatalities.  Damn!
Personally I love this game, so I recommend it just due to it's absolutely beautiful visuals and true visceral impacts.   It's not a game for the squeamish, and it's just so brutally violent.  But it's also just beautifully brutal, if you can handle it, it's a fantastic game.

Mortal Kombat 9 was one of those games where it properly rebooted the series back to form. Because, Mortal Kombat as a series wasn't being taken as seriously as it should as a fighting game contender. It went through a very awkward phase during the 2000s where after Deadly Alliance, we saw rehashed game after rehashed game in Deception and Armageddon, which we were lied to by Ed Boon when he initially commented on how Armageddon was to have been the 'last' game of the series. Before turning around immediately by saying that it's the last of the chapter of MK. Right, Boon.
And not to mention, we were subjected to horrid handheld ports of previous MK games to boot. Throw in some awkward spinoffs and you have a very weird mix. Mortal Kombat was experiencing an identity crisis.
It wouldn't have gotten any better with MK vs DC either since, the logistics of both universes colliding in a fighting game made absolutely no sense, IMO. So the series plunged into a 2 year silence until this installment came and finally, we can acknowledge that this entry is a proper reboot.
Everything we've remembered MK of being, is all here and all modernized. Most importantly, MK can finally be seen again as a fighting contender.
MK9 looked sharp and crisp for what it brought to the table. It toned down a lot of the silliness that plagued the series for all those years and got down to business.
I've played it first on console before hesitantly buying the PC port and I wasn't disappointed when things ran smoothly. There wasn't much to have been disappointed about this game. Except a little of the online community is kindof dead, the Krypt makes a return (yay, worthless stuff like in DA) and the beginning of guest characters. I'm not a fan of guest characters, regardless of who's who. Freddy Krueger? Come on now and yes I'm aware Predator and Jason Voorhees are like on MKX. Logic? Whatever.
Besides those minor things, MK9 is a great reboot and the step in the right direction. MK might not be as mechanically deep in fighting like KOF/SF/Tekken.etc are. But we've come to enjoy MK again for what it is and was. That's where it counted and I can't recommend this enough to a fan of fighting games or MK.

Before you say anything about the time, I finished the entire game and the bonus world... moving on...
TL;DR: The actual platforming elements are wonky and generally just a mess (as is kinda standard for comedy games), the comedy is nonexistant, and the concept fails completely. Do not recommend.
This game's concept is really interesting. You can read that above.
This game's execution of its concept is really bad.
For the conept to work, the game has to make sense both in forward and reverse. If either direction doesn't make sense, the game is very flawed.
Heads up: spoiler alert. I'm suggesting you not play it, so I don't see much reason for me to try to avoid spoiling it (and the game is asking for it).
Logically, the place to start in checking if a game makes sense is in the forward direction, I'd think.
Okay, first level,  intricate spike placement combined with floor tiles that change the speed at which you move combined with projectile shooting enemies. K. That's... K.
Err... first world's boss. Hit button, turns on laser that reflects enemy attacks then... turn it off when you're done and turn on a different one? Oooookay. It drops coins and then (at least whoever played it before the player gets there) avoid all the coins that it randomly poops out because reasons. K.
......
Last level! One goomba. Six coins. Boss that dies in one hit. K.
Okay. Forward doesn't make sense. Therefore, the execution of the concept is horribly flawed.
The game is calling itself a comedy platformer, so I can excuse that the actual platforming is kinda crappy (I mean, DLC Quest isn't fun because of the actual things you do in it), but it HAD to get the concept right, which it didn't.
Even outside of the entire level design failing, there are specific things that break the idea. The projectile-shooting things from the first level? They look injured when their projectiles get back to them. Shouldn't there be a smug "I'm going to shoot you!" look? There's disappear-for-a-moment-after-you-touch-them blocks, which would have been a really cool concept for a game like this. They're disappear-then-reappear-right-before-you-touch-them blocks... but they don't work like that in this game. They just disappear for a moment after you touch them.
The only actual joke it makes is at the end/beginning where it tries to handwave why it is that the game doesn't make sense forward... but... it doesn't work. By the time you get there, you're already so tired of the game not making any sense, that any explanation at that point is too little too late.
I also did the mariachi bonus world. It's not fun either and it has the same problems.
So... the actual platforming elements are wonky and generally just a mess (as is kinda standard for comedy games), the comedy is nonexistant, and the concept fails completely.
The only way I recommend getting this is as a part of the gamemaker pro weekly humble bundle that will probably be over by the time you read this because it's on the $1 tier and you get other (better) things.

... This game is a masterpiece. I'm sure you've probably heard this a lot from others, but it has to be said again. Bastion and Supergiant Games make phenomenal titles. Now... Let me explain why I praise this so much.
The story of Bastion is a simple one: The world has ended. An event called 'The Calamity' has destroyed the world, its inhabitants, and left it in a crumbling state with only a handful of survivors and the beasts that remain. You play as The Kid, an unnamed young man with quite a past, trying to rebuild the Bastion, a powerful artifact that holds the key to fixing everything. Throughout the entire adventure, your exploits are narrated by the wisened old man, who offers tidbits on how to survive post-Calamity Caelondia and even offer personal insight onto what's left of the world.
Gameplay itself is relatively straight forward, an action-RPG with light platforming sections. Your goals are simple: traverse the level to find the necessary item and fight your way back, occasionally picking up a new weapon or object to expand the Bastion along the way. You'll fight against hostile enemies affected by the Calamity, be they the sluggish yet monstrous Gasbags, defunt machinery left behind by the long lost Caelondians, or the animals striving to survive. You'll have to rely on quick acting and timing to handle the vast number of enemies, because unless you're careful, you'll run the risk of falling to your doom.
Two other strong suits that keep the game afloat are the visuals and the music. Visually, the game is gorgeous, coupled with the unique artstyle and the destructable environment, you truly feel you're in a domain touched by the apocalypse. And the music... gods above, the music is PHENOMENAL. Alternating tracks between tense action segments to somber and sullen songs befitting to the emotion of the game. Easily among the best music I've heard in an indie game that conveys such emotion.
If you haven't picked this game up, please do. It is well worth the price, and will leave memories of your experiences long after you completed it and the multiple challenge runs. Just watch your step, Kid.

Thief: Deadly Shadows is the final installment of the original trilogy of Thief games. It runs on a new engine from the previous two games, and so things work a little differently, this time around.
The first thing you'll probably notice is the updated graphics, and the second is the fidgety movement. Deadly Shadows has the ability to be played from a third-person perspective, but unlike, say, Oblivion, it seems as though the third-person control was built *first*. As a result, Garrett jitters a bit when starting and stopping movement, and you can see your hands and legs as they actually are, and not, like with many first-person games, as two sets of limbs apparently growing directly out of your face. Of course, you get used to this after a couple missions, though you won't necessarily get used to occasionally seeing things in your hands at the side of your screen when you turn too quickly.
I jumped several times when carrying bodies, all the way from the first mission to the last.
There are ten missions this time around, as opposed to Thief Gold and Thief II's fifteen a piece. To make up for this, The City serves as a free-roamy hub area where you can thief around for additional loot, sell whatever loot you're carrying, and buy supplies for future missions. There are also main story objectives to complete, along with optional side quests should you seek them. Missions themselves are shorter, owing to the smaller level designs - undoubtedly a result of the engine change and graphical makeover. The relatively small levels are then chopped into even smaller segments with load screens in the middle. While it's, again, something you'll easily get used to, it does occasionally make building layouts seem a bit odd when thought of as a whole.
The enemy AI has been improved. Guards will notice bloodstains on the floor, doors which should or shouldn't be open, and other guards missing from their posts. On normal difficulty, however, Deadly Shadows is much easier than Thief II (which was, in turn, far easier than Thief Gold). Series veterans looking for a challenge will absolutely want to play through on hard or expert. The difficulty of levels never really increases much over the course of the game (indeed, the toughest level for me was the third or fourth one I played). Though later in the game the hub world does take a couple difficulty spikes, by the final third I was carrying the maximum amount of all available equipment, with more than enough cash left over to replace anything I might use by the end.
Speaking of the end, all difficulty aside, the finale felt appropriate enough to earn a mention, here. The final level is a perfect fit for a game about burglary, and the final sequence is a perfect fit for this specific game about burglary. Even the ending cutscene wraps the series up nicely, allowing me to walk away feeling very pleased with my time spent with the series as a whole.
There are some other notable differences, here and there. There are now factions, so you can ally yourself with or against the Pagans and/or Hammerites. Levels now have loot-collecting requirements based on the difficulty you are playing on. Darkness is blueish, rather than stark black, so you can see what you're doing easier. Also it looks prettier, if you're into that (especially with the shafts of moonlight which pour in from any window they can). Lockpicking is now a little more involving. You have to get closer to knock people out, now. Stabbing requires closer quarters, as well, as Garrett now carries a dagger instead of a sword. And there's now a large emphasis on the Keepers' use of glyphs, which seem a little out of place when there was no mention of them even being a thing in previous installments.
The differences take some getting used to, but I urge you to keep playing until you do. Thief: Deadly Shadows is a worthy addition to the franchise, and once you're steady on your thief legs it's every bit as fun as the previous games. So get settled in, plug in your favorite pair of headphones, and let's take a walk on the Thief side.

So in Thief, you're a Thief.
Despite the misleading title of the game, however, shadows do not actually harm you in any way. Rather, it is advised to stick to the shadows as much as possible. I did not know this, and so had a very troublesome first few hours of gameplay.
In Thief, you steal things. That is because you are a thief. When you steal things, they belong to you, and so you can sell them to people and get money to buy other things that make stealing things easier. With this unique system in place, you can achieve a near-constant cycle of owning and disowning various objects in the game world. It is systems like these that contribute much of the immersion to Thief: Not Really Deadly Shadows.
You can posess a myriad of useful tools, like a knife. That is sharp, and so it can be used to stab guards, often causing them to die. While to some, like the guards, this may be seen as unhelpful, for a thief, it is actually quite useful.
With well thought-out game systems, a very well implemented loot ownership gameplay style, and the ability to own things, I highly recommend this game with something like a 7 or 12 out of 10.

Seven days. That doesn't seem like a long time, but seven days ago Hilderich was a founder of the Poor Sods mercenary company, an axe weiding terror who once beheaded three men in one battle, but this morning, he's a rotting corpse with his skull split down the middle. Anton the Brave, he's now Anton the deceased. Good ol' Bjarne, a beggar who signed on for a chance at something better was gutted and bled out as he begged for just one more breath. Steinar fared no better, his blonde head was cleaved from his sturdy farmhand shoulders. That's a lot of blood for one week.
Who knows, maybe the dead are the lucky ones. The rest of us knit our busted bones and stitch severed muscles nearly starving on a gray paste of grain and water. Of course some wounds can't be fixed with bandages and a bowl of gruel, poor Robert the Juggler took a pick to the head that scrambled his eggs and hasn't been the same since.
Yes, we have a a juggler on our fighting line. As I write that, I realize that we're barely a mercenary company at all. We've only two soldiers in the whole group. The rest: a brain-damaged juggler, a gravedigger drunkard, a fisherman, an apprentice of questionable loyalty and a cripple with no ears. Our gear is the broken bits we scavenge from the bodies of our enemies, or post-mortem hand me downs from our own fallen brothers.
But despite our dearth of battle-ready fighters and our rummage sale gear, we've somehow got another contract. Another benefactor with clean skin and white clothes who'll pay our rusty asses 400 crowns to murder some nearby inconvenient thugs.
My share of the 400 isn't enough to get me out, but maybe they've a cache of gold to loot, or captured princess to rescue. You know, with just a few more contracts and a few lucky breaks; I could turn this bunch over to Niels or Rumar, buy Robert a new set of juggling balls and retire somewhere green and quiet.
Poor Sods form up!
We're off to battle.

Alright so after many hours of pain and rage, I finally got a 100% achievement clear on this game.
It's a very basic tower defense game, but I cannot blame it for that since it pretty much a phone app.
It's extremely hard for me to talk about this game without mentioning all of its references. You will recognice voicelines from  things such as: Harry potter, Star wars, Die hard, Lord of the rings, Scarface, Ghostbusters, The Sixth sense, Teenage mutant ninja turtles, The shining and they even put in ''All your base are belong to us''. While it was fun to notice all these things, it feels like the game has less of a personality of it's own because of it.
Now to the part everyone is gonna jump straight to.
+PROS:
+Very addictive, you always strive to just clear one more map, or do one more challenge. My sleeping pattern got messed up when I started playing.
+A really cool skill tree that you use stars to lvl up, stars are earned for playing the maps. If you do a good job you get more stars, meaning you can upgrade more skills and be better prepared for the next map.
+Most towers feel usable depending on the situation.
+Most tower upgrades are usable depending on the situation.
+Some really strategic planning can go into this. Especially on the latest maps in the challanges.
+Big enemy variety.
+Many different heroes you unlock as you clear maps. When you beat the original campain, you have them all. They all come with a very different skillset, so you have to consider who will make the best ally on a map.
+Quite a few bosses, they all do different things and some can be a real challenge to work around sometimes.
+Alot of the achievements for this game are just fun little interactive things on the maps.
-CONS:
-Once you earn all the stars you need to lvl up everything in your skill tree, earing stars doesn't feel rewarding at all anymore.
-A few towers just doesn't feel good enough to be used. I'm looking at you, Big Bertha.
-Some tower upgrades are lackluster, such as the mage tower upgrade that turns enemies into sheep.
-While there are alot of different enemies in the game, many of them just feel like reskins of eachother.
-Some achievements are not explained well enough. Made me waste alot of time and had to backtrack.
Overall:
Am I glad I did a 100% clear on this game? Yes.
Would I do it again? Most likely.
Will I play this game just for fun in the future? No.
Is it worth full price? I'd say no.
Do I recommend it? Yes.

The game honestly went through development hell, and, it seemed like for a while, it would never be released from beta.
A great way to sum up a majority of Starbound is variety. There is a variety of enemies, environments, and just things to do in those environments. Well, or at least there is a lot of visual variety. On the more technical scale, there are quite a few different types of enemies, yes, but many environments feel very similar overall.
The combat offers a decent amount of weapons, as well, and works as well as it would be hoped for to. There are quite a few enemies with differing movement and techniques, making this one of the better areas of the game when it comes to having actual technical, and not just visual, variety.
Lastly, I have to admit the moving and platforming seems decent at first, however, once it's time for fine movements, it's incredibly frustrating. Your character automatically accelerates to full speed with only a tap of the A or D key, which can send them hurling to their doom off of a cliff or into a trap before you even register what you just did wrong. I think the problem could be fairly easily fixed, as all the devs would have to do would be add starting acceleration, however, alas, I am still accidentally going bungee jumping. Without the bungee.
The game may not be perfect in areas such as when it starts feeling repetitive after a while, and may have moments of instability and frustration, however, I overall found it enjoyable and would recommend at least a trial of this weird little indie game to those who just want to explore some environments and maybe do a little building, at least if it can be found on sale.

I've followed the development of this game since alpha, and have played the game since day 1 of Early Access. You'll see every other review saying this is like "Space Terraria" and lemme tell you(just like a thousand other people), Starbound plays MUCH differently. Terraria's worlds are almost always identical to each other "every world has a dungeon, jungle, etc.) but Starbound not only has an infinite amount of worlds, but those planets have a HUGE amount of variety in them. Now, most people would argue "But 2 planets with the same biome are pretty much the same!". Almost every planet has not only sub-biomes, but towns comprised of various species, a large variety of dungeons, and even MORE stuff underground.
I'll try to keep this review short but here's my main warning; if you go in to this game trying to play it like Terraria, you will HATE it. Play it with creativity, curiosity, and especsially discovery in mind.

My rating: 6.5-7/10
I love starbound and recommend it, but maybe wait for a steam sale if you're unsure about paying full price, because it'll probably be hit and miss for some of you. People looking to build and create will have a pretty good time. For explorers, it’ll keep you entertained a few hours. People looking for a good story-driven game? Not so much.
Pros:
-	Great character customization! For pixelated characters, there's a decent amount of stuff to customize.
-	Diverse biomes! You'll definitely spend some time just taking in the scenery and collecting some specific blocks.
-	Diverse characters! Albeit a little trope-y, but design and personality-wise, they're pretty unique.
-	Diverse weapons, armor, monsters, farmables, and collectibles! Crossdressing is also permitted, which should be handy for some people.
-	Great soundtrack! The music is very atmospheric and changes depending on climate and time of day.
Cons:
-	Illogical placement of biomes. (Lush fields in eternal midnight planets with sub-zero temperatures/tundras on volcanic planets with searing hot climates. I don't think it used to be this way either, so I'm not sure where that came from.)
-	Some racial NPC villages don’t seem to strictly follow spawning rules despite what the game tells you, and some get damaged or destroyed by the planets they spawn in. (I had a floran village spawn on a volcanic planet and it started burning to the ground minutes later.)
-	Quests are VERY repetitive. (All fetch/escort quests with some combat.)
-	Subterranean structures and biomes are repetitive. (There are some rare subterranean biomes, but most of the time you see a lot of the same types of structures spawning underground.)
-	Forgettable story. (It's your classic "find 6 treasures and save the galaxy," which is fine, but there isn't a lot that makes it very memorable. There's a twist before the final mission, but it doesn't really influence the story much at all.)
-	Forgettable characters. (It's more wasted potential, really. The characters are really cool! But they hardly get any sort of development. You pick one up at the end of each of their story missions and then they're just 'there.' Two appear in combat once during the second last story mission, and then a couple cheer you on at the final boss, but that's about it really. Their quests aren't too memorable either.)
-	Novakids are completely disregarded from the story for some reason???
-	Unlocking story missions is a pain. (You need to find villages of different races and scan items there, but if the village has insufficient items to scan, you'll have to find another one to complete it.)
-	Food spoilage is hard to avoid early on, and is difficult to store. (Food doesn't stack, and fridges are difficult to craft early in the game.)
-	Several unique decorative items are unobtainable and break when hit. (Not necessarily hindering gameplay but it just feels like a missed opportunity for more decorative items.)
-	Ship pets and crew block access to interactive items when standing in front of them. (I had my pet fall asleep in front of the ship's controls. That was pretty frustrating.)
-	Ally AI is kind of problematic and needs work. (Running into lava/poison, no self-healing, doesn't try and avoid deadly confrontation if wounded.)
-	Bugs can cause HUGE problems for people playing survival or hardcore. (Randomly loses ability to move until you attack, as well as falling off the map into space and dying when teleporting back to the ship.)
This review is more from the perspective of an average buyer/gamer. I did grab this thing back during early access, but I haven't been actively involved in its progression over the years. (Binge played it at the start of early access, and then once more about two years ago.) This is also solely based on what I’ve experienced so there might be some content I won’t touch down on here. I’ve also tried to keep the review spoiler free.

One of the best games in the franchise, this kind of feels like an "Ultimate Mortal Kombat" release because there's just so much content.
It essentially rebuilds MK1/MK2/UMK3 into one new package, and the story mode reflects this as it essentially moves through each of these era's during the narrative. The main annoyance with story mode is the unskippable cutscenes, which on occassion can be very long, and you have to wait through them even if you just want to quit back to the main menu.
The challenge ladder in the game is great, it essentially just throws a whole bunch of unique combat scenarios at you, and throws in some "test your might challenges" mixed in as well. Finally the Krypt has a ton of unlockable content, and an area where you can view each character model, their alternate uniforms, and your stats with that character.
I probably can't say enough about just how complete of a game this feels like, really feels like good genuine fan service for fans of the original MK games, but at the same time still making sure its not stuck in the past either by bringing a new story mode structure and some inventive challenges.

Bastion is an amazing game, with amazing gameplay, a great narrator, beautiful visuals, and a soundtrack so good your ears will ♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's upgrade system is good, it has very fun weapons, and overall the gameplay just feels like it's exactly how it should be. The story is very good. It is simple but creative. How is the story told? Well, as you're playing the game, it is narrated from a future point of view. This not only answers questions you have while playing the game, but it leaves you unanswered with the biggest question; To whom is the story being told? Anyways, what is the story about? You wake up, with the world around you shattered and abandoned. As you move on, it soon just seems like you're trying to just fix everything after an apocalypse. Though while you dig deeper into the game, you find out what it's really about. It's about war, and the affect it has on not just people, but on the world. The game lets you make some huge decisions, big enough to make you think "Am I doing the right thing?". It's so well put together it made me question who I was and if I knew enough to make decisions that big in real life.
The game is one of the most original titles I have ever seen. Supergiant did everything right with it.

TL;DR Version:
The long awaited Fallout game for 2015... back then, people jumped on the hype-train left n' right without a thought. Now, people jump on the hate-train with the exact same reason. I was interested and excited, too... but the flaws shows itself in the trailers.
This game has TONS of cons that outweigh the pros... so let's start off with the bad points first.
Well, the first big disapointment is that this game has is that it uses an upgraded 'Creation' engine; which is actually an upgrade of another engine, the 'Gamebryo' engine. The older engine was used for Fallout 3, New Vegas and Oblivion while the 'Creation' engine is used for Skyrim and Fallout 4. Ancient engine used throughout 4 games for the span of 8+ years? The age really shows in the games; tons of bugs, crashes, glitches and bugs.
Another big problem the game has is the lack of dialogue options. Only four choices; (1) Positive, (2) Negative, (3) Sarcastic/Humor and (4) More Info. So in reality, you only have two real choices that makes any difference. Sometimes there's speech checks in place of one of the four choices. It seems very dumbed-down and very Mass Effect-like.
The voiced protaganist contributes to the problem above, as having a voiced protaganist limits the amount of dialogue the game can has, therefore cutting down on the more dialogue options this game can has.
And of course we have the infamous DLCs that were released within this game's lifespan. The Automatron was a nice lil' piece, Far Harbor seems to be heavily influenced from Fallout 3's Point Lookout; which is both good and bad. Nuka World is an odd one, as it seems very bland and empty.
"But you've missed some DLCs there", you might ask. Nope. I don't count the Workshop bunch as DLC... they should've been priced lower and seperate from the rest of the bunch as 'Workshop Settlement Packs'. They could've made more better DLCs if these WSPs didn't get in the way.
Oh, and who could forget the Season Pass? $30 before, then an increase to nearly double of it's original price? Yes, they gave people a chance to "buy it cheap" before the prices change, but it's still scummy.
And let's not forget the most recent disapointment: The Creation Club. Paid mods, a cheap cash-in. nothing else.
I might also add that the VR version of the game is poorly made. Save yourself the trouble by just sticking to PC or Console release of the game.
The Legendary enemies/items are a grindfest, as after you fight a hard♥♥♥♥♥Super Mutant or something and it drops some lousy metal armor. And it happens a lot. All RNG and no crafting option for it? Is it so hard to have Effect Crafting like in Skyrim?
Speaking of Crafting, the way it's designed is okay... but still pretty bad. One weapon, many types. Make it so that pistols are pistols, and rifles are rifles. This makes the total count of weapons in the game drop a lot, and it's even less than what New Vegas has.
Unique weapons are a joke, just like in Skyrim. A renamed item with a Legendary prefix that any other Legendary item can also have? Not good. Unique weapons should be like what Fallout New Vegas did. Yes, I know the game still has some truely unique weapons like the
, but it still doesn't justify the lack of creativity.
Too. many. RADIANT QUESTS. Y'all know the meme by now... I don't even need to reference it here.
Not a lot of side quests, too. Many revolve around settlement building; which contradicts what Todd says about them during the big reveal.
The gunplay in the game is a massive increase, being able to take cover and peeking out to shoot is a nice upgrade.
With the B-side of the crafting system aside, it's still quite good. Make scopes, silencers, you name it. It also ties in with the junk around the world, as there's no such thing as 'useless junk'. Everything has it's use, some might even be pricey and rare...
V.A.T.S is now not some OP God-like power that you can use with no side-effect, as now time slows down instead of being totally frozen in place... so you can receive damage. Criticals are now a 'build-up' kind of power instead of the RNG based versions of the older games.
So overall, it's a good FPS game with little RPG and TONS of Settlement mechanics. Still not a 'good Fallout' game, anyways. Only buy if you wanna play a post-apocalyptic loot n' shoot type of game with base-building elements.
With the recent practices by Bethesda, it should be a clear indicator of what future Fallout and The Elder Scrolls games might end up be, and it's sad that it's going down that road.

An excellent stealth based game with some pretty good A.I.  This game is all about being a thief and staying hidden.  If you're looking for fast paced action, this game is not for you.  The main focus is on the story.
Pros: The city is well crafted  with easy to recognize light and dark areas.  The clearly visible hiding spots are blended well into the environment making for some great atmosphere.  As you move around the world picking locks, extinguishing fires, and stealing valuables, the guards will notice anything out of place.  You really will feel that your actions have meaning in the world.  The stealth mechanics are almost unmatched.  But the best thing about this game is the story.  With excellent voice acting and plenty of cut scenes you will be immersed in the world.
Cons: Although the city is completely accessible, the game is a little linear.  As with most games the mechanics aren't perfect and you may find some funny quirks.  Nothing game breaking though.
Overall, a pretty amazing game for the time.  The stealth and guard A.I. are phenomenal, not to mention a great story to boot.

I've yet to finish this game and I still love it and would recommend it. At first, I thought it was just going to be a basic "do bunch of criminal activities while secretly a cop", but I was so wrong. There is a legitimate story here, and the intensity with which it builds surprised me greatly. In fact, after a major event close to halfway through (not going to spoil it, but you'll know it when you see it), I actually nearly shed tears. For the game to make me that invested in the characters and what happens to them is proof of how great it is. Wei Shen is a badass, but the game clearly pushes his character HARD, and it's amazing to see the difference in him as the story progresses and he's drawn further and further into not only the goings on within the Triads, but his mission as a cop as well.
I personally love that there's a HUGE RPG aspect to this as well. You have three different experience sections. Cop Experience which increases as you do cases for the police and drug busts, but also completing missions without any damage to people or property, Triad Experience which is given for kicking♥♥♥♥♥and being as violent as you can possibly be, and Face Experience which is gained through favors for various people around Hong Kong. I don't think there's any reward/penalty to working one over the other and leveling each allows you to pick new perks. Overall, it felt like the rewards for progression were quite valuable.
There's a lot to say, but obviously I'm not going to write a novel about it :P In short, you can level up, you can buy new clothes that also give passive bonuses for wearing sets (or just look whatever part you want), you can spiff up your apartments if you just need to blow some cash, there's stuff to collect to gain more money, increase your HP, or learn new moves as part of a side quest....basically it's filled to the brim with anything an RPG fan would want.
So yes....give a shot. It's an impressive game and one I've let go for too long.

There is many games within this genre that came to be, but many fail to make themselves special. Sleeping dogs is incredibly special.
The game has many strengths and weaknesses. Strengths include the emphasis on the melee combat, which almost always feels reliable and fantastic to watch. Weakkness would be the gun play in this game, especially some of the guns dlc has advertised like the assault rifle but you cannot take it anywhere with you without alerting authorities and cannot conceal it (sometimes it's best for video games to focus more on being a game than being a life simulator). There is a handful of bugs, but none that are so bad it ruins the experience. The atmosphere is great, the graphics carried its weight and should please anyone, very little is actually wrong with the game.
Its greatest strength would be the storyline. The story feels very professionally made. Without spoiling, the gist of it is you're a cop and you're after some really bad guys. They have you do this by using one of your friends as a network into this criminal world. Obviously, feelings and morals conflict. The set up is incredibly cliche, it's done all the time, but the rest of the plot is well done. In fact, even the parts that have been done a million times in movies or games, they written it in a way to where it didn't feel recycled. The writing made everything feel fresh, even the parts you probably have seen before.
This is a game worth picking up. It's strongest weakness that probably hurts the most for people like me is its lack of multiplayer, some form of coop would have been great. However, it's a game you play for the first couple of playthroughs and not again for a long time if ever. It's a great experience, one that I feel truely deserves full price, especially since now it includes the definitive edition and dlcs, you lucky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. One thing is for sure, this will be one of many games this decade that will age very well.

Lets say that Starbound is a cake. In it's early access stages, everyone was trying out the cake batter. "This is some damn good cake batter!" they said. "It just needs to be mixed more and sent into the oven." The Starbound dev team continued to mix the batter, determined to make it just the way fans wanted it. 2-3 years later, they remind everyone that the cake is still being made, and it's almost done. People have been waiting for this cake for years, and they are hungry. Starbound dev team takes the cake out of the oven, and says "We removed the eggs and sugar, we didn't want them in our cake. Also, forget the frosting, just eat it plain." Understandably, the people were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ "What the hell guys?! You promised us a good cake! We even tried out the batter and TOLD you to keep the cool stuff!"
If you don't get the analogy, the dev team basically removed what made people exicted about the game. Various worlds with plenty to do? Nah, we just made all of the different planets basically the same thing with a new tileset. You'll only find abandoned buildings and mine shafts. Cool NPC settlements and cities? No, those are only in space stations, and boring ones at that. A large and expansive single player mode? Instead, lets have a few fetch quests, and remove the race lore too, because who cares about interesting plot.
Now mods make the cake right. It's a rookie job for the most part, but they at least make the cake tasty.

I'm sorry, i gave this game a chance. I tried 17 hours of it and i've only had around 2 hours of fun.
It's boring, there's nothing there. I shouldn't say there's nothing there, i should say that everything in this game means nothing.
Adventuring - Nothing is there that you want or would need. You only need to adventure to find colonies where you left click on everything or get extremely boring and monotonous quests of sending you on a wild goose chase to get to the fun parts of the game which last around 1 hour each quest and there's 6 of them. So i've spent roughly 14 hours adventuring and i've only gotten 1 hour of actually fun content from it. Great game right?
Building - This game does give you one thing though, and that's cosemetics and blocks. Both of them are useless. Cosemetics don't add anything truly substantial to the game and the blocks are just useless. Lets put it this way, they give you an infinite number of worlds to "adventure" in. By that, i mean an infinite number of rocks in space that mean nothing to you after you leave them. Sure you can build on them but what does it matter? they're forcing you to fly from planet to planet anyways. You can't stay on one planet at all. So you must be able to build on something right? You need a base. Well they give you one for free that automatically expands itself. You can't expand it though and there's almost no room for any fun building to be done. You HAVE to build your crafting stations and storage in the ship, you literally cannot make anything cool or substantial in the small base that they give you. It's been 17 hours and i've only gotten one expansion to it.
Quests - The quests are mainly the only game you'll find. But the only fun quests are hard to find or they're the main story quests. Imagine WoW's quests... now take away every ounce of fun and effort from them and make the reward a dog turd. You made a starbound quest. They're short, boring, and do nothing but give you money to eventually buy a new weapon that's replaced by an item from the main story quest anyways. Now this "main story quest" is not only where you find your items but it's the only motivation for playing this game. Basically, they're quests where you get sent on a wild goose chase for colonies where you have to adventure around on planets, which gets boring really fast, and you pray to god that you didn't waste 10 mintues on another planet. Once you finally finish the first part of the main story quest, you get sent to a fun dungeon. The items were great, the dungeon was fun, the enemies were challenging but not impossible and it was something new. Then it ends after around 30 minutes to 1 hour. And if the story is correct, you do this 5 more times, and then fight the final boss.
TL;DR - The game is fun, if it allows itself to. There is fun in the game but it's hidden under hours and hours of monotonous, tedious, boring, lifeless, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ quests which give you nothing. You can adventure, but there's nothing gained form it. You can mine but there's nothing gained from it. You can do quests but they're boring. The only thing fun is the main story quest, but that can be boring also. I just can't recommend this game after taking 17 hours to have around 2 hours of decent content. It's just not good. It doesn't matter what game there is or what i missed, if i played and  did almost every aspect of the game for 17 hours and finished a sixth of the main quest, i should have gotten somewhere or had fun at some point. If i've missed something "fun" then tell me, I really want to enjoy this game, but it's a huge disappointment as of now.

First off, let me just mention that I loved Terraria back when it was released. A two-dimensional minecraft with tons more unique creatures and biomes, not to mention unique bosses for different sections of the world.
Now we see this beautiful casual gaming masterpiece we know as Starbound; much like Terraria, but on a much, MUCH larger scale. It may not have as many pre-designed creatures, and the procedurally generated ones may not be much to talk about either, but when combined with the variation of the different worlds' landscapes and scenery, procedurally generated or not, they fit in very nicely with the worlds around you. There are many more block types, most of which share a theme with other blocks. If put together correctly, you could even create a style completely different from that of the rest of the game. The bosses are okay. In a way, they feel like your average boss in Terraria; quite tough when you get to it, possibly even inspiring during your first time fighting it, but once you beat them once, it's like riding a bicycle.
And although the gameplay is solid, addictive, and most importantly FUN, I will admit that what really caught my attention when I started playing this game was the character customization, whether it be via the character creator, cosmetic items found in-game, or a combination of the two. And this leads in to another topic of discussion: roleplay. I'm quite into it, and believe me when I say that this game is bursting with potential in terms of roleplay. The game has a linear storyline with non-linear gameplay, allowing the player to complete the game at their own pace, or simply choose not to complete the game at all. With this in mind, the player may choose to complete the game in order to get it out of the way or simply not do anything and stop tracking Esther's quests if that furthers their concentration on whatever activities they may be pursuing, such as roleplay, building a colony, exploring, or any combination of those.
Now if you'll excuse me, I have an appointment to kick Big Ape's @$$ in about half an hour, so enjoy the game and its future updates. This game is definitely recommended by me and earns my seal of approval (which doesn't really mean much and is only meant to emphasise my fondness for this game)

Alright, to start off the review, there will be spoilers, my own opinions, and all that jazz. Another sidenote, I didn't actually beat the game, but my friend told me the ending and what you get and I've played enough to give this a solid review.
First things first, the gameplay.
While it did take things from other games that I liked, a lot for me stemming from Terraria, it still felt like a pretty original experience. The space element I really liked, uh, I liked the fact that you didn't have to have different tools to break blocks and other enviromental items. I mean, that's about it for the positive stuff, just because this game was so lack-luster. Seriously, if I were to make a game where the beta had so much great features then remove most of what the fun was, I would really contemplate my life and why I would even do that. There were mechs, specie weapons, real combat, and even more that they removed for no reason at all. That's probably what threw me off the most about this game, the lack of content. Other stuff about the gameplay is even if you choose Survival, it's still pretty hard, actually, not hard, straight up annoying. You would have to cook items and eat them in order to live, which for me, is pretty ridiculous, since you would probably have to worry about that more than anything else, you would drop your items that may have taken a very long and tedious time to even recieve, and on top of all of it, on top of all the stuff I already ranted about, the mode itself didn't do anything to the game really, but to me emotionally. I swear, I have never been more anxious to grab my 800 copper and silver that took literal hours to get, and in the end, wouldn't even get them because I would KEEP DYING.
Next up, story.
It sucked. Period. I saw this in one review, but I might as well repeat it. All you do is talk to an old woman, go to a bunch of planets, where you have to waste resources to get to, suffer dying, dying, and more dying, until you find a village, in which you scan stupid posters and furniture, go back to the woman, do some cooky dungeon then beat either a really easy boss or a really hard boss, and in turn, do the same thing like 6 more times. Seriously, and in the end, you get 25,000 pixels, which I will say is the only good thing, some upgrade modules and manipulator modules, which I might add, won't do anything, and a Thank-You Card. A Thank-You Card. No legendary weapon that destroys planets, no clothing or ship additive that makes the game more fun, a flipping Thank-You Card. How lousey is that, to finish a, might I mind you, A SANDBOX GAME, AND NOT GET ANYTHING TO ENHANCE THE EXPERIENCE. Overall, it sucked.
Finally, everything else.
Since I've already expressed how I felt, it also sucked too. Weapons, don't really enhance anything, since there's a very small select few that are actually good, clothing and armor, which again, do nothing to benefit, and your crew mates and companions don't really even help that much. Seriously, it was really useless in the end.
Final Review: 3.5/10
