This is an Early access review of course; and it should be noted that the review is also being written only about a week since the game was initially released upon STEAM so I've played the "bare bones" version so far with only a few updates or content added.  Will have a "TL;DR" at the end for anyone that wants to see my underlying thoughts.
Stranded Deep is another classic survival game, but this time it takes place upon the open ocean with small islands scattered about with the supplies you need to survive.  You start off on a plane and it crashes, leaving you afloat in a life raft.  This is where the game currently starts and requires you to go from island to island to gather materials needed to survive and build.
Now before anyone pushes aside the game as just "another survival game", there are a few things that are unique to the game however that I personally quite enjoy that I want to make note off.  First off is the crafting system.  As with many other survival games you are able to craft and make new things to help you survive longer.  Most of the time, most games have a UI or type of tab pull up that you simply throw your supplies onto, and then craft.  Stranded deep does it differently; you have to actually pull your items out of your inventory, place them on the ground, group them with whatever other "ingredients" you need for the crafting recipe, and then craft it that way.  No longer do you simply craft a camp fire and have it instantly placed in your inventory for placing; no, you gather the sticks, throw them down into a pile, then craft it right there in front of you where it will then immediatly be placed.  It's rather a pleasent change from the usual crafting schemes that most survival games have.  Coupled with this is cooking; you don't just use a user interface to throw a fish on the fire, have it cooked, then pick it back up from said UI.  No, in this game you have to hold the fish over the fire and actually wait.  It won't cook immediatly; it will sizzle, smoke, and take a while before it will finally be cooked.  Now, you can either hold it over it manually, or you can craft a type of rotissery, but either way, its nothing simple like "fish + fire = instant dinner in UI".
Second thing that is largely unique to the game is the exploration factor.  At the surface, yes, going from simple island to simple island doesn't seem very exciting.  But in this game there are many a boat that has been wrecked in the ocean depths below you, holding tools, treasures, and weapons that you need to go diving down into to loot.  The underwater world is beautiful, and often (if you have a good enough graphics card/the sea bed is shallow enough) you can catch glimpses of coral formations and fish swimming about underneath your raft as you move around the ocean or as you are on a beach.  Some areas may be very shallow, others much deeper.  And of course, while you do this, you have to worry about predators; sharks like to pop up and go after you for a quick snack as you treasure hunt, or even as you are on the beach.  They are tough predators to take down and they like to tease you a bit it seems with they way they act.
Lastly the world is rather beautiful.  For an early access game, the environment is great and I love seeing the sun rise and fall because of the great graphics engine and how beautiful it can be.  Fog can roll in, heavy rain can pound down on you at any moment; the environment is great and very beautiful.  And this is coming from a guy that doesn't have the best graphics available either.  I can only imagine how great it looks with the proper system and build.
Crafting itself is fun; nothing too unique to be honest here.  You can make tools, build certain items for a small house or base, etc.  The real world crafting system is thrown in here too; you have to place sticks onto a foundation for instance to be able to craft supports that will allow for roofs or walls.  You can make a bed to sleep through the night, a spear for fishing, axes for cutting down wood/keeping away sharks etc.  Combine this with you have to figure out the recipies/being able to further break down items (for instance break a rock in two and make rock shards which are necessary for the spear) and you can spend a good amount of time trying to figure it all out.
Now, sadly, to the Negatives.
First and foremost, the game IS Early Access.  I PERSONALLY (this is my opinion) have lost faith in Early access games.  Too many here on STEAM start off strong, then die away slowly till they are no longer updated and taken care of.  I'm not saying this will happen to this game, but its always a possibility.  Again, the game has only come out recently, so the developers have not had time to post up any time maps, guides, or similar tools on Steam to help show whats coming up, their development, etc.  Its possible they have a website that does this, but I have yet to look myself for such.  Combine this with the fact that as this is the initial early access release, and after a few hours of gameplay, you will have largely done most of what you can at the moment.  Not that it isn't fun, but until updates come in and more content is added, don't expect a huge world full of possibilities just yet.
As said above, while crafting is fun, it is limited.  So far, from what I have found, there are a good amount of recipies but stop rather short of what I'd personally like to see.  You can craft everything thus far, but again, you'll be done in a while after you find the required materials.
The islands are FAR FAR away from each other.  I know that Islands are not going to be uber close to one another, but I mean they are FAR.  Now, this may have been a developer's choice to do such, but it can get rather long and tedious of just having to row for such a long time from one island, clean it of the supplies it has (which, is a good amount but nothing huge that allows you to spend a good day in the world on the island) and then have to go to the next.  This is also coupled with that most islands are the same with one another; some are actual copies, some are different, but most are all teh same size and have the same features except for maybe a few wrecks here and there that are in the ocean close to it.
Game is currently buggy; I've seen rafts dissapear out from under you leaving you in open water randomly at times.  Sharks behavior, while good at times, seems slightly sporadic as well, and the spawn rate is high.  Items can glitch at times through floors if you leave them in a safe place for instance, and at times I've found loot that I couldn't carry, but when I came back, the loot mysteriously dissapeared.  I can only assume a shark swam off with the flashlight for who knows what...
TL;DR/ The bottom Line
I'm still playing the game, still working at it.  Bottom line, I personally enjoy it.  It's a survival game yes, but its different then most out then with the concept and I think with enough hard work it can become quite a gem.  Can I say buy it now at it's current state?  That is up to you.  Its fun and will pass the time for a while.  But if you are wanting a more developed game or one with more options/more features added in for the support of the game, I'd suggest you follow the game and wait till more has been applied to it and it has been patched/added too.

Another great entry in the Fallout series. The whole thing feels like an improvement over Fallout 3 and New Vegas. The amount of content is absurd, the story is stellar as always, and there's always something to do. I have a few complaints however. First off, the karma system is gone. I don't know who was the genius that removed it, but it disappointed me a bit. It's not even that hard to implement. Next complaint; there's technical issues abound and crashing at times, and some poor optimization. Third and final point; the story is slightly more linear than 3 and New Vegas. While I don't necessarily count that as a bad thing, as Fallout 2 was pretty linear and was still great, it eliminates some potential opportunities that can be found in 3 and NV.
Overall, while having some flaws, and retaining a few flaws from the previous games, Fallout 4, in my opinion, is the best Fallout game since New Vegas. I highly recommend it to anyone who's a fan of the series. 9/10.

Sleeping Dogs is a very enjoyable GTA-style game set in a well detailed Hong Kong. The story is engaging and has great pacing, with an interesting supporting cast and several funny moments there is a lot to love about the story in Sleeping Dogs. The main attraction of the game is the great kung-fu style hand-to-hand combat of which there is thankfully plenty, the gunplay is average and the driving is pretty good. The graphics though now a little outdated still looks quite nice particularly at night, there is some great animation work in the combat but facial animations are a little weak. Overall an easy recommendation if you like open-world style games.
In Sleeping Dogs you play was Wei Shen an undercover officer with the Hong Kong police who is infiltrating the Sun On Yee triad. The supporting cast is interesting, if a little two dimensional. The overall plot is well developed and gripping although it does leave some mysteries especially in regards to the secondary characters and their motives. The main attraction of the story is the unique and often unexplored setting, Hong Kong.
The gameplay of Sleeping Dogs is incredibly fun. The highlight here is definitely the kung-fu style melee system, despite its simplicity the feeling of the hits and the slow-motion moments are great. The other important part of the melee system is the environmental kills, which are canned moves that instantly kill enemies, it's a very important part of the melee system though it does get a little repetitive seeing the same animations throughout the game.
The other part of combat is the gunplay, which is not really present in the first quarter of the game though really comes into play later on. The gunplay is probably the weakest part of Sleeping Dogs and the guns all feel quite similar and quite inaccurate, with the only redeeming feature being the bullet time slow-mo which is activated when jumping over cover and other key moments in the combat.
The driving mechanics are sound. Cars feel quite heavy to drive which is good for larger vehicles like vans or sedans though unfortunately even high end sports cars have a weak turning circle at high and low speed. Despite this the races in the game (of which there are many) are for the most part very enjoyable and using the handbrake to do a sharp turn is fun. You can also ram other vehicles by using a button and direction, which feels quite odd at first though the effects are very enjoyable because the impact feels very strong. The motorbikes were the most enjoyable and what I would recommend you use mostly.
There is also several minigames such as karaoke, which plays as you might expect. There is mahjong poker which I played a bit of, unfortunately it is almost 100% luck but it's fun enough for little minigame. There is also cockfighting though I didn't do any of that.
The graphics are pretty good as well. Considering the game is not really new it does look quite nice especially if it is raining because the reflections of the puddles on the road is really nice. The characters look standard and facial animations are average. The animations during the hand-to-hand combat is very good, though when using a melee weapon they become noticeably stiffer. Hong Kong is beautiful at night with the bright neon signs and layout, it also provides several diverse suburbs from the high-end CBD to the coastal slums and factories.
The music is one of the best parts of the overall presentation with GTA-esque radio stations, my favourites were the Chinese club/rap music, the classical station and the electronic station though the other stations also have a great variety of tracks and there should be something here for everyone. The only downside to the radio stations was that there is not really that many tracks per station, probably only ~6 so get used to hearing the same music regularly, it would've been nice to have custom radio stations with our own music. There is also music during certain moments outside of the radio stations and for the most part these are good background pieces.

Sure, there may be some glitches here and there, like teleporting back to your ship for no apparent reason, but all games have some glitches. The game honestly went through development hell, and, it seemed like for a while, it would never be released from beta.
A great way to sum up a majority of Starbound is variety. There is a variety of enemies, environments, and just things to do in those environments. Well, or at least there is a lot of visual variety. On the more technical scale, there are quite a few different types of enemies, yes, but many environments feel very similar overall.
The combat offers a decent amount of weapons, as well, and works as well as it would be hoped for to. There are quite a few enemies with differing movement and techniques, making this one of the better areas of the game when it comes to having actual technical, and not just visual, variety.
Lastly, I have to admit the moving and platforming seems decent at first, however, once it's time for fine movements, it's incredibly frustrating. Your character automatically accelerates to full speed with only a tap of the A or D key, which can send them hurling to their doom off of a cliff or into a trap before you even register what you just did wrong. I think the problem could be fairly easily fixed, as all the devs would have to do would be add starting acceleration, however, alas, I am still accidentally going bungee jumping. Without the bungee.
The game may not be perfect in areas such as when it starts feeling repetitive after a while, and may have moments of instability and frustration, however, I overall found it enjoyable and would recommend at least a trial of this weird little indie game to those who just want to explore some environments and maybe do a little building, at least if it can be found on sale.

The ninth entry in the well-known fighting franchise, Mortal Kombat (or MK9 for short) serves as a reboot to the franchise’s story following the events of it’s predecessor, Mortal Kombat Armageddon. With that said, all of the playable characters (minus Cyber Smoke) from the first 3 games of the franchise are in attendance for this game.
Any Mortal Kombat game can make an excellent game to play with friends, but what makes MK9 great is the content it provides for those who wants to play the game alone.
The game offers a story mode and a Challenge Tower, a mode in which you must best at least 300 trials with predetermined fighters. As well, the game has the familiar single or tag-team arcade modes.
The controls in this game feel at times very precise. When you need to pull off a high combo, where the number of inputs is more than 4, the amount of time to make sure the input is registered gets smaller & smaller.
But that’s not where my frustration is really at, rather, it’s the Enhanced moves. Enhanced moves can increase the number of attacks and the amount of damage done from that fighter’s move set. Problem here is that the timing to initiate them is very small.
Personal Note: This could also be a case where there’s actually nothing wrong with the controls, rather my controller not working well for this game.
When it comes to playing online, there’s not a lot of good to talk about. Whether it’s the lag from the servers or the consistent connection issues, the online matchmaking for MK9 is atrocious… or was atrocious.
The only reason for the “was” is that I haven’t been able to test to see if the servers are still running or not. Last time I played the game, there was no one in the online lobby & with the game’s successor, Mortal Kombat X, being released last year, it’s possible that the servers are shut down.
MK9 is a fantastic game and an excellent choice for newcomers looking to get into the fighting genre. Just a notice that the online multi-player might not be working anymore for those who would be looking to play this for competitive purposes.

Wave of Darkness is an isometric action RPG title set in a common phantasy world with elves, undead and magic.
Absolutely unique story: Waves of monsters suddenly envade the land and people are in desperate search of a hero. You never had such story before yet, right? The gameplay lasted about an hour until I decided to uninstall. You run around almost aimlessly since the quests only provide you local tasks and no big picture. Once you are done with the quest it just disappears from the log and you dont even know who to talk to to finish the quest. The ingame systems are clunky and require a lot of time and patience just to get used to.
The combat I had for the first hour of the game consisted of holding the right mouse button down when you want to hit an enemy. Thats it. I would like to write more but there simply isnt.
The graphic is insanely bad for a 2015 title. Some games from 90s look better and more detailed than Wave of Darkness. The interface is clunky, loaded with tons of icons and the inventory management is one of the worst in an RPG game. Howering over a mouse makes your screen get covered in information about that item, however you dont find the needed or important information quick enough.
The progress I made in the first hour so far was to run around finishing the few quests I receive talking to random NPCs standing around and killing some monsters. I was tasked with warning the king and what not but did not really feel inclined to do so. The bad optimization and crashes did not really speed up my progress.
The audio was so far the only positive thing about the game. The smoothing music in the background made me last longer with this game while the battle sounds were not too disturbing or clunky as the rest of the game.
There are not many games that I could not stick through, especially being RPGs or action games. Sadly, Wave of Darkness is one of them, so after playing a bit more than an hour it felt like an absolute waste of time to even try continueing in this game. I cant recommend Wave of Darkness to anyone, even hardcore RPG and oldschool action game fans should avoice it.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

-	Diverse characters! Albeit a little trope-y, but design and personality-wise, they're pretty unique.
-	Diverse weapons, armor, monsters, farmables, and collectibles! Crossdressing is also permitted, which should be handy for some people.
-	Great soundtrack! The music is very atmospheric and changes depending on climate and time of day.
Cons:
-	Illogical placement of biomes. (Lush fields in eternal midnight planets with sub-zero temperatures/tundras on volcanic planets with searing hot climates. I don't think it used to be this way either, so I'm not sure where that came from.)
-	Some racial NPC villages don’t seem to strictly follow spawning rules despite what the game tells you, and some get damaged or destroyed by the planets they spawn in. (I had a floran village spawn on a volcanic planet and it started burning to the ground minutes later.)
-	Quests are VERY repetitive. (All fetch/escort quests with some combat.)
-	Subterranean structures and biomes are repetitive. (There are some rare subterranean biomes, but most of the time you see a lot of the same types of structures spawning underground.)
-	Forgettable story. (It's your classic "find 6 treasures and save the galaxy," which is fine, but there isn't a lot that makes it very memorable. There's a twist before the final mission, but it doesn't really influence the story much at all.)
-	Forgettable characters. (It's more wasted potential, really. The characters are really cool! But they hardly get any sort of development. You pick one up at the end of each of their story missions and then they're just 'there.' Two appear in combat once during the second last story mission, and then a couple cheer you on at the final boss, but that's about it really. Their quests aren't too memorable either.)
-	Novakids are completely disregarded from the story for some reason???
-	Unlocking story missions is a pain. (You need to find villages of different races and scan items there, but if the village has insufficient items to scan, you'll have to find another one to complete it.)
-	Food spoilage is hard to avoid early on, and is difficult to store. (Food doesn't stack, and fridges are difficult to craft early in the game.)
-	Several unique decorative items are unobtainable and break when hit. (Not necessarily hindering gameplay but it just feels like a missed opportunity for more decorative items.)
-	Ship pets and crew block access to interactive items when standing in front of them. (I had my pet fall asleep in front of the ship's controls. That was pretty frustrating.)
-	Ally AI is kind of problematic and needs work. (Running into lava/poison, no self-healing, doesn't try and avoid deadly confrontation if wounded.)
-	Bugs can cause HUGE problems for people playing survival or hardcore. (Randomly loses ability to move until you attack, as well as falling off the map into space and dying when teleporting back to the ship.)
This review is more from the perspective of an average buyer/gamer. I did grab this thing back during early access, but I haven't been actively involved in its progression over the years. (Binge played it at the start of early access, and then once more about two years ago.) This is also solely based on what I’ve experienced so there might be some content I won’t touch down on here. I’ve also tried to keep the review spoiler free.

I'm more of a 'maybe' than a whole-hearted recommend, but it's not nearly as bad as everyone makes it out to be.  I rather enjoyed my time with the game, but ultimately stopped playing because of the glitches.  There's a good game trapped in here.  If it was finished properly it could even be a great game.  As is, it's interesting with hints of greatness mixed in a bag of random pain.
Unlike what others have said, this honestly has very little in common with Diablo, Gothic, or other RPGs.  It's definitely a retro, no-hand-holding RPG, but it quite simply doesn't have the depth the other big names do.
Yes, there are significant issues.  The game plays like an unfinished beta:
- certain mobs glitch
- the tutorial is unclear
- the camera is godawful and needs constant handholding
- locks are totally unused (after the tutorial), but you still find keys and runes everywhere
- the combat system is rudimentary (no skills, just stats and spells)
- performance is pretty bad
- achievements are a mess
- itemization is bland
- terrain can sometimes hang you up and you have not option but to reload
- the UI could really use some work.
- my character would get stuck running and only a full restart would fix it (this ultimately caused me to quit playing because it was way too annoying and frequent)
If you can ignore all that, the base game is completely playable and relatively fun.
+ The world is very large and there's lots to explore, with secret stashes hidden about liberally.
+ The spell system is unique.
+ Monster visual design is excellent.
+ The quests and world are interesting, if a bit barebones.
+ The voice acting is surprisingly good for such a low-budget game.
+ Music is quite good.
Unfortunately, it seems the dev team is no longer working on the project, and they have a shady past of 'updating' their games, so it seems this game will remain in the current unfinished state.  As such, I can only recommend this if you're able to look past the large number of negatives and see the good parts forged by an indie developer with some unique vision.  There's fun to be had, but, honestly, you're probably better off with other big name games.  5/10 ... without the bugs, would be 7/10.

Wave of Darkness is a hack n' slash action RPG similar to the Diablo series. There is lots of loot, enemies, and exploration.  You can craft your own spells with the runes you find. There is also a simple harvest and crafting system where you have to find recipes and ingredients.
At first, the controls were a little tricky, but after I remapped the keys and sped up the mouse, it became much more manageable. The game gives virtually no guidance after the short tutorial, leaving exploration and discovery entirely to you. This can be very fun, but at the same time can often leave the players with a feeling of confusion about what they're even doing in this world.
I love the openness of the game. You can go virtually anywhere so long as you find a way there and are able to survive. After discovering spells, I was leaving town when I saw a broken bridge and some interesting enemies across the river. You will begin to drown in deep water, so I found the narrowest part of the river I could and ran through the river. I emerged on the other side almost dead from drowning when I was attacked by a skeleton. I quickly blasted it with a fire spell, and it went down. I allowed myself to rest before slowly heading forth. The creatures here were 15+ levels above me, so I had to be sure to destroy them with spells before they reached me. Eventually, I came to some sort of shrine where I found a powerful ring which I sold for 1000 gold (at this point, selling an item for 1 gold was a big deal).
Not every location is loaded with treasure, which is nice. I found a frozen grove with wolves and some sort of ice creature. I searched the entire area, and I don’t believe I found any loot. So while most of the time loot seems a little too easy to come by, this is not always the case.
Combat is fairly simplistic. Target the creature and get close enough to swing your weapon. Spells are very powerful; I found myself fighting monsters 20+ levels above me using spells; creatures just a couple levels above me were giving me trouble with melee. It is fun to craft your own spells, though you may quickly find your packs getting overloaded with runes! These spells gain levels with use, and the only limit to how many you can create is the number of runes you possess and how much backpack space is remaining (each spell takes a backpack slot).
While loot is plentiful, after 9 hours of playing, I have only found one or two items that are better than what I started with. This is not necessarily bad; I like the idea that more powerful items are rare. After all, how many fantasy books have you read where the protagonist changes his weapon every other battle?
The crafting system is somewhat frustrating. There appear to be hundreds of recipes, but so far I have only found the ingredients to make a few of them, and most of the time the item is useless to me. I had to start selling a lot of the recipes and crafting components as my packs are getting full, even with over 400 slots! However, I was able to craft a weapon that is better than what I was using.
Speaking of packs, you can eventually get a lot of backpack space. There are 15 pack “types”, each of which can be upgraded to 70 slots (for a total of 1050 slots).
There are some odd visual bugs. Sometimes, after killing an enemy with a spell, the enemy remains standing in place as though I were casting a taxidermy spell. Even when the bodies fall, if they were in the middle of an action when the spell hit, they would fall a few moments later. Skeletons all seem to be female since they let out a feminine scream when they die. It would be nice to be able to jump or climb since I have gotten stuck on ledges and had to reload. However, I have yet to find anything that would break the game or ruin my enjoyment of it.
Overall I would say the game is fun if redundant. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes hack ‘n slash action with strong character development.

Art and Story- 11/10
The art is amazingly beautiful, the storytelling is immersive, the combat system is nostalgic while still being effective even amoung all the plethora of systems out there, and did I mention the art yet?  Because... woah!  Hand-drawn with pen and pencil on physical paper, rather than digital, which while digital is not inferior, creates an amazing nostalgic effect.  Really, overall, this game is beautifully done to create a wonderful sense of nostalgia while not skimping on the story or incorporating new ideas.  And the music is so well done, too!  I just can't say enough about how beautifully this game has been made.
Choices- 9/10
None of the choices felt very heavy or intimidating to me, though I've only played through Ylianne's story so far, and only once at that.  In fact, I probably couldn't enumerate the points where I did have to make a choice if I needed to because I can't remember many of them, let along any of them being very important.  Additionally, I haven't had the courage to play through the game a second time, so I'm not sure of it's replayability factor.
Finishing Feels- 10/10
Honestly, it did feel a little short, but I had played through the first bit a while back on a different account.  However, part of that feeling of it not being long enough is simply because the complete storyline is in 3 parts.  This is just the first portion of the characters' lives, and the vision for the whole storyline is absolutely inspiring.  When I got to the end of this part, I couldn't believe it was over and so desperately craved more.  Can't wait for the sequel to officially release!
**Note:  I spent a large amount of time playing this game in offline mode, so I do have a decent number of hours logged, more than steam says I do.

Honestly, not a terrible game by any means, but suffers from several issues. Graphics and art in general is pretty good, even though there's not much variety of enemies/places. Music is pretty solid, but again not much of it. Story is pretty poorly written but the setting is solid so it could have been better, the interesting parts only start in the last 15mins of the game. I found characters to be particularily unlikeable, while the royalty characters tend to be pretty common in this type of game, they're usually balanced by having different point of views. Only Yliane provides a different point of view in this game out of the 6 characters, and her point of view is cliché and always the contrary of everyone else so it becomes dull also.
The game suffers from a few bugs such as NPCs twitching when patrolling as well as some technical issues like the lack of proper resolution or keyboard+mouse support(can't click on most stuff, have to use up/down on keyboard to move through everything, can't Esc out of stuff but instead have to use the Cancel button etc, so definitely play this with a pad, not with a keyboard).
Difficulty felt very uneven, with most of the game being easy, but tedious(combat against trash mobs takes about as long as boss fights when you get the large groups, but pose no real threat if you use a proper setup... nor do the bosses really). However here and there some spikes in difficulty, like the last boss which proved to be unkillable with the particular set of chars/skills I had, I had to reload a save and change my skill build to kill him(I don't mean I was dying, I meant it was a permanent standoff, with the boss simply healing for more than I could damage him and with no way to prevent it because his heal has low enough cost that draining him of stamina wasn't enough). On the other hand I feel if I hadn't played the setup I had(tank+healer+DPS), the game would have been a lot harder. Monsters seem to hit for stupidly high damage with very little ways to prevent it due to how restricted you are in your skill usage by the basic combat mechanics, so having someone who taunts and having someone to heal that character felt almost necessary.
Customization felt minimal, there's very little gear to use and most of it is very standard stuff so no choice there, there's skills and passives, but a lot were redundant or weren't balanced properly when considering their cost versus their effects. I feel most characters only had very few swaps to be used, and most of it was fairly obvious, they were mostly stuck into their primary role. Which isn't necessarily bad, but there just wasn't much to do in these. You give your healer a single target heal, an aoe heal, a way to remove debuffs and that leaves one skill only. And obviously the passives will be stuff that increase healing or similar, so no real choice there. Every characters felt built like that.
I'd say the most negative aspect is it's basically not a full game, it's like the first act of a game. The price is relatively low so it's not so bad, but don't expect a great rpg, this is just the opening act, a teaser, and not a particularily appealing one. This is especially blatant when you have to make certain choices during the story that have absolutely 0 impact on this game's story. I assume they'll matter in the next game maybe, but that feels pretty bad.

Great Roguelike Turn-Based Squad Game, if a bit grindy at medium and higher difficulties. Three difficulty levels, and veteran's (middle difficulty) is definitely misleading - it is very hard (or the difficulty of the missions and enemies themselves and enemy scaling are poorly detailed in game, depending on how you look at it). And this is coming from some who likes X-Com 2's difficulty, and enjoys other roguelikes like toee.
After putting in 60 hours, I think I've figured out Veteran Ironman enough to get to day 100 with level 8+ characters and maybe 3 deaths of non-level 1 characters. It's grindy as it seems the best tactic is killing enemies weaker than you because it is very expensive to lose great characters.
That being said, I really like the equipment, stat, and perk system as it is very deep. Axes, Cleavers, Flails, Swords, Maces, Daggers, Spears, and Polearms, as well as other weapons, all represented. Each weapon has 2 attacks - a basic attack with a small secondary effect, and a special attack. Characters level from 1 to 11 and each level gain a perk, which each level unlocking 6 new pickable perks. There are unique items, but very rare - have only seen one that a merchant had.
Planning out your team, their equipment, their stat boosts, their perks, and their formation are very important at medium/veteran difficulty. At this point I've probably done 12-15 veteran ironman runs, although it's hard to actually lose, it's easy to get into that downward spiral point.
The secret seems to be focusing on buying your troops great armor first and great weapons or great recruits a distant second, focusing on survivable and hit chance, and making sure they gain experience and not die. It actually was very satisfying to finally come upon this, as before this it was frequent that one battle could instant wipe you.
All in all, a good game that scratches that TBS Squad Combat itch, with good sound effects.

How could I possibly write a review after playing the game only for one hour? Simple: I've beaten the singleplayer portion of the game. The game itself is fun and it would be a blast if it only had more singleplayer enemies and missions.
It's supposed to be a multiplayer title but did they really think the game will be a commercial success selling hundreds of thousands of copies? Did they expect hundreds of people playing this title 24/7?
There's no story. You play against four enemies. The first enemy has four fairly easy tutorial missions. The second and third enemies only have two missions and the third enemy has 3 missions. It took me exactly 60 minutes to play through the game. It's possible to get lucky and finish a mission in one turn. Chances are that your playthrough won't be even one full hour.
How does it play? Each match starts with an empty "board". You're given your fleet: fighters, carriers etc. Each unit has a certain amount of hitpoints and can move a certain amount of tiles. You start the match by placing your units on the "board" as you see fit and the game starts. You make the first move. The goal of the game is not to destroy the entire fleet the enemy has. You only have to destroy the main ship...The queen...The general of whatever you'd like to call it. It only has one hitpoint so everything can destroy it. The enemy can also win the match by simply destroying your "queen" without even touching the rest of your fleet. It makes for a fun turn-based strategy game.
Plays just like the singleplayer campaign but against real people. Now the cool thing is that the matches keep going even after you've closed the game.
You make your turn, close the game, go to work, run the game, see what the enemy did and make your next turn. All you got to do now is wait for the enemy to return and make his/her turn.
The matches can be played live as well but it's cool to have such a feature. However the game doesn't have a steady amount of players. This issue is kind of fixed by allowing you to exit the game and return to your match later on but this also means that one single match could take forever and you end up playing the game in short 2-5 minute sessions. These short sessions make you ask the question: Was it worth the money?

Kingdom Rush is a tower defense game with heroes (which you do not level or equip) and a skill tree of sorts.There are many types of monsters, and four different towers, each of which can be upgraded to do different things. Your strategy is completely up to you, though there are some challenges that restrict you to certain types of towers.
Yes. I'm probably a little less experienced in Tower Defense games than most, but I have mostly enjoyed my time playing Kingdom Rush. There is a lot more strategy involved than you would expect (and probably more than I have figured out yet), but I will say that, even on the "Casual" setting, you can't just plop down towers and let it go. You do have to think.
It can start to feel monotonous, which I suppose is normal for a tower defense game with this much content. It's a game that you have to know when to put up and play something else. I also wish there was something to do with those stars that you get beyond the initial skill tree. Although there are quite a few end game maps, you very quickly fill the skill tree up to max.
People new to the tower defense genre, as well as veterans who have somehow not played this version of Kingdom Rush, could all enjoy this game. It has a good enough tutorial that it doesn't just expect you to know the genre, yet it is completely skippable for the veterans, and it is interesting enough to keep skilled players engaged.
For the amount of polish and content, the $10 asking price is more than fair. Also consider that this game bundles very often, so keep an eye out for bundles with this included if you want to get a really good deal. I know there is a free, web-based version, but there is more content here, and we all know how to get free games anyway, don't we? This one is worth paying for.
It's very, very well balanced. You will fail a mission because you set things up incorrectly, then change your setup and win easily the next, just because you chose the right towers and tower upgrades the second time around.
The graphics are okay. This game started as a browser game, years ago, and it shows, but that's okay. The graphics aren't bad enough to distract from playability. It is not graphically intensive. You can probably play this game on an abacus.
Very few tracks for regular play, one track for the rare boss. Gets boring very fast. BYO playlist.
Most of the sound bytes are silly pop-culture gaming references. Some are pretty funny, and worth hearing at least once. Beyond that, very repetitive, and the mage tower sound is irritatingly shrill.
The gameplay is excellent. Very well balanced and easy to pick up, but not easy to master, yet rarely does it feel impossible. Just like a good strategy game should feel.
The game feels more than finished, and that's because it is. The developers have gone back and added content to the already finished game. The only stability issue that I encountered is that, when I alt-tab out when it is in full screen, it will sometimes freeze. So I leave it in windowed mode. No big deal.
This game already has a sequel out (Kingdom Rush: Frontiers), which is just as highly rated. This game last received a content patch in 2014, but it did get Steam Cloud support in 2016, so although I doubt there will be anything like content updates or DLC, I'm sure the developers will patch it to keep it stable going forward. In 2017, this game is currently 3 years old, and looks older, but it's not something that I really care about when playing a tower defense game.
Completed in 37.5 hours with all achievements.
Personally, I can't see myself wanting to replay this game once I'm finished, but that's only because Frontiers exists, and because so many other tower defense games are out there waiting to be played, should I need them. As for this game, nothing would change, so I don't see it as replayable. (Edit: I did end up getting all of the achievements. That's a rarity for me - I'm not usually a completionist.)
Overall, I'd give this game an 8/10. A very strong recommendation.

The game honestly went through development hell, and, it seemed like for a while, it would never be released from beta.
A great way to sum up a majority of Starbound is variety. There is a variety of enemies, environments, and just things to do in those environments. Well, or at least there is a lot of visual variety. On the more technical scale, there are quite a few different types of enemies, yes, but many environments feel very similar overall.
The combat offers a decent amount of weapons, as well, and works as well as it would be hoped for to. There are quite a few enemies with differing movement and techniques, making this one of the better areas of the game when it comes to having actual technical, and not just visual, variety.
Lastly, I have to admit the moving and platforming seems decent at first, however, once it's time for fine movements, it's incredibly frustrating. Your character automatically accelerates to full speed with only a tap of the A or D key, which can send them hurling to their doom off of a cliff or into a trap before you even register what you just did wrong. I think the problem could be fairly easily fixed, as all the devs would have to do would be add starting acceleration, however, alas, I am still accidentally going bungee jumping. Without the bungee.
The game may not be perfect in areas such as when it starts feeling repetitive after a while, and may have moments of instability and frustration, however, I overall found it enjoyable and would recommend at least a trial of this weird little indie game to those who just want to explore some environments and maybe do a little building, at least if it can be found on sale.

I've followed the development of this game since alpha, and have played the game since day 1 of Early Access. Terraria's worlds are almost always identical to each other "every world has a dungeon, jungle, etc.) but Starbound not only has an infinite amount of worlds, but those planets have a HUGE amount of variety in them. Now, most people would argue "But 2 planets with the same biome are pretty much the same!". Almost every planet has not only sub-biomes, but towns comprised of various species, a large variety of dungeons, and even MORE stuff underground.

The game features a small campaign full of unbalanced missions (the AI is given powerful ships in greater quantities), more fair skirmishes against the AI, and asynchronous online multiplayer. Doomstar incorporates the basic game rules of the classic board game Stratego (simple attack ratings, unknown ship attributes until attacked, highest ship number wins) with a reduced number of units for faster gameplay. The goal is to destroy the enemy command ship with any vessel. Mines don’t  move but destroy everything except light fighters and carriers. Fighters can move as many spaces as they want across the board. Battle cruisers and dreadnoughts are the most powerful units on the board. Black holes allow units to move multiple spaces in a single turn, and two set of fighters can attack the same enemy in the same turn. The AI is decent enough at the game to provide a good challenge, although online multiplayer is where the true action lies. Fans of Stratego will enjoy Doomstar, but the feature set is fairly basic.

Even at the hardest possible difficulty it's just a walk in the park and feels like a waste of time.

If you think this game requires skill, you're wrong. You can spam everything and do the same thing as an experienced player. Buy it if you like fighting story-based games, you can easily fool the AI, but as to multiplayer or 1v1, 2v2, etc, just...no.

I have been playing Town of Salem (ToS) since the early days of the game, and I have to say that I love it. The game has an excellent interpretation of the traditional "Mafia" game and the User Interface clearly explains your role, a feature that I have found many "Mafia"-like games to lack. Furthermore, the ToS community is excellent, complete with a wiki and a "meta" for the game (for example, rapidly voting then unvoting an individual two times in a row is a code for being blackmailed).
Despite how my I enjoy the game, I must admit that it comes with its own set of shortcomings and troublemakers (some people just want to watch the town burn), as every game does. To mitigate this, BlankMediaGames set up a "Trial" system that allows veteran players to process reports (similar to CS:GO's Overwatch system). As far as non-community problems go, the only issue I have with the steam version of Town of Salem is that it has lagspikes that result in a drastically reduced typing speed rather frequently. For this reason, I suggest you play ranked and rapid modes on the web version.
Regarding microtransactions and DLC, BlankMediaGames did extremely well with Town of Salem in their marketing plan. The web version of the game is free, however the steam version and Coven expansion are not. I feel that this is fair as far as a paywall goes, one can always play the web version without the steam version, and the Coven expansion does not feel like the "traditional" Town of Salem. The microtransactions present in the game do not give players any advantage over others once the game starts - as only cosmetics and "scrolls" can be bought using the in-game currency that can be purchased with real-life money. I believe this system to be fair as well, such cosmetics and "scrolls" can be earned without paying a dime, and those only change the appearance of the player avatar or the likelhood that a player will be certain role.
All in all, I highly recommend Town of Salem. BlankMediaGames has done, is doing, and will do well with the game, and if you absolutely cannot pay for the steam version, you can still join the fun on the web version.

Stratego in space.  If you are not ok with Stratego, it probably isn't the game for you.
The UI feels... compatible with mobile. This is a turn off for some. The mobile UI compatibility didn't feel like a significant hinderance in this game (it has in others). Don't go into this expecting an experience that is optimized for desktop.
The gameplay itself has skirmish, which is your classic Strategoesque environment. There is also a campaign which allows for unlocking additional opponents.  The campaign has asymmetry to the pieces.
There are variations on the power scale compared to the more "pure" numerical environment of Stratego. There is a piece that always wins if it attacks, and always loses if it is attacked. There are fighters - which you can move two per turn and have two attack the same spot. There are mines - which behave like mines... except for the bit that light fighters aren't blown up by them.
The board placement area has more options than the number of ships - some mobility there.  The black holes (those circle things in the center) allow for slingshot movement, which can give fighters (with lots of movement) some sometimes surprising movement options.
I'm not overly impressed with the AI, but its not awful. There's the "I sent that fighter down the outside edge to scout out that ship and... oh, I won."  Incidentally, there is an achievement for that.
All in all, its what I expected and would be on the "I'll play it again" side of things. I got it on a 25% off sale and that felt about right. If you're on the fence, wait for a bigger sale or wait to see if it comes out for mobile at a lower price point.

My rating: 6.5-7/10
I love starbound and recommend it, but maybe wait for a steam sale if you're unsure about paying full price, because it'll probably be hit and miss for some of you. People looking to build and create will have a pretty good time. For explorers, it’ll keep you entertained a few hours. People looking for a good story-driven game? Not so much.
Pros:
-	Great character customization! For pixelated characters, there's a decent amount of stuff to customize.
-	Diverse biomes! You'll definitely spend some time just taking in the scenery and collecting some specific blocks.
-	Diverse characters! Albeit a little trope-y, but design and personality-wise, they're pretty unique.
-	Diverse weapons, armor, monsters, farmables, and collectibles! Crossdressing is also permitted, which should be handy for some people.
-	Great soundtrack! The music is very atmospheric and changes depending on climate and time of day.
Cons:
-	Illogical placement of biomes. (Lush fields in eternal midnight planets with sub-zero temperatures/tundras on volcanic planets with searing hot climates. I don't think it used to be this way either, so I'm not sure where that came from.)
-	Some racial NPC villages don’t seem to strictly follow spawning rules despite what the game tells you, and some get damaged or destroyed by the planets they spawn in. (I had a floran village spawn on a volcanic planet and it started burning to the ground minutes later.)
-	Quests are VERY repetitive. (All fetch/escort quests with some combat.)
-	Subterranean structures and biomes are repetitive. (There are some rare subterranean biomes, but most of the time you see a lot of the same types of structures spawning underground.)
-	Forgettable story. (It's your classic "find 6 treasures and save the galaxy," which is fine, but there isn't a lot that makes it very memorable. There's a twist before the final mission, but it doesn't really influence the story much at all.)
-	Forgettable characters. (It's more wasted potential, really. The characters are really cool! But they hardly get any sort of development. You pick one up at the end of each of their story missions and then they're just 'there.' Two appear in combat once during the second last story mission, and then a couple cheer you on at the final boss, but that's about it really. Their quests aren't too memorable either.)
-	Novakids are completely disregarded from the story for some reason???
-	Unlocking story missions is a pain. (You need to find villages of different races and scan items there, but if the village has insufficient items to scan, you'll have to find another one to complete it.)
-	Food spoilage is hard to avoid early on, and is difficult to store. (Food doesn't stack, and fridges are difficult to craft early in the game.)
-	Several unique decorative items are unobtainable and break when hit. (Not necessarily hindering gameplay but it just feels like a missed opportunity for more decorative items.)
-	Ship pets and crew block access to interactive items when standing in front of them. (I had my pet fall asleep in front of the ship's controls. That was pretty frustrating.)
-	Ally AI is kind of problematic and needs work. (Running into lava/poison, no self-healing, doesn't try and avoid deadly confrontation if wounded.)
-	Bugs can cause HUGE problems for people playing survival or hardcore. (Randomly loses ability to move until you attack, as well as falling off the map into space and dying when teleporting back to the ship.)
This review is more from the perspective of an average buyer/gamer. I did grab this thing back during early access, but I haven't been actively involved in its progression over the years. (Binge played it at the start of early access, and then once more about two years ago.) This is also solely based on what I’ve experienced so there might be some content I won’t touch down on here. I’ve also tried to keep the review spoiler free.

Celestian Tales: Old North is a good first act of a game. But it's not a good game.
Sadly, the game is largely undone by its ambitious pitch. A low fantasy RPG about grey morality and realpolitik sounded right up my alley. While Celestian Tales has plenty of opportunities to capitalize on these ideas, it seems like they didn't make the final cut. The characters and the plot are very compelling in a way similar to Game of Thrones (albeit much less dark), but they don't get enough time to grow and blossom. The tone and setting are intruiging, but the game ends right as it all bubbles to the top. What the game's description promises just isn't delivered.
The game itself is a pretty standard RPG, nothing worthy of note. There's a few technical bugs that show a lack of polish, but it's pretty easy to overlook them. The game does have some incredibly bad signposting issues, where it's not at all apparent how to progress the game. The final boss is not immune to instant death attacks. An entire chapter of the game is simply backtracking through the first few areas. It's pretty damning when your game is less than five hours long and it still has padding.
As for the good: The character art is absolutely phenomenal, and the music is generally pleasant too.
Celestian Tales has potential. However, when Ekuator Games says it's the first installment in a trilogy, what they really mean is they don't have the resources to make the full game they want to and will instead release it in parts. Even at the $12 price tag, this game is too expensive.
Hopefully the sequel will live up to its ambitions, because this game clearly didn't.

Spoiler Alert manages to cram more tedium and stress into 30 minutes than most games tens of times longer.
Looking over the concept it seems solid enough: beginning at the end, Spoiler Alert plays in reverse as you run backwards attempting to recreate your past movements as you go. It’s not all the different from what the excellent Retro/Grade was doing a few years ago, but where that game used time reversal as an interesting hook to wrap a rhythm game around, Spoiler Alert betrays its concept immediately and seems to really just want to watch you fail while wagging a metaphorical finger in your face.
It traps you into an auto running cage and then expects you to somehow predict when you need to jump (your only means of interactivity), which is easier said than done when your character moves like a blob of jello, your window of opportunity is seconds small, and hit boxes are all over the place. The simplicity of level designs and how they get more difficult the closer they are to the start of the game also helps to destroy the impression that you’re playing through a game backwards instead of just a really boring runner that decided to be edgy and go left. No game would ever design levels like this, but somehow Spoiler Alert seemed to forget its most fundamental concept in every way that actually matters.
I legitimately burst out laughing when I exited the game to find I had spent only half an hour clearing every level in the game, as I could have sworn I had been stuck in Spoiler Alert for days cursing its cheap kills and Casiotone Christmas themed mariachi soundtrack (which is every bit as horrifying as it sounds). If Spoiler Alert is a joke it’s one nobody is laughing at, not even the game itself. If anything it felt like Spoiler Alert had come preloaded with its own self contempt, begrudgingly going through the motions as quickly as possible so I’d leave it alone and we could both get on to better things.

I enjoyed this game for what it was. It felt very much like a love letter to Playstation 1 era JRPG's. The main game for your first playthrough will take you about 9-12 hours to complete.
For me, the story was decent enough that I wanted to know what would happen as it continued. At various points you're given choices, but currently they don't seem to affect anything really in the storyline for THIS game. Its hard to justify this design choice when there's still only the first of a trilogy for play. However, it does raise hype to see what may happen once the next title is released, and I am deathly curious about what occurred for some characters because of choices I let my characters take.
The battle system is pretty simple, but I do like that pretty much all the party combinations I've tried so far had some sort of synergy. That's pretty tough to pull off when you have six characters you can pretty much switch out anytime between fights. However, I wish the gear choices were a bit more varied to further push characters into certain playstyles. This is something I hope occurs for when the second title is released.
Music is pretty respectable, especially love the battle theme. The art direction is great too, my only complaint in the art is sometimes it is difficult to tell what is higher/lower in perspective planes. Some extra shading/lighting for this would have gone a long way to dispel confusion in these areas, especially in the capital town you start the game off in.
Also, if you're purchasing, I HIGHLY recommend adding the Howl of the Ravager DLC. The party you use for it is different than the base game's, but it really fleshes out some things that occurred in the main title. Plus, the fights in it are more challenging and interesting.
Definitely think this game series has a lot of potential depending on how the next title in this series goes.

On the originality part, I really liked this game concept: Replaying a platform game in reverse, with things to do or not to depending on the state of the different objects: For instance, you need to jump on a dead enemy but you do not need and in fact should not jump on an alive enemy. If you do otherwise, then you need to do the whole level from start due to a "time paradox": It would be kinda strange to have, when you play a platform game, invisible coins that would turn visible when touched, right?
The music is present the whole game and is neither intrusive nor impressive. The thing I remember the most about this game sound effects is the kinda reversed sound that plays when you get a coin. So overall, the sound aspect is not memorable but add to the game response feeling.
The graphics are kinda cartoon-like and simple and I really enjoyed them. The only thing I would complain about is that there are only a few different sprites but why this is will be seen more in depth after. The animations are smooth.
Now on the gameplay side. Even though the game is enjoyable, there are some dark sides that taint it in my opinion: Sadly, the game is so that you have only one possibility to complete the levels: The devs have decided on one path, one moment to jump or press Z (special powers), this is to say, they decided exactly which pieces are invisible and which enemies are dead. Between this and the length of one level (between 5 and 20 seconds depending on the level), the game falls a bit short and sadly, the level design is really simple which can make it quite repetitive at the end of the 100 levels.
It includes 10 bonus levels and a speedrun mode (You just play the game again without it asking you to press 'Z' when you finish a level.
Collector's edition includes a level editor.
I think 3 extra dollars for the level editor and some external to the game content is quite expensive. Therefore, if you plan on buying the game and do not expressely plan on creating new levels, buy Standard edition.
Consider buying when on sale.

Thief 3: Deadly Shadows was a brave attempt by a declining Ion Storm Austin to create a worthy sequel and ending to an amazing trilogy. On paper, they did everything right. They got the vast majority of Looking Glass Studios staff on-board to make it, they swapped technology to the Unreal Engine and set out to make the series more appealing to a broader audience. The end result however, was a different story.
In Thief 3, Garrett is once again the lovable misanthropic protagonist, stealing and hiding his way through another adventure. As expected, you will visit a wide variety of interesting locations and settings to foil yet another attempt to destroy The City.
The story of the game is incredibly well written and maintains the high standard of story telling that Looking Glass prided themselves in writing. The musical score and general ambience is handled by Eric Brosius and, as expected, the atmosphere is just as gripping as it was in the previous games.
Instead of playing mission after mission like in the previous games, the game is based around a 'hub' system; Garrett will have to make his way from his apartment through The City's streets to his next chosen objective, all the while keeping an eye out for pockets to pick or people to mug. Just make sure the City Watch aren't around before you attempt to hold someone up in the street. You'll need to visit fences around The City who will sell your stolen goods for you and shops to buy the equipment you'll need for your next mission.
The game plays out over the course of 9 days. Each day, you'll have to leave your place of residence and explore the streets. Each day will bring something different so it encourages you to investigate areas you've previously explored to find things to steal or to find new story elements. You'll be exploring a City that has largely recovered from the aftermath of Thief 2 and is slowly sliding back into a more magical steampunk state, visiting grand cathedrals, mansions, museums, libraries and, of course, The Cradle.
If you've never heard of this legendary level, the game is worth purchasing for this level alone. I won't go into too much detail about it but I'll say this... It's an amazing horror experience that will have you terrified from beginning to end.
The AI is both much improved over previous games but incredibly stupid at times. They'll remember past events and people they've met in the streets, monsters or otherwise. They'll remember if they've been robbed, found bodies in the street or seen blood on the floor and run away if they're outnumbered. Unfortunately they'll end up trying to hide in the middle of the street or accuse you of crimes you may not have committed.
There is some top quality voice work in here too especially for the monsters. The monsters up close sound so creepy that it'll send shivers down your spine!
For all its good points however, this game has some major problems. Thanks to this game being primarily designed for the Xbox and it's 64MB of RAM, the levels of the game, whilst being incredibly detailed for the time, are small, cramped, fairly linear and had to be split up into sections so the Xbox could cope. The PC port truly got shafted by this decision.
Ion Storm Austin also, for some insane reason, decided to take their completely butchered version of the Unreal Engine they used for Deus Ex 2 and made Thief 3 with it, albeit with some drastic improvements. The engine was a pretty damn impressive renderer for the time and does great dynamic lighting but performance wise, it was terrible. It runs fairly well on the PCs of today though but, back in 2004, you were lucky to see even 30 FPS on the most powerful of computers of the day.
Overall, it's a satisfying end to a trilogy that was truly amazing from start to finish. Even though Thief 3 is considered the weakest of the series, it has its good points and I can highly recommend it!

For the amount of people complaining about this game on the forums, i don't understand. First off, yea, there is a couple of bugs, but there not game breaking. One is when you 1st load up the game, the game is unresponsive, but that is easy to fix, you close it, close it in the task manager, and start it up again. This fixes it. The other bug i found is some enemies teleport around. I actually thought it was a monster skill at 1st, but i guess it is a minor glitch. As far as im concerned, neither of these bugs break the game much. I am having fun with it. I just did enough quests to own my own house in the game..shame i only had enough money to buy rugs and tables.
AS far as the game, yea, it does not hold your hand. First off, the quests do not mark where you go. You must explore where to go to the next quest. Older rpg's were like this. In a way, this does not really bother me, as you explore alot of the world for looking for your quest goals.
The other thing people complain about is the lack of inventory space. This is not a Final Fantasy game where you can carry 99 of every item in your backpack. I feel this game is more realistic in the respect you can carry only limited supplies. Even diablo 1 and 2 was like this, get used to it or play an easier game. Yes, this game is hard. It does not babysit your character. In that respect, i actually find that quite fun and refreshing not to being handheld on what to do in the game. Sure, if i wanted to play an easy game, i might like that, but i find this way also fun.  I recommend it if you can bypass the small bugs, and ignore the item limits you can hold. Don't let those turn you off the game. It has some strategy and fun aspects.

Update 12 March 2017:
**Patches/State of the Game:
Well, despite Iggy's claims they're still supporting the game, the last patch notes are from 2015( see these two images- iggy claiming it's still supported, but latest patch notes being from Nov 2015
. Check the discussion boards if you don't believe me) and from all I can see it's still utterly broken.
which is their official site for WoD updates reinforces this.
**Graphics:
Just..dont buy it. Please. For your own sanity. Look at this screensnip I just took. Marvelously detailed armour and then the actual character model...
(note that's on the highest settings I could find, with a very recently built gaming rig, skylake processor, GTX1070 etc etc)
**Previous Titles:
Oh and a big hint that the game is just a pretty poor rework of LOD (Legends of Dawn), one of their previous, also negatively reviewed, games? The game executable itself is called game_lod.exe. That and a lot of the models, lore, etc are awfully similar.
**Bugs and misc:
Alt-tab still tends to hang the game to the point you have to Task-manager crash it out.
Still able to get stuck in far too many places- and there's no unstuck, so you have to go back to your previous save
Random crashes- no obvious source, seemingly purely random.
They don't appear to have spell-checked or grammar-checked a lot of the quest text/conversation text, glaring errors in most text that pops up.
As in original review, the inventory system is a crippled mess. you'll end up with 50 or so different kinds of materials and recipes that you can't craft for ages, weapons and armour you probably won't ever be able to use and everything else, and a confusing inventory upgrade system on top of it.
Original Review:
Still seems to be a broken, clunky mess...and the crafting is ridiculous- you'll find your inventory quickly filling up with a massive number of crafting materials and recipes, but none you can actually make because you're missing one or two bits (some of which show up on vendors, but they have randomised inventories, so..yeah..may not even have simple stuff, not to mention it's often pricey as hell).
Plus on the point of inventory, there's an odd system of bags..where you buy a bag and can upgrade it's size by adding more bags (up to a limit), which is a cool idea..except a) a lot of the bags look the same ( I don't mean similar, I mean the exact same icon), and they no longer show their name once you've equipped them so it gets confusing which is which. They also don't list anywhere on them the maximum number of upgrades (total slots) they can have, which can lead to you buying too many of a bag and essentially wasting gold.
Despite what seems like a massive world, the whole place really is rather linear, and still confusing at the same time.
A lot of the quest texts are unclearly written, which can lead you to attempt the wrong thing (or go the wrong place) which gets frustrating fast.
You don't really get many skills in the game, you (mostly) get Spells. Spells are odd too- you'll combine Runes (which, sadly enough is the name for both an item to unlock certain chests, and the items to make spells) to craft a spell, but that doesn't teach you the spell..you still have to carry the spell around in your bags, taking up inventory slots. Some spell combinations are ridiculous (both good and bad), and a lot of it really, really doesn't make sense.
Honestly, I wouldn't recommend getting this game unless you're prepared for a lot of frustration

In order to enjoy this game, you have to accept 3 things:
1) You will get curb-stomped at the start. There's no tutorial, no hand-holding, no tactical advice. The game just tells you how things work and you have to figure out how to make it work in your favour. You might decide you are good at strategy games, and that you can make it on a difficulty above 'beginner'. You are wrong.
2) Everyone will die sooner or later. Unless you save + reload every fight until you can do it with everyone alive, everyone is headed to the grave. How quickly they get there is down to you, but it's difficult not to get attatched when every character has their own unique feel, and you start to remember your survivors. I'll never forget my one-eyed butcher with a knack for dodging past swords that felled many a orc warrior, only to be shot down by goblins. Or my farmhand-come-knight that could cleave 3 men in one swing, but was the last to fall in a doomed raid on a vampire's lair, ending the company's short, bloody life.
3) Sometimes, RNG will ♥♥♥♥ you. Yes, sometimes you miss 4 attacks in a row that all had 70% + chance to hit. Yes, sometimes your favourite guy with high melee defence thats holding up a shieldwall will somehow get stabbed through his armour and die.
If you can accept these things and still think, "i want to play this game" then boy oh boy is this the game for you.
The best thing about this game is it's strange charm. The feeling when you lose all your men in a fatal ambush, overrun by ghouls, is rarely one of, "oh thats BS" but, "Damn, I'm gonna try again and this time do better".
The huge array of weapons and armour give a lot of variation to the viable tactics you can employ, and coming up with your own ideas and character builds is half the fun.  Finding the right character for that build is something else that many other games skip lightly over, but in Battle Bros it's absolutely pivotal. No use giving a heavy crossbow to the guy who cant stand up without passing out from exhaustion.
Plus the devs are pretty cool, and seem to genuinely care about making a good, finished & polished product after taking feedback from the community.

After finally slogging through to the end of the story (the need to scan npc structures in order to progress got quite tedious by the last race; especially if you remember that the glitch structures form on volcanic planets that have the fire-rain weather which destroys the structures on contact and you can only scan placed items. I'm just saying, if these intelligent robots settled on volcanic planets for their homeland, you would think they might take steps to prevent fire damage.)
Ok, rant over, I'll continue: after finishing the story I must say that the gameplay otherwise is what you get the game for. That's not to say the story is bad, infact I enjoyed it (I had hoped the shadowy race would be a twist near the end but hey ho).
Overall Starbound boils down to three simple principals: Gathering odd materials from odd planets to use in future creative moments. Grinding monsters and dungeons for currency and weapons. Making healing consumables.
Unfortunately gameplay-wise the advantage the player has from the ability to regen health puts most fights firmly in your favour. Nevermore-so when it comes to boss fights: the boss fights of Starbound require a lot of movement, a lot of aiming in the general direction and  A LOT of eating up salves, bandages, medkits and nanowraps. Maybe I am simply not good enough at dodging in the game, but honestly I had far more success with the bosses when I avoided most, rather than all damage and then just healed up.
Conversely, this does not deter me from reconmending this game for the creative and excitable alike: while the above points do apply to the combat, it fails to make the fights any less enjoyable: some of those hellish bullet hells really did make me smile when finally beating the big beasties. I also thoroughly enjoy making structures, often attempting to recreate some of the pregenerated buildings on a larger scale because damn do some of them look nice.
So, if you enjoy any or all of: building, exploring, fighting, farming, grinding, planning, caring, gliding, fleeing, hiding or even if you just want to bully a few npcs into a fight with your overpowered character. I would reconmend you try Starbound.

After a few years they announce that you can move in, you've seen the plans, you've seen the pictures, it'll be AMAZING. After an hour of playtime, i decided to make a review about this game.
This game's main focus is on tower def. Keep in mind, this game was design to be played by a controler (but i much prefer mouse+keyboard) so some keybindings wil be kind of awkward, for example: to aim down your scope you have to press the ctrl rather than right click. Instead right click is to use your weapon's secondary fire. All though the multiplayer is kinda hard to find a game with deacent ping (because there aren't any official servers. Players are the ones who host the servers) it still works, unlike Homefront: The Revolution. For a beginner, it's really easy to hop straight in the game without any knowledge what so ever about the game. The tutorial is really easy to understand, campaign mode isnt too hard (The first-half of it, the other half might need some more assistants from other player(s)).
Now about the cons of the game. Like i said before, the servers are hosted by the players them self, therefore some servers will be laggy (For example: You want to play with a friend that lives on another country) and the controls are abit awkward for some PC gamers. But there is one con that stood out to me the most. When you launch the game, for some reason they limit your FPS on the menu screen to about 30. I've confirmed this using the steam FPS counter interface and overwolf's FPS counter aswell. The main menu shows some landscape of the game, but because of the 30 fps limiter, the menu screen looks very unprofessionally made. I haven't ask other people if this "FPS limiter" shows up on their games but it did to mine. I looked at the settings and it seems that there is no way to turn it off. Maybe in the future they will realese a patch about this concern although it's highly unlikely considering this game was made in 2013, we'll see.
This concludes my review on this game. It's not bad, i recommend this game to all of you PC gamers that are looking to try out a tower defense game. It mixes FPS+TD really well. I don't recommend playing this with a controller though, because you'd need to aim at the enemies while they're moving, i don't know if the game supports aim assist but i still dont recommend it either ways.

First let me say, wow this game is pretty. The underwater scenery is seriously breath taking. I could not believe how interactive this world was for early access. The ocean alone boast a wide variety of wildlife from those you can eat, to those wanting to eat you. Basically the premise of this game is you are a survivor of a plane crash, who is stranded in the ocean with multiple islands within rowing distance. Once on the island you must survive with whatever fate plays you. The crafting system allows for the creation of a variety of tools which will aid you in this endeavor. A watch accessed by pressing F allows you to see your health, hunger, and thirst, all of which must be kept balanced in order to make it through the day.
Gameplay (don’t judge too hard, it was my first time also make sure to set it to HD)
Currently the game can get a bit boring after a while, as the crafting is basic at this point, and there is really no end goal (you cannot be saved). However this is highly promising. Heck they really couldn’t have added more detail, for example if you stay out in the sun too long you get a sunburn which negatively impacts your health thus forcing you to build shelter.
Overall if you enjoy survival games, and beautiful oceanic graphics, then this game is for you! I cannot wait for more objectives, and a multiplayer to be implemented.

I played well over hundred hours of this because I was assured that this would get better by the end.
It didn't.
I started playing the series with Fallout 2 back when it came out and got the first game soon after. Fallout 3 was a slight dissapointment, but I loved New Vegas. The first twenty or so hours were rather enjoyable just walking through the wilderness and doing the odd quests.
The problems really started when (NO BIG SPOILERS!)  I went back to the main quest and met the leader of the Institute and got to ask about the central question of the game: why was my baby taken from the Vault? Where is he now? The answers were unsatisfying and felt like lies, with no opportunity to ask for clarifications. This was big minus when the whole game turned around this one encounter.
This was few weeks ago and I'm still angry. The most important conversation in the whole game, done in haste to get back to shooting enemies. Traditional part of the Fallout-games is an end-scene where the repecussions of your actions are revealed. This game didn't have that scene. Which is natural, as the world in the game was never one that was going anywhere: it was always just a place where to shoot and kill.
