As someone who has played Transistor beforehand, I had a rough idea of what to expect from Bastion. Wasn't quite right on all counts, but it does nothing to take away from the enjoyment of the game itself.
I'm not too good at writing these, so I'll be brief: the gameplay is simple, but solid. The story is great for it utilizes a completely novel way of narrating it and wouldn't be too bad when portrayed ordinarily. It never feels too difficult, but it can provide a challenge that can be further adjusted with your choices. The game itself is pretty even today and aged well.

It has some definite replayability as well, though I've yet to actually breeze through NG+. Nevertheless, Bastion scores a big plus in my book.

Firts of all, let's take a look at the description of the game by the developer: "Celestian Tales: Old North is a refreshing take on the classic turn-based Japanese style RPG, where your decisions in its dark and gritty storyline shape the world of tomorrow." Naturally, such a description begs the question of what kind of decisions you can make during the game, how they affect the world, and implies at least some degree of freedom of choice to the player. Alas, that is not true. Firts of all, the game is extremely linear. Even though it suggests that you see the "end" of each character, there is little difference to the story except the prologue and epilogue of each characters, while the game play exactly the same, save for some very rare situations where you are given the opportunity to make some trivial choice (out of two possibilites, always). So, bascially, they expect you to play the same game six times just to have some minutes of different dialogues during the entire experience. The game simply doesnt have this replay value.
The game is made using unity but it accomplishes little more than well polished Rpg Maker games deliver. The sound track is good, but does not justify the game. the battles are very easy and simple, requiring little to none strategy at all. The enemies are no more than a handufl constantly repeating and respawning. The dialogues are poor, the characters are bidimensional, and the plot is weak and full of loopholes  at best. Unfortunately, it simply doesn't deliver an experience that many rpg maker games provide you, for free most of the time.
Highly Recommended!!

When it comes to JRPGs, I'm very easy to please. If there's an overworld, towns, lots of monsters to fight, and levels to gain, then I'm usually satisfied. This is what I consider to be my "comfort" genre. Even with that in mind, I find myself not recommending Celestian Tales: Old North. Why is that exactly? This is an ambitious JRPG with multiple protagonists, decisions to make, and a number of other interesting ideas; surely it should be considered a cut above the mundane. Unfortunately, all this game really has to offer is promises. Its intriguing elements aren't fleshed out enough to satisfy fans of the genre.
One of the first aspects that is liable to catch your interest is the choice of main characters. There are six to choose from, all with their own introductory sequences. There are also a handful of character-specific cut-scenes. For my play-through, I decided on Cammille. During the quest, she frequently came across as the most level-headed person in various situations. I also thought that she was one of the only likeable characters. Part of what makes ambition a double-edged sword is that the player develops their own ideas on how the story should progress. A few decisions in this game are made, and I imagine they will have serious ramifications in the sequel, but I'd also like to cut a little dead weight.
Aira. Aira, Aira, Aria. For her it's always Deus this and Deus that. Yes, I get it, her beliefs are strong. I just can't shake the feeling that one day, 10 years from now, I'll want to backhand her. Reynard, whose personality can be summarized by the words "giant axe", looks like a donkey when he talks. Then there's Ylianne... blech. Yli talks in third-person because Yli is absolutely insufferable. When she's not playing up the "sweet and innocent" angle, she's crying about how terrible humans can be. Maybe in 10 or 20 years I can send Yli back to the dinky Elven forest she came from, and then burn that over-sized toothpick-stand to the ground.
These are the sort of consequences that are rarely explored in RPGs. Kingdoms rise and fall, worlds are driven to the brink of ruin, but you're hardly ever given a reason or even an excuse, to bring misery to your closet allies. Admittedly, I'm asking for a little too much, but I guess what I'm really trying to say is that there are too many protagonists. Having six party-members is fine. The problem is that in order to get the full-story, you're obligated to play through the game as everyone.
franchise toyed around with this idea, but they were still reasonably large and involving RPGs. A play-through of Celestian Tales: Old North is going to take around 5 hours. Not many people are going to replay a mostly un-changed adventure 5 more times just for a few extra cut-scenes, even if it is really short.
There are a few incidents in Old North where you decide the fates of others as well as yourself, but you won't know the results until the next game. Now I'm perfectly alright with this aspect, to a certain extent. Less significant decisions should have its results known to the player before the current game's end. When I choose to allow apprehended bandits a trial, instead of executing them outright, I should get to know how the trial went. Unfortunately, I have to wait for the next game to find out that important piece of information.
It's doubly frustrating, because the next game is supposed to take place at least a few years after the events of the first. Those bandits could very well have escaped from prison, formed a small army, razed a nearby town, became farmers, settled down, and started raising children. This news would eventually be relayed to Cammille (or whoever the main character is) and... there's nothing that can really be done about it. Basically, there's too much of a time-skip for decisions to continue to hold weight. I might have also angered one or two nobles, but if they aren't attempting their revenge in a year or less, they'll probably forget or stop caring.
Even with a scant 5 hours, Old North still manages to wear itself thin. There are not that many enemy-types, the dungeons aren't numerous or expansive, and there's even a some padding. Near the end of the game there's a part where you have to backtrack. This adds very little to the storyline, and there's no pay-off in the form of an additional dungeon or a boss-battle. It's more like "Here, run this errand because it'll take up a few minutes of your time". There aren't any side-quests, aside from a bonus boss if you find all of the hidden medals.
This is another reason why ambition can sometimes come at the expense of the game. The in-battle sprites are nicely animated, but I would have traded them all away for different kinds of enemies, and some more areas to explore. The battle-system is pretty solid, as it's based around managing stamina for various skills and spells. The problem is that there isn't enough variety to every encounter. The bosses don't necessitate tactics. I cruised through all of them in just a few rounds. The only time my party-members were defeated, was due to some oddly high-damaging attacks in end-game random battles.
I played a lot of RPGs with poor or even nonexistent storylines, but they still felt like complete games. With Old North, I get a few portions that don't really add up to enough. I have to settle for the expectation that the next two games in the trilogy will deliver a complete adventure. Honestly, I would have preferred a 15 or even a 10 hour RPG, with just one or two main characters (instead of 6). All that really needed to be done was offer some decision-making with consequences that occur in a reasonable time-frame. The character-specific scenes could still be implemented, only without relying on the player doing 6 play-throughs. More variety in the enemies as well as dungeons would have been welcome as well. Even with all of those changes, there would still be plenty to look forward to in the following games. As it stands, my advice is to wait and see. Right now it looks like Celestian Tales is trying to do too much with too little.

I have been bored with this post-2000 generation of games, few are the complete package the games in the 90's were. Old North is a traditional turn-based RPG, with leveling up, equipment customization and all these thing a RPG has. It's not long, but each of the 6 main characters (one of which must be chosen at start) has his or her own story, leading to a lot o replayability. It's a beautifully made 2D game, the soundtrack is quite good, all the characters are very well portrayed, with complex and believable personalities and the story is absolutely amazing. It looks like an interesting cross between The Banner Saga, Game of Thrones and Suikoden 2, so just buy it, you won't regret.

After reading reviews, and seeing a sale, I decided to give this one a shot.
It did not live to the hype, sadly.
I'd like to preface the below with this:  buy it at $5 or less, $15 is a joke.
While thoughtful and clever at times, the story missed the mark for all of the glaring holes, in particular, one of the characters is a functional macguffin, whenever the story requires a relevation, it falls to her.  Let's call her... Velma.
Thankfully, the party is formed of intelligent characters, which shows in their converstations and the paths they draw upon.  Too bad the supporting cast of NPC's, which the story spends a good amount of time establishing as sane, falls apart in plot-driven Chaotic Stupid. Naturally, as with any morally astute story there's a moral compass, and as such she plays the child very well.  Plus she finger paints and spent most of her years high (Upon a Tree)  in the clouds with other hippies.  Let's go with Shaggy here.
I liked the combat system, especially the concept of juggling aggro.  To bad that this means your healer will probably suck it all up with skills and items, like the uptown girl who plays jack of all healing trades and can't tank... I dubbed her Dauphney.
Rather than buying new weapons, the game has you upgrading existing ones, while each person as enough to adapt to a particular playstyle.  Sucks that there's no real way to compromise for a middle road though, like the pragmatic-yet-idealistic soldier-woman who's equipment can't agree on giving or taking♥♥♥♥♥♥.. Madame Fred, I call thee.
Of course, they've also implemented a skill system, which further allows you to customize the characters to whatever playstyle you enjoy.  It's a shame when you realize certain characters are a far superior than others, like the po' boy poster child-turned murderhobo's E-skill.  Such a lovely character, that Scooby-Doo. (Pro-tip: Just feed Isaac power and the highest dps you can, and he'll wipe an Andori... Rons... Or... ...Blue-thing a turn.)
The problem with these two systems, though, is some characters clearly blur without synergy, especially towards the end, their skills and equipment make them prime for backwards strategies and I can't decide if it's intentionally clever or a natural reaction to the emplaced system(s).  Prime culprits include the loud-mouth who's character growth chart looks like a big O expression.  Rather 'Scrappy' fellow.
If the above seems somewhat harsh, and you're still here, I'd like to soften a little: This game isn't bad, but it has two flaws, It's rushed, and it's not complete.  Yes I know there's supposedly more, but this isn't EA, and while well done for a group of hindi trying their hand at Western motifs and imagery it's no GoT.  (Though it's on par with Tactics...'till the end...)
Yep, that final boss  soured the whole thing for me, and if you sit back and think, it probably will for you too.

I don't usually write reviews for games, however. This is an exception. This'll be a short review.
This game is a perfect example of early access gone right, the developers know what they are doing.
Gameplay -
At first, you may be overwhelmed by the UI but it is easy to learn the mechanics of the game. The main idea of Battle Brothers is that you run a medieval mercenary company, you hire your men and feed them, train them, and fight with them. Once you establish yourself well enough you may purchase more equipment such as weapons and armor from cities and towns.
The quests in the game can be somewhat repetitive but is an easy makeup for every battle is not the same as the last. You will be taking long patrols to hunt down those terrorizing the roads of the realm, or prehaps to disperse that group of orcs taking up hold in the fortress in the woods.
Graphics -
While being a 2D game, the visuals are very appeasing to the eye and contrast well for the timeline. Armours and weapons are diverse and different from the last and the combat is one of the most satisfying moments in the game. The world map looks very nice and colourful while also looking grim.
Combat -
The combat in Battle Brothers is among one of the most satisfying i have ever experienced in a turn-based strategy game since X-Com. Will you poke as many holes as you can in your enemy with a Boar Spear? Or prehaps make heads roll with that mighty greatsword you just got your lad Fernidand after stopping for some drinks?
The game is hard. That is farely evident. You will win some and you will lose some. The AI is very good and fairly unpredictable, making every encounter possibly one of your last.
Soundtrack -
The soundtrack fits the game amazingly well. The combat themes are one of my favorites and the instruments perfectly fit the dire situations you will experience while playing Battle Brothers.
I spent 20$ on this game in hopes for something unique, however what i got out of it was enjoyment worth 40$. I will be playing more of Battle Brothers in the future.

At very steep discount this game may still be worth buying for the few hours of single player mode, or if you have friends who still play this instead of the sequel. When I first saw Spoiler Alert, the book was judged by it’s cover. At this point in life I should be over that by now, but what are you going to do. As the name implies, you start Spoiler Alert at the end of the game. It’s a counter intuitive romp filled with unkilling baddies and uncollecting coins. You start by defeating an evil looking bunny and get to the princess! That’s when the real game starts.
What ensues is a basic platforming game with nothing super special until you reach the end. I know that seems a bit harsh, but other than the quirky artwork and the fact that you are a chili pepper, there isn’t anything much different other than the main draw of constantly running backwards. That is a different approach to how I’ve been playing platformers my whole life. However, that backwards challenge is conquered after the first half of the the third world (which is the first world you play). The rest of Spoiler Alert felt more like a practice run for the end game.
After you’ve unbeaten Spoiler Alert, a few more options open up to you. You unlock an extra world called Mariachiworld and Speed Runner Mode. Mariachiworld is a set of ten levels that are tougher than the original worlds (thirty levels each, why only ten here?). They did have at least one level that took me more tries than the norm to get gold (unsurprisingly the last level).
Speed Runner Mode is a different beast entirely. While the other levels can be tried and retried again and again fairly easily, you won’t be grabbing gold that easily this time. You’ve got to make it through the entire 90 levels without making a single mistake to achieve gold. After one mistake you’re down to silver and so on. It’s tough for me to decide if I’m just going to restart and try for gold or just finish to get practice with the rest of the game. So far, I’ve just restarted, but I’m fairly sure I’m going to try to get gold one of these days.
tinyBuild Games also allows you to build and share your own levels. Think you’ve got what it takes to make the cruelest level out there? Well, this definitely gives you a chance. You’ve got all of the tools and toys in the game at your disposal. It’s pretty simple to use, but I’m sure if you don’t want your level to be just another shovelware level, it will take some practice to get that perfect level out of your head and onto the drawing board.
Score: Gewd.
I don’t fully appreciate the bulk of this game. However, if I view the first three worlds you encounter as a “prolonged” tutorial for the end game of Speed Runner Mode and the ability to create your own levels to share and torture other people over the net with, Spoiler Alert is a fun game. I may have appreciated the main game more if the levels were longer, but they are all mostly eight to ten seconds long as stated above. It’s neat in concept when you mess up and don’t have that far back to go, but it makes for a shallow experience. Still, the hand-drawn effects are nice, the music is fun and the mechanics are smooth. If you’re looking for some easy achievements, here you go. If you’re looking for a challenge that barely anyone you know on Steam will ever get, look no further. Speed Runner Mode will be the toughest thing to do in this game hands down. You’ll could get it with tons of practice, but do you have the determination to stick it out?

I think the devs have made some interesting decisions about gameplay and would like to provide feedback and suggestions. First, of course I want bug fixes and things to be completed like the watch showing actual temps... or rafts disappearing half way when going to another island.
Crafting on the ground - Nice idea for sure. Not sure I like having to hold a hammer for certain things etc.. The only thing I can think that really needs a hammer might be the foundation since the posts would be hammered into the ground. I would do away it, unless the hammer is actually needed. Like using the axe, you don't hold the axe unless it is needed. And the colours being different for "normal" crafting and building. Just make it the same and just require all the items being on the ground unless it actually needs a tool.
So, hammer use. How about things get a little more free. Let the building be free. What I mean is, no 8 sticks for foundation. Let us use a hammer on one stick and pound it into the ground to a certain depth. Then do it again for 3 more to make a kind of square. From there we connect them with more sticks. From there you piece together sticks with rope to the size you want to make the floor and place it when it's done. Same for walls etc... (except there is no hammering posts into the ground first, that is already done right....).
With the posts each pounded to a certain depth, players couldn't go too crazy with thier builds because the land isn't flat, only so much could be used depending on where you are building.
I would agree with others, remove the shark music. And make them faster if they are attacking or chasing you. If you're in the water and a shark is after you, it should be pretty damn difficult to survive that.
It would be great if sharks actually took physical damage when you strike them with a spear etc..   if they are very dangerous it will give players courage to see damage. And yeah.. no killing sharks with a damn knife.
Please, let us use beds any time and add a fatigue meter. So then we can't just swim and swim as long as we have eaten and drank, you might just drown if you swim while super fatigued. Also, sun would fatigue, lack of food would fatigue you (more so when starting to starve), lack of water will fatigue you,  injuries would fatigue, disease would fatigue you. Not crazy.. just added depth to survival.
When the temp gauge on the watch is fixed and there is temp in the game, please allow us to cool off in the water. But of course this would be risky!! Shade and shelter helps. Also, should be able to use some kind of fan in your hand to help cool yourself. But of course you can't do much else....
Another use for the hammer. Be able to bash rocks off of stone outcrops on the shore. Not all boulders in the game, just the outcrops. So there are rocks found on the ground but also you can work to get some more.
Enough for now.. may come up with more.

Graphics are beautiful, as you'd expect from a CryEngine game. Trees and vegetation look nice and are generally placed in a realistic, natural way, although I did see some floating grassy plants in one area. Rain and puddles are nice, too. I believe most, if not all, of the graphics are freely available CryEngine assets.
I did notice a few holes in the geometry, and the numbers 1 through 8 down the left-hand side of the screen should be removed, too. It's like the developer left it in debug / development mode.
Graphics options are limited, but sufficient: resolution, full screen / windowed mode, and a single detail setting. Performance was adequate in full HD on 'very high' detail on my five-year-old gaming laptop; modern gaming PCs should have no trouble whatsoever.
Sound is limited: a nice mellow rain sound, footstep sounds of various types, and other standard CryEngine sound effects.
Find Out plays like any other CryEngine FPS, except with no S. It's essentially a walking simulator set in a forest glen, surrounded by a stone-walled maze.
There's no story or instructions. You start at your tent in a forest. You begin walking forward, find an empty cabin (which you can't enter without enabling a CryEngine cheat), and then find out that the forest is surrounded on all sides by high stone walls. Eventually you make your way through these into a maze and have to find your way out.
The game seems to be heavily influenced by the Maze Runner, but doesn't go as deep. It's more of a technical or proof-of-concept demo, and is very limited in scope.
The starting area is well designed and the atmosphere is good, but the 'game' doesn't provide more than an hour or so at most of interest; you'll have a hard time playing for long enough for all the Trading Cards to drop.
Pros:
+ Pretty graphics
+ Interesting premise
+ Reasonably good level design
+ Trading Cards
Cons:
- Short
- A few problems in level geometry
Find Out is basically a single-level CryEngine demo made with freely available assets. It would make a nice addition to the developer's portfolio, but I don't recommend it as a game.

Terrible.
The game starts in a pointless forest area with no instructions, floating vegetation, and no way to interact with anything at all. All you can do is locate one single door and go through it, at which point the actual game begins. The only reason why this forest area even exists, seems to be that it provided material for 4 of the screenshots that advertise the game, which mask the fact that the rest of the game's graphics consist of the same boring wall copy-pasted literally thousands of times.
Gameplay is as dull as it is simple: You walk through a large maze of rectangular walls (20x50 squares plus a smaller annex), and have to find 8 pressure plates and the exit. With a simple technique like "hug an outer wall and occasionally peek into paths leading inward", doing this takes about one hour. After escaping, you see a text "Thank you for playing" and the game resets. That's all there is to it. There is no way to interact with anything in the maze, there are no special places in the maze, no story, no puzzles, no enemies, no timer, no randomization, nothing except you and the walls. Everything looks exactly the same apart from the occasional plant, crate, or bench, none of which serve any purpose whatsoever.
The gameplay description on the product page is a blatant misrepresentation of the actual state of the product. The "dynamic environment" is in fact completely static unless you count two automatic sliding doors. The "interaction with different mechanisms" consists solely of stepping on 8 identical pressure plates. The "day-night cycle", if it exists, must be so slow that I found it impossible to notice. The "spectacular effects" don't exist, even the graphics may very well be just stock assets. The "unique atmosphere" is exactly the same as in any other uninspired maze game. Honestly, this looks like someone was learning the ropes with CryEngine for a day, and spent the least amount of effort possible to put something out that might still qualify as a game. Selling this as an adventure game is like selling a "Hello World!" program as a visual novel.

The first of a series of games (three? I think?) CT:ON is fairly good. The story is intriguing, the characters are well-written and developed versions of typical fantasy tropes, the combat system is turn-based (which after all the action RPGs coming out lately is a nice change), and unlike most fantasy games, the party is made up of more women than men (4:2). The music is good, if a little repetitive in the field (though I think I liked every event score), and ultimately I enjoyed it.
There are a few flaws, though. For one, given that to unlock all the achievements (and likely the different story paths) you have to play the game 6 times is a little annoying, especially since it seems the deviation is really only about 5 scenes (prologue, 3 scenes within the game, epilogue). So I imagine it'll get boring fairly fast and it feels like a way to artificially add time to the game, when the game play itself could probably be finished in 5-6 hours (especially if you're like me and you spent your first playthrough running around over-leveling and making sure you do everything). Also, when you get to the epilogue, the English gets a little messy... like missing words and sentence fragments (possibly for stylistic effect that's just gone wrong). Finally, when you finally do get the world map open, it frustrated me a little to see all the areas I couldn't visit in this game.
Basically, I'll probably run through the game 2-3 more times, with the characters I liked the most, but I don't expect the kind of replay they really must have wanted with the 6 different stories.

This was a delightfully short but sweet indie title with plenty to offer for fans of the top-down action genre. Granted, the game can be far from short with all of its additional content the game has to offer, but in the age of the perpetual backlog one can't always be asked to spend the extra time on it. The game received high praise for its beautifully crafter maps, and a vast array of weapons, customization options, and additional content. Even after 5 years, the game's style ages incredibly well and works with the environments and the dysmal mood it succeeds in creating. While I wasn't a fan of the narration at first, it certainly grew on me, as well as the excellent voice acting from the supporting roles. I will also say that the soundtrack worked with the game's mood and themes, but I wouldn't have it as a selling point for the game.
Though the objectives of the game can feel grindy or simple, the developers succeeded in weaving an interesting story about the city you're trying to repair (called the Bastion) and the "Calamity" that caused its exhile and near-destruction. The breadth of enemies in this game will also surprise you, and will never make you feel bored or annoyed with their placement or cheap gameplay shenanigans. Combat is fair, and borders on being a bit too easy for seasoned gaming veterans.
This is a must-buy game on sale.

Problem for me was, by the time that the stamina points would fill up to the point where I could actually use a nice skill, the enemies were already dead. So basically you're using the low stamina cost skills all the time, or just hit "attack" repeatedly.
Also, theoretically a syngery between the characters different skills is possible (f.e.: With Camille i give the enemy a "bleed" status effect, and then I have another character do extra damage when the enemy is affected by "bleed").
This is nice in theory - but it seldom ever works, because the enemies will either already be dead by the time you manage the combo, or you are. And when you die, you lose all the stamina points you already built up..

This has to be one of the worst games I've ever had the displeasure to play, and it's all because of it's terrible block mechanic.
I know this review will get a lot of negative ratings from fans. I don't really care.
Enjoy hitting that "unhelpful" button without reading.
So in order to appease you fans of this game, let's start with the good:
-The game is gorgeous. Despite how absolutely dreadful some of it's aspects are, art isn't one of them.
-The game's soundtrack is great.
-The narrator is also very good. Actually, the whole sound design (things getting hit, things exploding) is rock solid across the board.
-The game does an adequate job of letting you know where you are and where you need to go without leading you by the nose. There are a couple markers early on. I don't recall too many after that.
-Upgrade materials are placed in intuitive locations; you won't need a walkthrough to find the last upgrade material for a weapon or anything annoying like that. Story bits are also intuitive.
-Game takes a while to complete, which I always count as a positive. Even in games I dislike, like this one, because for those who do like it that means more stuff to do and more entertainment time per dollar.
-Customizable difficulty beyond just "The monsters are stronger!" or "The monsters are weaker!" in the "gods" system; each god can be activated individually, and grant the monsters special bonuses (such as: explode on death, increased damage reduction, regeneration, increased damage etc).
Now, where to start on my list of gripes?
-Let's start small: the game constantly swaps out your loadout whenever you get a new weapon or skill. This is frequent, as there are many weapons and skills in the game. This isn't praise, though, as they're mostly useless.
What this means is that the game will take away your favorite, highly-upgraded power weapon in favor of some worthless piece of unupgraded junk, then tell you to complete a level with it.
This is all the more appaling considering we have TWO weapon slots, but the game will not default to taking away the first or second; melee ones will equip the first, ranged the second, and you can't possibly know what random junk the game will throw at you without reading a walkthrough (which will ruin the whole story aspect of this story-based game).
-Gods are not unlocked from the beginning, and must be earned even when you do unlock the shrine. Also, gods are only for increasing difficulty, not decreasing it.
Players who struggle with the game will realize that it's got no "easier" mode. While I believe the game to be fairly easy when it doesn't cheese, I've been playing for most of my life, and those who haven't and are struggling will be annoyed by this.
-Next up: targetting. How do you ♥♥♥♥ up targetting? Well, if you're bastion you do, because you're "special".
Normally, if I want to target something I indicate those wishes to the game by pointing at it with my mouse. In general, a game will pick up targetting within a reasonable range of the target (and not exclusively on top of it).
Bastion, though, begs to differ; not only do you have to point directly at the target, you also have to keep your mouse on the target to shield from it when faced with multiple enemies.
Where this fails spectacularly is that there are multiple high-speed or teleporting enemies in the game, and they just vanish from your mouse cursor, making your character turn around and target an enemy outside your field of view and who isn't attacking you.
-Okay, perhaps those could be excused (they can't). What's next?
Upgrades. All the upgrades in this game are boring.
They are all "faster reload by X%" or "X% more damage" or "+X ammo capacity". And when it's not that it's "more knockback" or "can now stun" - absolutely generic, boring, and frankly unworthy of a world in which we are constantly on freaking flying pieces of rock.
Couldn't you have invented something a bit more interesting?
-There is no invulnerability frame after taking damage. Dust: An Elysian Tale did this on it's hardest difficulty too, and it was just as stupid there; there, if you touch spikes it's pretty much a game over (across several minutes as the spikes take 1-2 health away per second out of your 700+ total).
In Bastion, if you ever find yourself in a position where you are flanked (and you will, because the game spawns enemies behind and in front of you simultaneously) then because of the aforementioned ♥♥♥♥♥♥ blocking you're likely to have the character try to block a guy who isn't attacking you, take damage, rotate around to the guy who just hit him, take more damage from the previous guy and either die or rotate again... Which means you take more damage. Repeat until either dead, use a special skill, manage to get your mouse cursor over one of them or get out of range and line them up.
-The enemies are stupid. They run around like headless chickens, fall into pits, slam into walls and keep running into them for a fair few seconds.
Bosses? Ones that can move will very frequently just fall off into a pit and die instantly, even if you don't want them to.
A leaping boss fairly late into the game was apparently so terrified of me, he turned right and just jumped off when I approached.
-The story is non-sensical. It's about as stuck up it's own rear end as Final Fantasy XIII 2.
Seriously, I have no idea what the hell am I supposed to be working towards; every time I gather something (shards, cores, whatever) some rampaging plot device comes and undoes my work. Why should I even bother to keep trying again? Because allow me to ask... "Have I ever told you the definition of insanity?"
-Challenges are pointless. Again, unless it rewards you with an upgrade component for your main weapon(s) (which most won't, as two of three of their rewards will be an upgrade component and a skill for them) then they're about as useful as throwing peas at the screen when you see an enemy, because you won't be using them. There isn't even a way to know what enemies you'll find or what the terrain will look like, so you can't know what weapons will be good.
All in all, I give this game a "broken essential mechanic / 10". If you can get over how horrible blocking is, this could easily be a 7/10 or even an 8/10, but I can't.

The idea to choose from different perspectives is really neat and interesting, but the actuall difference is so shallow that it hardly warrants an actual replay. The most you get for playing different characters is a few cutscenes, nothing that drastically changes the game. Maybe if I beat it with all 6 characters I would see a greater impact, but as it stands now, it isn't worth the investment.
The story had a chance to be interesting, fighting giant barbarian like creatures in an epic war, however you never actually get to do that. Your ragtag band of "squires" just run around doing meanial tasks that frankly, just feels like filler. I get that you're squires, and not exactly battle tested, but you don't do anything exciting. The boss fights are weak (and I'm just assuming the dire wolf and pig you fight are the boss fights) except for two of them, and one of them you don't even fight as the squires.
Then there is the end of the game. After about 7 hours of boring chores and vague cutscenes (which at the times I just assumed would be better explained later, but now I'm pretty sure that if you want a better understanding of them you have to replay the game as said character) there is a drastic plottwist, a boss fight (which was pretty challenging and fun) and then an abrupt end. No explanation at all, just a massive cliffhanger then the credits roll. Which is a shame because it ends right as the game gets interesting.
There are other minor cons and pros, but anything else I could say would just be parroting other reviews, and honestly a lot of them are just opinionated remarks that players could take as either or depending on what they like in a game. I just wanted to hit some major fall offs so anyone thinking about getting this game knows what they're in for. The game info is pretty accurate when it says "you are not special".

Once again players take control of Garret, a master thief, one that turned stealth and robbery in an artform. The game also features an interesting sandbox-like experience where you can go around the city and observe the life in town and access missions via this way.
I also found myself very welcome even though I started with exactly this title and had no idea of what the previous games held, so you shouldn't be ashamed of this being your starting point... Give it a try.

I love this game. It is hands on the most immersive game I know. This game really makes me feel what is to be a mercenary.
Glory? Nope.
Honour? Of a sorts.
Hard choices? Plenty.
Death in every corner? Defenitely.
Make your own ideal characters? In your dreams.
Let's elaborate a bit and point out the good in this game.
The mood. This game delivers what it promises (and that already in early acess!) A low power fantasy world where ten man are a force to keep an eye on and a hundred an army. The descriptions of quests and events really fit this mood and remain at all times in that mood. Yes, there is comic relief but it doesn't break immersion at all. It only furthers it more.
The details. There are so many things to keep track of. Food, supplies, the wounds of your men, your weapons and armor and yet it never feels like a chore or even anything but enjoyable. I don't know how they did it but this game makes a certain degree of micro management fun.
The difficulty. This game isn't a cakewalk but neither is the combat impossible. You really have to pick up the right recruits (Backgrounds and traits and affinities with certain stats count here.) and the right fights and equip your lads accordingly to what you think to face. A whole squad of longbowmen at night in a dense wood is not ideal for one. Nor is a group of swordsmen against heavily armored foes.
You also have to pace yourself in combat, getting cut off and surrounded means death. On top of that, a lucky enemy shot or blow can do you in as well but you can minimize risks by proper skill use.
Replay value. Pretty good as each game means you're on an entire newly generated map with differant people, settlements and nobles houses. Currently the dev's are working on so called late game calamities. This doesn't mean you will crash in late game, it means certain events will happen such as a huge orc invasion, an undead invasion or two noble houses going to war. With all of that no game will feel the same.
Pricing. This game is a steal for twenty bucks for all the awesomeness it delivers.
Now the bad things!
In conclusion I would like to heartily recommand this little gem of a game to everyone that loves a good turn based free world exploration roleplaying game.

TL;DR -- If you played the original way back when, then get this and install the KAM remake mod. Otherwise you might want to check out Anno 1404 or other RTS games instead.
This is a historical real-time strategy (RTS) city builder with plenty of combat. The game dates to about 1999, but it has aged well. If you want better graphics and a scenario editor, google "KAMremake" for a fan-made mod. If you had this game on CD-ROM a long time ago, then definitely get the KAM remake mod.
Most scenarios follow a pattern of:
1. build up your settlement to get resources
2. use resources to build an army
3. use army to defeat computer players' settlements before they take you out
Sometimes it takes 2+ hours just to build up your settlement...only to have it wiped out by a probe from the opposing army.
As you build up your settlement's economy, better buildings are unlocked, Use wooded shields and leather armour to start your army. Eventually use coal and iron ore to buy metal weapons and armour. But everybody needs to eat, so someone has to grow the food. Resources for construction (wood and stone) have to come from somewhere, too. There is a nice tension between the civillian and military economy. However there is also alot of micromanagement YMMV.
This game predates the Anno series of RTS games, and is sort of a land-locked cousin in terms of game play and settlement building. If you never played games of this genre before, you might want to try a more recent title before investigsting this one. But if you already are a fan of the genre, then definitely get this title.

I haven't finished a Grand Theft Auto game - yet I own 4 of them and have played each. Sleeping Dogs on the other hand has gripped me from the start. It's an open world game centered around a rather boilerplate crime thriller narrative that's elevated due to the impressive voice talent behind it, including Emma Stone, Lucy Lu, Tom Wilkinson (Batman Begins, RocknRolla, Shakespere In Love etc. - if you love movies you know), & legend James Hong (Bladerunner, Big Trouble in Little China) among others.
Set in Hong Kong the game offers a nice level of visual enticement and variety for a game set in the present. As with any open world game there is the main narrative or side objectives to explore as well as the city itself, all of which keep you engaged as you sift through its different layers. The soundtrack (via radio stations) is also particularly outstanding, offering a catalog of tunes from Warp Records and Ninja Tune among others (for those in the know). Sleeping Dogs isn't exceptional or unique in its offering, but it is exceptionally competent and a worthwhile adventure.

This game is clearly a case for the missing "neutral recommendation"-button in Steam. I can't quite decide if I should vote "yes" or "no".
It has many nice aspects, like the artwork, animations and interesting story dialogues. I really liked the resolve of the major event (a war) storywise, and it generaly gave me a very good feeling, reminding me of why I am a big fan of the Suikoden-Series. (Is it just me, or does the running animation seem almost copied from the Suikoden artstyle?)
That being said: It is super-short.
As soon as you think, that the "main plot" would be starting (in most other full-priced games of this genre), you will see the credits rolling. The game proposes replaying the game for the "different perspective" of another character. But as much as I see it, the differences will only be a slight sub-plot which runs in parallel and is shown between different situations of the main event. I can't really say that I am too eager to rinse & repeat through it with the other characters.
Conclusion: It is a nice game, done with some artistical love.  If you want a short but involving story in Suikoden-Style, you really won't regret it.
BUT 13$ is way overpriced from my point of view. Get it when it's 50% off or something. I'd say 5-7$ (per chapter, as the Devs seem to plan a trilogie with it) would be a more appropriate price.

Pretty good!  ...if very, *very* short.  But I'm not a fan of the reviews giving 6/10 or whatever; what game there is here is pretty good, even if it's extremely blatant the team ran out of cash.  I'd still be happy to support it so that we can see some more game, as the first ~10% or so that we can see seems interesting.
Anyway.  The combat system is interesting and plays well.  Encounters are very easily avoidable which is nice, with the proviso that this means that it's very possible to have unwinnable boss fights until you go grind a tad.  The setting is interesting enough, and most of the characters are fine with 1 exception.  The writing is...  a tad erratic, but I'm mostly positive.  Sometimes it's *great*, offering compelling in-setting justification for some of the weirder "involve the characters" angles where the characters react properly (surprise) but then puzzle out what's really going on.  Sometimes it's a bit...  1st-time author / fanficcy, where it's a tad too blunt/sincere about the Big Point they're trying to make here.  But hey, I'd rather that then no point at all, so I'll take it.
If you're curious about the one character I didn't like, it's the half-elf; she has all the "I am an alien outsider so let me ask naive questions about human culture and then have the others explain how brutal and illogical we are, as if to a child."  Think Star Trek Spock except way more cloying and saccharine.  This kind of character can work, but it doesn't here.  Oh well.  She isn't that important anyway.
It's good!  And short!  Recommended.

A fine little medieval RTS game.  Quite similar to the settlers series - somewhere between S2 and S3 (you have control over your army, but still need to build roads to connect your buildings).
Gather materials and build your town, train and feed your workers and army, beat the enemy - easy huh? Not that much, let me give an example:
To be able to train a basic bowman, you must cut lumber and bring it to the sawmill to have lumber, from which you can have a bow made at the weapons workshop. You will also need a basic leather armor, which you can have by butchering swine and have their skin brought to the tannery. There the tanner will make leather from it, so you can bring that to the armoury workshop to have a leather armor made. Have your men carry these to the barracks and you can equip a recruit to become a bowman.
Still, most of these things are automaticly done by your workers so don't be afraid. The battle control is a bit chaotic (because of the group control), but fun nevertheless. There are a couple of levels without 'base building', but even those are entertaining. The story is not really worth mentioning and the music gets a bit annoying on the long run, but (in my humble opinion) the perfect balance between battle and town building/management makes up for those.
If you like The Settlers, than this is a 'must have' for you.

Twenty-four days, we've been trying to rebuild V Company to it's former glory. For twenty-four days, I've watched men, young and old, join up for different reasons; Escaping their mundane lives, to provide for their families, to avoid consequences for their past indescretions. For the lucky few, they achieve what they've come here to achieve.
Unfortunately, fate hardly ever deals a fair hand. Most of the men who have joined up over the past twenty four days have been left where they have fallen; on the battlefield. I've watched as these green recruits have been struck down, time and time again. Tormel was struck low by an arrow, a lucky shot, fired by a weaseling bandit. It was his first combat with the Company. Gulfrich was slaughtered mercilessly by Orcs, almost split entirely in half by a mighty blow with a crude axe.
Many of these men had hoped to make a name for themselves, only to be trampled into the ground, nothing but a short lived memory. People say that the dead and gone live on forever as memories.... I have found this to be false in the case of mercenaries like us. As those who remember them, soon meet a similar fate...
------ I haven't reviewed a game on steam before, but if I were only allowed to recommend one game, it would be Battle Brothers.
My review won't be based around the technical aspects of the game, many other reviews do that, and I am pleased with how the game is played. My review is more based around how you feel while playing it. I've never had such a deep emotional struggle while playing a game without a linear story, before.
Battle Brothers takes you for an emotional journey as you build up your band of mercenaries, and complete contracts, to earn glory, fame, and of course, gold. You hire men from different backgrounds, to fill in your battle lines and quite frequently watch them die. They could be with the company for a day, they could be with them for a month. None of your mercenarie's survival is a sure thing in Battle Brothers, and when you make a strategic error, your men pay with their lives.
I quite enjoy Battle brothers, and without the linear story, I'm set to use my imagination to make up their stories as I play. 10/10 and four thumbs up.
--UPDATE--
Some people have given the studio flak for releasing the game and stopping development. Here's what I have to say about it.
Battle Brothers accomplishes everything it set out to be at the start of its development, and accomplishes it well. The game had not been abandoned, but actually finished from early access and worthy of a full, finished release.
They said that they would continue to provide bug fixes, tweaks, etc. Which they have followed through with and done, and now they're throwing in a completely unexpected content update for free. Other studio's have sold less content than this update to consumers under the guise of it being DLC many, many times before so this shouldnt be a problem whether you consider it free dlc, or just a content update.
Anyone who demands or expects more from these developers on this particular title(No matter how Absof***inglutely awesome it would be to get), is just selfish and ignorant to the fact that there comes a time where a studio needs to wrap up a project, and look to new things.
I sure as hell know that with the quality of this game, I'd love to enjoy another title by this crew.

Have you heard?
Jerry Seinfeld as a bee?
Bee Movie? A movie?
He made it? Seinfeld?
I know, I mean, can't DreamWorks Animation publicize it at least? It's been, what, 10 minutes since I've last seen a poster or heard a commercial or watched a teaser or noticed a cute bee sticker on a sidewalk? Oh, it's been only two minutes? I mean, I drove to work, it's 8 a.m., I haven't heard a peep about Bee Movie since, what, 7:35? Who is marketing this thing? I mean, hey, WHO ARE THESE PEOPLE?
Bee Movie, which opens today, at last - not to be confused with wife Jessica Seinfeld's new cookbook for children, a peril in our contemporary self-promotional industrial complex - is not the second coming of the animated feature, and despite the heat blast of hype coming off it, the nice thing about the film itself is how it has no desire to rock Toon Town, or reinvent a single thing. Jerry talks about this film like it's a modest doodle, something to do between practicing his true love, stand-up comedy, and despite the gazillions DreamWorks have spent on it, and his own heavy promotional lifting, the funny thing is, he's right - it's a piffle of a cartoon, a cute whim.
It's also about something.
Which is a disappointment.
Seinfeld, the sitcom, of course, was famously about nothing - "No learning!" was Larry David's often repeated mantra - but the conventions of the contemporary digitally animated holiday blockbuster don't allow for lots of ambiguity and serendipitous bad karma springing back on anyone. The lesson, I think, is that, as Jerry's bee dad says, "Every job, well done, means a lot." Also, we need bees to pollinate. Which doesn't distinguish Bee Movie from the dozens of other animated critter pictures featuring very famous celebrity voices.
What does, within limits, is Seinfeld himself, who lends the film a sensibility and curiosity that, like his stage act, rarely panders. The premise is pure Seinfeldian minutiae taken to an extreme, an extended riff on bees: Barry B. Benson (voiced by Seinfeld) graduates from bee school and learns that bees have a few jobs they do - regurgitator, pollinator, crud picker, heater. And what you choose is what you do for the rest of your life (span). This leads to the film's two most inspired, enchanting sequences - a trip outside the hive with the "pollen jockeys," who dive on Central Park, dodging balls and rain drops; and a homage to The Graduate, with Barry floating in a pool of honey, Dustin Hoffman-style, as his parents bicker over his chances.
The rest would fill a 10 minute routine: Barry decides to sue the human race when he learns we bottle honey and sell it - "I will not be a honey slave for the white man," he shouts, Seinfeld-style (meaning, with a wink in his voice). He befriends Renee Zellweger, who helps the suit. Oprah voices the judge. John Goodman hams around as the Southern defense lawyer. The animation is colorful but undistinguished. The bee puns are constant. And gentle Jerry, not so far from New Yorker Jerry, has trouble sounding sincere, which is not a deal breaker, but Bee Movie lacks the sting to make up for the cold stab of that familiar yammer. Jerry Seinfeld has a job.
It's telling jokes.
Bee Movie, which probably should have been a children's book and not a major cultural event, tells a few good ones but never cross-pollinates much: I've met someone, Barry tells his mom, who asks, "Is she Beeish?" He replies: "Well, she's not a wasp." See? Cute. Buzz. (Ouch.)

The idea at the base of this game is simple but clever: Everything goes backwards!
As in  all the classic side-scrolling platforms, the game is split in Worlds, each of them is made by some sub-levels.
Considering that everything goes backwards, you will start the story from the last level of the last world, “advancing” backward until you arrive at the start.
The uniqueness of this game is the upside-down approach to the level: you will have to revive the killed monsters and put back the gold coins you took without creating time paradoxs!
A nice thing is that the game menu is backward as well.
It’s not really difficult: Sometimes you will need the right timing to jump, but nothing too hard.
I found it original, funny and witty.
A nice filler for your time out.
Cons:
- Short
- Really low replayability

L'idea alla base di questo gioco è semplice ma geniale: tutto si svolge al contrario!
Come nei più classici platform a scorrimento laterale, il gioco è suddiviso in mondi, ognuno dei quali è composto da un numero variabile di livelli.
Considerando però che tutto si svolge al rovescio, affronterete la storia partendo dall'ultimo livello dell'ultimo mondo, avanzando mano a mano a ritroso nel tempo fino ad arrivare all'inizio.
La particolarità del gioco sta proprio nel dover affrontare ogni livello all'inverso: dovrete far tornare in vita i mostri uccisi e rimettere a posto i gettoni presi, stando attenti a non creare dei paradossi temporali!
Carino il fatto che anche il menù di gioco sia completamente al rovescio.
Non è particolarmente difficile: ogni tanto serve la giusta dose di tempismo per i salti, ma niente di veramente impegnativo.
L'ho trovato comunque originale, divertente e spiritoso.
Ottimo riempitivo per i tempi morti.
Punti negativi:
- Corto
- Scarsa rigiocabilità

I can't say enough good things about this game. Spoiler Alert's mechanics and concept are so unique. Unlike some games, where you can willfully manipulate time forward or backward, the game begins at the end while your character is perpetually stuck in reverse and forced to undo every action they had previously taken (whether it's restoring coins collected, or unkilling enemies, etc).  Rather than failing at a level by dying, you fail by creating a "time paradox" and disappear from existence completely.
The art is vibrant and the cast of characters are cute, the music is catchy, and the gameplay itself is highly energizing, despite the occasional bout of frustration. You will find yourself unable to stop playing until you've completed every level (90 total, plus 10 bonus levels). There is also a level editor, which you can use to create your own maps. It's definitely worth buying if you're looking for a simple and fun gaming experience.

Being such an incomplete game (look at the dev's road map for a list of awesome upcoming features!), it will leave you with a smile. Graphics are absolutely gorgeous, the sounds are nice, and you really get the feeling of being alone (immerse yourself with head phones for 100% awesome-sauce). For a 2D Backward Side Scrolling Platformer where you play as a Chilli with a bucket on its head... I thought this sounds like my type of game. However, after playing it I am left a little disappointed and wanting more of it. With this said take a look at the Pro's and Con's I found below:
Pro's:
♦ Fun
♦ Good Concept (Work Backwards)
♦ Funny Characters and Enemies
♦ Great Sound
♦ Awesome Graphics
♦ Great Workshop Potential (Maps created in Level Editor can be put on Workshop)
♦ Simple Controls that just work (Only have to press 2 buttons)
♦ Cool looking Trading Cards
♦ Easy Achievements and 100%
Con's:
♦ Storyline seemed weird
♦ Way too short (Finished it 100% in 55 minutes can possibly be done in 50 or less)
♦ Not Challenging at all (Way too simple)
♦ If you buy Standard Edition you have to buy the whole game again just for the Bonus Content
♦ Bonus Content isn't a DLC Option (Should have been cheap DLC for what it is)
♦ Not much Workshop Content and the content isn't moderated (Only 25 levels and some are unfinishable Levels)
♦ Hardly any replay Value (Unless you want to beat your 10 second level time, which is pointless)
♦ Leaderboards don't work (Mine shows up as White, possibly because I didn't get a time on Speed Runner Mode. But with that said then why aren't the Leaderboards Global?)
♦ Can 100% the game without getting all Trading Card Drops
Overall, I'd recommend buying this game if you want something really short to 100%. You will have fun and enjoy the concept whilst it lasts but once you finish it there isn't much incentive to replay it unless you want to try and beat your level time of average 10 seconds or less. Don't get me wrong if you have the "Bonus Content" you can do the Speed Runner Mode which will take you a while to get gold in, but there is no achievement or incentive to do this and can get very repetitive and boring quickly. You can however create your own levels and play other user created levels via the Workshop but there is few actual working Workshop levels available. So, for what the game is and for the relatively miniscule content in the game, it is good. However, I wouldn't say it's worth the $8 for the full game and to pick this up really cheap if not free if possible.
PS: My total time to complete all worlds (World 1, 2, 3 and the Bonus World minus the Speed Runner World) was 18 minutes, so if that doesn't say how short the game is and how much content it's lacking than I don't know what will.

Sanctum 2 is a 2013 FPS/tower defense hybrid, developed by Coffee Stain Studios and runs on Unreal Engine 3, and is the sequel to the critically acclaimed game of the same name, Sanctum.
The game takes place on the fictional colony of Elysion One, and follows the story of veteran soldier Autumn Skye as she is called in to protect and defend oxygen-generating cores from the planet's native species, called the Lumes. To do this, the player(s) must construct a maze using the resources available to them and arm it to the teeth with turrets, cannons and whatnot, then join the fray themselves, fending off the swarms of invading Lumes in the maze.
Sanctum 2 adds a lot of new key features, such as being able to aim down sights and have an actual ammo system instead of a percentage telling you when a weapon is about to overheat, Lumes are now able to harm and kill players instead of simply knocking them back, an experience sytem unlocking more weapons and tower types up to level 50, and a proper story mode, told in the style of comic book pages during loading screens. There's also new Lume types and bosses which are able to destroy the player's towers as well.
Building on the new weapon system, players are now not just limited to just playing as Autumn, but her younger sister Sweet joins in, armed with a REX missile launcher, as well as a hulking robot armed with a sniper rifle and a shotgun-wielding scientist.
The game's difficulty settings have also been replaced with a new feature: Feats Of Strength. Before each map, players can choose whether or not to activate a particular Feat, which will result in various buffs for the Lumes: Faster movement speed, health regeneration, more damage dealt to the player, player respawn is disabled...
Sanctum 1 was pretty challenging on its own, but the sequel ramps it up. A lot. Even with a full lobby of friends together trying to crack some of the maps, each player's damage output is divided between them to balance it out. A strong sense of foretelling, planning and of course, flawless executiom is needed to prevail.
Oh,and of course, the text-to-speech. Who can forget the text-to-speech?

This has to be one of the worst games I've ever had the displeasure to play, and it's all because of it's terrible block mechanic.
I know this review will get a lot of negative ratings from fans. I don't really care.
Enjoy hitting that "unhelpful" button without reading.
So in order to appease you fans of this game, let's start with the good:
-The game is gorgeous. Despite how absolutely dreadful some of it's aspects are, art isn't one of them.
-The game's soundtrack is great.
-The narrator is also very good. Actually, the whole sound design (things getting hit, things exploding) is rock solid across the board.
-The game does an adequate job of letting you know where you are and where you need to go without leading you by the nose. There are a couple markers early on. I don't recall too many after that.
-Upgrade materials are placed in intuitive locations; you won't need a walkthrough to find the last upgrade material for a weapon or anything annoying like that. Story bits are also intuitive.
-Game takes a while to complete, which I always count as a positive. Even in games I dislike, like this one, because for those who do like it that means more stuff to do and more entertainment time per dollar.
-Customizable difficulty beyond just "The monsters are stronger!" or "The monsters are weaker!" in the "gods" system; each god can be activated individually, and grant the monsters special bonuses (such as: explode on death, increased damage reduction, regeneration, increased damage etc).
Now, where to start on my list of gripes?
-Let's start small: the game constantly swaps out your loadout whenever you get a new weapon or skill. This is frequent, as there are many weapons and skills in the game. This isn't praise, though, as they're mostly useless.
What this means is that the game will take away your favorite, highly-upgraded power weapon in favor of some worthless piece of unupgraded junk, then tell you to complete a level with it.
This is all the more appaling considering we have TWO weapon slots, but the game will not default to taking away the first or second; melee ones will equip the first, ranged the second, and you can't possibly know what random junk the game will throw at you without reading a walkthrough (which will ruin the whole story aspect of this story-based game).
-Gods are not unlocked from the beginning, and must be earned even when you do unlock the shrine. Also, gods are only for increasing difficulty, not decreasing it.
Players who struggle with the game will realize that it's got no "easier" mode. While I believe the game to be fairly easy when it doesn't cheese, I've been playing for most of my life, and those who haven't and are struggling will be annoyed by this.
-Next up: targetting. How do you ♥♥♥♥ up targetting? Well, if you're bastion you do, because you're "special".
Normally, if I want to target something I indicate those wishes to the game by pointing at it with my mouse. In general, a game will pick up targetting within a reasonable range of the target (and not exclusively on top of it).
Bastion, though, begs to differ; not only do you have to point directly at the target, you also have to keep your mouse on the target to shield from it when faced with multiple enemies.
Where this fails spectacularly is that there are multiple high-speed or teleporting enemies in the game, and they just vanish from your mouse cursor, making your character turn around and target an enemy outside your field of view and who isn't attacking you.
-Okay, perhaps those could be excused (they can't). What's next?
Upgrades. All the upgrades in this game are boring.
They are all "faster reload by X%" or "X% more damage" or "+X ammo capacity". And when it's not that it's "more knockback" or "can now stun" - absolutely generic, boring, and frankly unworthy of a world in which we are constantly on freaking flying pieces of rock.
Couldn't you have invented something a bit more interesting?
-There is no invulnerability frame after taking damage. Dust: An Elysian Tale did this on it's hardest difficulty too, and it was just as stupid there; there, if you touch spikes it's pretty much a game over (across several minutes as the spikes take 1-2 health away per second out of your 700+ total).
In Bastion, if you ever find yourself in a position where you are flanked (and you will, because the game spawns enemies behind and in front of you simultaneously) then because of the aforementioned ♥♥♥♥♥♥ blocking you're likely to have the character try to block a guy who isn't attacking you, take damage, rotate around to the guy who just hit him, take more damage from the previous guy and either die or rotate again... Which means you take more damage. Repeat until either dead, use a special skill, manage to get your mouse cursor over one of them or get out of range and line them up.
-The enemies are stupid. They run around like headless chickens, fall into pits, slam into walls and keep running into them for a fair few seconds.
Bosses? Ones that can move will very frequently just fall off into a pit and die instantly, even if you don't want them to.
A leaping boss fairly late into the game was apparently so terrified of me, he turned right and just jumped off when I approached.
-The story is non-sensical. It's about as stuck up it's own rear end as Final Fantasy XIII 2.
Seriously, I have no idea what the hell am I supposed to be working towards; every time I gather something (shards, cores, whatever) some rampaging plot device comes and undoes my work. Why should I even bother to keep trying again? Because allow me to ask... "Have I ever told you the definition of insanity?"
-Challenges are pointless. Again, unless it rewards you with an upgrade component for your main weapon(s) (which most won't, as two of three of their rewards will be an upgrade component and a skill for them) then they're about as useful as throwing peas at the screen when you see an enemy, because you won't be using them. There isn't even a way to know what enemies you'll find or what the terrain will look like, so you can't know what weapons will be good.
All in all, I give this game a "broken essential mechanic / 10". If you can get over how horrible blocking is, this could easily be a 7/10 or even an 8/10, but I can't.

This thing is absolutely brilliant, a real gem!
I love the fusion of philosophy and communication theory they have pulled off. This is one of those masterpieces that can show that video games have become a form of art, way beyond pure and sometimes simple entertainment. The integration of the players actions, the general strangeness and abstraction, Alan Watts lectures and the quirk of the different size scales accomplish something that most other art forms nowadays fail to do (with the rare exception of some theater plays and clever movies and ofc books): They get you into interesting discussions.
If you loved Stanley's Parable and the Tiger-heist-thingy, you will also like this.
Having said that ... this probably is not something I am going to play for a very long time. Nevertheless, I am very happy that I bought this game, as it will be one of my personal milestones of great, surprising and fulfilling gaming moments.

Sometimes, you get a game initially not thinking much of it - You haven't researched it, and you haven't heard of it before. However, because it's on sale/free, you think "Meh, may as well pick it up, it's free at the moment". Then you play it, and you cannot believe you've never heard of it before. In the past week or so, I've extensively played the game, and it has very, VERY quickly become my absolute favourite. The soundtrack is brilliant, the visuals are excellent, the art direction is unique and interesting, and the gameplay is rock solid. I'm not the biggest fan of FPS games usually, and I'm most certainly NOT a fan of Online games. However, Sanctum 2's online is great with players popping in to help you complete missions, and the cool mixture of first person shooter and tower defense really works! I really cannot recommend this game enough; I think that way more people should give it a chance! Although I got it for free (It was a giveaway on Humble Bundle not so long ago), if I'd known how much I'd love the game, I would have spent £11.39, and not regretted it for one second.
Final thought: If I were to rate this game on a scale of 1-10, I would genuinely give it a 10. This game is absolutely stunning and it doesn't get the attention it deserves.

Minimalistic rhythm-based platformer.
The game's physics are very basic, as are the initial graphics and level designs. However, as you proceed, you collect orbs that each add a new layer to a catchy electronic soundtrack and activate new stage elements. Almost every obstacle in the game moves in time with the music, and making your way past them requires that you do the same. Challenges that would seem to demand superhuman precision become easy when you take the time to plan your approach and count the music's beats.
The game is very short, and thus has no time to get stale. Stage elements are never over-used, checkpoints are frequent, and each level ends with a boss that mixes up the game's mechanics.
Very satisfying.

Fallout 4 in a nutshell:
Good game? Yes
Fun As Hell? Sure
Good Shooter? Yep
Best Roleplaying/Fallout Game Ever? HELL NO
The biggest problem with this game is the fact that the role playing factor has been substansially lowered due to several things including a voiced main character, less meaningful choices during the main and side quests, less explored and interesting characters, and finally the lack of interesting quests in general (minutemen quests don't count that's just repetitive BS). Don't get me wrong there are definatley some great quests, but this game pales in comparison to the weight and variety Fallout: New Vegas or even Fallout 3 possessed. I'd also add the fact that even though the gun play is FANTASTIC, there is a lack of gun variety. Bethesda decided that they'd put a few guns in and let you tinker with them (at end game there are only 1 or 2 attachements per gun you'll actually use), and as a result you get sick of the lacking amount of guns (reference New Vegas for how it should be done).
Overall it's not a terrible game, but as a long time Fallout fan I feel like no matter how much I mod this game it still lacks when compared to previous titles. At the end of the game you get a LAME ending cutscene that feels weightless, and not much changes after your massive decision. Also has a bit of a LAME cliffhanger which NEVER got addressed in the DLC. Massive Bummer :(
**FYI the Far Harbor DLC is better than the whole base game and addressed MOST of these issues, so do yourself a favor and pick it up at least**

The artist(s?) is clearly the top member of the development team. As bad as most of the game is, at least the models for everything are high-poly enough to look pretty decent. Granted this doesn't work for any of the animals as they look as flat and devoid of any fur detail as your average PS1 game.
Disregarding the now infamous events surrounding the game, expectations should be tempered considering it is an independent game title from a studio you've never heard of. Even then, it disappoints.
You can do stealth kills on the amazon women... with the same death roar as the men you kill. You can kill every animal in the game with a single pistol bullet (even from the awful double barrel "old pistol") yet it takes 3 pistol rounds or 2 M9 rounds to kill a completely unarmored person. Nearly all interaction animations end up throwing the camera underground, zooming in the camera so much you can't see the animations, or having the model clip through the camera. Most crafting is trial and error as even when there are recipies oddly drawn on some rock, half the ingredients are "helpfully" displayed as scribbles. Granted all you ever need are bandages and the leather water jug anyway. Lighting is all sorts of wrong and broken... but then again it is an Unreal Engine 3 game.
There was a $50k kickstarter for this game, which failed, and I think that explains the game. The kickstarter failed, so the developer probably just gave up and put the unfinished beta into Greenlight. With the absolute zero quality control there of course it got accepted. I hear all but one guy left the company some time after release, which explains the tiny insignificant update made two years after release.
Also, optimization/performance is unacceptably poor. I may not have the toppest of the line rig, but an overclocked i5-3570k, GTX780 Lightning, and enough RAM to run a large server should not be struggling to keep above 30 while running Crysis 3 on Max hovers around 45-60 and keeps games with similar-yet-better graphical fidelity to this one like Dead Island and Far Cry 2 well above 100 FPS.

Using gamebryo was a step backward and they've been made painfully aware of this. Object physics and ragdolls are unrealistic by today's standards, you can see the fallout 3 bleeding through when you shoot a target in VATS. The voiced protagonist... it's purely subjective but I can't stand it, and it just seems so shoehorned in because it doesn't really affect how the person you're talking to reacts to you. If you want the classic, PROPER fallout experience then the mods "silent protagonist" and "full dialogue interface" are a MUST, I discovered them late in my game but it improved the experience and immersion exponentially for such small mods.
Making the power armor a modular shell that requires batteries... I'm a little torn about this, on one hand why create a fully modular shell like that which can be built upon when the suits should be seperate and unique, on the other making it require batteries was probably the right idea, but the time each core lasts vs. how hard they are to find is unbalanced.
TL;DR - the game is a step back in the series, spend your money on similar games instead and hope bethsoft will get it right next time, or even better let obsidian make all the fallouts from here on out.

I don't play a lot of games anymore due to time constraints, but Fallout 4 is one of the few exceptions I'm really glad I made. I've happily spent hours just exploring the vast Wasteland and coming across all sorts of interesting places, characters, and quests. The world is beautiful and densely packed, and it doesn't feel like you'll easily run out of things to do. I love the addition of settlements and the freedom to build however you want, though at the moment settlements don't serve that much of a purpose and doesn't yet impact the game in a meaningful way. Combat and enemy AI are very well done. The ability to craft / mod armors and weapons add welcome variety, and Dogmeat is just absolutely adorable - at least, when he's not getting in your way :p As many have said, the dialogue and storyline fall short of expectations, and Bethesda still needs to iron out some bugs and glitches, BUT I don't think they take away from what is most definitely a fantastic game, and one of the best games I've played. Overall I'd certainly recommend Fallout 4, especially if you like wandering around at your own pace and collecting indecent amounts of (not-so-useless) junk :)

Its environments are fun to explore and often atmospheric, but it doesn't have as many wide-open or weird levels as previous Thief games.  The lack of rope arrows is also unfortunate.  But it's a strong Thief experience that you're not likely to get elsewhere, and its story nicely concludes the trilogy.  It also adds to the Thief recipe with a bit of sandboxy-ness in the City that joins missions together.
My major gripe is that blackjacking can solve almost all situations, at least on Normal. I didn't play Expert because the high loot requirement can get tedious, but maybe on Expert you'd have more need to use other tools.
