Indie games come in all shapes and sizes. With a far more limited budget and development team, many indie titles focus on one particular aspect of a game and accentuate that as much as possible, while shedding the negatives. For games like
and
, it’s the narrative that shines through. For games such as
and
, it’s the unique underlying game mechanic that drives the game home. Then, there are games that rely on humour and/or unique gimmick to build intrigue, including games such as
and
. This final group is by far the least interesting of the bunch, and is typically the least successful. Sadly,
falls into this group.
For reasons that I can’t describe to you, you play as a walking chilli pepper. Very early in the game, you face the final boss and voila, the credits roll. Have you completed the game? Of course not – this is merely the beginning. The game then forces you to go through the entirety of the game in reverse.
The game is split into three main worlds, each with 30 mini-levels which are approximately 10 seconds long. Your goal is to walk from the right hand side of the screen to the left. Each level has a number of enemies and/or obstacles for you to un-tackle. For example, if there’s a flattened enemy in your path (i.e. you jumped on it earlier) then you have to jump on it again whilst backtracking to un-flatten it. Similarly, some of the coins in the level may be slightly faded out, indicating that these coins were retrieved. Whilst playing the game in reverse, you have to grab these faded coins (to “un-collect” them), whilst avoiding the non-faded out coins which are coins that you apparently never collected in the non-reversed playthrough. It’s an incredible simple concept that’s difficult to put into words.
Aside from jumping, the game also occasionally gives you various other abilities to work with. The dinosaur/dragon powerup, for example, allows you to shoot fireballs. However, because you’re playing in reverse, the fireballs come out from your enemies and you’re tasked with “catching” the fireball. The hammerhead shark power-up works similarly, except you’re catching a hammer (which travels in a parabolic arc) rather than a fireball (which travels in a straight line).
There are two ways to fail each level. The first is death, which can occur when you touch an enemy/projectile/spikes. The second is by causing a time paradox by doing something you supposedly didn’t do the first time around. For example, if you encounter an enemy that’s alive, jumping on it and killing it will create a time paradox and you’ll have to start the level over. A similar thing occurs when you collect a coin that wasn’t collected the first time. After you complete each level, you’ll be given a grade, which lies somewhere between “Perfect”, if you don’t die or create any time paradoxes, to “Good”, if you die/create paradoxes more than once. You read that right – the worst you can do in this game is “good”. This is the kind of condescending♥♥♥♥♥♥that would put primary school teachers to shame.
And that’s it. No, really. The game is the textbook definition of a one-trick pony, and it’s not a particularly mind-blowing trick by any means. When the novelty of traveling backwards wears off (and this will occur very early on), all you’ll be left with is a very empty shell of a mediocre-at-best platformer. The enemies are bland and uninspired, the power-ups are dull and none of the platforming elements are particularly challenging. Furthermore, your characters on rails – he constantly walks backwards at the same speed and there’s nothing you can do to change his velocity. What the whole game boils down to is a simple game where you have to press “jump” when appropriate. If you fail, you try again until you time it correctly. Often, you’ll find that the game plays more like a rhythm game than a platformer, and a very shallow one at that.
With that in mind, it’s both a blessing and a curse that the game is incredibly short. After completing the game, you unlock a “speedrun mode” which connects each of the levels back-to-back from the end to the beginning. Even with my frail-old-man-reflexes (which required me to attempt some levels multiple times), my final time was a tiny bit over 20 minutes. I would wager that the majority of the more competent platformer players could do it in 15 minutes or so. The fact that the game and its gimmick gets tiresome well before the end of its short lifespan speaks volumes.
The aesthetic is made up of the same old flash style found ubiquitously through indie titles, perhaps most famously in
and
. It’s colourful and eye-pleasing and suits the cartoony tone of the game. The upbeat and Mexican-influenced soundtrack complements this further, although each track is short and loops repeatedly, which may bother some of you. The only sound effect that I remember from the game is the weird “HRGUGH” sound that your chilli bean produces upon death.
It saddens me to hear that this game was in development for two years. The developers certainly had a goal in mind, and for the most part they did capitalise on their one idea and did successfully build a game around it. Unfortunately, the final product feels lacklustre. It tries to exploit one little gimmick that can’t stand on its own two feet, and there’s just not enough quality content surrounding the gimmick to solidify the game. It’s something you’d expect to find as an averagely-rated flash game on Newgrounds rather than a fully-released Steam title. For that reason, I can’t really recommend this to anyone.

An excellent blend of shooter / strategy & co-op elements. Sanctum 2 looks great, sounds great & is a joy to play.
The shooter elements are solid & there are 4 (+1 DLC) characters to play as - all with different loadouts & play styles (which you can further tweak to fit your preference). The game features perks, weapons & towers to unlock via a fun (but maybe a little slow?) leveling system. On top of that, numerous modes besides the campaign exist & difficulty modifiers are available as well.
The strategizing through the immense number of turret types & the working area on each level leave countless combinations & tactics up to the player(s) - I often find myself surprised by another's approach on levels I've completed 10 times.
The enemies are fun, varied & distinct, from lumbering tanks, to bat-like flyers, to skittering little critters - you won't be disappointed by the number of threats coming your way.
The levels don't get too crazy at first, so one can get acclimated, but I'm genuinely surprised & pleased at how eclectic the levels can get (from simple, flat plains & courtyards to swamps, bridges, & debris-littered forests).
I am nothing short of impressed & would recommend this title to anybody who likes shooters, co-op titles, or has any interest in a tower-defense game.
The only thing I can think to nitpick might be how the story transitions from level to level - there are short animated still sequences where the characters may lightly discuss something or other. I might call them hard to follow because of this, but so far, they have some good ideas & I find it interesting nonetheless.

This game is not so much like "Rashomon" – everyone agrees on what actually took place – so much as it’s like "Pulp Fiction." Every character is much more complex than he or she first appears, and no individual has the full picture. With each playthrough, characters that I’d dismissed as one-dimensional suddenly became sympathetic, and their perspectives lent new emotion to scenes I’d seen before. One playthrough just isn’t enough to judge the game.
Each run, assuming you take on the secret boss and don’t grind, takes about 5-6 hours or so. That “don’t grind” bit is really important; the combat becomes considerably more interesting, since you're forced to be resourceful and creative instead of steamrolling everything.
Every time you clear the game, it creates a clear game save file, which will be imported into Part 2 with your choices. Speaking of choices, some of them are not available for certain characters. Depending on their history and psychological profile, some are only going to be able to take one of the choices available to other characters. It seems to me this creates a real sense of foreboding: There’s just no way this ends well for everyone. It’s pretty clear that as difficult as the events of this game were for some of the characters, Part 1 was the idylls of their youths; you get the distinct feeling that by Part 2, when they’re all likely to be knee-deep in intrigue and deception, they’re going to look back at these simpler days with a sense of longing.
All this points toward a game series with a great deal of replayability; it’s pretty clear that you’ll have to take all six characters through the three games to get the full experience. Definitely recommended.

I really wanted to like this game...but although there are some upsides, the downsides dominate.
This game draws inspiration from traditional turn-based RPGs, and personally I got quite some Suikoden vibes...but that's about it. The graphic and overall visual look is really good. There could have been more varied enemy types but it's ok. Character design and animations fine as well, for an indie game it's rather more than I had expected.
Music and sound effects are nice, nothing feels out of place.
On the other hand though...what bugged me the most about the game is the characters, their behaviour and "character developement" if it can so be called. Same goes for the story, which feels kind of shallow, there isn't that much to talk about, and the plot twists are unexpected because things turn up you can't possibly know, so not the good kind of plot twists (except one very obvious).
There are 6 playable characters in total, because nonsensical reasons you can only have 3 fight, the actual reason probably being it had made the game too easy. The biggest problem is, that the characters don't add replay value, not to me. Differences in dialogues and "cut scenes" aren't that notable. Almost every character has despicable traits he/she doesn't get rid off, or only partially gets rid off. This may just be my personal taste, but I don't like to play characters that put religion above all else, or feeling okay with treating the less fortunate like they're my possession.
I could go on.
On top of that there are some bugs/glitches and plot holes. Bugs/glitches like characters having their top level skills when starting a new game or graphics popping up behind the character when they should be in front, or vice versa (i.e. walking in front of a house's corner, but said corner suddenly popping up over the character leaving only the feet visible).
All in all the game is rather small and short. Max Level is 30, max playtime should be 7 if you're really slow. If you're quick and know what you're doing you can finish the game with everry collectible in well under 4 hours. Take this into account if you want all achievements. Finishing the game with all characters is a chore. It's not hard, just time consuming.
Though there are some upsides, the downsides are too much for me to recommend this game. Though that doesn't exactly make it an actual bad game. It's just wasted LOADS of potential, and anyone with expectations should step away from thinking of buying this game.
If you're fine with short and simple turn-based RPGs go ahead and buy. If you expect something of the style, quality or complexity of a Suikoden or anything like that, you should only get this on high discounts.

Not entirely sure where to begin. I'm extremely disappointed. I wasn't expecting anything as grand as Suikoden, but when a game promises moral choices that shape the world I don't think it's unreasonable to expect moral choices that shape the world.
I played through as Cammile. There were three moral choices. None of them had any far reaching effect on the game. I know that the devs are supposed to be putting out other parts for the game, but that's not an excuse to put out a lacklaster game in hopes that customers will stick around just to figure out what three choices MIGHT have influenced.
Plus when random interesting things did happen, you don't get any choices. Big things are happing that cause actual moral dilemma? You watch them play out. *SPOILER* I just have to say that taking a ♥♥♥♥ing recipe book that's in a forgein language does not count as a god damn ethical conundrum. I don't care if it's in some crazy dude's lab. I don't care if the recipes are for "evil" things (which the game didn't really explain exactly what kind of recipes were in it. They could have been foreign pastry recipes for all we know).
The art style is okay. The character portaits are nice, but the background art is meh. Near the end of the game I still got stuck in random objects. Slightly different colored ground in the middle of the layout? You probably can't walk over it. You'd be going along in a town and SURPRISE you can't actually go that way, but you thought you did because that wall that looks like it should be further back is actually right in your path. There's really not a lot of depth, and I dreaded having to go through the first town. Sprites are okay.
I didn't like the chacacters. I hated the elf. I honestly think that the devs only put her in the game so she could go "Oh my goodness! I don't understand your strange human ways! Explain this odd thing to me!", and then you get force fed history, culture, etc that every character that grew up in the game's country knew but wouldn't have any reason to spout off for the player to learn. The rest of them are flat too. Any character development that does happen does so suddenly and without proper explanation as to why they're having these changes of heart.
The war that your taking part in does have an intersting ending, but what should have been spread out across more time gets thrown at you in a span of like ten minutes, tops.
Also, soooo many unanswered questions. They introduced quite a few things to pique interest, and I stuck around despite all the things that annoyed me because I wanted to see what would happen. The story had so much promise, but it's so slap-dash and rushed and worse left unfinished that you're just left with disappointment.
And the ending? I hated it. I can not stress this enough. I hated the ending. Utter garbage, and it made it worse because I thought *maybe* I'd actually get to make a decision to effect the outcome. Nope. After everything is all said and done *then* you get to make a decision that, you guessed it, doesn't make a damn bit of difference in the game.

Celestian Tales: Old North is a wonderfull indie JRPG, probably one of the most well made Indie JRPG’s developed in recent years, and it could surely be put in a same sencence with some much more expensive AAA titles.
Celestian Tales offers six different perspectives represented as playble characters that will make the player question their approach to a variety of moral dilemmas and puts you in a awkward place in the middle of a full-scale war where your every action counts, but not in a "western" way we are all accustomed to.
Classical turn-based battle is represented much like in Final Fantasy titles where the player can attack, use skills, items, and defend against enemy attacks. It offers one of the best aesthetics in an JRPG game that i’ve came across in a long time, indors and outdors. The music is absolutely fantastic, and is beautifully orchestrated all throughout the game. It really blends in well and sets the tone for the game.

It's easiest to compare this game with Mount and Blade, but with turn based combat.
The turn based combat feels satisfying and has kept me playing for quite a while, but the game only superficially resembles Mount and Blade in other areas. There are no real characters or relationships to develop, trading is simplistic and you can never settle down.
Imagine a Mount and Blade campaign map where you can't increase your party speed but you still have to run after other groups. It doesn't seem like they thought it out well enough.
There's also very little interactivity in the towns that are scattered around the campaign. You can't even buy accommodations at the local inn for your company. Maybe I just expected more when I saw the lovely town windows which reminded me of Betrayal at Krondor.
There's even less interactivity outside towns, where the few things you can interact with are enemy bands. You can't talk to peasants, buy food from farms or anything else, really. Just begin combat (remember, you never fight while inside a town).
If it was meant to be this light on features, I wonder why the game needed a real time campaign map at all? My main activity in it has been waiting and getting bored. It would have worked much better if it was turn based, since then I could just spam next turn until I got to my destination, keeping an eye out for eventual enemy bands in my line of sight, instead of just waiting for 5 minutes.
The enemy encounters get boring pretty quickly as well, because you always fight (there's no negotiating with them), there's always more of them (and of mostly a single type) than there are of you, which leads you to apply the same tactics every time.
I would've loved an encounter with a witch and some channeling tentacles or some cultists which needed to sit in a pattern for the witch to be able to cast a curse (would have been interesting to disrupt that with shield bashes or something), but no, you get to fight 18 wolves in the woods... again.
I'm not saying the game needed to be turn based Mount and Blade (though how awesome would that have been?), but it needs to be something, anything. I know it's early access and a few more things will get added in, but it hardly looks like enough, especially when considering the price tag and graphics (I love the graphics, but come on, you don't get more budget than that while still being able to ask money for it).
I played it a lot because I love games like this (I also left it running in general because it's very light on system resources), I'm not saying there's something better out there, but that doesn't mean this one is good.
It might end up good once out of early access, but with an "early 2017" release date, I can't help but think it'll still be underdeveloped.

This is technically an "early access" review, because I got to try this game before it came out when I went to an arcade/pinball/retro gaming convention, right off the bat I talked about how I felt like I was in the 80's when i tried the game on an actual cartridge.
The game's ost is interesting and deffinately gives off that catchy/classic retro kind of creepy feel that you'd expect from horror style games during the NES era and the art style reminds me strongly of Double Dragon and River City Ransom on the NES, but the question remains, is this game a good game?
The game is an interesting game and deffinately lives up to "Nintendo hard" in terms of how tough old school games were, with basic gameplay (go to the right, just like a beat em up) but with platforming elements and difficult placements similar to Mega Man
However, where the game's problems are can be "located" if you will, with no ability to use passwords if you run out of contiunues  or a file to save (although the game may be trying this to capture NES nostalgia, it can feel like a chore if your required to play througout the game in one run, especially with no way of getting back to where you were if you run out of continues) and some of the bosses (to my knowledge) take no effort to beat, for example you fight bigfoot on level 2, all I had to do after losing 1 life was stand on  a tree stump without moving and beat that boss fight easy
Overall, the game is a nice game and deffinately feels like an old NES game and its nice to know that new games are being made these days for old consoles, however, I feel as though (unless this game gets patched) that due to it trying to hard to "match" the NES, it might actually turn off some people from trying the game, I would get the game if its at a discount or on a physical cartridge, but be ready for a challenge and be aware that the game can be slightly unfair

Grind sessions to get the materials you need for a new armor are obligatory : since the devs couldn't figure out how to make the game challenging, they just removed knockback , nerfed mobility and added damage on contact. have fun fighting 5 monsters at a time. and what monsters they are , by the way : apparently, the whole "INFINITE AMOUNT OF RANDOMLY GENERATED MONSTERS !!" thing got pretty much removed : the majority of the mobs you'll witness are handcrafted, and they're EVERYWHERE. on planets, on asteroids field, everywhere. you'll see the same yellow slime thing  everywhere. fighting them is also a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ since starbound combat is really mediocre (there are no tactics really, you try to put as much enemy to one of your side and you hit there with your sword)
Also, there are radiant quests (bring me this, kill this mob, escort me there). i'll skip over thoses, since they are really boring.
so now, you have a decent armor, and you're tired of fighting the same enemies over and over. well, fear not ! there's the main quest ! a magnificient main quest where you can :
-fight bosses who are easier than random monsters ! (the final boss literally has only 2 attacks, i don't know how you can die from him)
-explore planets because you're supposed to "scan" items to progress ! (yeah , since there's no point in exploring the world, just force the player to do that)
and that's it. you've done it. you've finished starbound, after 20 hours of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gameplay and forced exploration.
Honorable Mentions :
-I was in awe after discovering that yes, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ pixel art game can in fact bring my 390x and i5 6600K to 20fps
-the fact that a SINGLEPLAYER game can actually LAG : everything freeze and restart again a few seconds later , as if you had a lagspike.
-the fact that the hoverbike (one of the two vehicles in the game, the other being a boat) makes your game crash/ put you under 10FPS if you reach max speed with it (but you will never reach max speed , since it won't be able to move on something that isn't flat, therefore making it useless.)
-the fact that the devs thought adding a ghost to moon planets (they're only here for providing you fuel) was a good idea : you will NEVER land on a moon for something other than fuel. so why adding a monster that will NEVER kill you ? why making such a decision, when the outcomes is that it's completely pointless ? he just slowly follows you, and that's it. you just need to WALK to avoid him, or you can just buy your fuel in the outpost (you should, since you can't store your money anyway in early game)
-the fact that this game seems to have more removed content than actual content (randomly made bosses, mechs, planet-chat etc...)
i could go on and on about how this game was clearly in dev hell for a while, and how for a game called STARBOUND, there's so few "STAR" related stuff.
if you're rich, or a furry, or you like building♥♥♥♥♥♥ get this game. (yes, most servers are ERP servers for furry. have fun.)
otherwise, just play a better game. (hint : it's also a 2D sidescroller where you can mine stuff, but it's actually good.)

This is a great old RTS game that I ever played. It is a RTS game with realistic features together with stupidity :p
What you need to play this game is a micro-military management and patient
Let's see the overall.
: The graphic was ok but think about it that it was a game created around Win95 or Win97. It is acceptable for me.
: Simple UI. You can only move your military. Labourer and Slave will move according to your build plan and need. Other characters will move according to their role.
: Very slow if you want to have a big army and grand city. It will take you more than 2-3 hours per map. However, once I get used to it, I can finish some maps within 30 mins without having to build the whole city with army micro-management.
: If you want to build a block of road, once you clicked on the map, your labourer will come and adjust the land. Then a slave will come with a block of stone. After that, your labourer will finish a block of road. As for the building, labourer will adjust the whole plot. When the road connected to the entrance of the building, your slave will start building it. However, if you build another roads or land plot, the labourer will move there to adjust the land and build the road. So, you can't build a whole city in one go.
: In this game, the fundamental resources are almost unlimited. Wood can be planted which will be turned to timber. Wheat can be planted over and over again. However, you should build the building in order as in one map, I forgot to build the saw mill and focus on the food to feed my army. As a result, I can't build any building at all as all the timbers are used in farming.
Food is matters. Your citizen can starve to dead if there is no food.
Melee: Once the melee battalion engages the enemy, they won't back down until all the enemy or your battalion are annihilated. If you want to flee, you have to hope that the remainings are not engage the enemy. The soldiers is very loyal to your command. If you command them to destroy the building, if the enemy hit them from behind, they won't fight back and keep attacking the building LOL. If you run into the bigger army, bye.
Cavalry: Unlike your foot soldiers, the calvary will not chase down the enemy. I like to hide them somewhere when the archer units pass and strike them.
Archer: I like this unit unit and mechanism a lot. It is very realistic. Your archer was trained to fight in the long range, so if the enemy close in, the archer won't fire any single arrow. There are eight directions for your army to form a line. Your archers can't fire the enemy if they can't see! This mean if your archer units face to the east and the enemy comes from the west, say goodbye to your archer.....
So, the battle is as simple as it seems like melee at the front, archer from behind. BUT, if you make a wrong move, you have to take a pain-relieve pill. However, with the good plan you can win over an army of 500 by just only 50-100 soldiers. Or in one map, I won over the huge army by killing a farmer, without food, all the soldiers were starved to dead.
In conclusion, if you have a lot of free time, try this game and your time will be gone.....

Fallout 4 is set in Boston, where you are forced into a roll of a Minuteman who protects The Commonwealth. Bethesda, did you not learn from Obsidian when they made Fallout: New Vegas? We want freedom to express ourselves as any character our minds can conceive. We want our destiny to be shaped by the choices we make, the characters we choose to side with. I was quite dissapointed with the main story. The DLC Far Harbor had amazing storytelling and you could create the ending you wanted to pursue. You could make peace with every side if you so wanted to, but that wasn't an option in the main storyline.
The graphics are lacking I would say for a game that released 2015, and the performance isn't great. I wish you would scrap the creation engine, and use other more streamlined 3rd party engines, like Unreal Engine or CryEngine.
Aside from the negative aspects, the gameplay of this game is perhaps the greatest of any game I have ever played. The side quests are extremely interesting and exploring the openworld Boston keeps you on the edge of your seat, what could I possibly come face-to-face with next in this irradiated wasteland?! There are several fascinating points of interest like small communities that all have many characters with radiant individuality.
The gunplay is AMAZING, with infinte possibilites of creating your own weaponry almost anyway you want to. The same goes for armour and the such. The crafting in this game has it all, except for the possibility to create ammo, which was a small nuisance.
The modding community like always is amazing on this game, and the playability extends hundreds if not thousands of hours with all the great mods that are out there.
This game gets 8,5/10. The story is pretty bad, but with such a massive interesting open world you never really felt like following the main storyline anyways.

I have been a long time fan of RPGs, ever since I first played Star Wars: KotOR when I was 12 years old, and they are easily my favorite game genre. The first time I had ever played a Fallout game was back in 2012 with New Vegas, and not long after, I picked up Fallout 3. Both have remained in my top 20 games of all time. Fallout 3 is my favorite of the two, as it has an amazingly immersive world, and a more personal and heartfelt story.
Then Fallout 4 released, and I can safely say that this is my favorite entry in the series. It took almost everything I loved about the first two 3D games and just did it better. The world is amazingly immersive and fun to explore, the voice acting is some of the vest I've heard in a game, the combat is great, the crafting, the story, and characters are wonderful, as are the choices you can make with them, and leveling up a character, while it's a little more simple than in previous games, is no less fun.
Honestly, the only common criticisms that I can agree with are the fixed number of dialogue options, the occassional lack of seriously different dilogue choices, and the lack of non charisma checks in dialogue. But the fixed options and lacking non charisma checks were hardly a hamper, and the lack of dialogue choice happened only happened twice on my count, and the quests that had them had more than satisfactory options by the end of them.
I know this glowing review makes me a Bethesda shilling filthy casual that doesn't know what a good RPG is, but that's my honest to god opinion. Is it as great an RPG as, say, Dragon Age: Origins (my favorite RPG ever)? No, but I think that it is an incredible experience that a worthy entry to one of my favorite series, and one of my favorite games ever made.

This is a fun little tower defense game for a casual gaming session but very basic with low replay-ability. 7/10 will finish it but won’t be back after.
At a 9,99 euro list price this game is a little above the price mark where I would expect a ‘mobile look and feel’ casual tower defense to be. You will likely not spend more than 20 hours on it even if you are a completionist. As far as the Tower defense segment goes there are games out there that will give you more value for money.
is a cutesy approach to a tower defense game set in a straight forward cartoonish fantasy world. The involved reading is limited, to the point and has some fun parts to it but the game leaves you to figure out stuff yourself after the first mission and given its overall simplicity that’s perfectly fine.
The addition of a hero unit to your tower defense setup helps work out little weaknesses in your defense or allows you to mount the occasional offense together with some summon-able re-enforcements. Given the controls though the hero needs to be re-selected constantly to use efficiently often tempting the player to just use it as a roadblock at critical intersections or resort to tapping space continuously to keep the thing moving (A simple way to rebind the key was not found).
The game is very much linear (especially in the beginning) and levels are static so if for some reason you get stuck or bored you probably won’t pick it back up again after you quit even if you do decide to throw different heroes at it.
The controls lack mouse support a little and while this is not a huge issue it does add a bit of superfluous clicking to the game that could have been avoided. The heroic and iron modes available after you finish a level restrict you further to give you more of a challenge but regularly do this by taking the unique aspect out of the game that give it it's edge over other Tower defense games (i.e. no more hero unit, see below).
The developer(s) did put some thought into the achievements adding a bunch of small little Easter eggs to the game that are straight forward to discover and add a little bit of a reason to look outside of the paths the monsters travel on.
All in all I enjoyed my first 10 hours in this game and I am happy with it mostly because I bought it when it was on sale. If there ever is a DLC added I am not likely to buy it and re-visit this game since as far as tower defenses go there are far superior options available. I am not entirely sure how people manage to put in more than 20 ish hours in this but if I find out I'll be happy to update this review.

You love Plants vs Zombies and love the idea of tower defence but want something a bit more hands-on.
Kingdom Rush is, quite possibly, the best tower defence game I've ever had the joy of playing. Exceptional fun, challenging and honed to near Indie-gaming perfection.
There were 2 things I loved immediately with this title. Firstly, it was the graphics. For its cartoonish simplicity, the game looks
. Pair this with the fun voices and numerous cultural references - you end up with a title as inviting as a bloody great big mug of hot chocolate.
The second was the barracks and reinforcements. An elegantly simple, yet inspired, addition. What this gives you are troops on the ground; able to intercept and stall the enemies that try to get by. No longer are you idly sitting by the road and lobbing crap at a bunch of enemies casually taking an unperturbed evening stroll... Now you actually get to get stuck in! It adds a refreshing depth to the game, as well as brilliant tactical leverage where stalling enemies gives your other towers the chance to finish them off. It makes for so many more gripping "hold the line!" moments as you desperately send reinforcements to plug your creaking defensive lines as they take an utter battering. It makes the game richer and so much more hands-on than most other titles.
The range of towers are also simple, yet great fun. At the 4th upgrade they split into 2 possible top-level variants; each with their own uses, extra abilities and (quite delightfully) fun personalities. On the whole, they're reasonably well balanced (with the exception of the Tesla Coil, which is a bit overpowered) and the additional 4th level upgrades add a lot of interesting utility. The vast range of enemies are also brilliant - each bringing with them their own collection of nasty traits and challenges. Overall, it keeps the game fresh and interesting over its very generous collection of levels.
In another nice touch, the 3 difficulty levels are very well calibrated, so whether you're a casual gamer or want a brutal challenge... you should be able to find it here.
Ultimately, with the exception of the somewhat basic music, this is a game that feels lovingly crafted with barely a stone left unturned. From the cunningly crafted challenges to the charming Easter eggs - the game is as tricky as it is fun. A very rare, yet impressive, feat to be able to boast about.
And better still... there's a sequel!

Spoiler Alert is a 2D side scrolling comedy platformer that has you running backward from right to left in very small levels. Why do you run backward? Because the start of the game kicks off with you completing the game. Then you're forced to play the levels in rewind. Dead enemies will need to get hopped on to unkill them. Live enemies will need to get avoided. Transparent coins need to get collected and standard coins need to get avoided.
If you do something the game doesn't want you to do, then it creates a 'Time Paradox' and you're forced to restart the level. Each level runs for about 5 or 10 seconds, so its pretty easy to get right back where you were. Not just that, but the game is very easy. There are 90 levels broken into three worlds of 30 levels. Then on top of that there are 10 extra levels in the collector's edition for only $4 more! Wow 100 levels you say? Sign me up! No, again they're all around 10 seconds long, making for a game that you can complete all its content in under 30 minutes. Maybe 45 if you're awful at the game.
Oh but wait, there's a level editor so you can make your own levels! That sounds cool, but then you need to select a small, medium or large level. Even the largest level feels short. It feels like it should be a mobile game for how bare bones this is. The $3 price tag proves it is better suited for a mobile platform and not Steam. Think of the creative possibilities. You can make your own challenges, because the game sure didn't do it for you! Game too easy? Well make a super difficult challenging level that's over in a mere 10 seconds! Want a level full of exploration? Nope, you're out of luck, because you're stuck going one way at the game's own pace.
The controls are super simple! Jump button and well... jump button. There is no actual movement like left or right, you're stuck moving one way at the game's pace. Not just that, but even when you step onto tiles that make you run fast (or slow in the bonus content), when you jump off them there's no momentum. So you're going fast and then you jump into a slow standard jump, then land and you're going fast again. The game is super easy, so its not like you'll get killed or anything.
Does only jumping sound dull? Well there are three power ups that consist of headgear! Amongst the three of them, they do two different things. The dragon head and hammer head will let you extinguish fireballs and blow out hammers that get thrown at you. The moon helmet lets you roll underneath of low platforms and spikes. To get them you need to jump on where they are and you're forced to lose them when the game wants you to or else again, it will create a time paradox.
Man its so cool having a game this restrictive. You do exactly what it wants! Well except for the three secret blocks. You don't need to get those. There's no time paradox there.
At the end of each level, you're greeted with a menu that lets you view your time, go to the next level, select a level or replay. It breaks the flow. Heck it buffers a 15 minute game into a longer game. Super Mario didn't have something asking if you'd like to retry the level you've just beaten. I guess Spoiler Alert knows you want a perfect score with 0 time paradoxes. You're obsessive. You speed run things all the time and want to shave seconds off your time... but well you're stuck running at the same speed. The only way to shave those seconds off is to not die. So everyone will have the exact same time. You can also select any level you've unlocked.
Not only do you have to unkill enemies, but there are certain ones that when you unkill them they spawn back into their space ships on top of you. So you need to time your jumps to get on top of them before they reassemble. Not just that, but some dead enemies don't need to get unkilled, even if they're dead. How can you tell? Are they different colored or different enemies? Nope. You just jump over them so they can come back to life and throw a hammer at you. Then using one of the mandatory power ups, blow the hammer back at them. Because apparently whomever went through the game originally that the game doesn't show you, must have thrown a hammer at an enemy to kill it.
Its a mind bending game. The power ups don't really blow things out, because they must spit fire from the dragons head and throw hammers from the hammerhead. The fire isn't aimed in the right direction though. Its coming from enemies when it should be coming from you. The hit detection is a little iffy too. Landing on spikes or getting a coin that you shouldn't have will pause the game to tell you its a time paradox. Well in the pause I could see that I wasn't touching spikes, nor did I collect a coin that I shouldn't have. Hey whatever, it didn't cost me ten minutes of gameplay.
I ended up replaying the game to get all of the achievements and it took me another 40 or so minutes. Hey at least its all the achievements in 90 minutes. The $3 or $7 for the collector's edition really boils down to how do you value your time per dollar. Its a boring game, but you're only there for 30 - 90 minutes in all. If you're a creative person, you can get more out of the level editor, but there are better games with better level editors out there.
Avoid this game. Its a quick money grab with a gimmick. On a phone it might be worth it to play through if you're stuck somewhere for 30 minutes. Who knows maybe you have an iPad that you'll be stuck somewhere with. On a train, on a bus, in a car ride or a hot air balloon. You never know!

Overall a great game despite a handful of glitches that hopefully will get worked out as the game development progresses. Can get boring when traveling between islands but regualrly finding new items keeps it interesting. After loading a save things can be a little jacked up such as my raft being gone and all of my items having fallen through the floor of my humble abode. I'd still recommend this game though because its fun and has kept my interest and should only get better from here.

Spoiler Alert is a PC and Mobile title that claims its gameplay tests your platforming skills. Developed by Megafuzz and distributed through tinyBuild, this game had recently dropped on the Steam marketplace as a collector’s edition. However, it wasn’t until recently that a standard edition of the game had become available at a reduced cost. But does this indie title end up a brilliant “comedy” entry, or is it nothing more than a running gimmick that goes on for way too long?
Spoiler Alert tells the tale of a red chilli pepper who on a quest to reach a princess, whisks her away, and then is forced to go through the events in reverse. Every move must be done moderately close to the original, or else he will wind up a in a time paradox and have to redo that section until he gets it right. The tale is divided into three worlds that clock in at ninety stages total (with a bonus world that offers ten more, a speed run of the entire game, as well as a level editor to design your own stages).
Like many casual games, this is based on a one to three star rating system. Each of the ninety levels and ten bonus base this on your skill, which is basically how often you trigger a time paradox. This leaves you grabbing and avoiding coins originally missed, collecting the ones that were picked up, and jumping on defeated enemies to bring them back to life. The placement of a lot of these, other than the mushrooms you bounce off of and certain platforms, are incredibly random and often illogical, making you feel like you’re backtracking a new gamer’s save and not one from a competent player.
While Spoiler Alert sounds like a fun idea with plenty of potential in theory, it actually ends up a wasted opportunity overall. Nearly all the stages are two to three seconds long, maybe five to six maximum, and most have the same general outline as well. An obstacle is introduced and plays a role in a few levels until something new is brought in like a power-up you need to impale yourself on spikes to obtain once more. Your character also moves on its own, so all you’re really doing is timing your jumps, which gets tediously boring after five minutes of gameplay at the most.
The music doesn’t really help much either, being corny performances that are fun for about the same amount of time, if not less. The sound effects being in reverse is a nice touch, but the voice over when you create a time paradox (i.e. fail miserably) is annoying after the first few times you hear it. The graphics are nice for the most part, having an upbeat hand drawn touch that those who played Super Mario Bros. games could kind of appreciate. The characters themselves look like they stepped out of a children’s book, while the backgrounds look like something out of any Nintendo or Super Nintendo title of that franchise complete with smiling trees and three hidden treasure boxes you open by jumping up and hitting them with your head.
Even with the bonus modes and additional level editor, Spoiler Alert can become rather tedious after a brief while. It took me a little less than two hours of playing everything the game has to offer, obtaining three star ranks on all one hundred stages, doing a single speed run that clocked in at about thirty minutes, as well as unlocking all the achievements the Steam version comes with. Others who played this title claim to have done all this in about an hour, which does seem possible to accomplish with how easy the game actually is. While the concept of Spoiler Alert, a game played in reverse, has plenty of potential, it’s squandered for the sake of an incredibly short and basic title. While this “standard edition” isn’t bad, really only being worth a shot if you get this on sale at the cost of mere pocket change or or even in a Steam bundle somewhere, its still not that memorable, or even entirely enjoyable an experience.
Review originally posted at Apoch's Metal Review

Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2. The mere concept of a sequel to last year's surprise hit is enough to send chills down the spines of the game's die-hard fans. Luckily, those chills are not in vain - Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 is the perfect example of how to make a sequel to an already amazing game. The levels are bigger, the trick catalog is more plentiful, the number of goals per level has been doubled, and the already stunning gameplay has been honed even further.
All of the professional skaters from the first game have returned, and new skaters like Rodney Mullen, Eric Koston, and Steve Caballero have been added to the roster. Also, you can create your own skater, choosing from different skin and model types. All of the first game's modes are back. You can opt to skate a two-minute single session, freely skate around a level with no time limit, or enter the career mode. The career mode here is much more than the first game's. Completing level goals in career mode earns cash, and you spend that cash on higher attribute points, new boards, and new tricks. This makes the game pretty customizable - if you don't like your skaters tricks, a little money and some time on the trick screen and you can set any trick to almost any button combination you want.
With the exception of the three competition levels, each level in the game has ten different goals, each with a different dollar value assigned to it. Three of the goals are score-based, and you still have to spell skate and collect a hidden tape as well. Four of the goals are fairly level specific. In New York, you'll do things like collect subway tokens, 50-50 grind on a sculpture, and grind on a set of subway rails. In Philly, you'll have to drain a fountain, find four lips and do lip tricks on them, and collect small liberty bells. In Venice, you'll ollie over five "magic" bums, tailslide the Venice Ledge, collect spray paint cans, and find four specially marked transfers. Finally, the goal in each level is completed when you've completed the other nine goals and collected every piece of spinning money. In competition levels, you earn 90 percent completion by earning the gold medal, and the remaining 10 percent comes from collecting all the cash in the level. Later levels are opened up when you've collected a certain amount of cash. You don't need to get 100 percent completion in each level to beat the game's final level, but you'll be too addicted to the game to settle for anything less.
The multiplayer game is just as exciting as it was in the original. With the exception of horse, all of the other modes are played simultaneously. Trick attack is a timed score contest. Graffiti tags a surface with your skater's color when you include it in a trick - if you do a better trick on a surface owned by your opponent, it switches to your color. Tag gives each player a timer, which only counts down when you're "it." The first player to run out of time loses. The game still runs at full speed in the two-player split screen modes, though most of the levels have been altered a bit for multiplayer - for instance, the Skatestreet level loses its outdoor areas, and the Bullring no longer allows you to get up into the stands, which have been replaced by draw-in shrouding fog.
Tony Hawk 2 looks so good that you may occasionally have trouble believing it's a PlayStation game. The textures are large and colorful, and some levels include lots of nicely detailed graffiti. The levels themselves are absolutely enormous, each containing at least one hidden area. Yet even with the large levels, the game runs at a nice, solid speed at all times. The camera works extremely well in almost any situation, though it would have been nice to see a look function in the game, like the skater's eye function found in Sony's extremely Hawk-like Grind Session.
The only real problem with the original Tony Hawk's audio was that the soundtrack was a little singular - if you didn't like that style of music, you were essentially out of luck. Tony Hawk 2 breaks up the monotony nicely, a wide range of artists including Naughty By Nature, Powerman 5000, Rage Against the Machine, Dub Pistols, Papa Roach, Anthrax (featuring Public Enemy), and Bad Religion. The game's sound effects are outstanding, mixing a nice balance of ambient sound (nearby cars, trains, announcers at the skate competitions, and so on) and the sounds of skating, such as the clink of your trucks hitting a rail, the different textured sounds of varying surfaces, and, of course, the sound of your skater's body slamming to the pavement.
The first game already had extremely tight gameplay - the levels were designed with big trick combos in mind, but there was room for personal style and innovation. Tony Hawk 2 opens up the concept even further with the addition of manuals - essentially front or back wheelies - which you can use to link trick combos together when crossing flat land. The larger levels of Tony Hawk 2 are extremely manual-friendly, yet the manuals never give the game a gimmicky feel. Instead, they really give you even more control over your skater and open up the scoring for even bigger combos. Also, the first game had gaps - small bonuses that gave you points for transfers, jumps, and long rails. Tony Hawk 2 is packed with these gaps; some levels have well over 40 different gaps. A gap checklist on the options screen helps you keep track of which gaps you've yet to find.
Another amazing addition is the skate park editor. The editor gives you an empty room and lets you fill it up with rails, ramps, pools, boxes, and just about anything else. It's extremely easy to use, and you can set it up for single-player and multiplayer play. Also, in case you aren't feeling terribly creative, Neversoft has stashed a ton of levels on the disc for you to mess around with. The skate park editor is great on its own, and it justifies owning DexDrive, as well. Surely a smattering of fan sites will offer large collections of created levels for download to such a device.
Near the end of a platform's life , most of its software falls into one of two categories. The first is shovelware - cheaply produced games hoping to cash in on the platform's large installed user base. Games in this category fail to innovate and come off as games that would have been decent three or four years ago, but simply can't compete with a system's better offerings. The second category is a fairly elite club, containing games from developers that clearly know how to exploit the aging hardware for all its worth. The PlayStation's final year is coming to a close, and in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2, Neversoft has put together a game that clearly belongs at the top of the second category. As most major publishers' development efforts shift to any number of next-generation platforms, Tony Hawk 2 will likely stand as one of the last truly fantastic games to be released on the PlayStation.

When to buy: Wait for a bundle. The brevity of the game does not justify the price. It's also worth noting that there is no upgrade DLC of sorts from Standard Edition to Collector's Edition, so wait for Collector's Edition to hit a bundle.
Ultimately, a weak recommendation from me. However, I would like to add that I did enjoy the Collector's Edition extras - the music is aurally beautiful and there's even an old game jam demo of the game.
I did have my share of fun with the game, the comics and cutscenes were rather funny. Ultimately, however, Spoiler Alert falls
(pun intended) of being worth it. That does not mean to say that the game is bad, but people will find it hard to pay three dollars for a game that won't last them more than an hour at the most.
Here's the kicker: it does not take long to 100% the game. Each level does not take long on average to complete (even if you repeatedly escape to the main menu just so you can get a gold trophy after a failure), and with only around 60+ levels excluding the bonus Mariachi levels, you're going to be done with this phenomally quick. So quick that in fact I hadn't even gotten all my card drops yet. No matter, idle the game until I got the last one. The short length proved to be quite a downer for me.
Levels vary from "stupendously easy" to "require the darndest bit of perfect timing". Levels that fall in the latter category have to be played incredibly precisely. The jumping and hit detection feels off at times - sometimes I jump at the correct moment or think I dodge a particular coin or enemy...OH NO YOU DON'T!, I hit it instead, causing a time paradox. Pretty much about the only challenge that's stopping people from completing the game faster than expected.
Spoiler Alert is a side-scrolling platformer that's already been completed before you play it - the goal of the game is to "un-complete" it, i.e. go in reverse. And, as you can clearly see, this review is also pretty much the same way.

The first game to be released out of a planned three part series, Celestian Tales is a game fashioned after JRPGs of yore. It has all the charm of many older games while having modern polish and refinement. CT is a very character-centric, story based game. There are 6 playable characters, each of whom has their own perspective on the events taking place. Allthough all are young, each has a unique background that shapes who they are today. The plot of the story isn't anything special; it's a typical european-style feudal society dealing with politics and war. The shining point of the story is watching how the characters interact and grow while they travel through the events that take place.
All non-scripted enemy encounters can be seen on the field ahead of time, and players are able to choose whether to stand their ground or to attempt to bypass the fight. The battle system utilizes a traditional turn-based menu system in which both friendly and enemy characters take turns choosing their actions based on their quickness. Character skills and abilities synergize not only with the unique skills each individual character possesses, but with their teammates' abilities as well. Even with your team size limited to three characters at once, there are many varied squad compositions that are perfectly viable without any grinding needed to prop up their workability. Upon completing a battle, you are automatically restored back to full resources, This allows you to continue to push forward through the story without having to constantly backtrack to an inn after a random encounter gone bad.
There is only a single experience bar, and all 6 characters level up together even if not used in combat. This allows for constant access to multiple characters without having to worry about grinding them up to par first. Each character has access to 3 weapons which can be upgraded by using materials gathered from encounters. Each weapon ends up having a vastly different specialization from the other two making the choice between weapon lines meaningful, despite having limited options. You are also allowed one piece of armor and two accessories to customize your characters farther. The choices in armor are just steps in increased survivability as you go through the story; there aren't really any interesting options there. The accessories on the other hand give you dozens of ways to customize your characters, though very few, if any, give choices as meaningful as you're given with your weapons.
As far as difficulty goes, I think Ekuator did an amazing job balancing everything out considering the experience of the team and the budget and scope of the game. I enjoyed the entire time playing through and never felt like I had hit any steep difficulty curves. As someone who grew up playing JRPGs on the NES, I would have enjoyed it if the game was a bit more challenging overall, but I think that it is challenging enough as is for the average gamer.
Due to automaticly replenishing resources I did my first playthrough with an extremely aggressive team build, wondering how far I could get before I would have to rely on something safer. I never ended up having to swap out my main line-up in order to progress, despite it basically being a rogue+ranger+assassin team. Although I would have liked to have had the option to tune up the difficulty a bit, I think the only thing that actually bothered me was how easy it was to level up. I felt like I had gone days out of my way to grind, when I had only made sure to not skip any enemies the first time through, and skipped almost all of them when exploring or backtracking. I'm not advocating for any forced grinding, but I think the games challenge might have held up better if exp was 20-30% slower. This is especially true since the party members that aren't currently fighting get the same exp as everyone else.
I would say its a 6-10 hour game your first time through, but it could have easily been 20-30 hours if, like older games, it inconvenienced you with more random battles and forced you to backtrack to an inn 2-3 times per dungeon to replenish suppliess and resources if you wanted to make sure you explored every corner. In all, I'd say its definately worth the buy, just be ready to wonder what's going to happen to all the unresolved threads of the story while they work on part 2.

Old North is the start of a three-part series from Ekuator Games.  It was funded on Kickstarter, a campaign which I managed to miss although I certainly intend to throw some cash at them for the next one!
Old North is a JRPG-style game.  Fairly short - my first playthough was 7:46 - and easy.  Battles are turn-based, and your characters have stamina points which build up each turn to allow you to use skills.
The most interesting thing about the game is the six main characters.  You can play through as any one of them (and get an achievement for finishing the game as all six).  While the main plot remains the same, each character has a unique viewpoint, with their own scenes and knowledge.  Camille, for example, learns something very important from her brother near the end of the game which the other five characters remain totally unaware of, while Aria, the dogmatic Paladin, seems a lot more human when you see her defying her father and struggling with honouring a dead soldier of another religion.
The overarching plot is that of these six characters becoming Squires, and taking part in a war and various political events which shape their world.  As the game is the first chapter of three, it ends of something of a cliffhanger.  Throughout the game you make choices - such as letting a group of bandits go to trial or be hanged by the villagers - which, in theory, will change the shape of the future games in the series.
The game is short and simple enough - with one hidden boss to beat and some weapons to upgrade as side-plots - that playing through it six times only feels like a bit of a chore, especially with the added intrigue of new scenes.

The community is fairly divided on Starbound because many people that have owned it for years have seen it regress over time. I'll try to put this into perspective for those that are unfamiliar with the game's development history.
Imagine that Minecraft is still in early access and you haven't played it in a while. After a prolonged period of time, a large update is released, so you go to check out how the game has changed. To your surprise, the developers have removed The Nether (the dimension that looks like Hell) and all the materials and crafting recipes that went along with it. They replace it with a crappy, linear platformer level where you are required to jump over subsequent pits of lava, with a time limit of a minute or so, to get some crappy prize, like a few mushrooms or a bucket or something. After searching for several hours without any luck, you discover on an online forum that diamonds and the associated crafting recipes are all gone. Instead, the developers have implemented a new kind of ore that is functionally identical to iron, but has a different color and allows you to craft iron items with that color instead of the normal color. Upon exploring underground, you notice there are WAY MORE underground structures than there used to be, each one being just a few meters away from each other, and that there are only 3-4 different types of underground structures... like the entire underground world is just a mosaic of these repetitive structures! In fact, they are so abundant now that the randomly generated caves are almost missing from the game because there is no room for them to exist.
You begin to scratch your head. You wonder why the developers would make these types of changes and why it took 6 months to do so. You notice that the entire community is also upset about these changes and that the number of people that like the new direction is nearly zero. Another 6 months go by and another major update is released. You check it out with the hopes that the developers listened to the players' complaints and reinstated some of the old content, or to see if any of the new content is worthwhile. Instead of reinstating diamonds, there are now 5 types of iron, again, functionally identical, just of 5 different colors. But now in order to unlock iron recipes, you now need to find a village and complete 10-12 'fetch quests' for the villagers. FOR EACH NEW GAME, you are now REQUIRED to spend 2-3 hours at the start catching fish, baking cakes, collecting wood, etc. to fullfill these quests before you can aquire recipes for iron items. Also, the Ender Dragon has been removed from the game entirely... for seemingly no reason at all, and isn't replaced with anything new or any new use for the Ender dimension.
Now, if it were your first time playing Minecraft, would you find this updated game fun? I think so... probably... I guess....? But for many that have been around for a while, it's almost painful to play the recent releases of the game. Almost every single example I gave for the theoretical Minecraft development scenario pertains to some analogous change that was made in Starbound over the years with very spread out updates. From many user reviews, I see development updates summarized as "one step forward, two steps back". This really isn't an exagerration. It isn't just a bunch of content-hungry impleasable fans whining about nothing.
It's been unfortunate, confusing, and painful to witness this game's development over the past few years. I hope new players that just purchased the game can enjoy their purchase, but I pity them for not being able to experience the version I loved 2-3 years ago. I pity all of us for never being able to play the game we envisioned would be the final release. It's almost as if whoever developed the game until 2012-2013 sold it off to a disorganized team of complete amatuers, who just screwed up the appeal and balance of them game. What really set this game apart from Terraria, Minecraft (and countless others) was the appeal of uncovering the unknown, and the promise for expansion in this direction. Minecraft and Terraria have more/less one world you can play in that becomes knowable in a few hours, whereas in Starbound, you were always excited to find out what the next planet would be like, what types of secrets it would hold. This is the partly why Star Citizen has raised over 115 million USD. It's why the new Mass Effect game is bringing back and expanding upon the planet exploration concept. It's why we are all eager to see how No Man's Sky turns out. This is what drove us to play Starbound, but even in beta, it never felt complete. This aspect, the most promising and differentiating aspect of Starbound, was simply never completed. In fact, it was 'benched'/reduced for game elements that nobody wanted, such as a linear, mundane quest line.

Sometimes I hear people say that games cannot be art, as they're merely for entertainment and if they try too hard to become art their gameplay will suffer. Bastion begs to differ.
In creating this, Supergiant Games has managed to develop a game that is great both in its gameplay and in the realm of art, something that few games can manage to do. Granted, Bastion's gameplay is nothing revolutionary, being similar to a lot of games in the hack n' slash genre, but the game does offer a sufficient amount of customization to allow one to "personalize" the game to their playstyle. A player can choose their weapons of choice, upgrade them to their liking, choose their favorite alcoholic beverages (which are the game's passives), and if they're up for a challenge they can invoke the gods to buff enemies in a variety of ways in return for more spoils. Then if a player wants to, they can change all of those aspects 5 minutes later for their next adventure. Despite all this, my main complaint with the game is that it's fairly short, being about 6 hours a playthrough, but thankfully the game's customization and various modes give it some nice replayability.
Of course, I can't forget to talk more about Bastion's artistic side. The game's plot is almost entirely told by its narrator, who follows the experiences of "The Kid" following a strange apocalyptic event known as "The Calamity." Unlike some games which only elaborate on their stories between levels or during times of rest, Bastion's story is constantly expanded upon by the narrator, who provides frequent commentary (with his soothing voice) on the games events and lore as the player explores a ruined world. Now the phrase "a ruined world" may paint the picture of a crumbled and rustic land in some minds, but in reality the game's artwork depicts much of the opposite, as the world is vibrantly colored and the surviving parts of it are mostly in tact (except for the whole floating around an abyss in chunks deal). But I digress, if you are in the mood for a hack n' slash game with exceptional storytelling and artwork (or even just one or the other), give this game a try sometime.

A fundamental flaw in sailing survival games is establishing a base. Much like Salt, each island is dotted with "some" resources. More likely than not, the island you begin upon has enough resources to start a small house, get some food, and maintain a fire for a few days. Yet, eventually, you'll have to sail in order to restock on either rocks, sticks, coconuts, or whatever you need at that moment.
At this point, you'll feel inclined to simply gather the supplies and head back to your home island. However, you'd be wrong in doing that. The islands are so vastly apart from one another, the traveling can be ridiculously long (I'm not even going to mention the fact that your vessel sometimes just disappears; it's a bug). Not only that, you can only carry so many items at a time. Could you, technically, take a small handful of items over and over back and forth between the islands and your home base? Yes, but why would you?
Think about it: eventually, even the nearest outlying islands (despite how incredibly far apart each island is) will eventually run out of materials. Eventually, you'll have to move your base. Now, moving your base - the act in of itself - is not so terrible. However, what makes base-building fun is a sense of satisfaction. You created a castle and have the ability to admire it. You rule the lands and its farae naturae through your ingenuity and sheer architectural domination. The only time you are then inclined to leave is after you have thoroughly enjoyed the fruits of the land, and that's the issue.
In Stranded Deep, you are not given a chance to really enjoy your satisfaction. Instead of enjoying your ability to survive, your time is mostly - nearly all - is spent finding the few meager sources you have and then sailing off. Quite literally, you spend about 20 minutes finding and using supplies/surivivng and 40 minutes sailing. The best example I can think of is a buffet but the plates are super, super small. You are not satisfied after a plate; you did not get to have your salad first, then your protein, and then your dessert. Instead, you are given your salad but one lettuce leaf at a time. Will you eventually get your whole meal? Well, yes, but ♥♥♥♥ if it isn't tedious.
There's nothing wrong with establishign a need to relocate. Minecraft, The Forest, and The Long Dark all have that feature. However, those games do not immediately force you to relocate after 10 minutes. Your first base, in all those games, give you enough time to get a feel for the game, understand the mechanics, and prepares you for the next journey. Stranded Deep just sort of keeps you walking at all times with no sense of fulfillment. In this sense, imagine running a marathon. You're at the start and you get prepped, prepared, and maybe even assign a friend to meet you half-way for a bottle of Gatorade. That beginning prep is what gets you excited for the struggle to survive. Stranded Deep, on the other hand, slaps your♥♥♥♥♥across the starting line while you're still trying to kiss your mum goodbye and goodluck and forever extends the finish line.
There's no rest. There's no fulfillment. There's no real point. You  re-establish a home base because you have no other option, not because the game just happens to tell you to do so.

I got Everything at a very low price and I don't regret this purchase at all. The concept and design is very interesting, but it has some hits and some misses. This game is beautiful in its depictions of wildlife, especially birds, insects, ocean life, and microscopic life. The ability to become any object and explore various levels of the macro and micro worlds is mindblowing. There are so many random objects that the hunt for something you haven't seen before becomes an obsession. The exploration alone has provided hours of entertainment and the many philosophical lectures make it even better.
There are some things about Everything that are not as beautiful, however. I was rather disappointed by the continental and cosmic parts of the game. They weren't as aesthetically pleasing as they could have been and are far too limited in their features and appearance. For example, the only landmasses are green continents, sand continents, ice continents, rock continents, alien continents, and city continents. It would have been nice to see volcanoes, mountain ranges, jungles, islands, you know, a world more like our own.
There was a disappointingly limited number of celestial objects as well, even more-so at the planetary level. The planets are just as boring and cookie-cutter as the continents. For example, the only explorable planets are ice planets, green planets, sand planets, rock planets, and alien planets, so you get the idea. As for non-explorable planets, it's just the dwarf planets and mesoplanets. There are no gas giants and if you see a moon then you won't be able to get to it, since moons are apparently just purely cosmetic extensions of planets rather than seperate objects.
I also wasn't a fan of the rolling land animals or the frogs that couldn't hop. I know there is an artistic explanation for it, but it still came off as a real shortfall on the animators part. The fact that only four-legged land mammals have to move by rolling while pretty much every other living thing moves in a relatively natural manner only makes it seem more like laziness in my eyes.
The city portion of the game was also not my cup of tea. The city itself felt incomplete and just seemed very strange and out of place. Honestly, I think this would have been a better game if the developers didn't bother with the city portion so they could have devoted more time and resources to improving the natural aspects of the game.
Despite the nitpicking complaints, I am really enjoying the novelty of this game and it should make a nice screensaver once that novelty wears off. Everything is a good game that provides a unique and relaxing experience. Though I'm glad to have purchased this title at a discount, I would definitely recommend it at full price.

I recommend this game! Very interesting concept of a tower defense game. You need to think logically about creating the path for the enemies and using your towers in the most efficient way to pass a level. It differs from other TD games. Why? Because in most of tower defense games you just build your defense, sit back, relax and watch your towers crush the enemies. Updated review (I have completed all routes with 100% achievement) :
If you are looking for an RPG with a long playthrough and tons of contents, I won't recommend this game. All this game has to offer are its aesthetics & super short story. Also, most of the choices you make in this game do not have a long-term effect in the game yet which will make some people (especially hardcore RPG fans) left dissapointed.
If you are looking for an RPG that can be completed in just a few hours because you are too busy in real life and if you are a completionist who are looking for easy 100% steam achievements, this game is for you.
If you want to get into more details about this game, continue to read, which you should.
There are 2 things that I found after I completed this game with every single character :
1. If I want to recommend you which character to play :
Reynard (he has the highest amount of moral choices in the playthrough. he's probably the one with the real character development)
Isaac (he has the best background story & plot twists)
Cammile (interesting ending, play as her if you wanna know about what is going on in the game)
Aria (interesting whole story, play as her if you wanna know more about the potential villains in the game)
I find Lucienne & Ylianne story as the most unexciting, uninteresting ones.
2. The harsh truth about this game is there is almost no reason for you to replay the game with another character unless you are a completionist like me. Even if you want to know the story, you can simply ask someone else who have completed the character's story that you are curious with. Besides that, the only thing that makes this game a bit longer is because you are forced to re-visit the same place over and over again.
Pros :
- Interesting story and lore.
- Distinct character personalities makes dialogues more interesting & enjoyable.
- Beautiful hand-drawn environment combined with plenty of great soundtracks.
- The whole party level up at the same time including the characters who do not participate in battles.
- The game encourages you to explore each map to find honour medals, weapons, and some items.
- No random battle. You can avoid all monsters if you want to.
Neutrals :
- Typical old school JRPG turn based combat system. Nothing special except for the stamina system. Some might enjoy it, some might find it pretty boring.
- 30 max level. Some may think it is too low, but some may not because the game itself is pretty short. I don't see any reason for the developer to increase the level cap above level 30 for a game with short playthrough.
Cons :
- Even though the developer has added a few mechanics to add more depth in the combat (stamina, skill builds, whole party level up, 3 upgradeable weapons for each character), combat still feels unexciting that I wanted to skip most of the encounter. But sadly, I couldn't, or I'm gonna get wrecked at the last chapters because of the next con below.
- Combat difficulty spikes at late game.
- For an RPG, the amount of places you can visit is lacking in this game. You will be forced to visit the same places over and over again just to prolong the length of the game. This makes your adventure a bit boring and less exciting.
- Choices you make do not matter on this episode, but probably they will matter on the next episode. I can see that maybe your choices you make now will determine your characters personality & backstory in the next episode. Celestian Tales is a trilogy after all.
- For an RPG, I personally think the game length is super short. I suggest the sequel to be at least twice longer than this.
