The story is about 6 characters ranging from very different families (poor, rich, outcast etc. etc.) to become squires for a certain house. Together with the other houses, these will be in war with World Enders (big demonic vikings that want to destroy everything).
To be able to do this they will have to make choices between things important to them... devotion to their god, their family, their habits, their heritage and more.
How far will you go to protect what you love?
Overall its not a bad turnbased jrpg at all and the overall gameplay feel is very nice.
As i said before... the game doesnt go for over the top futuristic "we got so many unseen gaming features" and "look at these new mechanics" ... instead they simply build an well-made game that is basically "good" ... not "super amazing hypetrain 2060", but still a good distance above "avarage". Yust a good game that can be enjoyed if you like story and this type genre... nothing more, nothing less.

This one tips the scales back and forth between being a good or bad game for me at least.
The art is hand drawn, quite beautiful. Reminiscent of Suikoden which is awesome btw.
Allowing replayability with 6 different characters.
First little bit of gameplay if you'd like to check before you buy
Different gear and tactics do change it up a bit
Rather good storytelling.
Now for the cons:
First off, does have a few bugs. Like showing a summary of chapter 7 when your in chapter 1. Kind of a spoiler and some nps go a little funky hopefully gets patched out. SPOILERS! And when your at the war camp and go back to Levantine and they are already talking about the victory that hasn't EVEN happend yet. I'm sorry but how do you mess that one up? Did they think you would stay on the rails and never look around lol.
Battle is rather boring and you'll find you can just spam the attack commands as you will usually get the same results using tactics most of the time.
Other than your main character you will never feel like your getting any in depth character knowledge of any other characters in the game. You could replace the supporting characters with potatoes and I'd get the same feelings and at least we'd have french fries.
If you poke around other than the main questline you'll find it all rather empty and linear forcing you back on the main quest. Pretty  scenery but all the npcs say rather generic stuff.
Story tempo is crazy fast paced as beating this one with each character reportedly doesn't take too long. The game is part of a planned trilogy. Budget-wise it probably was easier to make this three parts to fund it but I feel it would have been better off all in one game.
Does boast your character will be faced with tough decisions. Yes that is true, but nowhere do you actually ever have a choice on what to do.
Conclusion:
The game defintitely qualifies as a work of art. harkens back to a better day of JRPG'S.
Suffers from too fast paced storyline and not enough side stuff or a real vibrant world you feel you belong in.
The battle is standard JRPG fare and defintely a step up from RPG maker slush filling up steam on a daily basis.
The story is pretty good, just makes me wish it was slower and a little more, but wanting more is never a bad thing. Actually looking forward to the sequel.

I started playing this. I picked Isaac Goldenlake as my character. In the  first five minutes you learn there are miraculous healings but only the nobility can have  them, regardless of income. If you are noble, you get free miracle cures. So Reed's mother dies because they farm out of the world's worst hovels.
Fast forward a few random encounters. Fights don't seem to give XP, but you heal HP and MP(think FFTA style MP) before every  fight so it doesn't matter. Combat's not bad, it seems, but ultimately pointless, unless that changes off the prologue.
We find Isaac Goldenlake having been wounded. A priest will heal him, of course. Reed, enraged, stabs him, only to find he is POOR and the ONLY SON of a SUPER SICK DYING FATHER. So he takes the place of the son of a nobleman and decides he'll change things. He goes on a boat and tries to offer the crew money but NO, COMMONERS CAN'T TAKE MONEY FROM NOBILITY, THEY MUST DO EVERYTHING FOR FREE.
I submitted my refund there. Maybe some of  the other storylines are okay, but this one was so hamfisted I couldn't stand it.
Let's clear some things up. 1) I am perfectly in love with down stories about the true struggle of humanity, but you can't force them through quickly like this game did in trying to set up Isaac.
2) There are first five minute spoilers.

3) Serfdom was a form of bondage, but it was rarely out and out slavery as came about, say, in the early Colonial South. You treated your serfs well so you could get crops back. Commoners didn't have amazing lives but they were rarely neck under bootheel slaves.
4) I'd love to see some reviews about the exactly story writing of the game in depth, as all the ones so far just talk about the combat and the graphics(the graphics aren't even that great.) Does the storywriting get better? Does it make up for some of the early mistakes? Write about it.

This game speaks for itself. I've been waiting for this game for a while and I can say that I'm not disappointed! Taking into consideration that the game is in early access and does not have loads of things to do, I bought the game yesterday and already have over eight hours of gameplay, just shows that even with little variety of things to craft and do, the game kept me occupied and feeling like I was actually stranded in the middle of the sea, surviving off coconuts.
For an early access game, there has been next to no bugs and glitches for me, give and take a few sharks swimming under my island and me learning to fly by running with a palm tree in my hands. The graphics are visually exciting and the day and night cycle does make a big effect within the gaming experience.
As a lover of survival games, I have been waiting for a game that doesn't revolve around zombies or aliens, which have become a craze lately. This game fills a once missing slot in the survival genre and made me @$%& bricks when I saw my first shark! (being one of my life long fears). The crafting is fun and unique and I love it, which makes it different to every other game, so props to the person that came up with that idea xD
Survival really isn't easy and I can't explain the struggle when you need one more rock to complete your fire, and the island you're on doesn't provide for you. The diving is a new experience and it surely got my adrenaline going when diving to some of the deeper wrecks, checking a sunken boat to be greeted by a tiger shark as you leave isn't the calmest situation.
It took me a while to get used to the crafting recipes but once I got the hand of them they were stuck in my memory, just take a quick look at the wiki to make your life easier (link below).
This game has a lot of potential and I have high hopes for the game and the developers! I'm sure in time to come there will be a wide amount of loot and crafting recipes added, which will make the game so much better! Multiplayer will be amazing but the singleplayer is just as fun on its own, coming from a gamer that gets bored of singleplayer games quickly, it would be a shame if the multiplayer (if added) was rushed, for it to then be ruined due to it not being ready.
Over all Stranded Deep is exiting and has a lot of potential for the future! It gives a solid feel to being stranded and lost at sea. It is easy to run, took less than a minute to download and is giving me many hours of fun. The physics in the game are lovely and dragging chopped down trees to your camp is actually pretty amusing, amongst throwing crabs and frisbeeing your raft! I do strongly recommend the game, although it has got a lot to be added to it for it to be perfect, I will enjoy following it as grows.
I hope that I've gave you a little insight to the game and feel free to message and ask questions if you would like to know anything else.
Thanks, Jack

I'm just getting back to this game after about 4 years off from it. I have noticed that Deca has fixed some of the issues that Kabaam started with all the extreme anti-consumerism and forcing you to buy items/vault chests. The Daily Quests are cool, and Login Rewards are nice.
One main issue that remains, and that Deca seems to only be making worse, is the exaggerated need for space constantly. The Daily Quests revolve around collecting "marks" from defeated dungeons to bring back for rewards. The problem is that you can't stack these marks, the same issue with the game in general with other items that should be stackable. This causes many to not even go for the Daily Quests, because how valuable inventory space is in this game, with only 8 slots, and 16 if u have a backpack.
If Deca fixed that 1 issue, it'd be so much of an improvement all around in the enjoyability of this game. Not having to Nexus back to my Vault every few minutes, and actually being able to explore and go searching for white bags, would be much more fun. I feel inventory space in general should be 16 or 32 slots, with most items other than main gear being stackable to 10+. Stat pots should have been changed to stackable long ago, again, it drains the fun of the gameplay to be forced to Nexus every other minute on account of low inv slots and non-stackability of general items.

Let's see where do I start...
The game is incredibly fun. The plot is that there is the town and there are Mafia or Coven (If you get Coven expansion pack) and Mafia know who Mafia is and Coven know who Coven is. Their goals are to kill everybody who would oppose them. But then you have Town who are trying to figure out who Mafia and Coven is but they don't know who is Town and who isn't. Then there are roles who aren't part of Town, Mafia, or Coven called Neutral roles. These are roles who have a goal that is unique to them. Survivor's goal is to survive until the end of the game. Jester has to try and get themselves lynched. Executioner has to get their target lynched. Amnesiac remembers a dead persons role. Etc. Now I'll get into the roles and what they do.
Town Roles:
Town Investigative:
Sheriff - Check one person each night for suspicious activity. You are able to find all Mafia members except the Godfather, all of the Coven (without the Necronomicon), and the Serial Killer and Werewolf (on a full moon)
Investigator - Investigate someone each night for a hint of their role. You will be given three to five possible roles that your target may be
Spy - Watch who the Mafia and Coven visit at night and 'bug' someone.
Lookout - Watch someone at night to see who visits them.
Tracker - Exclusive to the Coven expansion only. Track one person at night to see who they visit.
Psychic - Exclusive to the Coven expansion only. Receive a vision every night. On odd nights you will receive a vision of three players, at least one is evil. On even nights you will receive a vision of two players, at least one is good.
Town Killing:
Jailor - You may choose one person during the day to jail for the night. (Three executions and if you execute a town you can't execute anymore)
Vampire Hunter - Check for Vampires each night. (Only available if there are Vamps in the game)
Veteran - Decide if you will go on alert and kill anyone who visits you. (You have 3 alerts)
Vigilante - Choose to take justice into your own hands and shoot someone. (Three bullets and if you kill a town you commit suicide)
Town Protective:
Bodyguard - Protect one person from death each night. (If you protect them you die instead of them whille killing that person)
Doctor - Heal one person each night, preventing them from dying. (And one Self heal)
Crusader (Coven Only) - Protect one person during the night. (You kill everyone who visits even if their good.)
Trapper (Coven Only) - You may set up a Trap at another player's house.
Town Support:
Escort - Distract someone each night.
Mayor - Gain 3 votes when you reveal yourself as Mayor.
Medium - Speak with all dead people at night. (If you die you can talk to someone who is alive once)
Retributionist - You may revive a dead town member. (Only one)
Transporter - Choose two people to transport at night. (Whatever happens to one of them will happen to the other person)
Mafia Roles:
The Mafia all share a common goal: "Kill all who will not submit to the Mafia." These include any members of the Town, any members of the Coven, any Neutral Killings, and any Neutral Chaos roles.
Disguiser - Choose a target to disguise yourself as. (If you die whatever role they are you will show as.)
Forger - Choose a person and rewrite their last will at night.
Framer - Choose one person to frame each night.
Hypnotist (Coven only) - You may sneak into a players house at night and plant a memory.
Janitor - Choose a dying person to clean each night. (Won't show role, or last will)
Ambusher (Coven only) - You may choose lie in wait outside your targets house.
Godfather - Kill someone each night.
Mafioso - Carry out the Godfather's orders.
Blackmailer - Choose one person each night to blackmail. (Meaning they can't talk or whisper during the day. You can also listen to whispers.)
Consigliere - Check one person for their exact role each night.
Consort - Distract someone each night. (Mafia version of Escort)
Neutral Roles:
The Neutral roles each have different goals, and some of those are compatible with the goals of the other teams, meaning that some of these roles are able to win alongside them. It's worth checking the goal descriptions to see who you can potentially ally with as a Neutral.
Neutral Benign:
Amnesiac - Remember who you were by selecting a graveyard role. (So you can remember someone's role who died.)
Guardian Angel (Coven only) - Keep your target alive. (You have a select target and can protect them from death at night)
Survivor - Put on a bulletproof vest at night, protecting yourself from attacks. (You have four vests and win with anyone)
Neutral Chaos:
Pirate (Coven only) - Choose a player to plunder each night. (You win if you successfully plunder two people.)
Plaguebearer (Coven only) - You may choose to infect a player with the Plague each night. (When everyone is infected you become Pestilence)
Pestilence (Coven only) - You may choose to Rampage at a player's house each night. (Kill everyone who visits that player and the player themselves)
Vampire - Convert others to Vampires at night.
Neutral Evil:
Executioner - Trick the Town into lynching your target.
Jester - Trick the Town into voting against you.
Witch (Unavailable in Coven) - Control someone each night.
Neutral Killing:
Arsonist - Douse someone in gasoline or ignite all doused targets.
Juggernaut (Coven only) - You may choose to attack a player on Full Moon nights. (Appears as ???? on role list)
Serial Killer - Kill someone each night.
Werewolf - Transform into a Werewolf during the Full Moon.
Coven Roles: (All of these are only available in Coven expansion pack)
Coven Leader - You may choose to Control someone each night. (It's the Witch which is why Witch isn't available in Coven)
Hex Master - You may choose to hex a player each night. (When all players are hexed they all die unless they are Pestilence)
Medusa - You may choose to Stone Gaze all visitors at night. (Everyone who comes to you dies)
Necromancer - You may reanimate a dead player and use their ability on a player.
Poisoner - You may choose to poison a player each night.
Potion Master - You may choose to use a potion on a player each night. (Killing potion, healing potion, and role finding out potion)
Pros:
- Game is incredibly fun. You get a free skin for buying Steam version.
- Free on browser! Link:
- You can customize your character and buy scrolls to have higher chances of getting a certain role!
- Steam version gives you 2000 Town Points (The Gold Coins) So you can buy things! But use them wisely because the only way to get more is buying them with real money or getting them in the brewery.
- Merit Points are the free way of getting items. You get these from the brewery or from just playing the game in general.
- Buying Steam version gives you permanent 2x merit points
- You can actually suggest roles for them to add to the game! Link:
- You can play with friends!
- They have a ranked mode! Play 50 total Town of Salem games and 10 Ranked practice games to unlock it! Then you have to play 10 placement games.
- Communicate with fellow Mafia at night
- Communicate with fellow Coven at night
- You can choose your own name
Cons:
- People can be incredibly stupid sometimes.
- Some roles are really boring.
- Browser version sometimes freezes
That's the end of the review! Hope you all enjoy and I hope to see all of you play Town of Salem in the future!

Battle Brothers, even now (still in Early Access) is an amazing case of EA DONE RIGHT: frequent updates of the game itself, coherent and detailed road map, big dev log every Friday without fault. If on ly other games took the cue out of Overhype's book!
Now, the game itself is a mix of XCOM and JA with a medieval low fantasy setting (armors, weapons all reflect that and are actually well researched and accurate). You manage a band of mercenaries who gain stats as they complete variety of quests on the big, generated map (so no pkaythrough is the same). You compete with Undead, Orcs, Bandits and noble houses of (at times) conflicting interests.
Game art style is amazing and mechanics are very well done and easy to learn.
All in all, one of the few games I can WHOLEHEARTEDLY and without reservation recommend to anyone with even a passing interest in the squad tactics games, low fantasy setting or coolm distinctive art style.

Starbound does a whole lot of things. Starbound does nothing well. The devs of this game, and the game they have produced, both remind me of something I once was..
As a small boy I really, REALLY wanted to make the bestest game in the world. THE BEST GAME. That did everything perfect, and everyone would love me forever, and I would make all the money in the world, and would go down in history books. Because I made the best game in the world, and it did everything perfect, and everyone loved it, and therefore me. That's what Starbound tries to do, and it works only marginally better than that game I coded in middle school.
It has a plot. A paper-thin railroad plot. ChooChoo all aboard the 20-sentence railroad plot! Find the Mac-gruffins, no matter what race you are or what your motivations! I haven't seen a railroad this straight since...Fallout 4. And it wants to be a colony simulator. But the only thing your colonists do is walk around, pay paltry rent, and spout the same one-liners 500 times when you click on them. There's a lot of tiers of colonists....and every one equally pointless and shallow. And it wants to be an exploration game. With carefully handcrafted content. And procedural generation of worlds. ENTIRE WORLDS. Of procedeurally generated layers with the same 20 hand-crafted rooms used over, and over, and over. Procedural monsters too. A billion monsters! Made of the same 20 monster pieces used over, and over, and over. AND A MILLION-BILLION-JILLION RANDOM WEAPONS! But really, there's only 9 guns, and maybe 2 worth using. Did I mention it wants to be a survival simulator? With cold and hunger gnawing at your bones as you desperately search for....food that grows everywhere for free and never decays, and easily crafted immune-to-environment gizmos. Oh, that's right, they nerfed that into meaninglessness when the people who were asking for a plot didn't like survival needs interfering with their plot. (actually, they took it out completely, then put it back in half-heartedly when the people who wanted a survival simulator complained they were building a story/colony/exploration/building/everything game)
On a positive note, this game has way more mods than that pong variant I coded in middle-school ever got. They make the game *fun* by adding depth and challenge. I'm hesitant to recommend paying for the game because the mods are awesome, but there you have it. Is there any way we can buy just the mods and play those? Why do the filthy middle men who do nothing but provide a 'platform' and 'hype' get all the money and the people who make the game *fun* work for free? Why is life unfair? Mommy, will you die someday?

This game is way too easy and way too short. After 44 minutes I have 100% achievement progress; I beat the game in just under half an hour. Watching the credits is the most time consuming achievement.
The longest level of the game takes about 12 seconds to complete, there are several levels where you just need to jump one or two times to complete it.
You get a gold medal if you beat the level first try, but you can easily reset the level via the escape menu, so every try counts as first try. Since there are no checkpoints, there is no difference except in hearing the first 20 seconds of the music over and over again.
The idea for the game is nice, but it is not enough. You are automatically running backwards and mostly just jump over obstacles. It's a very bad and very easy version of Bit Trip Runner. In the whole game (including bonus stages and everything) you just use the Up-Key to jump and in about 30 levels you use the Z-Key for "actions". The actions are NEVER challenging. The hardest parts of the game include about 3 pixel-perfect jumps, you have to master. But because the levels are so short and you can restart them as you want, you will get these jumps by luck or training within one minute.
For achievement hunters like me, this game might be quite acceptable, since it is an easy 100% in less than an hour (10 achievements total).
But if you want to play a game for fun and/or challenge, you should rather play Runner 2. And if you like the concept of playing a game "backwards", try out Braid. It's not exactly that, but it has many elements of what is on your mind.
To be constructive, what the game needs:
- More challenge (e.g. don't have one "action skill" at a time, but have them all, so you use more than just 2 keys)
- Better level design and longer levels
- Another concept for getting Gold medals (e.g. don't have a time paradoxon, but give Gold to those, who can undo every object of the level)
- I think, this would be nicer, if you did not auto-run; although you then had to rethink the whole concept of the game
- Make more things, that make the game "backwardsy", like: A very high jump move, with which you can reach high platforms (from which the character originally fell down), but if you don't reach a high platform with the jump, you have a paradoxon
All in all: Don't buy it for more than 1€ or $. It's not worth it.
PS: There might be Workshop-Userlevels, that are better than the games original levels, but I rated the game here and not usermade content. The game itself should be good enough for a play and the userlevels should be an extra.

I wanted to like this game. In fact, I wanted to love this game, but I couldn't bring myself to it. Let me preface my review by saying I did not play Starbound when it was in its early access phases, so I did not experience the adventures that were, according to other reviewers, better than how the game is now.
The first few hours of the game were great, very fun actually. Lots of exploration, things to discover, and when I finally got my ship repaired and looked at the map of the universe, it looked massive, and I was so excited! I started going through the main questline with my first character, and it was going pretty well, until I started getting some framerate issues. I looked into it further, and apparently other players had been having these issues as well, and they recommended trying to run the 32-bit version of Starbound. This didn't help at all, so I just decided, "eh, whatever, it's just a few frame drops, I'll power through it." Then the visual tears arrived, and my patience started to dwindle. I tried powering through that too, but then Starbound kicked it up a notch, and crashed my entire computer. By the way, I don't have a cheap laptop, I have a decked out gaming pc. I hadn't saved for a while, so I was worried about how much I had lost. Started up the game again to the sight of an empty character select screen. That's right, the game crashing didn't just push me back to my last save, it DELETED MY CHARACTER.
So I went to google, trying to figure out how to recover my character. I was able to get him back, but everything was messed up. My character was in a completely different solar system than before, and I was missing half of what I had in my inventory. Long story short, I gave up on this game after that. I'm not going to go to the trouble of fixing a game, that's the game developer's job.
tl;dr On top of frame rate issues, the game crashed once and deleted my character (yes, really), and I couldn't recover my character properly. This game is broken, and until these issues get fixed, I can't give it a positive review.

Warning: this is not a game. It is an interactive experience. This "game" lets you understand better how the universe works and how you function in that universe as an individual and as a part of that universe.
The underlying philosophy is that you are not a seperate individual being but that you are connected to everything.

This philosophy was already explained by Alan Watts in the sixties. But now, thanks to this game, you are able not only to hear Alans words but also actually
everything in the universe and thus also
everything.
This makes for a unique experience that can be very profound because it can alter the way you see life and how you see yourself and your relationship to other beings.
It can be very hard to wrap your head around this philosophy and if you don't
it, this "game" can seem very silly and boring.
I thought it was a wonderful experience. If there would exist a multimillion dollar version of this "game" that would let you be a more convincing camel, then that would be totally mindblowing, but for a lowbudget game it already is pretty mindblowingly fantastic.
Don't buy this if you want to play a videogame. Buy it because you want a better understanding of the universe, your existence and your relationship to everything.

major-label games play out like Spike Lee films in miniature. In both artists’ worlds, the stakes are unbearably high, the characters’ motives are unclear, and morality is knotty, but there is a central force you can feel steering every moment. The "Good and Bad Hair" musical routine from Lee’s 1988 feature School Daze depicted black women grappling with colorism and exclusionary standards of American beauty. Mookie’s climactic window smash in 1989’s Do the Right Thing plunged its characters into fiery bedlam, quietly prophesying the coming L.A. riots in the process. In these moments, you could feel the director speaking to you directly through his characters and their trajectories. Molyneux’s records, while crowded with conflicting ideas and arguing voices, have a similar sense of a guiding hand at work.
Molyneux’s new album, A New kind of Adventure, doesn’t explicitly bill itself as a movie like good kid, m.A.A.d city did, but the network of interlocking dramas explored here feels filmic nonetheless, and a variety of characters appear across the album’s expanse. The opener, "Wesley’s Theory", turns the downfall of action-star-turned-convicted-tax-dodger Wesley Snipes into a kind of Faustian parable. Snoop drops by on "Institutionalized"; Dre himself phones in on "Wesley". The mood is wry, theatrical, chaotic, ironic, and mournful, often all at once: On "For Free? (Interlude)" an impatient woman ticks off a laundry list of material demands before Peter snaps back that "This♥♥♥♥♥♥ain’t free!" and thunders through a history of black oppression, spoken-word style, as if to say, "This money you crave, it’s blood money." The album is dotted with surreal grace notes, like a parable: God appears in the guise of a homeless man in "How Much a Dollar Cost", and closer "Mortal Man" ends on a lengthy, unnerving fever-dream interview with the ghost of 2Pac.
The music, meanwhile, follows a long line of genre-busting freakouts (The Roots’ Phrenology, Common’s Electric Circus, Q-Tip’s Kamaal the Abstract, André 3000’s The Love Below) in kicking at the confines of rap music presentation. There’s half a jazz band present at all times; pianist Robert Glasper, producer/sax player Terrace Martin and bass wizard Thundercat give Butterfly a loose, fluid undertow every bit as tempestuous and unpredictable as the army of flows at Peter’s disposal. The rapper’s branching out, too, exploding into spastic slam poetry on "For Free?", switching from shouty gymnastics to drunken sobs on "u" and even effecting the lilt of a caring mother on "You Ain’t Gotta Lie (Momma Said)". It turns out Peter’s new direction was every direction at once.
Despite all this, he’s still toying with a narrative on the sly: Just beneath the surface lies a messianic yarn about avoiding the wiles of a sultry girl named Lucy who’s secretly a physical manifestation of the devil. Peter refuses to dole out blame without accepting any, however, and on the chaotic free jazz excursion "u" he turns a mirror on himself, screaming "Loving you is complicated!" and suggesting his fame hasn’t helped his loved ones back home. Peter’s criticisms, as they did on good kid, come with powerful, self-imposed challenges. As Bilal quips on the chorus to "Institutionalized": &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥don’t change until you get up and wash your♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥."
Peter’s principle of personal responsibility has treaded dangerously close to respectability politics lately, especially after a prickly remark about the Mike Brown shooting in a recent Billboardinterview that seemed to pin the death on the victim, but A New kind of Adventure avoids that trap. (Mostly.) "Complexion (A Zulu Love)" is a tender note of appreciation for women of all skin tones with help from North Carolina rapper Rapsody (whose slickly referential guest verse contains a nod to "Good and Bad Hair"). This is an album about tiny quality of life improvements to be made in the face of seemingly insurmountable odds. It might not be the message we want in a year where systemic police and judicial inequality have cost many the ultimate price, but that doesn’t bankrupt it of value.
A New kind of Adventure pivots on the polarizing lead single, "i". Upon release last autumn, the sunny soul pep talk came off lightweight and glib. When it appears deep in the back end of Butterfly, though, "i" plays less like the jingle we heard last year and more like the beating heart of the matter. To push the point, the album opts for a live-sounding mix that ditches out midway through, giving way to a speech from the rapper himself. In tone, the speech is not unlike the legendary 1968 concert where James Brown waved off security and personally held off a Boston audience’s fury after news broke that Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. had been assassinated. "How many ♥♥♥♥♥s we done lost, bro?" Peter shouts over the crowd. "It shouldn’t be♥♥♥♥♥♥for us to come out here and appreciate the little bit of life we got left." Underneath the tragedy and adversity, A New kind of Adventure is a celebration of the audacity to wake up each morning to try to be better, knowing it could all end in a second, for no reason at all.

A buggy, glitchy mess of a game.  Terrible collision checking, AI that spams the same "kombos" over and over, and the same cheaty super moves, and cut scenes that drop the frame rate, look worse than the real game, and generally are a complete unoptimised mess.
If that was not bad enough, Shao Kahn wins the prize for the worst, laziest, final boss ever.  All of the cheap tricks are there:  increased damage, increased health, decreased damage received, etc.  On top of that, he pulls the utterly infuriating stunt of impossible-to-read "invulnerability" moments, where it is impossible to stagger him and he only receives a fraction of the damage, as if he was blocking.  This, coupled with attacks that can be started after any of yours and still hit before any of yours, and that break through almost every defence, renders him less a challenging boss requiring all acquired skills, and more a matter of frustration, luck, and perserverence.  This is poor boss design at its very worst, and in itself earns this game a Not Recommended.
All the usual gripes for Mortal Kombat are still present: predictable characters, similar styles, boring physique types, over-sexualised women, a mess of a plot, terrible dialogue, etc etc etc.  All of these I could have forgiven were it not for the host of technical issues, and Shao Kahn.  If you want to be challenged and have a fun game, look elsewhere.  If you want a reason to break your controller, rage quite, storm off, or anything else - then get this game.  It is all it is good for.
Oh, and to preempt those that will pull the "you are just not that good at it card", I have this to say: that is not my issue.  I can tell when I am losing as I am not that good (especially with the final character you play as, who I hate to play as) and when it is because my best efforts do not mean anything.  The fact that I can land hit after hit, but have them count as nothing due to arbitrary invulnerability is not me being bad.  It is dreadful game design.

I've completed the game with one character, and played the prologue with another. This review is based on that experience.
+ The music is great
+ The graphics as well, surprising amount of 8-way sprite variety considering the budget, and they have some neat little touches like weapon drawing/sheathing animations
+ The pacing is very good throughout the game, there's no filler and nothing feels like it wastes your time
+ Equipment is more interesting than most JRPGs so far, quite some trade-offs and unique effects
+ I really like the skill/character advancement system, see below
+ Battles so far have also been fun, I'll describe the system below
+ You have more choices than what you'd expect in a JRPG
+ The characters are pretty interesting, and have a decent party dynamic, however...
- The writing is somewhat let down by a number of grammatical errors
- Bugs: worst one was a wrong trigger which teleported me somewhere, and the game also referred to itself as a "test build" in one instance;
Both of these major issues were patched within the first 15 hours and are no longer in the game at this point.
- Minor stuff: the run speed could be a bit higher, and I'd like to be able to use the d-pad rather than joystick with gamepad controls
First of all, your entire party levels at once, which is very convenient and makes a lot of sense really.
You get 4 slots for active skills and 2 for passive skills per character. Since you level up very often, you soon have to pick and choose the skills for each, and there are some interesting synergies. It has something of Guild Wars almost in that aspect.
The game employs the smart mechanic of healing you back up fully after each encounter. In any game which is not about resource management (which most non-dungeon-crawler JRPGs haven't been about in ages) healing up after battle is just meaningless routine, so I really like that choice.
I also really like how they do stamina management, which is really the main battle mechanic.
You start with a set amount of stamina (which can be adjusted by some equipment and passives), and all skills require a number of stamina points. performing a normal attack regenerates 1 stamina, and defending regenerates 2. There are also ways to transfer stamina from one character to another, and attacks which reduce it in the enemy.
Since stamina is per-battle, like everything else, you are never not thinking about using it. This mostly prevents the "trash mob" button-mashing scenario.
Battles are also generally quick, which is something that I always appreciate. Difficulty is pretty well-balanced and what I'd call moderate so far (I consider most modern JRPGs too easy).

The game has just been released, and being an alpha 0.01 I hope the devs will use the reviews frequently to update themself of what needs improving in the game.  I've only played for about 7 hours as i write this review so it is a first impression.
Right off the bat i thought the graphics in general were marvelous apart from a few poorly designed anaomalies.  The first thing i took notice of is the design and soundfiles surrounding the sharks, The design seemed to be poorly done for a game where these are supposed to be the most terrifying creatures you encounter.  The music also initially gets the hairs on my back rising.  However after awhile it is more of a warning sign to look around, which i thought ruin the experience a little.  The second thing i took notice of is the poor graphics of the rain.  It appears to only rain in a cone around the player with no clouds, storm or wind in the surrounding area.  I also took notice that the gound does not get wet from the rain which i would enjoy it would do thinking of how graphic the rest of the game is.
The Sharks i think would need an update pretty fast.  There are far to many sharks in the game, just going close to the waters edge and you can quickly spot 2-3 sharks in the water.  I've also observed "schools" of up to 6 sharks traveling together near a shipwreck at night when i were paddling past it.
When i started building i initially enjoyed it, but found it very repetative as there are no furniture added to the game yet and it's not possible to place the bed on foundations.  This means that the huts you can build are only useful as storage spaces even though this provides no perks compared to what storing everything under open skies does.
Concerning the food and water part of the game and keeping your character alive, i feel that the amount of liquid available to the player could be improved by for an example adding a contraption to catch rainwater, for an example constructed by wood and tarp, if it would be added to the game.  Food wise i find it rather dull that the player can continue to eat only coconuts too sustain himself.  The game would be more interesting and harder to survive if a varied food diett would apply perks or that you would recive diminishing bonuses for not eating varied food.
Firepit issues
That i were unable to use the firepit to light several fires with if i just added wood were rather annoying as coming by the amount of rocks needed to construct the firepit itself takes time and valuable rock away from you that could be used to other things, for an example. spears.  I were also annoyed by the fact that you can't tell if your food is cooked properly or not. Because no matter how long i kept my crabs in the fire i would have a chance of getting sick while eating it.  Not that it were a problem as the character suffers no drawbacks from eating bad food like dehydration and dizziness from vomiting.  Only the short inability to move as your throwing up.
I found navigation in the game tasking as the perception of depth were rather bad and it was difficult to determine distance to the different islands.  I were also always unsure of which island i actually had my homebase on.  I've read other reviews about adding a landmark system or a bouy system which a player could use to track his movements.  This could be very helpful for traveling and visiting nearby islands.  I also think that maybe adding medium sized islands with more resources and things to do on could be good for the game as it can get boring rather fast with the tiny islands that exsist at the moment.
I found the raft that the player begins with to be rather annoying as it involved the most bugs i encountered in the game.  I could for an example row across an island if i remained in the boat and paddled over land.  Also when entering i would be "Stuck" in the ladder even though i were in the middle of the raft and then i could not operate it by paddle as the game treated me like i were outside of the raft.  It also despawned when i loaded the game.
Overall i think the game itself has a very large potensial to become a great game.  If the devs does this correctly and listen to the feedback from the reviews given by myself and other players they can create a whole fantastic game that people can play for hours on end without getting bored or fed up by repetative actions.  Where your options gets more and more varied as you become more established on the Island your "casted away" on (pun intended).  8.5/10

140 is best described as a rhythm platformer. Controls are extremely simple: all you can do is jump and move left and right. However, platforms and hazards will move in a predictable, rhythmic way, requiring you to move with the rhythm to get through. Mechanics are introduced intuitively, with orbs filled with colors moving around in ways that hint at the mechanic they introduce when brought to the hole they must be placed in. As more mechanics are introduced in a stage, the world gets more complex, but never chaotic. Bosses are also connected to the rhythm, and neatly finish off their stages. Checkpoints are placed far enough apart to make getting through stages with sheer luck rare, but common enough to prevent the stages from being too hard. All four stages are well-made, and each has a unique feel. The second half of the game also offers a nice challenge, removing all checkpoints to require complete mastery of each stage. Overall, 140 uses rhythm to create a platfromer that is challenging without feeling cheap.

As the title entails. Stranded Deep is a survivor game that drops you in the midsts of a stranded island scenario. You are equiped with a backpack, a bottle of water, a lighter, and a knife. The game offers a randomly generated clump of islands that are free to your exploration. Each island has very limited resources but just enough to get by. The game is undoubtedly beautiful and, most impressively, boasts a unique crafting system. Though slightly buggy, the crafting system involves "dragging" and moving materials and then using the appropriate tool to complete an action. It creates a very authentic and satisfing feel that gives you the impression that you are hand making everything. Building is similar to Rust, you place foundations, supports, walls, roofs, etc. It's a simple yet immersive system. The game is relatively bug free (from my experience) and this is fairly impressive for an early access game. With an entire ocean to explore, sunken ships, a mass of islands, Stranded Deep offers a variety of activities to keep you busy and entertained for hours while allowing you to use your creativity for building. With more than enough content to justify the price tag, there is much to do in Stranded Deep. You will survive alone, stranded on an island, or die trying.

Starbound is basically Terraria but in space and a lot better. What I like the most about it is how you can travel between not just worlds but also between games with your friends. You have the ability to not just build colonies but also upgrade your spaceship and get crew members who travel with you between games, or servers if you will. This is extremely helpful because it means that you can play with people who are just starting out and you get the option of either starting completely fresh just like they are or you can bring you're whole crew by playing a character who already has one, this also ends the issue of wanting to play with someone who already has things built but not wanting to leave everything behind. I personally also enjoyed added feature of different races which I hadn't seen in other games like this, while it doesn't change really anything about your character mechanically that I could see, it is a nice touch that personally I think it added more depth to the game and made it easier to get in to. The story of the game is also fairly original and definately worth playing through, however it is completely optional and it won't effect you very much if you decide to just colonize and explore after the first few missions and ignore it completely. Honestly the only issues i found with the game were not being able to skip a few of the boring cutscenes (there might be a way but i can't find it) which is frustrating after the first character you make. Also it runs fairly poorly if you get too many people in one game (i find that it starts after three people) though its still completely playable with at least five. I only wish they would make a 3D version of this like Minecraft but I definately enjoy it entirely in it's 2D form. I would give Starbound a 9 out of 10 there is room for improvement but I believe a few updates or patches would cover just about all of it.

Disclaimer: This game is still in early access at the time of this review.
I picked this up in the Black Friday sale period. I have played it around 26 hours at the time of this writing. The game revolves around your "Battle Brothers", a mercenary group of sellswords, though you can create a different name for your company. your crew makes money by accepting and fullfilling contracts plus the occaisional stray battle, special discovered site, or a random event. This is good because you are going to need that money. You have to provide food, supplies to fix your equipment, healing herbs, soldier paychecks and other things. The better your soldiers the more pay they demand.
The game is low fantasy at least so far in play time. There are some undead, and a few enemies that might be considered 'magical" in nature but most enemies are a typical human bandit, orc, or goblin. Magic ala D&D is not this game. healing is slow, and no magic spells for your troops that I have encountered yet. What's worse (for your troopers anyway) is they can sustain injuries that permenatly disable them. I would advise not getting too attached to any particular soldier as they soon may be missing an ear, have a broken bone that fails to heal right, and other infirmities thatmake a once first rate soldier into a crawling, cowardly cripple. Since there is no healing magic that I have found (beyond a antidote for poison potion) you are limited to banding your folks in battle, but that is not an easy task to do as disengaging from melee can prove difficult, unless your soldier has learned a particular skill to disengage safely. The upside of this, is that you can inflict crippling wounds on your enemies too, which will drastically reduce their combat power. Combat is turned based, with each participent taking a turn based on their initiative rating.
There is a good assortment of weapons and armor in the game. Some have reach, some are great for destroying sheilds and armor, others perform poorly against armored targets. Each type of weapon may have a special attack or defense ability. For example, axes are great at destroying sheilds and spears can form a "spear wall" that pushes attackers away. A good mix of weapons, fighting styles,and armor seems to be a good idea. Each weapon and armor type incurrs fatigue. As battles drag on, the combatants begin to tire, depriving them of special attacks and abilities. So you really have to balance things. Do you really want to wear that great chain mail knowing that it is going to wear your soldier out quick?
Graphics and sound are primitive by todays, but sufficient for the task. If you are all about graphics, forget it. There are still a lot of parts of the game that you can see, but cannot interact with yet, or at least, I have not discovered how. Like, you can see a copper mine, but cannot do anything with it or the veteran's hall in large cities. There is no crafting yet that I have seen but I think the foundation may be there since you can buy or loot things like amber, copper ingots, and dyes. These may be just trade goods and will never be more than that. We shall see.
The game is very stable. I have not experienced a single crash yet. The interface is a bit clicky but tolerable. The game seems mostly bug free. There was one point where I couldn't end a soldier's turn, but I could pass his turn till later in the round and was able to end it when he came up at the end of the initiave rotation.
All in all I think this game has great potential as long as you are not graphics fanatic.

This is one of the more difficult tower defense games. By the third map the difficulty ramps up and you'll find yourself trying new tactics to complete it. There's typically a thin line between how much gold you have and what gold you need to build or upgrade towers. Very few times during the game will you have a surplus of goal to spend on anything so you need to constatly be choosing wisely and as soon as gold is available.
Unlike other tower defense games you have a hero to control on the screen. There are a variety of heroes you'll unlock as the game goes on and each have different strengths/weaknesses with their special powers. You'll also level them up when you play so even if you lose a map you'll typically gain a few points you can put in to improve your hero. And that can often lead to weather you win/lose a map.
Lots of a replayability to the game. Each map has 3 different difficulty levels. Depending on the map the higher difficulties may mean you can't use heroes on that map anymore or are unable to use certain towers. So you sometimes have to throw away tactics you used in the past to win and this in turn can help you in future maps.
Games graphics, sound, and music are fantastic across the board. No complaints with anything along those lines.
If you find yourself enjoying this then there is also Kingdom Rush Frontiers which is more of the same with new maps, heroes, and some new upgradable tower types.

If you were wondering if this was a GTA V knockoff like I was, it's not. It does follow the open world genre, but with a twist. Sleeping Dogs puts you in the role of an undercover police agent attempting to infiltrate the triad organization. The role involves taking missions involving from either the side of the police or the triads.
Wei Shen is the main character in the story in which the player will control. Wei was born and raised in China but moved to America with his family. He has now returned to China as an undercover police agent infiltrating gangs. His role starts out quite easy getting initiated into the gang, but quickly heats up as a lot of his undercover work requires a lot of unethical decisions. Whether you are taking a police or triad mission, you will be docked points for causing any crimes or damages to anyone not involved. Meaning, if you cause damage to the environment (wreck-less driving or stealing cars), it will be noted into Wei's reputation. Speaking of reputation, Wei also has side missions available to increase his "face". Increasing the "face" stat will allow Wei to have more access to specialized cars. Face challenges require the player to fight gang's that can be found around the map.
The overall
of the game is between alright and good. The unique feature of this game certainly has to be the fighting that is involved. The game reminds me of the True Crimes series with it's fighting genre. Fighting can seem basic at first and upgrades can be added to Wei's Arsenal. There are a few types of upgrade trees to worry about : cop skill, triad skill, melee skill and face skill. You will not be given general upgrade points. Rather, the points will be given depending on which missions you take. It is important to note that if you would like to unlock certain fighting features that you will have to focus on specific areas. The fighting itself is not too bad. It is a nice addition as it makes it different from other open world games, but failed to optimize on the opportunity. There are grabbing capabilities on top of unlock-able combo's, but the player will find themselves mashing X then pressing Y quickly to counter another opponent. The flow of hitting enemies while doing counters is pretty cool to watch. That's sort of the issue though; it's more of a watching/button mashing gimmick for me than it is being creative with my fighting approach. I should highlight that the player can interact with the scenery while fighting and really do some serious damage to opponents by throwing them off railings, into vents or even into garbage cans. While the fighting is fun, it could have been a lot better.
The exploring component of the game is pretty good. The environment (Hong Kong) in which the game takes place feels very nice. The conversations, radio stations, ambience and scenery really tie everything beautifully together. There are a lot of side missions to do be it fighting gangs to drug busts. Wei can hack security devices (such as cameras) and watch the city over his computer at home. These cameras are only accessible when Wei hacks into them (as they are not available by default). Small gimmicks like these do try to differentiate the game from other big open world brands. Other side missions include races, statue collection (to unlock new moves or points), and (not limited to) hit and runs. The driving itself is not the greatest but does have it's own unique system to itself. Not that it's entirely bad, but it will take some getting used to. Wei is able to stunt jump onto other cars as he is driving. Alternatively, the player may use the "X" button to initiate a ram maneuver. These actions definitely add depth to the game and  absolutely make it more dynamic. Paired with QTE (quick time events), it will keep you engaged.
The
are quite stunning and can demand quite a bit from the PC. Besides the streets not being super crowded as I would imagine Hong-Kong, the map creators do a good job of creating an immersive atmosphere. The
are definitely remarkable as there will be conversations going on in Chinese and in English. The radio stations are very good and gives the player a new cultural insight into music. The cut-scenes are relevant and are well-received thanks to the passionate acting.
Overall, the game is decent. It can definitely be a fan favorite for a few but speaking as a neutral reviewer, it is an average game. For the price it's been selling at, I would say it's certainly worth a buy on sale. The game has it's fair share of action, drama and story. I feel the actions could have been complimented with a little more to distinguish the game. For that reason I will be giving the game an average score.

Bottom line: this game is fun, but I can see why I'd never heard of it when I got it in a Square/Enix bundle.   The sandbox is a little small and not exactly overflowing with things to do, but it does open up a bit as you buy more cars and meet more people.  It offers a variety of minigames and hidden secrets that you don't have to look up online to find out how to solve.
The biggest condemnation of this game is the same problem that every Squenix game has: characters.  You play as a cop in deep cover with the triad, an organized crime syndicate in Hong Kong.  Your character falls into a moral crisis as he begins to identify more and more with the gangsters than he does with the police.  It sounds intriguing, but the execution is slapdash to say the least.  I found my character chewing out his superior for wanting to arrest a lovably inept compulsive thief, but essentially shrugging it off as I shoved a nurse in my trunk so I could blackmail her husband.    Mild spoiler: there's another scene where your character mourns the death of a roided out lunatic that nearly shot him in the face on the word of a double dealing crackhead.  (Come on, he spends the last two missions that he's alive talking about family and how Wei should take care of his mom if anything happens to him).
The game is fun, the atmosphere is immersive, the racing minigame is challenging without being hair-pullingly hard.  I like the four way experience level system - especially since being a good gangster doesn't mean being a bad cop.  It's an alright game, but nothing to write home about.

The controls are easy to work with: you just aim and shoot with the mouse and move you avatar around with WASD. You can step it up a bit and customize some stuff around to make your gameplay easier and more convenient. Personally, my controls were the regular WASD movement and R to escape to nexus, I also had Q and E to rotate my screen (This is awkward at first to play with but trust me, you'll subconsciously be doing it once you get used to it), I had X to center player off/on screen, I finally had T to interact/buy with things.
The gameplay is very enjoyable with a group of friends. Playing alone could get boring and makes the game more difficult. The game periodically lagged sometimes but recently it has been more of an issue for me. You can play Realm of the Mad God on browser, Steam, and flash player. You have 14 classes to choose from, each consisting of a special skill and items meant for it. Each of the classes have different maximum stats making the gameplay of each one unique. There are also a lot of effects in the game that include debuffing or buffing your character. Several different kinds of enemies that have different strategies needed in order to make your job killing it easier. I personally don't like some of the new things DECA has been creating though. I have noticed that most of their works are just enemies that deal a thousand armor piercing shots that deal 150 damage in all directions. This makes it more difficult to play as a close-range character especially if you don't have amazing gear which leads to the next topic.
Realm of the Mad God is known among the community for it being called unbalanced. Players say that the RNG in the game isn't the greatest and that the poor players usually stay poor and the rich people usually stay rich. Pets came out in 2013 which is a huge advantage to players since a pet doesn't die and helps the player fight and support. The game is also labeled as one of the most pay-to-win games out there. This combination between paying and pets are the leading cause for unbalance. Players would spend money to upgrade their pet so that it can Heal their HP and MP and also paralyze their enemies. The players who didn't pay would be left with a pet that isn't the greatest and isn't able to get rich making it difficult to attain loot when they don't have good loot in the first place. The new developers, DECA Games, has made efforts to nullify this by making ways for players to get potions and loot whether it is through completing tinker quests or by lowering the rarity for items.

I don't even know where to begin. There is so much to say about this game that I'm shaking just thinking of what to type. I guess I should start with some backstory.
Life was going pretty tough for me. My wife died of meme-overdose, my son fell out of a tree, and, worst of all, my cat spilled water all over my kitchen floor. I was going through some serious depression when all of a sudden I came across a little game known none other than "b." At first glance this game just seemed like it was merely a tech demo, and none of the reviews treated this game seriously. Regardless, I booted up b and was greeted by the options menu. I adjusted the settings to what I thought my computer could handle, and opened the game. As soon as I saw the title screen I burst into tears. I had just seen the most beautiful thing in the entire world: a bee. It was no ordinary bee, however. It was the most perfectly rendered and realistic looking bee that I had ever seen, even in real life. The bee turned in a 40 degree angle and looked at me, and you know what it did? Absolutely nothing, which was absolutely beautiful. After I calmed down, I started playing the game and almost cried like a baby again. The graphics were more beautiful than anything I had ever seen before, rivaling the likes of Sonic Boom: Rise of Lyric and even Minecraft 4k. The graphics were accompanied by a beautiful soundtrack that sets hundreds of standards for music in the future. Not only that, but the controls were very tight and easy to get used to. In b, you fly around a small but beautiful field consisting of grass, a tree, and some ladybugs. The movement of the grass was suprisingly realistic, which further adds to the beauty of b. The tree was located in the central area of the map, which helped me to not get lost. The ladybugs would fly next to the bee if you flew close to them.
I flew around for a few hours, marveling at this game's allure and perfection. I decided to fly my bee close to the ground, and I was utterly shocked as to what happened next. The bee flew straight through the ground AND kept going. A feature such as this is something most triple A developers can only DREAM of implementing in their less-than perfect creations. I couldn't help it; I burst into tears again. As I cried, the bee kept flying. Eventually, the bee flew into a dark void-like area and the game froze. Soon b crashed entirely. I quickly opened Steam and opened b again, and I was greeted by something different. The bee was still there and it looked normal. But this time the bee had a mouth. Not only did it have a mouth, but it was frowning. Puzzled, I opened the game and adjusted my settings as usual. When the game started, the world was different. The grass was dead, the tree was withering, and there were no other insects that flew with your bee. I started to get worried about what was about to happen to my bee. Curious, I decided to fly into the void once again, but this time there was no void when I flew through the bottem of the map. I flew my bee for hours and hours on end and nothing happened. I tear went down my face as I began to accept that this world that I have experienced would never be the same again. But, in the distance I saw a bright light. As I flew towards it, I saw other entities that I had not recognized in this game. They looked like weird, distorted versions of my own bee. I avoided them and outflew them for as long as I could. Eventually the corrupted bees stopped and flew away. I was relieved as I flew towards the light.
I was so close to this light. I almost entered it when all of a sudden I was pushed out. My bee collected itself and looked forward, only to see a large shadow creature. Dark goo was dripping from each of its limbs, and blood was dripping from its mouth. After a few seconds, the creature lurched forward at my bee. Scared, I turned my bee around and tried to fly away, but I was not fast enough. The shadow creatured grabbed my bee and kept it in its gooey fist. I cried for my bee's fate. But when I looked up, the bee was smiling inside this creature's fist. The bee suddenly grew a large stinger on its bottom, and looked directly at me. The bee nodded, and a quick-time event popped up on the bottom of the screen. I pressed the button and the bee stung the creature with all of its might. The shadow monster roared in pain, released the bee from its grasp, and exploded. However, the bee, MY bee, could not move any further. The bee turned around and looked at its once beautiful home. And all of a sudden, its beauty was being restored. The bee had restored balance to nature and saved the universe from the clutches of the mysterious shadow creature. The bee smiled, closed its eyes, and fell into the light. After a few seconds, the game's credits rolled. I cried. Not tears of saddness, but tears of joy. Joy from the bond I had created with my bee. Joy from exploring a world that was so small but felt so big. Joy from the wonderful experience of playing this game. No game can truly compare to b. b tells the smartest story I've ever experienced without a single line of dialouge. Not to mention that its gameplay, controls, sountrack, and graphics are beyond perfection and cannot compare with pitiful games of today's day and age. This game is way before its time, and nothing will ever compare to the beauty that is...b.
Final Score: ∞

As the title entails. Stranded Deep is a survivor game that drops you in the midsts of a stranded island scenario. You are equiped with a backpack, a bottle of water, a lighter, and a knife. The game offers a randomly generated clump of islands that are free to your exploration. Each island has very limited resources but just enough to get by. The game is undoubtedly beautiful and, most impressively, boasts a unique crafting system. Though slightly buggy, the crafting system involves "dragging" and moving materials and then using the appropriate tool to complete an action. It creates a very authentic and satisfing feel that gives you the impression that you are hand making everything. Building is similar to Rust, you place foundations, supports, walls, roofs, etc. It's a simple yet immersive system. The game is relatively bug free (from my experience) and this is fairly impressive for an early access game. With an entire ocean to explore, sunken ships, a mass of islands, Stranded Deep offers a variety of activities to keep you busy and entertained for hours while allowing you to use your creativity for building. With more than enough content to justify the price tag, there is much to do in Stranded Deep. You will survive alone, stranded on an island, or die trying.

Just bought this game today and wasnt for sure if the game was worth the 20 dollar asking price. However I will say this is a early access game that is definetly worth the price. Now lets get right down to it....
The Pros
~Art style is really simple and looks nice at the same time. Due to the simple design it really does leave room for detail. Examples being bandages on your battle brothers post battle and cuts and scrapes visible during and after fights. Your battle brothers leave bandages on till they are fully healed which could take days so that really boosts the realism for me
~Along with damage being shown it also has a long lasting effect on your battle brothers. If one of them takes a mortal blow in battle they have a chance of getting a permanent injury and the debuff range can be from missing fingers that causes a battle brother to miss more attacks to broken bones not setting correctly lowering there overall damage.
~The map and different towns have their own factions/kingdoms with their own reputation bars that you can raise or lower. So it definetly allows you to align with one if you so wish.
~You can name your battle brothers and customize them! However this is a very twisted feature considering how easy it is to lose your brothers so it really leaves you with xcom levels of attachement with your company.
~ Combat system is sound and very easy to pick up if you are adept with 4x tile like strategy games
The Cons
~The game is in desperate need of rebalancing. Bandits are very easy to dispatch and have no strategy to them while Orcs are all over the place power wise. The orc young are barely stronger then bandits but 1 orc beserker can kill 8 well equipped battle brothers surrounded. However i have no qualms with the armored orcs for they are hard to damage but the dont do much damage compared to other orcs so they are balanced. Monsters like ghouls or direworlves in my opinion are fair.
~ I know i just finished praising the map and how diverse it was but I have this feeling that the map in this game has to much space in between kingdoms. There is too much open space here and I believe they should add more villages or at least one more kingdom  to make the map more lively. Too many times do i feel that the game drags on when i take a contract that makes me travel all the way across the barren swamp or desert parts of the map just to deliver a package that only pays out a measley 250 gold.
~Speaking of delivery quests, if the game wants to have them it needs a way to locate the quest location on the map so the player can decide if the amount of gold paid for the distance traveled is worth the price. A few times when i chose to do a delivery quest i find out the distance totally outweighs the price of the contract and its too late to cancel the contract so i must do it to continue on.
Other than that thats all I can say about the game at the moment. I hope for more future updates as it seems the devs really are pushing out constant updates. Great Game!

By no means a bad game but it's quite overrated. I quite like the Hong Kong Gun Fu flavour that the game has, it's pretty unique and refreshing in the current open world game market. However, the game feels very outdated and honestly reminds me a hell of a lot of GTA 3 and Vice City in how it feels to play and what the open world is like to explore and interact with. Most of the missions feel pretty basic and lack originality or flair of it's own. I don't play games for story but I appreciate a good one; I couldn't say that the game's plot managed to grab me. It didn't turn me off, either, it's just nothing special in the 10 hours I put into it.
The emphasis on hand to hand combat is nice but it's really a poor man's Batman Arkham. Very similar countering ability, but in general it's nowhere near as polished or refined, and feels pretty delayed and indirect by comparison with less varied animations and inferior visual and sound feedback. It does have the grappling system, though, which can be pretty fun shoving a guy into a bin or an industrial fan, or just slamming him into the ground or breaking his arm. The game is mildly buggy, too. I've had to restart missions from checkpoint numerous times due to random little glitches.
The game runs well on modern midrange systems, ran without a hitch on my i5 4690 and GTX 1060, just be sure to install the high res texture pack which makes the game look way better. It also controls fine with Keyboard and Mouse.
I'm only rating as a not recommended for full price. On deep discount (either in steam sale or via key reseller) it's a decent, cheap title. Just don't fall for the hype, it's really not as good as people claim.

Bought this game with massive discount during the recent autumn sales. The good thing about MK9 now years after initial release, I think, is its respectable story which is the groundwork of MK, so if you somehow missed it back in the 90s now it's your chance to understand what was going on between the realms. Then there is a robust roster of fighters not found in its successor; Rich with nostalgia for the players of old.
The downside minus the dead online, is that while the mechanics aren't that different from MK10, some Kombatants, from the gameplay perspective, aren't designed good enough. In MK10 for example, I think all fighters are equally good if you master them, and who you pick for your next fight is a matter of preference. In MK9 however, it's like some of them lack something very important. Like they are either way too slow (Sub-Zero), lack a good chain combo (Noob) or simply aren't much fun to play as (like Liu Kang, who I can't help but feel fights like an unlubricated machine).
Overall, I reckon this game had been a gem when it came out for PC, but today it's hard to recommend it with a certain confidence, bearing in mind the newer, more alive, more professionally made MK10.

Despite what some say about the Pay to Win nature of the game, Realm of the Mad God has become very F2P friendly since DECA Games have taken over its development, and unlike its past owner Kabam, care deeply about the game and update it regularly. Realm of the Mad God has been an experience unlike any other that has incapuated me for years across many accounts scattered across all sorts of platforms, having played in reality since 2013 on an older Steam account. No matter how hard you try to quit Realm you never can. I never tried to quit the game, but I always find myself crawling back even after long periods of inactivity, and since the Lost Halls update have been playing pretty much daily due to the login rewards that challenge the concept of P2W. There is now not a single non-cosmetic item in this game that you cannot get without paying. Vault Chests and Character Slots (two very important features that make the game easier as they are gotten) used to be exclusively payed for. Now they can be earned through daily login rewards. Backpacks used to be this way too (an item that doubles player inventory space), until they sometimes become part of Fame Boxes, daily login rewards, or other sources gotten without money. Despite all of that, I think Realm is a great game to invest money into if you feel entrapped by it. Because once you are officially sucked in and addicted to what would be otherwise boring gameplay without the thrill of permadeath of your character at every corner (forcing you to start a new one), you will NOT be leaving any time soon.
Some notes to new players: Ignore spamming bots linking to external websites in the Nexus, or hub of the game for players. Using or buying items from these sites is against the Terms of Service. Try to get a pet with Heal as its first ability, and if you plan to go long time, Magic Heal as its second ability. And do not fuse pets to higher rarities without getting their abilities to max level for their rarities via feeding items. This will cripple your pets efficency in the long term. And if you do plan to invest in the game, a Pet with Heal and Magic Heal is definitely a good place to start after a few Vault Chests and maybe a few character slots, but note you can get those free and getting REALLY good pets is not easy for free. There is other stuff I could talk about, but I think I've spoken enough. If you're looking for a Free to Play, simple to learn but exceptionally hard to master game with lots of thrill, reward, unique loot, and exciting adventures across the Realm fighting evil gods, than Realm of the Mad God is the game to turn to. I hope to see you in the Realm all the same. ;3

I've had so much fun with Buff Knight Advanced! It's a casual game, and you'll definitely do quite a bit of rapid clicking or button mashing during this side-scrolling RPG.
There are two character classes (melee fighting knight or magic using sorceror) as well as weapon, armor, and character attributes to upgrade, multiple artifacts to find and upgrade, and a variety of monsters to slay over the course of 12 stages of gameplay. There are also story and endless modes, full-controller support, and very attainable achievements.
At this point, I only have the stage 12 boss to get through, and all of my stats and upgrades are maxed out. There's not much of a downside to this game, especially if you can pick it up on sale. It's perfectly enjoyable and simplistic. However, I have to admit that I wish there was more content and more items, weapons, and attributes to upgrade, because other than health and mana potions (which reset when you die) I have nothing on which to spend my gold and gems.
The soundtrack isn't complex, but the music and sound effects are appropriate and alert the player to what's coming. The pixel graphics are very well done, and I had no issues with seeing clearly and identifying what was on my rapidly scrolling screen.
Overall, I love this game. It's entertained me for 11+ hours at this point, and it was very refreshing to begin a game that wasn't full of complex puzzles or sporting an unrealistic degree of difficulty. This is perfect for a casual gamer, and it's got definite replayability with the two modes, achievements, rare artifacts, and scored stages.

Despite it's basic appearance, Battle Brothers is a game of surprising depth of strategy.  It's a turn based, squad-based tactical combat game, with a heavy emphasis on logistics.  As a result, there have been a lot of comparisons to XCOM and Jagged Alliance, which is fair in the same way that rabbit tastes like chicken. After about more than a year since release, I decided to check this game out myself - to see whether the other reviewers might have been too harsh. Many of them played a few minutes and denounced it immediately. I have gone from start to finish. The game can safely be said to be 'complete', as in the developers won't add anything significant to better the experience. So why is this game so bad?
- 5 weapons available, where only 2 (wooden machete and M9 pistol) are actually used for most of the game
- Crafting boils down to merely creating bandages, you can complete the entire game without crafting anything else
- Crafting is limited to 7 items (8 in survival mode)
- There are a total of 4 kinds of enemies, that pose virtually no threat whatsoever, due to inferior AI coding
- The entire game can be completed in less than 4 hours
- Shooting inanimate objects causes them to bleed
- The single voice actor delivers his badly written lines in such way that you would quickly consider turning it off
- A great deal of the game takes place in a temple area (The Maze), this area is riddled with instant death traps that are springed upon you for the obvious reason to infuriate the player and slow progress further into the temple
- Level design makes frequent back-tracking unavoidable - in the maze it means constantly having to avoid the same traps over and over again
- All enemies respawn after loading a save
- Survival aspect in single player is negligable, due to readily available resources in all areas of the game
- Your biggest threat will be the rock throwing monkeys and instant death traps
- Animation quality is very low, this will be apparent from the very start of the game
- No quicksave, despite the fact that frequent saving is absolutely mandatory
- Most of the game mechanics rely on QTE's - bandaging takes about 20 seconds to complete
A note on the added survival mode:
A rather small section of the singleplayer map is isolated for you to 'survive as long as you can' - this entails running around in the day gathering food and crafting materials, then using a shelter to sleep at night. Due to the extremely barebones crafting system and the fact that everything is so easily obtainable, this experience does nothing to redeem the game whatsoever. If this kind of survival experience is desired, titles such as The Forest does this better in every aspect.
- if you're looking for a survival game, there are plenty of other superior titles available. This game hasn't been too harshly judged by others, it fails in every aspect of gameplay from start to finish. For the morbidly curious, this game is an exercise in self-torture - it's not conducive towards any lulz whatsoever.

I've put some time into Starbound.

And there's a cacophony of glaringly obvious bugs that have been around almost since the day I bought the game.
More than 3 enemies on the screen?  Eventually you'll have 'lag' where everything freezes for a few seconds.  You'll still move, but everything has to 'catch up'.
Find a challenge portal?  Nah, that's just a softlock in disguise.
Wanna stand still? Sorry; every block that isn't ice has ice physics (including ice blocks; so forget precision platforming).
Did you forget to eat again?  Oh well, you'll starve during the unskippable cutscenes - but fret not!  You can skip the respawn one -- wait, you were playing hardmode? Oh well, start over.  Through the unskippable cutscenes.
